0.title: Jesus Is Better: The Letter to the Hebrews
0.overview:
Who wrote the Letter to the Hebrews? The honest answer is: we do not know. Origen, the great third-century scholar who knew the church’s tradition better than almost anyone, concluded that only God knows who wrote it. Paul has been suggested — the theology runs as deep as any of his letters — but the literary style is far more polished and rhetorical than anything Paul wrote. Apollos, Barnabas, Priscilla, Luke — all have been proposed. In the end the mystery serves the text: Hebrews forces us to attend not to the human messenger but to the divine subject. The letter is about Jesus, and everything else in it orbits that sun.

The recipients were Jewish Christians — almost certainly a specific congregation, possibly in Rome (see 13:24, “those from Italy send you greetings”) — under intense pressure. Some had already suffered public shame, imprisonment, and the plundering of their property (10:32–34). Exhausted and frightened, they were tempted to drift back toward the synagogue, toward the familiar world of Temple sacrifice and priestly ritual. The writer’s response is not to demand more willpower but to open their eyes: you cannot go back, because going back is going backward — from substance to shadow, from fulfillment to promise, from Christ to the types that pointed toward him.

When was it written? Almost certainly before AD 70. The writer speaks of the priests and sacrifices as still going on (8:4; 10:1–3), and a letter arguing that the old system was passing away would hardly have left out the destruction of the temple if it had already happened. Timothy is alive and recently released (13:23). A date in the 60s fits best, and it matters: the readers were being drawn back to a temple that was still standing, and within a few years it would be gone.

Hebrews is structured as a “word of exhortation” (13:22) — a synagogue sermon put into written form. It alternates deliberately between doctrinal exposition and pastoral warning. The five great warning passages (2:1–4; 3:7–4:13; 5:11–6:20; 10:26–39; 12:25–29) are not interruptions to the argument; they are the argument’s pastoral urgency breaking through. Each one follows the same logic: if the lesser covenant carried consequences for violation, how much more the greater? The warnings grow in intensity as the letter progresses.

The controlling word of the letter is “better” (Greek: kreitton), used thirteen times. Jesus is the better revelation (ch. 1), the better mediator (chs. 2–3), the better rest (ch. 4), the better priest (chs. 5–7), the better covenant (ch. 8), the better sacrifice (chs. 9–10), and the ground of better and enduring possessions (ch. 10). The heroes of faith in chapter 11 were all seeking “a better country” (11:16). The letter culminates in the vision of Mount Zion, “the city of the living God” (12:22), and the unshakeable kingdom that no earthly power can topple (12:28).

Read Hebrews as a sustained pastoral argument for the all-sufficiency of Jesus Christ. Every argument leads back to him; every exhortation is grounded in him. The great High Priest has passed through the heavens, has offered himself once for all, has sat down at the right hand of God, and now — this is the astonishing thing — he continues to intercede for us. He is the same yesterday, today, and forever (13:8). Whatever the pressure, whatever the temptation to settle for something less, Hebrews speaks with one voice: hold fast to Jesus. There is nothing better. There is no one better. He is enough.

1.title: The Majesty on High: God Has Spoken His Final Word
1.overview:
Hebrews opens with no greeting. In four verses the writer sketches the Son across all of history, from creation to the throne, and sounds a note the letter will return to: he sat down, because his work is finished.

The chapter then compares the Son with angels, through whom the law was given (Acts 7:53), and seven Old Testament texts show that he is not one of them.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — God Has Spoken by His Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One long sentence sets the theme of the sermon: the God who spoke in fragments through the prophets has now spoken in his Son, and seven statements show who that Son is.
verseByVerse.theology:
Radiance and Imprint

God has not changed speaker; he has spoken finally, in a Son. Verse 3 holds together what the church later had to defend: the Son is one with the Father in nature and distinct from him in person. And, having made purification for sins, he sat down.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jewish Christians under pressure were thinking of going back to what was partial.

Now: The way out of an old attachment is not to call it worthless but to see what it was pointing at.

verseByVerse.quote: Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Hebrews 1 opens the letter with a magnificent statement of who Jesus is. God, who spoke in many partial ways through the prophets, has now spoken his final word in his Son (vv. 1–2). Seven great claims about the Son follow (vv. 2–3), and seven Old Testament quotations prove him far greater than the angels, who are servants sent for those who will inherit salvation (vv. 4–14). The theme of the whole letter is set: Jesus is better, and to turn from him is to turn from God’s final word.

The setting. The author is not named. The Eastern church generally attributed the letter to Paul, the Western church long doubted it, and Origen, in the third century, said that only God knows who wrote it. The style is unlike Paul’s, and the writer received the gospel from those who heard the Lord (2:3), which Paul insisted he did not (Galatians 1:12). Apollos (Acts 18:24) and Barnabas are among those suggested. He was a close associate of Timothy (13:23), and the church received the letter as Scripture. The readers were most likely Jewish Christians, perhaps in or near Rome (13:24), and it was most likely written before AD 70, since the sacrifices are spoken of as still continuing (8:4; 10:1–2). Persecuted (10:32–34) and grown sluggish (5:11–14), they were tempted to drift back to Judaism. This sermon shows Christ better than angels, Moses, Aaron, the old covenant and its sacrifices, and calls them to hold fast.

A letter with no greeting. Hebrews has no name, address or greeting. It opens like a sermon, which is almost certainly what it is: a word of exhortation (13:22), the phrase used of a synagogue address (Acts 13:15). The writer does not introduce himself, because he does not intend to be the subject: the first word of substance is God, and the first thing said about God is that he spoke.

At many times and in many ways. The opening words in Greek are deliberate music: polymerōs kai polytropōs. The first means in many parts, piece by piece: a law here, a psalm there, a prophecy centuries later. The second means in many manners: a voice from a burning bush, a dream, a vision, a still small voice, a prophet told to marry an unfaithful wife and live the sermon in his own home. Both describe revelation that is real and incomplete: God genuinely spoke, but in instalments, with no single prophet ever holding the whole.

God spoke by the prophets. The idols of the nations had mouths and could not speak (Psalm 115:5); the living God broke the silence of the universe and addressed creatures he had made. The prophets were men carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1:21), so that what they said, God said. “To our fathers” names people who owned that history as family, and the writer does not begin by criticising what they are drawn back to. He affirms it: God really did speak there.

Fragments waiting for a face. The argument of Hebrews is never that the old was wrong. It is that the old was partial, and that going back to a partial thing after the whole has arrived is the tragedy. And the fragments were never random: the Spirit of Christ in the prophets testified beforehand to his sufferings and glories (1 Peter 1:10–11). Every piece God spoke through them was a piece of one portrait, and the prophets died without seeing the face. Whatever else divides the old covenant from the new, it is not a change of speaker.

In the flow. Verses 1 to 4 are a single long sentence in Greek, the overture to the whole sermon, sounding almost every theme of the letter. The letter then moves in a steady rhythm: it shows who Christ is, then warns what it would mean to stop listening to him.

Do I still need the Old Testament if God has spoken in his Son? Yes, very much. The Son did not replace the prophets; he fulfilled them, and you cannot understand the fulfilment without the promise. Jesus taught his disciples from Moses and all the Prophets the things concerning himself (Luke 24:27), and this very letter cannot say a sentence about Christ without quoting the Old Testament. The sacrifices, the priesthood, the tabernacle and the psalms are the vocabulary Hebrews uses to explain the cross. Read the Old Testament as a true word from God that is still speaking, and ask in each passage what it was preparing the world to see in Jesus.

For worship. God did not have to speak at all. He could have left the world in the dark it chose, groping after him among idols with painted mouths. Instead he spoke, and kept speaking, through a thousand years of prophets who were mocked, ignored and killed. Every fragment was true, and every fragment was a promise. The God who would not stop talking to a people who would not stop running is the God who, at the end, sent the Word himself.
verseByVerse.note: The author of Hebrews is not named; Paul, Barnabas, Apollos and others have been suggested. It was written to Jewish Christians tempted to turn back from Christ, probably before the temple fell in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed the heir of all things, through whom also he created the world.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In these last days. The prophets spoke of the last days as the time of the Messiah (Isaiah 2:2; Hosea 3:5). In the New Testament the whole stretch from Christ’s first coming to his return is the last days (Acts 2:17). The final era has started, and nothing that comes before the end will be more than this.

By his Son. The Greek has no article: literally in Son. The emphasis is on the kind of messenger: before, servants carried the message; now it comes in a person who is it. The prophets had the word of God; the Son is the Word of God (John 1:1, 18). Isaiah could foresee the suffering Servant without being him; here the messenger and the message are the same, which is why there can be nothing after him. God has said himself. So to know what God is like, you need not guess or wait for another prophet: the way Jesus welcomes sinners, touches lepers and weeps at a grave is the way God is. Whoever sees him sees the one who sent him (John 12:45).

Seven statements in a single arc. Seven statements about the Son run through verses 2 and 3: heir, creator, radiance, imprint, sustainer, purifier, enthroned. They move from the end of history to its beginning, into the being of God, down into the dirt of human sin, and back up to the throne: the whole story of Christ in one sentence.

The heir of all things. In the ancient world the son, above all the firstborn, inherited his father’s estate. Everything that exists is the Son’s inheritance, as Psalm 2:8 promised: ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage.

Through whom he created the world. The heir of all things is the one through whom all things were made (John 1:3; Colossians 1:16). He did not inherit an estate somebody else built. He made it, and then received it back, so the inheritance is not a promotion but a homecoming. And “world” is aiōnas, literally the ages: the prophets lived inside a calendar the Son had made.

Where Christians differ: is revelation still ongoing? Some charismatic teaching expects ongoing prophetic revelation from God alongside Scripture; some liberal theology sees revelation as continuing through human experience. This commentary’s view: God’s speaking in the Son is final. The apostles and their associates recorded and explained this revelation in the New Testament, and with them the canon closed (Jude 3; Revelation 22:18–19). God still illumines his word by his Spirit, applies it to our hearts, and guides us providentially, but he does not give new revelation equal to Scripture. Scripture alone is sufficient (2 Timothy 3:16–17). The reason is that the apostles and prophets were the church’s foundation (Ephesians 2:20), and a foundation is laid once. Many charismatic brothers agree that nothing they call prophecy may add to Scripture or share its authority, and this commentary honours their longing to hear God, even while it believes the gifts of new revelation ceased with the apostles.

What it does not mean. “Appointed heir” does not mean the Son was not always divine or that he earned his status. As eternal Son, he has always been Lord; as incarnate Son, having completed his work, he was appointed heir as the God-man.

If God’s word is final, how does he guide me today? Through the word he has already given, opened to you by his Spirit. He has not left you without direction; he has given you a complete Bible that is enough to make you wise for salvation and equip you for every good work (2 Timothy 3:15–17). Within what Scripture commands, he guides by wisdom, by the counsel of mature believers, by the ordinary providences of life, and by desires he has shaped in you. When an impression or a feeling comes, test it by the word and hold it loosely; never treat it as a voice from God that you must obey. The Son has spoken. To hear God speak today, open what he has said.

Is it narrow to say that God’s final word came in one man? Only if Christians had picked Jesus as their favourite teacher and declared him the best. But the claim is not that we found God; it is that God came looking for us. If God is real and personal, he is free to speak in the way he chooses, and the question is not whether the claim sounds modest but whether it is true. The evidence Hebrews points to is a life, a death and an empty tomb (2:3–4; 13:20). And see who this humbles. If the final word is a gift from God, nobody reached it by being cleverer or more religious than anyone else. The sceptic and the churchgoer stand in the same place: both need to listen.

parallels.desc: I will make the nations your heritage

verseByVerse.quote: He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature, and he upholds the universe by the word of his power. After making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The radiance of the glory. “He is” is present tense: what he eternally is. “Radiance” (apaugasma) is the light that streams from a source. You cannot have the sun without its radiance, and there was never a moment when the sun existed and its light had not yet begun. The radiance is not a lesser substance; it is the sun, reaching you. That is what the writer says the Son is to the Father. And “glory” (doxa) is the visible splendour of God’s being, which Moses begged to see (Exodus 33:18–23) and the disciples beheld in the Word made flesh (John 1:14).

The exact imprint. Charaktēr, which gives us character, is the die used for stamping coins, and by extension the impression it leaves: not a likeness but precise correspondence. “Nature” (hypostasis) here means the very being of God. To see him is to see the Father (John 14:9; Colossians 1:15). Later the church used hypostasis to mean person, but here it means being.

Both truths in one clause. Together the two images give both truths the church later fought for at Nicaea. Radiance: he is not a second God, any more than light is a second sun. Imprint: he is genuinely distinct, as a stamped coin is distinct from the die. One in nature, distinct in person. The great errors about Christ have usually had to cut one of these two words out of the verse: some made the Son a lesser being, others made Father and Son one person wearing two masks.

He upholds the universe. Not Atlas holding a weight steady: the verb means bearing something forward toward an end. The Son is conducting creation somewhere, and he does it by speaking: the same means by which the world was made is the means by which it continues (Colossians 1:17). If he fell silent, it would stop. Every atom in your body this morning exists because the Son has not stopped speaking it into being.

Purification for sins. Then the sentence turns, and the turn is the whole gospel: the one who carries the universe stooped to deal with dirt. On the Day of Atonement purification was made by blood (Leviticus 16:30), and had to be made again the next year. Christ made purification by his own blood, once for all (9:12–14, 26). What does purification actually mean? Sin does not only make us guilty; it makes us unclean, unfit to come near a holy God, as a man covered in mud is unfit to sit at a king’s table. To purify is to remove both the guilt and the stain, so that the conscience is cleansed and the sinner may draw near to God with a true heart (9:14; 10:22).

He sat down. The writer will hammer this in chapter 10. Priests in the tabernacle stood at their work every day (10:11), and among all the furniture Exodus lists there is no chair for them: the work was never finished. A seated priest is a priest with nothing left to do. Christ sat down because his work was complete (10:12). The right hand is the place of honour, authority and power (Psalm 110:1), and “the Majesty on high” is a reverent Jewish way of naming God without pronouncing his name.

Prophet, priest and king. These clauses are the seed of what later theology called Christ’s threefold office: he has spoken as the prophet (v. 2), made purification as the priest, and sat down as the king. In Israel the offices were kept apart: no priest of Aaron’s line sat on David’s throne, and when King Uzziah went into the temple to burn incense he was struck with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). The Son holds them all.

What it does not mean. “Sat down” does not mean Christ is inactive; he reigns and intercedes (7:25). It means his atoning work is finished.

If he made purification once for all, why do I still feel dirty? Because feeling and fact are different things, and the conscience is slow to believe good news. The purification is finished whether or not you feel clean, because it rests on what Christ did, not on what you sense. When guilt returns over a sin you have already confessed, do not try to make purification again by punishing yourself or promising harder. Bring it to him, and remember that he is seated: there is nothing left to add. If a sin is new, confess it, and the same blood that cleansed you once cleanses you still (1 John 1:7–9). Feeling usually follows faith, slowly. Let the fact lead.

Does Jesus really hold my life together, down to the small things? Yes. If he upholds the universe by his word, there is nothing in it too small for him: the cells in your body, the timing of a phone call, the weather on the day of the funeral. That is not fatalism, because the one who holds it is not a force but a person, the same person who made purification for your sins. The one who carries the stars is the one who was crucified for you. You can trust the details of your life to someone who already gave himself for the whole of it.

For worship. The light of God’s own glory took a body that could be struck, and the Word that holds every atom in place was silent before Pilate. The radiance was hidden in the darkness of Golgotha so that sinners stained past all cleaning could be made clean, and then that same light rose and took the throne. The face we will see there is the exact imprint of the Father, and it is turned toward us in welcome.

verseByVerse.quote: having become as much superior to angels as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Superior to angels. Why angels at all? In Jewish thought angels were the highest created beings and the mediators of the law (Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19; Hebrews 2:2). So to ask whether the Son outranks angels is to ask whether the new word outranks the old one. The question is not, at heart, about the ranks of heaven but about which covenant to live under.

Having become. What the Son became was superior in office, not in nature; verse 3 forbids reading it otherwise. As the eternal Son he was always above the angels; in his incarnation he was made for a little while lower than the angels (2:9); and by his death, resurrection and ascension, as the God-man, he was exalted far above them (Ephesians 1:20–21; Philippians 2:9). And “superior” (kreittōn, better) is the keyword of Hebrews, used thirteen times: a better hope, covenant, sacrifice, country, resurrection. Everything that follows unfolds it.

The name he has inherited. Which name? The next verse answers: the one thing no angel is ever called in this unique sense, Son. It may also include Lord, the name above every name (Philippians 2:9–11). And it is inherited, which is family language again. A servant may be trusted with everything and inherits nothing; the name comes with the relationship.

A gap measured by a gap. Superior in the same proportion as the name is more excellent: one gap measured by another, and since the distance between Son and servant is a difference in kind rather than degree, so is the other. The angels are not a little below Christ on the same ladder. They are on the other side of the line between Creator and creature.

Proof by Scripture. The writer now proves the superiority not by argument but with seven Old Testament passages in a row, assuming his readers will accept a text as settling anything.

Why does it matter to me that Jesus is greater than the angels? Because whatever you are tempted to put alongside him, it ranks below him. Few Christians today are tempted to worship angels, but many are drawn to something that feels more impressive, more immediate or more spiritual than plain trust in Christ: a powerful experience, a special teacher, a tradition, a technique for reaching God. The readers of Hebrews were tempted to go back to a system given through angels. The answer to every such pull is the same: nothing God has made is on the level of the Son who made it. If you have him, you are not missing anything higher.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–14 — Seven Texts, and Not One of Them About an Angel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer proves his point from seven quotations his readers already believed, and ends with a surprise about what angels are for.
verseByVerse.theology:
Texts About God, Applied to Jesus

Scriptures addressed to God, Psalm 45 and Psalm 102, are read as addressed to the Son, and the angels are commanded to worship him. A being the angels worship cannot be one of them.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Readers who had lost property and standing were told that earth and sky are the temporary things; the Son remains.

Now: The angels, far from rivals, are sent to serve those who will inherit salvation.

verseByVerse.quote: For to which of the angels did God ever say, “You are my Son, today I have begotten you”? Or again, “I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son”? And again, when he brings the firstborn into the world, he says, “Let all God’s angels worship him.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
To which of the angels. The argument is conducted entirely by quotation, and the question expects the answer none: search the Scriptures for the exception, and there is not one.

You are my Son. The first citation is Psalm 2:7, a coronation psalm in which God installs his King on Zion while the nations rage, and “today” is the enthronement day, not a statement about origins. It does not mean the Son began on a particular day; it means that on a particular day he was publicly installed. The New Testament applies it to Christ’s resurrection and exaltation, when his eternal sonship was openly proclaimed and he was declared the Son of God in power (Acts 13:33; Romans 1:4).

I will be to him a father. The second is from God’s promise to David about his offspring (2 Samuel 7:14). In its own setting it concerns Solomon, and the next line speaks of disciplining him when he commits iniquity: he could never be its final fulfilment. No son of David ever exhausted the promise of a throne established for ever (2 Samuel 7:13, 16), and the writer takes it as pointing to the one who would.

But are angels not called sons of God? Yes, but always as a group. Job speaks of the sons of God presenting themselves before the LORD and shouting for joy at creation (Job 1:6; 38:7): the heavenly host, the members of God’s court. What God never said to any angel is what he says here to one person: you are my Son, my heir, my king enthroned. The plural title describes a class of creatures. The singular names the one through whom God made the world (v. 2). Believers too are called sons of God, but by adoption, through the Son who is Son by nature (Galatians 4:4–7).

The firstborn. “Firstborn” does not mean first created; it is a title of rank, not chronology. God calls Israel his firstborn (Exodus 4:22), and David is made firstborn though he was the youngest of Jesse’s sons (Psalm 89:27). It means the heir, the one with pre-eminence (Colossians 1:15, 18). “Brings into the world” may refer to his incarnation, when the angels praised God at his birth (Luke 2:13–14), or his resurrection, or, as many think, his return in glory: the word “again” may go with “brings”, so that it reads, when he brings the firstborn into the world again.

Let all God’s angels worship. The words match the Greek Old Testament of Deuteronomy 32:43 (compare Psalm 97:7), and the quotation is decisive, because it commands the angels to worship him. Angels consistently refuse worship when it is offered to them: when John fell at an angel’s feet he was told to worship God (Revelation 19:10; 22:8–9). Only God may be worshipped (Matthew 4:10). The being the angels are commanded to worship cannot be a creature at all.

Textual note. The Dead Sea Scrolls contain a Hebrew text of Deuteronomy 32:43 that includes the line about the gods (or angels) bowing down, which supports the Greek translation used here as reflecting an ancient Hebrew form of the text. Most English Bibles translate the shorter Hebrew of Deuteronomy, so readers will not find this line there.

What does eternally begotten mean? It means the Son’s relationship to the Father is that of a son, sharing his very nature, without ever having had a beginning. A human father exists before his son; the eternal Father never existed without his Son, any more than the sun existed before its light (v. 3). Begotten is not made: a man makes a table, but he begets a son, someone of his own kind. So the Nicene Creed says the Son is begotten, not made, of one being with the Father. You do not need to picture it to believe it. It simply guards the truth that the one who died for you is not a creature God sent, but God himself who came.

How do I answer someone who says Jesus is a created being? Start where this chapter starts: with what Scripture says to him and about him. He made all things (v. 2; John 1:3), so he cannot be one of the things made. Angels are commanded to worship him (v. 6), and worship belongs to God alone. He is addressed as God (v. 8) and as the LORD who laid the foundations of the earth (v. 10). Ask your friend to read the chapter with you, slowly, and to say what each verse claims. Be gentle and patient; most people who hold this view were taught it, and the Spirit uses the plain words of Scripture to open eyes.
verseByVerse.note: The words of v. 6 match the Greek Old Testament of Deut 32:43, which is longer than the Hebrew.

verseByVerse.quote: Of the angels he says, “He makes his angels winds, and his ministers a flame of fire.” But of the Son he says, “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever, the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
He makes his angels winds. Psalm 104:4, in the Greek translation; the word for winds also means spirits. Wind and fire are impressive, and also transient and at somebody else’s disposal. The point is the word makes: angels are things God made and uses as he wills, however glorious they are.

Your throne, O God. Psalm 45 is a wedding song for an Israelite king, and in its original setting the king is addressed as God. Some translators render it “your throne is God’s throne” to avoid the difficulty, but the writer of Hebrews read it as it stands, addressing the Son directly as God, and built his argument on it. In its first setting it was a breathtaking way to speak of a human king; its full meaning is realised only in the Messiah, who is truly God. And the throne is for ever and ever: his kingdom is eternal (Daniel 7:14), against the changing winds and flames of the verse before.

Their own psalm. These Jewish believers confessed that the LORD our God is one. The writer is not smuggling divinity into the argument; he shows them that a psalm they had sung all their lives addresses the Messiah as God and give him an everlasting throne. The confession that God is one is not denied by the Son. It is filled out by him.

The scepter of uprightness. Uprightness is straightness, justice (Isaiah 11:3–5). History has known many thrones and very few straight sceptres. This one has never bent.

Loved righteousness. This is Christ’s perfect moral character: he loved what is right and hated evil, perfectly, throughout his earthly life (4:15; 7:26), and that perfect obedience, which none of us has matched, is counted to all who trust him (Romans 5:19). Loving right and hating wrong are one disposition seen from two sides, and an indifference to wickedness is not gentleness but a failure of love. Jesus could weep over Jerusalem and drive the traders from the temple in the same week, because the love and the hatred came from one heart.

God, your God. Two things are held together without embarrassment: the Son is addressed as God, and he has a God. That reflects the distinction of persons in the Trinity and the Son’s role as incarnate Mediator, who could say on resurrection morning, I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God (John 20:17). And “anointed” is the root of the word Christ: Messiah, Anointed One.

The oil of gladness. Oil was a sign of joy at festivals and coronations. His companions may be other kings, or his people (the same word is used of believers at 3:1 and 3:14), and he is anointed with more joy than anyone beside him. He endured the cross for the joy that was set before him (12:2), and now the joy is his.

Should a Christian hate anything? Yes: what Christ hates, which is wickedness, and above all our own. Hatred of evil is not a sin; indifference to it is. But the hatred of Christ is never contempt for people. He hated sin and ate with sinners. So hate the lie, the cruelty, the abuse, the thing that is destroying someone you love, and hate it most fiercely in your own heart, where you can actually fight it. Then love the person, as he does, enough to want him free of it.

Does following a righteous King mean I have to be grim? No. This King is anointed with the oil of gladness, and those who share his kingdom share his joy. Holiness and gladness are not opposites; in him they are one thing. A Christian who is serious about sin but has no joy has understood half the psalm. The sceptre is straight, and the throne is a wedding throne: Psalm 45 is a love song. Obey him gladly, because the one you serve is glad.

verseByVerse.quote: And, “You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth in the beginning, and the heavens are the work of your hands; they will perish, but you remain; they will all wear out like a garment, like a robe you will roll them up, like a garment they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will have no end.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
You, Lord, laid the foundation. The boldest quotation of the seven is Psalm 102:25–27, a lament: a man in deep affliction, whose days are like an evening shadow, who turns from his own frailty to the permanence of God. The one he addresses in these verses is unmistakably the LORD, Yahweh, the God of Israel, the creator of heaven and earth. And the writer of Hebrews says: this is the Father speaking to the Son.

Texts about God are texts about him. A psalm addressed to Yahweh is quoted as words spoken to Jesus. Paul makes the same move: in Isaiah the LORD swears that every knee will bow to him; Paul says every knee will bow at the name of Jesus (Isaiah 45:23; Philippians 2:10). It is the strongest form the New Testament’s teaching about Christ takes: not merely that Jesus is like God, but that texts about God are texts about him.

The work of your hands. Scripture now says what the writer said in his own voice (v. 2). The hands that shaped the heavens were later held out to Thomas, with the marks still in them.

They will perish, but you remain. The most permanent-seeming things there are, earth and sky, are the temporary items in this comparison. The Son is the one who lasts.

Like a robe. The universe as an old coat, folded and set aside (Isaiah 34:4). The Son will do with the stars what you do with a jacket at the end of the day.

They will be changed. Not annihilated but transformed. The old creation will give way to new heavens and a new earth (Revelation 21:1; Romans 8:19–21). A garment changed is replaced with something better, not with nothing.

You are the same. In this letter unchangeableness is not an abstraction. Hebrews is written to people whose world was coming apart: property confiscated, community shunned, some imprisoned (10:32–34). To them the writer says: the things you thought were solid are the garments, and the one you are being tempted to leave is the one who does not change. He will say it again in the plainest form: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever (13:8).

If the world will be rolled up, does it matter how I care for it? Yes. The world is the work of Christ’s hands, and that is reason enough to treat it with respect. Changed is not destroyed: God will renew this creation, not throw it away, and our bodies too will be raised, not discarded. So work done well in this world, kindness to neighbours, care for what God made, is not wasted. What the passage forbids is putting your final trust in anything that can wear out. Enjoy the garment, look after it, and do not mistake it for the one who wears it.

How does an unchanging Christ help me when my life is falling apart? Because he is the one fixed point when everything else moves. Your health may change, your work, your marriage, your church, your own feelings about God. He does not. The love he had for you before you were born is the love he has for you on the worst day of your life. His promises do not expire, his sacrifice does not lose its power, and his intercession does not pause. When nothing feels solid, do not look for a solid circumstance. Look at him, and say to him the words of this psalm: you are the same.

For worship. The psalmist felt himself dying, and he lifted his eyes from his own fading to the God who does not fade. Hebrews tells us whose face he was seeing. It was the Son, who laid the foundations of the earth and will fold up the heavens like a cloak, and who in between took our fading flesh, let it wear out on a cross, and rose with it renewed. Everything grows old except him, and he has promised to make all things new.

verseByVerse.quote: And to which of the angels has he ever said, “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet”? Are they not all ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sit at my right hand. The seventh quotation, framing the series with the question of verse 5, is Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament verse the New quotes most. Jesus used it to show that the Messiah is David’s Lord (Mark 12:35–37), and its fourth verse supplies the Melchizedek priesthood of chapters 5 to 7. Two things are given to the Son here that are given to no creature. A place: at my right hand, the position of royal authority. And a promise: that his enemies will be subdued, and that he may sit while it happens. Ancient kings placed their feet on the necks of conquered enemies (Joshua 10:24). Christ reigns now, and his enemies are being subdued, the last enemy being death (1 Corinthians 15:25–26).

Until. This word tells the reader where he stands in the story. The subduing is under way and not finished, which is why the readers are suffering. We live between the sitting and the footstool. The King is already enthroned; the victory is already certain; the last enemy is still in the field.

Ministering spirits. Having established that angels are inferior, the writer says what they are for. “Spirits” recalls the winds of verse 7, and “sent out” is present tense: continually being sent.

Those who are to inherit salvation. Here is the sting in the tail of the whole chapter: the ones angels are sent to serve are us. The glorious beings through whom the law was given serve ordinary struggling Christians the world would not look at twice (Psalm 34:7; Acts 12:7–10). And the word “inherit” ties back to verse 2 and closes the circle. The Son is heir of all things; those who are his inherit salvation. What is his by right becomes theirs by gift, and the angels, who inherit nothing, are sent out to look after the heirs.

In the flow. The first movement of the sermon ends here, built to lead straight into the first warning: therefore (2:1), if the message spoken through angels was binding, how much more the salvation announced by the Lord (2:2–3).

What it does not mean. It does not mean we should pray to angels or seek contact with them (Colossians 2:18). They serve at God’s command, not ours.

What about Matthew 18:10 and Peter’s angel? Jesus says of his little ones that in heaven their angels always see the face of his Father (Matthew 18:10), and the disciples in Acts thought it was Peter’s angel at the door (Acts 12:15). These texts show that God’s angels are concerned with his people, and that the least of them are not overlooked in heaven. They do not teach that each person has one angel assigned to him for life; the second is only what frightened disciples supposed. This verse speaks of angels as a company sent to serve all who will inherit salvation. We can be sure that God sends his angels for his people; we are not told more, and should not invent it.

Why do I never see angels, if they are serving me? Because their service is usually hidden, and that is by design. Most of what God does for his people is done out of sight: dangers turned aside that you never knew were coming, strength given in an hour you thought you could not survive. Elisha’s servant saw only the enemy army until God opened his eyes to the hills full of horses and chariots of fire (2 Kings 6:15–17). You do not need to see them, and you should not try to contact them. Trust the God who sends them, and thank him for protection you will only fully know in glory.

On a Tuesday. Take the hint the angels give: find one heir of salvation this week, a weary believer or an elderly saint, and do for them something unseen and unthanked. It is the work of angels.

For worship. The King sits, and the battle goes on, and the outcome is not in doubt. Every enemy of his people, sin and Satan and death itself, is on its way to becoming a footstool. And while he waits, the armies of heaven are sent out not to guard his throne, which needs no guard, but to look after his heirs. The one who for a little while was made lower than the angels now has them running errands for his brothers.
verseByVerse.note: Psalm 110 is the Old Testament passage most often quoted in the New.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets,<sup>2</sup>but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed the heir of all things, through whom also he created the world.<sup>3</sup>He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature, and he upholds the universe by the word of his power. After making purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high,<sup>4</sup>having become as much superior to angels as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs.<sup>5</sup>For to which of the angels did God ever say, “You are my Son, today I have begotten you”? Or again, “I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son”?<sup>6</sup>And again, when he brings the firstborn into the world, he says, “Let all God’s angels worship him.”<sup>7</sup>Of the angels he says, “He makes his angels winds, and his ministers a flame of fire.”<sup>8</sup>But of the Son he says, “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever, the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom.<sup>9</sup>You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your companions.”<sup>10</sup>And, “You, Lord, laid the foundation of the earth in the beginning, and the heavens are the work of your hands;<sup>11</sup>they will perish, but you remain; they will all wear out like a garment,<sup>12</sup>like a robe you will roll them up, like a garment they will be changed. But you are the same, and your years will have no end.”<sup>13</sup>And to which of the angels has he ever said, “Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet”?<sup>14</sup>Are they not all ministering spirits sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?

2.title: Lower Than the Angels: The Glory of the Humiliated Son
2.overview:
Chapter 1 set the Son above the angels; chapter 2 answers the obvious objection: if Jesus is this exalted Son, why did he suffer and die? The answer comes through Psalm 8, and it shows the humiliation as the road by which he brings his brothers to glory.

The chapter opens with the first of the letter’s warnings (vv. 1–4), against drifting from so great a salvation.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because of who the Son is, his word cannot be treated casually.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Danger Is Drift

The peril is not dramatic renunciation but neglect: slipping past the harbour without ever deciding to leave. The remedy is attention to what has been heard.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: If the law given through angels carried penalties, neglecting the salvation declared by the Lord is more serious still.

Now: The question is not whether you have renounced Christ but whether you are still paying attention.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore we must pay much closer attention to what we have heard, lest we drift away from it. For since the message declared by angels proved to be reliable, and every transgression or disobedience received a just retribution,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Hebrews 2 has two movements. First comes the first of what are often counted as the letter’s five warnings (vv. 1–4): if the law given through angels was binding, there is no escape for those who neglect the great salvation announced by the Lord. Then the writer explains why the Son became lower than the angels (vv. 5–18). Through Psalm 8 he shows Jesus humbled and crowned, calling his people brothers, sharing their flesh to break the devil’s power over death, and becoming their merciful and faithful high priest.

How Hebrews is built. With “therefore” the first warning arrives on the heels of the argument that produced it: doctrine, then an application with teeth, then more doctrine. The Son is the radiance of God’s glory and the enthroned King; therefore you cannot treat his word casually.

We must pay much closer attention. Not you must, but we must: the preacher puts himself inside the warning, and he will do it again and again. These passages are not a man lecturing people he considers less safe than himself.

Lest we drift away. The word (pararyōmen) means to flow past or slip away, used of a ring slipping off a finger; it suits the picture of a boat that slips its moorings and is carried past the harbour mouth by a current the crew never noticed. Nobody decides to drift; drifting is what happens when nothing is decided at all.

The commoner peril. This peril is far commoner than open apostasy. These readers seem to have been tired, socially battered and quietly attending less (10:25); the old ways were warm and familiar, and there was no particular moment at which they chose to leave. The remedy is not to try harder to feel, but to attend to what you have heard.

Moored to a person. What holds a believer is not a rope of his own making. The letter will later call the hope a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, fastened behind the curtain where Jesus has gone ahead of us (6:19–20). To pay attention is to keep looking at the one who spoke. The fixed point is not our grip on the rope but the Saviour at the other end of it.

The message declared by angels. An argument from the lesser to the greater. The message declared by angels is the law at Sinai, held to have been mediated through angels (Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19). It proved legally binding.

Transgression or disobedience. “Transgression” is stepping over the line; “disobedience” is literally mis-hearing, refusing to listen. Both were punished, and justly (Numbers 15:30–31). In God’s reckoning, not hearing is not neutral.

How do I know if I am drifting? Drift is hard to see from inside, because it feels like nothing. Look for small signs rather than dramatic ones. Prayer has shrunk to emergencies. The Bible is opened less, and with less expectation. Missing church no longer bothers you. Sin that once grieved you now merely irritates you. Christian friends have quietly been replaced by others. Your thoughts about God are mostly about what he has not done. None of these proves you are lost; each is a current. The remedy is not panic but attention: return to the word, to prayer, to the gathered church, and to the Son who is greater than everything that has been pulling you away.

For worship. The God who spoke at Sinai with fire and trumpet has spoken again, in his own Son. He did not have to warn us. A God who wanted to be rid of careless people would have let them drift without a word. Instead he raises his voice in love, like a man on the shore shouting to a boat moving toward the rocks. Every warning in this letter is the Father calling his children back to the harbour, and the harbour is his Son.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition held that the law was given through angels.

verseByVerse.quote: how shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation? It was declared at first by the Lord, and it was attested to us by those who heard, while God also bore witness by signs and wonders and various miracles and by gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to his will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
How shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation? The argument completes itself, and the logic is uncomfortable precisely because it is so simple. If the word that came through angels carried consequences, what happens to those who ignore the word that came through the Son? The greater the messenger, the greater the weight of the message, and the thing escaped is the judgment of God.

Neglect. Not reject, not deny, not blaspheme: the word means to be careless of. It is the word Jesus used in his parable of those invited to the wedding who paid no attention and went off, one to his farm, another to his business (Matthew 22:5). Nobody in this congregation was tearing up the gospel. They were letting it slide, and that is enough to be in danger.

Such a great salvation. The warning is heavy because the thing being neglected is enormous: a salvation won by the Creator of the ages. Neglect is dangerous in proportion to the worth of what is neglected. A man who loses a letter is careless; a man who loses a pardon from the king on the morning of his execution is something else.

Can a true Christian drift away and be lost? No, and the warning is still real. The escape in view is escape from final judgment, and the writer includes himself: how shall we escape. But he will also show that those who truly share in Christ hold fast to the end (3:14), and that warnings like this are among the means God uses to keep his people from drifting (compare 6:4–12). God does not keep his children in spite of the warnings; he keeps them through the warnings. The Christian who hears this and pays closer attention is doing exactly what the warning is for. The person who hears it and shrugs should be very afraid, not because a true child of God can be lost, but because the shrug may show he never was one.

Is it not harsh to treat mere neglect so seriously? It feels harsh only while we think of the gospel as advice. If a friend gives you a tip and you ignore it, little is lost. But if the pilot warns that the current is carrying the ship onto the rocks and points to the one safe channel, ignoring him is not a small thing, even if you never argue with him. Neglect is also how the heart most often says no while still feeling respectable. The decent person who never rejects Christ but is always busy with a farm, a business or a reputation (Matthew 22:5) is saying that something else matters more. That is why the warning is kind. It wakes up the churchgoer and the careless together, and it points both to a salvation so great that it is still offered to those who have neglected it.

Declared at first by the Lord. Three lines of transmission follow, the first being the Lord Jesus himself: the time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel (Mark 1:14–15). The salvation you are tempted to neglect was preached by its own author.

Attested by those who heard. “Attested” is from the root of reliable in verse 2: the apostles, as eyewitnesses, made it firm. The writer places himself in the second generation, which is one reason most think Paul did not write the letter (Galatians 1:11–12).

God also bore witness. The third line is God’s own, in the miracles of Jesus and the apostles (Acts 2:22, 43): signs point to a meaning, wonders astonish, miracles are works of power. The gospel arrived with three witnesses: the Lord, his apostles, and the Father’s own hand.

According to his will. God decides who receives what (1 Corinthians 12:11), which rules out treating any gift as an achievement or a right.

Where Christians differ: do miraculous sign gifts continue today? Pentecostal and charismatic Christians believe the miraculous gifts, such as healing, tongues and prophecy, continue in the same way throughout the church age. This commentary’s view: this verse describes the signs, wonders and miracles as God’s confirmation of the gospel through those who heard the Lord, that is, the apostolic generation (2 Corinthians 12:12). Their purpose was to authenticate the foundational revelation. With that revelation complete, the sign gifts have ceased in that form. God still works powerfully, answers prayer, heals as he wills, and gives every believer gifts for service (Romans 12:6–8; 1 Peter 4:10–11). Many faithful believers, some in Reformed churches among them, think these gifts continue, and often practise them with care and humility; their love for Christ is plain, and they are brothers. This cessationist view is held charitably toward them.

The order of the witnesses. The writer speaks of the signs in the past tense, as part of how the message was first confirmed. It has been confirmed, and it is written, and the same Spirit who once attested it with wonders now opens blind eyes to it through the word.

Should I pray for healing, then? Yes, with confidence and without embarrassment. Cessationism is not the belief that God has stopped healing; it is the belief that he no longer gives individuals the apostolic gift of healing at will. James tells the sick to call the elders, who pray over them and anoint them in the name of the Lord (James 5:14–15), and that instruction is for the whole church age. So pray for the sick, specifically and persistently, and ask the elders to pray. Then leave the answer to God, who sometimes heals at once, sometimes through doctors and time, and sometimes by giving grace to bear what he does not remove (2 Corinthians 12:7–10).
verseByVerse.note: The writer did not hear Jesus himself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–18 — The Founder Made Perfect Through Suffering
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer explains why the Son had to become lower than the angels: to fulfil Psalm 8 as the true Man, to call sinners his brothers, to break the power of death, and to become the high priest the rest of the letter will describe.
verseByVerse.theology:
Fear of Death as Lifelong Slavery

We do not yet see everything subject to man, but we see Jesus: lowered, crowned, tasting death for everyone. He shared flesh and blood to break the devil's hold through the fear of death, and to make propitiation as a merciful and faithful high priest.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A congregation that had lost property wondered why following a crowned Lord meant shame: his pattern runs down first.

Now: Because he suffered when tempted, he is able to help those being tempted, today.

verseByVerse.quote: For it was not to angels that God subjected the world to come, of which we are speaking. It has been testified somewhere, “What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you care for him? You made him for a little while lower than the angels; you have crowned him with glory and honor, putting everything in subjection under his feet.” Now in putting everything in subjection to him, he left nothing outside his control. At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The world to come. The world to come is the new creation, begun by Christ and completed at his return. Some Jewish thought held that angels governed the nations in this age (Daniel 10:13, 20), but the coming world will be ruled by Christ and his people: not simply the Son, but humanity, in the Son.

Testified somewhere. A curious way to introduce Scripture (also 4:4), not vagueness: the speaker that matters is God rather than the human author.

What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you care for him? The quotation is Psalm 8:4–6, following the Greek translation, and it is a psalm about the dignity of human beings. David is looking up at the night sky, overwhelmed by his own smallness under the moon and the stars God set in place. And the answer the psalm gives is not that man is nothing. It is that God remembers him, cares for him, and has crowned him. “Son of man” in the psalm means a human being. But the phrase also became the title Jesus most often used of himself (Daniel 7:13), and the writer sees the psalm fulfilled in Jesus as the true representative man.

For a little while lower. The phrase can mean a little lower in rank, or lower for a little while, and the writer builds on the second: a temporary humiliation followed by a crowning. In the Hebrew psalm humanity is made a little lower than God, or than the heavenly beings; the Greek translation has angels.

Everything in subjection. The creation mandate (Genesis 1:26–28): man was made a gardener-king under the great King, with the whole created order under his feet, under God.

Not yet. Then the writer says the honest thing: the magnificent text is visibly not yet true. We do not rule. We are ruled: by decay, by circumstance, by disease, by disasters, by the devil and by death. The fall disrupted God’s design (Romans 8:20–22).

A crown waiting for its head. The psalm was never only about humanity in general. Jesus took its second verse on his lips when children shouted hosanna (Matthew 21:16), and Paul reads its last line as fulfilled in the risen Christ, under whose feet God has put all things (1 Corinthians 15:27; Ephesians 1:22). The crown Adam dropped was waiting for a head, and the dominion humanity lost is restored in one Man first and then, in him, to all who are his. That is why the writer can admit the not yet so honestly: he knows whose name comes next.

In the flow. Chapter 1 set the Son far above the angels; now the writer faces the scandal his readers knew too well, that this Son suffered and died. Psalm 8 is the key: God always meant human beings to rule his world, and the road to that rule runs through the lowly Man who goes first (2:9–10).

If human beings were made to rule, why do I feel so small and powerless? Because you are living in the not yet, and the Bible does not pretend otherwise. The smallness you feel is real: one diagnosis, one redundancy, one bereavement can show how little we control. But it is not the end of the story. You were made for dignity, and the dignity is not cancelled by the fall, only delayed and damaged. In Christ it is being restored, and in the world to come the redeemed will reign with him (2 Timothy 2:12; Revelation 5:10). So feel your weakness honestly, and do not despise it. It is the place where Psalm 8 is waiting to be fulfilled in you.

Does this psalm say anything about how I treat other people? A great deal. If God is mindful of every human being and crowned humanity with glory and honour, then no person is beneath your notice: not the unborn child, the elderly woman with dementia, the man sleeping in a doorway, the colleague you find tiresome. Each bears God’s image and was made for a crown. Contempt for any human being is contempt for something God has honoured. Treat people as the psalm sees them, and you will find yourself treating them as Christ did.

On a Tuesday. Tonight, if the sky is clear, go outside for five minutes and look up, as David did. Let the size of it make you small. Then pray Psalm 8, and thank God that the Maker of all that is mindful of you.

verseByVerse.quote: But we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we see him. We do not see everything in subjection to man, but we see one man, and in him the psalm has come true: the sight of faith. The readers had never laid eyes on Jesus, but they could see him in the gospel more clearly than they could see their own circumstances.

Namely Jesus. At the point of humiliation the writer uses the human name for the first time in the letter: the carpenter’s son from Nazareth. He is the true man, the last Adam, in whom Psalm 8 is fulfilled (1 Corinthians 15:27, 45).

Because of the suffering of death. Crowned, and still crowned. The order is everything: the crowning is because of the suffering, not in spite of it (Philippians 2:8–9). The cross is not an obstacle he overcame on the way to glory. It is the ground of the glory. That is the answer to a congregation asking why following a crowned Lord has landed them in poverty and shame: the pattern runs down first, then up.

Taste death for everyone. “Taste death” does not mean sip; it means to experience it fully (Mark 9:1). “For everyone” is on behalf of each, and in the context the everyone are the many sons being brought to glory (v. 10), his brothers (v. 11), the children God has given him (v. 13), the offspring of Abraham (v. 16), the people (v. 17).

Textual note. A few manuscripts and some early church writers read “apart from God” (chōris theou) instead of “by the grace of God” (chariti theou). The two look similar in Greek. “Apart from God” might refer to Jesus’ cry of abandonment on the cross, or to his dying for all apart from God himself. But the great majority of manuscripts read “by the grace of God,” and that is almost certainly original.

Where Christians differ: did Christ die for every individual equally? Many read “for everyone” as proof that Christ’s death was equally for every human being, making salvation possible for all. This commentary’s view: the surrounding verses define the everyone as the many sons brought to glory, the brothers he sanctifies, the children given to him by the Father (vv. 10–13). His death actually achieves their salvation: it brings them to glory, destroys the devil’s power over them, frees them, and makes propitiation for their sins (vv. 10, 14–17). This is definite atonement (sometimes called particular redemption): Christ tasted death for each one of those he came to save, and none of them will be lost. Jesus lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:15). Yet his death is of infinite value, sufficient for all, and the gospel is offered sincerely to every person. Many faithful Christians read for everyone as all people alike, and they preach the same cross as the only hope; this commentary differs from them as brothers.

What it does not mean. “For everyone” does not mean all will be saved. Hebrews warns repeatedly that those who reject Christ face judgment (2:3; 10:26–31).

Can I tell an unbeliever that Christ died for him? You can tell him, truly and urgently, that Christ died for sinners, that his death is enough for anyone, and that whoever comes to him will never be cast out (John 6:37). That is how the apostles preached: they did not begin by explaining whom God had chosen; they called everyone to repent and believe. Definite atonement does not narrow the offer; it guarantees that the offer is backed by a death that actually saves. You can say to anyone with full sincerity: come to Christ, and you will find that he died for you.

For worship. He tasted death, the bitterness and the God-forsakenness of it, for each of his own, and grace was the whole reason. The crown he wears now was not handed to him at a ceremony. It was won on a hill outside the city, on the day the crown on his head was made of thorns. Every believer who closes his eyes in death will find that death has already been tasted for him, and that the one who tasted it is waiting to share his glory and honour.

verseByVerse.quote: For it was fitting that he, for whom and by whom all things exist, in bringing many sons to glory, should make the founder of their salvation perfect through suffering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It was fitting. The word is startling: the cross was appropriate, what you would expect once you know who God is. To most religious sensibilities it looks like a scandal, a stumbling block and folly (1 Corinthians 1:23). Hebrews says it suited him. Given his character, his holiness and his love together, no other method would have been in keeping.

For whom and by whom. The Father, the goal and origin of everything (Romans 11:36), with no obligations to anybody, chose this way of salvation, and it was worthy of him.

Many sons to glory. The sons are the redeemed, adopted as God’s children (Romans 8:14–17), and glory is final salvation, the dominion humanity lost. God is not merely repairing the damage; he is leading a great family home and completing the original design.

Perfect through suffering. “Founder” (archēgos) is a pioneer who goes first and opens a way, a champion who fights for his people (12:2; Acts 3:15). Then the hard phrase. “Perfect” means to complete, to make fully fit for a purpose; in the Greek Old Testament it is used of consecrating a priest. It does not mean Jesus was morally imperfect and needed improving; he was always sinless (4:15; 7:26). What the suffering completed was not his character but his qualification. He was made fully qualified as Saviour and High Priest by going through suffering and death (5:8–9). And he is out in front, on a road he has already walked, so that a suffering congregation was not lost in a wilderness. They were following tracks.

Does this mean my suffering is part of the path too? Yes. Not that suffering earns glory, which Christ alone earned, but that God leads his sons to glory by the same road their pioneer took. Your suffering is not a sign that you have taken a wrong turning, or that God has forgotten you. It is the country the founder of your salvation has already crossed. He is not shouting directions from the far side; he walked it, and he is leading you through it. And it has an end: the road goes to glory. Paul could call the heaviest affliction light and momentary beside the eternal weight of glory it is preparing (2 Corinthians 4:17).

verseByVerse.quote: For he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified all have one source. That is why he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying, “I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise.” And again, “I will put my trust in him.” And again, “Behold, I and the children God has given me.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who sanctifies. Jesus makes his people holy, sets them apart for God, by his blood (10:10, 14; 13:12). One makes holy; the others are made holy, and yet the next phrase binds them together.

All have one source. Literally all of one: most likely God the Father. The sanctifier and the sanctified belong to the same household.

Not ashamed to call them brothers. The phrasing concedes what it denies: there was every reason he might have been. These are the people described as drifting and enslaved by lifelong fear. The exalted Son of God, the radiance of the Father’s glory, is not embarrassed to be publicly associated with them (Matthew 12:49–50). Much of human life is spent trying to become someone nobody would be ashamed to know: the right job, the right look, the right record. The gospel cuts that anxiety at the root. The one whose opinion matters most has already said, in public, that he is not ashamed of his people, and no one else’s approval can add to that or take it away. On the morning of his resurrection, the first message he sent was to the men who had run away: go to my brothers (John 20:17).

I will tell of your name. Three quotations follow. The first is Psalm 22:22, from the psalm of the crucifixion, at the point where it turns from anguish to triumph: the brotherhood is announced by a man coming out the far side of dereliction, and the first thing he does is sing among his brothers in the congregation. When the people of God sing, the loudest voice in the room is his.

I will put my trust in him. The second is from Isaiah 8:17. Here is the Son, in his humanity, doing the thing that most marks a creature: trusting God (12:2). Whatever faith is asked of us, he exercised it first, in the dark, on a cross.

I and the children. The third is Isaiah 8:18, where the prophet stands with his sons as signs to an unbelieving nation. Here Christ presents his own, given him by the Father, of whom he will lose none (John 6:37, 39). Between them the three texts make the family complete: a brother who sings with them, who trusts alongside them, and who presents them to God as his own.

What it does not mean. “One source” does not mean believers are divine as Jesus is. He is the eternal Son by nature; we are sons by adoption. He is the Sanctifier; we are the sanctified.

How can he not be ashamed of me, when I am ashamed of myself? Because his acceptance of you does not rest on what you are in yourself but on what he has done for you and the Father has given him. He calls you brother not because he overlooks your sin, but because he has dealt with it: he is the one who sanctifies. Shame says you must hide; the gospel says you have been claimed. When shame rises, do not argue with it on its own terms by listing your good points. Answer it with his words: here am I, and the children God has given me. He is not ashamed to stand beside you before the Father, and he has already done so.

What does it mean that Jesus sings in the church? It means that when the congregation gathers to praise God, Christ himself is present, leading the praise. Our worship is not a performance we offer to win God over; it is joining the song of the risen Son, who declares the Father’s name to his brothers. That should change how you come on Sunday. You are not dragging your weary voice into a void. You are standing next to the Son, and your weak praise is carried in his.

On a Tuesday. Picture the believer you are most inclined to be embarrassed by. Jesus calls him brother, and to sit with him, invite him home or speak well of him is simply to agree with Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: Since therefore the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same things, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Flesh and blood. Two different verbs: the children share flesh and blood as a settled condition; he partook of it in a single decisive act, taking up something not natively his. He did not merely appear human; he became fully human (John 1:14; 1 John 4:2).

Through death. He became mortal in order to die: not primarily to teach or set an example, but to have something to lay down. God cannot die; a man can. “Destroy” does not mean annihilate. It means to render powerless, the same word Paul uses when he says Christ abolished death (2 Timothy 1:10). The devil has not ceased to exist. His weapon has been taken away.

How the devil held the power of death. The devil held the power of death in that he brought sin into the world, and sin brings death (Romans 5:12; John 8:44). He accuses sinners and holds them under death’s penalty. By dying for sin, Christ removed the ground of the devil’s accusation and broke his grip (Colossians 2:14–15; Revelation 12:10–11). He drove the Son of God to the cross and broke his own weapon on him.

Lifelong slavery. The diagnosis is that the fear of death is a form of slavery that lasts a whole life. It is what makes a man grasp, hoard, protect himself, refuse risks and cling to comfort. Much of what is called self-interest is fear of death wearing ordinary clothes.

Leverage taken away. The devil holds people chiefly through fear. Take the fear away and the leverage is gone, which is why the early Christians were so hard for the empire to manage: you cannot finally threaten a man who has stopped being afraid of the worst thing you can do to him. For the believer, death is no longer a punishment but a passage to Christ (Philippians 1:21–23; 1 Corinthians 15:55–57). That does not mean believers are spared dying: Christians still die, and the parting still hurts. But the sting of death is sin, and its power is the law’s sentence on sin (1 Corinthians 15:56), and Christ has taken both. So for the believer death is no longer the moment he goes to be judged for his sins. It is the moment he goes to be with the one who bore them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the devil now has no activity at all; he still prowls (1 Peter 5:8). His decisive power has been broken, and his final destruction is certain (Revelation 20:10).

I am a Christian, but I am still afraid of dying. Is something wrong with my faith? Not necessarily. The verse frees you from slavery to the fear, not from every feeling of it. Death is still an enemy (1 Corinthians 15:26); Jesus himself wept at a grave and was in anguish in the garden. What changes is that fear no longer has the last word or rules your choices. You can feel the dread and still trust the one who has gone through death and come out. Bring the fear to him honestly. Ask him to show you what death is now for you: not the jaws of judgment, but a door into his presence. Often it is the process of dying more than death itself we fear, and he has promised to be with you in the valley too (Psalm 23:4).

On a Tuesday. Fear of death rarely announces itself; it shows up as the clutch at safety and the refusal of risk for Christ. Freedom looks ordinary too: the gift given, the word spoken. And beside someone you love who is facing death, these two verses read aloud can say what is hard to say any other way.

verseByVerse.quote: For surely it is not angels that he helps, but he helps the offspring of Abraham.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not angels that he helps. The verb means to take hold of, used of Jesus catching Peter as he sank (Matthew 14:31): not help from a distance, but a hand closing on someone who is going down. Fallen angels have no redeemer (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6). The point is not that angels are neglected but that the incarnation was specific: he took hold of our nature, not theirs, because it was human beings he came to rescue.

The offspring of Abraham. For Jewish Christians wondering whether following Jesus had cost them their inheritance: far from severing them from Abraham, the incarnation is the fulfilment of what was promised to him (Genesis 12:3; 22:18). And the phrase reaches further than ancestry. Abraham’s true children are all who share his faith, Jew and Gentile (Galatians 3:7, 29; Romans 4:16).

Why did God not save the fallen angels? Scripture does not tell us, and speculation is unprofitable. What this verse says is not that angels were refused but that the Son took hold of Abraham’s offspring, and it says it as an act of sheer, specific mercy toward people who had no more claim on him than anyone else. The right response is not to work out why we were chosen and they were not, but to wonder that he took hold of us at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest in the service of God, to make propitiation for the sins of the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like his brothers in every respect. Not in most respects: body, soul, emotions, temptations, weakness, suffering and death. Everything human, except sin, and the letter will supply that one exception later: yet without sin (4:15). Hunger, exhaustion, grief, the fear in the garden were genuinely his. A high priest must be taken from among the people he represents (5:1), and a representative who had not shared the condition could not have represented anybody.

A merciful and faithful high priest. The letter’s great theme, unpacked in chapters 5 to 10, is named for the first time: Jesus is the true High Priest to whom Aaron pointed (Leviticus 16). The two adjectives face two directions. Merciful toward us, because he knows from inside what it is like. Faithful toward God, carrying out his task perfectly. A priest needs both, and many human priests manage only one: severe men who are reliable, or kind men who are lax. This one is both, standing on the human side of the gap and reaching across it.

Propitiation. The word is the technical term for what happened on the Day of Atonement; the related noun names the mercy seat itself, the lid of the ark where the blood was sprinkled (9:5). Propitiation means satisfying God’s just wrath against sin by an offering, so that he is favourable toward sinners. It includes expiation, the removal of sin itself. Christ is the propitiation for our sins (Romans 3:25; 1 John 2:2; 4:10). He bore the wrath we deserved: this is penal substitution. The people are the brothers of verses 11 to 17.

Not a bribe. Some object that propitiation sounds pagan, like bribing an angry deity. God’s wrath is no mood that a gift could sweeten; it is his holy, unchanging hostility to evil. And the decisive difference from the pagan picture is who provides the sacrifice. In paganism a man appeases a god. Here God, in mercy, supplies the offering himself and, in the person of his Son, bears it himself. That is not bribery; it is love paying the price out of its own heart.

Where Christians differ: did Christ’s death turn away God’s wrath? Some modern theologians reject propitiation, arguing that God’s love does not need appeasing, and translate the word only as expiation (removal of sin). This commentary’s view: Scripture teaches that God’s holy wrath is real (Romans 1:18; John 3:36), and that Christ’s death turned it away from his people by bearing it in their place (Isaiah 53:5–6, 10; Galatians 3:13). This is not an angry Father appeased by a loving Son against his will; the Father in love sent the Son to be the propitiation (1 John 4:10). Propitiation and expiation go together: Christ removed our sin and satisfied God’s justice. This is penal substitutionary atonement, the heart of the gospel.

If God is love, why does he need propitiation at all? Because his love is holy love. A God who shrugged at evil would not be loving; he would be indifferent to the victims of evil and to the ruin it brings. His wrath is the response of perfect goodness to what destroys his world and his creatures. The wonder of the gospel is that the same God whose justice must judge sin is the God whose love provides the sacrifice. The cross is not love overcoming justice, or justice overcoming love. It is both satisfied in one act, in one Person. That is why you can be completely sure of forgiveness: not because God has stopped caring about sin, but because he has dealt with it fully.

On a Tuesday. When you sin this week, notice which priest you go to in your mind. Some of us go to a severe one and expect a rebuke; some go to a lax one and expect a shrug. Go to the real one, merciful and faithful. Confess the specific thing, thank him that the wrath it deserved has already been borne, and, because he is faithful to God, ask him to help you turn from it.

verseByVerse.quote: For because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Suffered when tempted. The chapter ends not with a doctrine but a capability. The word covers both temptation and testing. Jesus was truly tempted: in the wilderness (Matthew 4:1–11), in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:36–46), and throughout his life (Luke 22:28).

Suffering in temptation. We tend to imagine that resisting temptation was easy for him because he was sinless. Hebrews says the opposite. Only the person who refuses all the way to the end knows the full force of the thing, because the one who gives in has stopped the pressure early. He felt the whole weight precisely because he never yielded, and that unbroken obedience, offered in our place, covers every time his people have yielded.

Could Jesus have sinned? Some Christians say he must have been able to, or his temptations would not have been real. The historic answer of the church is that he could not, because he is the eternal Son, and his human will was never set against the will of God. That is the more likely answer. But it does not make the temptation unreal. A bridge that cannot fall still bears the full weight of the train; a fortress that cannot be taken still feels the whole force of the siege. Because Jesus never yielded, he felt temptation’s pressure to the very end (compare 4:15).

Able to help. “Help” (boēthēsai) was the ordinary word for answering a call for help: not a sympathetic figure at a distance, but somebody arriving. Because he has been through it, he knows exactly what we face (4:15–16; 1 Corinthians 10:13). And those being tempted is present tense: the help is for the person in the middle of it this afternoon.

Competence and sympathy in one person.
