He is the radiance of God’s glory who carries the universe along, and he has been hungry, frightened and pressed to the limit, so that when you call he does not need it explained. The competence and the sympathy are in the same person. This is the note the letter will return to at its turning point: let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace (4:16). The whole argument about priesthood exists so that frightened people will ask.

What does his help look like when I am tempted? Usually not a feeling that sweeps the temptation away, though sometimes the pull simply loosens when you pray. More often it is a way of escape God provides (1 Corinthians 10:13): a thought of Scripture brought to mind, a door you can walk out of, a friend who calls, a strength to say no that you did not have a moment before. So when temptation comes, call to him at once, in a sentence, before you argue with it. Then take the way out he gives, physically if you must. And if you fall, run to him just as quickly. The one who helps the tempted also cleanses the fallen.

Does Jesus understand temptations he never faced in exactly my form? Yes. He was not tempted by every modern form of sin, but he was tempted in every way that matters: to doubt his Father’s goodness, to grasp for comfort, to take a shortcut to glory, to hate his enemies, to give up under pain and loneliness (Matthew 4:1–11). Every temptation you face is some version of these. He knows the pull from inside, without the corruption that makes our resistance weaker. You will never be able to say to him, you do not understand.

For worship. He knows. The Lord who upholds the universe by the word of his power has been hungry in a desert, exhausted on a hillside, betrayed by a friend and pressed to the edge of his strength in a garden at night.. So the cry of a tempted believer on earth reaches a throne where the one who hears it has been there, and he comes at the shout. The merciful and faithful High Priest is the swiftest helper in heaven.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore we must pay much closer attention to what we have heard, lest we drift away from it.<sup>2</sup>For since the message declared by angels proved to be reliable, and every transgression or disobedience received a just retribution,<sup>3</sup>how shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation? It was declared at first by the Lord, and it was attested to us by those who heard,<sup>4</sup>while God also bore witness by signs and wonders and various miracles and by gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to his will.<sup>5</sup>For it was not to angels that God subjected the world to come, of which we are speaking.<sup>6</sup>It has been testified somewhere, “What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you care for him?<sup>7</sup>You made him for a little while lower than the angels; you have crowned him with glory and honor,<sup>8</sup>putting everything in subjection under his feet.” Now in putting everything in subjection to him, he left nothing outside his control. At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him.<sup>9</sup>But we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone.<sup>10</sup>For it was fitting that he, for whom and by whom all things exist, in bringing many sons to glory, should make the founder of their salvation perfect through suffering.<sup>11</sup>For he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified all have one source. That is why he is not ashamed to call them brothers,<sup>12</sup>saying, “I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise.”<sup>13</sup>And again, “I will put my trust in him.” And again, “Behold, I and the children God has given me.”<sup>14</sup>Since therefore the children share in flesh and blood, he himself likewise partook of the same things, that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil,<sup>15</sup>and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery.<sup>16</sup>For surely it is not angels that he helps, but he helps the offspring of Abraham.<sup>17</sup>Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest in the service of God, to make propitiation for the sins of the people.<sup>18</sup>For because he himself has suffered when tempted, he is able to help those who are being tempted.

3.title: Greater Than Moses: Do Not Harden Your Hearts
3.overview:
Moses was the supreme figure in first-century Judaism. Hebrews honours him fully, “faithful in all God’s house”, then makes one decisive distinction: Moses was a servant in the house; Jesus is the Son over it.

The chapter then turns Psalm 95 into a warning. The wilderness generation had everything and still fell through unbelief. The danger for the readers is not dramatic denial but slow hardening. The remedy is practical: other believers, speaking to them every day.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Jesus and Moses: Servant and Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer asks tired believers to fix their minds on Jesus, and compares him with Moses. Both were faithful; but Moses served inside God’s household, and Christ is the Son over it, and its builder. The household is the church, and holding on to the end is the mark of belonging to it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Servant and Son

Moses is not demoted but placed: faithful in God's house as a servant, while Christ is faithful over it as a son. The honour goes to the builder.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Jesus is both apostle, sent from God, and high priest, going to God for us.

Now: The letter's standing prescription is to consider Jesus. Holding fast does not create the reality; it shows it.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, holy brothers, you who share in a heavenly calling, consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession, who was faithful to him who appointed him, just as Moses also was faithful in all God’s house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Hebrews 3 shows that Jesus is greater than Moses and then gives the second warning. Moses was faithful in God’s house as a servant; Christ is faithful over it as the Son, and we are that house if we hold firm to the end (vv. 1–6). The warning (vv. 7–19) is built on Psalm 95: today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as Israel did. So the readers must watch that none of them has an evil, unbelieving heart, and must encourage one another daily against sin’s deceit.

Therefore, holy brothers. “Therefore” (hothen, for this reason): because of all that Jesus is as the merciful and faithful high priest (2:17–18). This is the first time the writer names his readers, and he uses the warmest terms available. Holy (hagioi, set apart): made holy by Christ (2:11). Brothers: Jesus calls them brothers (2:11), and so does the author. That matters for how the warnings in this letter are heard. The man who is about to say, take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil, unbelieving heart, begins by calling them holy brothers. He is warning people he believes are Christians, which is the only way such warnings ever work.

You who share in a heavenly calling. “Share” (metochoi) means partners, partakers, the word used of the King’s companions in 1:9. The heavenly calling is a call from heaven, issued by God, and a call to heaven, to glory (Philippians 3:14). Israel was called to an earthly inheritance in Canaan; these believers are called to a better country, a heavenly one (11:16). That is why losing property and standing in Rome could not touch the thing they really owned.

Consider Jesus. The verb (katanoēsate) means to fix the mind on, to think something through: attentive study rather than a passing glance, the word Jesus used when he told his disciples to consider the ravens (Luke 12:24). And it is the letter’s standing prescription. To a congregation drifting, tired and frightened, the instruction is not first to try harder or to examine themselves. It is to look at somebody (12:2). The earliest manuscripts name him simply Jesus here; the KJV’s Christ Jesus follows later ones.

The apostle and high priest of our confession. The two titles are given together nowhere else in Scripture, and this is the only place Jesus is called an apostle (apostolos, sent one). He was sent by the Father to bring God’s word to us (John 17:18). An apostle is one sent from God to men; a high priest goes from men to God, representing us before him. Every mediator in the Old Testament held one office or the other. Moses was the sent one; Aaron was the priest. Jesus is both, which is why this chapter compares him with Moses and the chapters that follow compare him with Aaron. In one person, God’s word reaches us and we reach God.

Of our confession. “Confession” (homologia) is the faith we publicly profess, the thing they had said aloud, probably at baptism, and were now under pressure to unsay. The word will return at 4:14 and 10:23, each time with the instruction to hold it fast.

Faithful in all God’s house. Jesus perfectly carried out the task the Father gave him (John 17:4). And the comparison begins with a compliment. The quotation is from Numbers 12:7, where God defends Moses against Aaron and Miriam: Moses is faithful in all my house. “House” (oikos) is God’s household, his people Israel. The writer does not begin by diminishing Moses. He begins by agreeing with the highest thing Scripture says about him.

How do I actually consider Jesus? Take time to think about him on purpose, as you would study something you wanted to understand. Read a passage of the Gospels slowly and ask: what does he do here, what does he say, what does this show me of his heart? Turn the titles of this letter over in your mind: Son, Creator, radiance of God’s glory, apostle, high priest, pioneer, brother. Sing about him and pray to him, not only to the Father in his name. When you are anxious or tempted, deliberately turn your thoughts from the problem to the person. Considering Jesus is not a feeling you wait for; it is a direction you give your mind.

parallels.desc: He is faithful in all my house

verseByVerse.quote: For Jesus has been counted worthy of more glory than Moses—as much more glory as the builder of a house has more honor than the house itself. (For every house is built by someone, but the builder of all things is God.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
More glory than Moses. It is difficult now to feel how large that claim was. To these readers Moses was the man who spoke with God face to face, through whom the law came, the founder of the nation’s entire religious life. Moses’ face shone with reflected glory when he came down from the mountain, so that he had to veil it (Exodus 34:29–35; 2 Corinthians 3:7–18). Jesus is the radiance of God’s glory itself (1:3). The moon is beautiful; but it shines because the sun does.

The builder and the house. The writer does not argue it by finding fault. His argument is structural, and it is not about merit: however fine a house is, the honour goes to the one who built it. Moses is not being demoted; he is being placed, inside the house. Jesus stands outside it, as its maker.

The house is a household. God’s house is his people. So Moses belongs to the people of God, whereas Christ constituted them. Moses was a stone in the wall. Christ laid the foundation, chose the stones and set every one in place.

The builder of all things. This parenthesis is easy to skip. Every house has a builder. God is the builder of everything. Jesus is the builder of this house. The writer leaves the conclusion for the reader to draw, the same one chapter 1 reached by quoting Psalm 102 to the Son: Jesus is identified with God, who created everything (1:2, 10).

Is it wrong to admire great Christian leaders? No; Scripture itself honours Moses, and tells us to remember our leaders and imitate their faith (13:7). Admire them, learn from them, thank God for them. The danger comes when admiration slides into dependence, so that a preacher, author or movement becomes the house rather than a part of it. When a favoured leader falls or disappoints, a believer who trusted the builder grieves but stands; a believer who trusted the stone collapses with it. Give leaders the honour due to a faithful servant, and keep the glory for Christ.

For worship. The Son designed the household of God before the world began, chose its members in love (Ephesians 1:4), and paid for the building with his own blood (Acts 20:28). He is not a landlord who visits now and then; he lives in what he built, among people who were rubble when he found them. The builder of all things is God, and the house he delights in is made of forgiven sinners.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant, to testify to the things that were to be spoken later, but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son. And we are his house, if indeed we hold fast our confidence and our boasting in our hope.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As a servant. Now the comparison is stated exactly. Both were faithful, and the writer says so twice. The difference is standing: in the house against over it, servant against son (1:5). The word for servant is not the usual doulos but therapōn, a more dignified term for an honoured attendant, the very word the Greek Old Testament uses of Moses in Numbers 12:7. The writer picks the most respectful word available, and still it is not son.

To testify. That is Moses’ function, and it is not a small one. The tabernacle, the priesthood, the sacrifices were testimony given in advance about something not yet said. Jesus said it plainly: if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me (John 5:46; Luke 24:27).

Over God’s house as a son. “Over” (epi) means set over, in charge of, and “as a son” names a standing no servant has: heir and master of the household (1:2). The title Christ appears here for the first time in Hebrews (in the earliest manuscripts), at the very moment the writer sets him over the whole household of God.

And we are his house. The argument turns without warning from Christ to the congregation. The house is them, sitting in somebody’s room hearing this read (1 Timothy 3:15; Ephesians 2:19–22). The tabernacle Moses served in has gone; the house Christ rules over is made of believers.

If indeed we hold fast. Then the first of the letter’s conditions about belonging. “Hold fast” (kataschōmen) is keep a firm grip. “Confidence” (parrēsia) is boldness, openness of speech; “boasting” is exultation. Membership in God’s house is shown by holding firm, and the call recurs (3:14; 6:11; 10:23). The KJV adds firm unto the end here, following later manuscripts; the phrase is certainly original at verse 14.

Where Christians differ: does this conditional mean true believers can be lost? Arminians (Christians, many of them Methodist or Wesleyan, who hold that a true believer can finally fall away) read the if as meaning that a genuine member of God’s house may fall away and cease to be part of it. They hold this out of real seriousness about the warnings, and they are brothers in Christ. This commentary’s view: the verse says we are his house if we hold fast; it does not say we will cease to be his house if we do not. Holding fast is the evidence of genuine membership, not the cause of it. Verse 14 makes the logic clearer: we have come to share in Christ (perfect tense, already true), if we hold firm to the end. Perseverance proves that we have truly come to share in him. Those who fall away show they never did (1 John 2:19). The warning is real, and God uses it as a means to keep his people persevering (Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5).

The grip and the hand. These clauses do not say that a Christian is kept by his own grip; Christ is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him (7:25). God keeps his people precisely by means of warnings like this one, which is why a genuine believer reads them and holds on tighter rather than despairing. A child on a cliff path holds his father’s hand, and the father holds the child’s wrist. The child’s grip is real; the father’s is the reason he is still on the path.

What does confidence and boasting in our hope look like? Confidence is the freedom to speak openly about Christ and to come to God without cringing. Boasting is not arrogance but glad, unembarrassed pride in what God has promised, the way a bride speaks of her wedding day. These readers were tempted to go quiet, to keep their faith private so that the neighbours would leave them alone. Holding fast means refusing to be ashamed: still saying, at work and at the family table, that your hope is in Christ, and still praying as a child who expects to be heard. The opposite of boasting in hope is not humility. It is embarrassment.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–19 — Today, If You Hear His Voice
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer reads Psalm 95 as the Spirit speaking now, and holds up the generation that came out of Egypt and died in the desert. It moves from the danger of one unbelieving heart in a congregation to the remedy of daily encouragement, and ends on the root of Israel’s failure: unbelief.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Remedy Is Other People

Because sin deceives, a hardening heart cannot diagnose itself. So the safeguard is outside the individual: exhort one another every day.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Those who fell in the wilderness were the ones who had come out of Egypt.

Now: They stayed out through unbelief, so belief is the way in, and no one is too far gone to exercise it.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion, on the day of testing in the wilderness, where your fathers put me to the test and saw my works for forty years. Therefore I was provoked with that generation, and said, ’They always go astray in their heart; they have not known my ways.’ As I swore in my wrath, ’They shall not enter my rest.’”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says. The tense is present, and the speaker is the Spirit. The writer quotes Psalm 95:7–11, a text roughly a thousand years old, which he will later say God spoke through David (4:7), and introduces it not as what the Spirit said but as what he says (10:15). When you open your Bible, the Holy Spirit is not reminiscing. He is speaking to you.

The wilderness generation. The psalm recalls the people who came out of Egypt, saw the plagues and the pillar of fire, ate manna every morning for forty years, and never entered the land. Psalm 95 began as an invitation to sing joyfully to the rock of our salvation, then turned suddenly to this warning. Worship and warning belonged together in Israel’s songbook.

In the flow. Verses 1 to 6 ended with a condition: we are that house if we hold fast. Now the writer shows what failing to hold fast looks like, from the very generation Moses led out of Egypt. The argument runs on to 4:13.

Today. “Today” (sēmeron) is the key word of the warning, repeated in verses 13 and 15 and in 4:7. Psalm 95 was already using today to reapply an old event to its own generation; Hebrews now reapplies the psalm. The offer has a date on it, the present one, and it will not last for ever.

Do not harden your hearts. “Harden” (sklērynēte) means make stiff, stubborn, and the verb is addressed to them. The heart becomes hard through repeated refusal to listen, as Pharaoh hardened his heart when the frogs were taken away (Exodus 8:15); each refusal makes the next easier. Elsewhere Scripture can say that God hardened Pharaoh; here the hardening is something people do to themselves, and the two truths sit side by side without either cancelling the other.

Meribah and Massah. The Hebrew place names, quarrelling and testing, become in the Greek rebellion (parapikrasmos) and testing (peirasmos). They come from Exodus 17, where Israel demanded water and asked whether the LORD was among them or not (Exodus 17:1–7). They had walked through a parted sea a few weeks before, and still they asked.

They saw my works. And there is the tragedy in one line. They tested him, demanding that God prove himself again, after the plagues, the Red Sea, the manna, the water from the rock, the cloud and the fire. Forty years of visible miracle produced no faith in that generation as a whole; only Caleb and Joshua stand out. Evidence does not manufacture trust.

The voice at Massah. The voice Israel refused in the wilderness is the voice that has now spoken in the Son (1:2), and the letter will say so: see that you do not refuse him who is speaking (12:25). Paul goes further and says that the rock which gave them water was Christ, and that they put Christ to the test (1 Corinthians 10:4, 9). Then the Son went into his own wilderness, hungry for forty days, and when Satan urged him to make God prove himself, he answered from the very chapter that remembers Massah: you shall not put the Lord your God to the test (Matthew 4:7; Deuteronomy 6:16). Where Israel tested God and hardened, Jesus trusted and obeyed, perfectly and in our place. The today of the psalm is his voice, and his obedience, not our uneven record, is the one in which his people stand.

Provoked. “Provoked” (prosōchthisa) is God’s holy anger at persistent unbelief: not the irritation of a bad-tempered deity but the grief and indignation of a Father whose children watched him feed them every morning for forty years and still called him a liar.

They have not known my ways. God’s verdict locates the problem in the heart, not in the difficulty of the desert. “Not known my ways” is not intellectual ignorance, for they saw everything. They knew his works; they did not know him.

The oath. God bound himself (Numbers 14:21–23, 28–35): there was a point past which the offer, for that generation, was withdrawn. “Rest” (katapausis) was originally the rest of the promised land, where God would give his people peace from their enemies (Deuteronomy 12:9). But, as Hebrews 4 goes on to show, the land was only a picture of the rest God himself entered on the seventh day, which he still offers to his people.

Would I believe if God showed me a miracle? Many people think so, and this psalm says otherwise. The wilderness generation saw the sea part, ate bread from heaven and drank water from a rock, and still asked whether the LORD was among them. Jesus said the same of the rich man’s brothers: if they will not listen to Moses and the Prophets, they will not be convinced even if someone rises from the dead (Luke 16:31). The problem is rarely a lack of evidence. It is a heart that does not want God to be God over it. That is not to say every honest question is rebellion: Jesus gave Thomas the evidence he asked for (John 20:27), and the gospel invites examination. But it humbles the sceptic, who may need to ask what he would lose if Christ were true, and the churchgoer, who has seen God at work and can still grow hard. Both need the same thing: a new heart that hears his voice today.

What if I am afraid I have already hardened my heart? Then you are hearing his voice, and it is still today. A truly hardened heart does not worry about being hardened; it has stopped listening and does not care. The very fact that this warning troubles you is evidence that the Spirit is at work in you. Do not sit and analyse your condition. Do what the psalm asks: hear his voice and respond, now. Confess the specific thing you have been resisting, turn to Christ, and ask him to soften your heart. He has never yet turned away anyone who came to him (John 6:37).

On a Tuesday. Hardening rarely feels like rebellion. It feels like postponement: the apology that can wait, the sin you will deal with after this busy month, the step of trust you will take when life is calmer. The psalm’s word for all of that is today. If something has been on your conscience while you read, the kindest thing you can do for your own heart is to answer it before you sleep. Tomorrow is the word hardening always uses.
verseByVerse.note: Meribah (“quarreling”) and Massah (“testing”) were where Israel tested God for water.

verseByVerse.quote: Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil, unbelieving heart, leading you to fall away from the living God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Take care, brothers. The direct address returns, with brothers again, in the middle of the sternest sentence yet. “Take care” (blepete) means watch out, be on guard, and it is addressed to the whole community of professing believers.

Lest there be in any of you. Not lest you all fall away, but lest it be in any one of you: even one. A congregation can be broadly sound and contain one person quietly going the other way. A shepherd with ninety-nine sheep in the fold still counts.

An evil, unbelieving heart. Literally a heart evil of unbelief: the two words are welded. We tend to treat unbelief as an intellectual difficulty and evil as a moral one. Hebrews will not allow the distinction here. Unbelief is not merely intellectual doubt; it is a heart that refuses to trust God.

Fall away from the living God. The verb (apostēnai) is the one behind our word apostasy: to stand off from, to withdraw. And what is being withdrawn from is not Christianity or the church but the living God. The readers imagined they were considering a change of religious arrangement, going back to the temple, which was after all God’s own institution. He tells them what the transaction really is: a step away from a God who is alive, and who has spoken to them in a Son (1:2).

Is it fair to call unbelief evil, when I cannot help what I find believable? It is fair, because unbelief in Scripture is not first a matter of the head. No one is blamed here for finding a hard question hard. The heart this verse describes has heard God speak, seen what he has done, and decided not to trust him, which is to treat the living God as a liar (1 John 5:10). Between people we know the difference: doubting a stranger is not wrong, but refusing to trust a friend who has never once let you down is an insult. God has given more than enough reason to trust him, above all in the Son he did not spare. Unbelief at its core is not a lack of light but a preference for the dark (John 3:19). That is said of a heart that has decided against him; someone still honestly searching is not being called wicked here, and is invited to keep looking at Christ.

How do I tell doubt from an unbelieving heart? Doubt struggles toward God; an unbelieving heart walks away from him. The father who cried, I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24), had a great deal of doubt and brought all of it to Jesus. Ask yourself: do I want to trust him, even when I find it hard? Do I bring my questions to him, or use them as reasons to stay away? Am I still praying, still reading, still with God’s people, even if haltingly? If so, you are a struggling believer, and Christ is gentle with such (Isaiah 42:3). If you find you have stopped wanting him and are glad to be free, that is the condition this verse warns against, and the remedy is to turn back today, while it is still called today.

What should I do if someone in my church seems to be falling away? Take care, as the verse says: notice, and do not look away. Go to him personally and gently, not with an accusation but with love and a question: how are you, really, with the Lord? Listen before you speak. Pray for him, specifically and often. Keep inviting him, keep in touch even if he stops coming, and tell the elders so that they can shepherd him too. The aim is always restoration (Galatians 6:1; James 5:19–20). You cannot change his heart, but God often uses one faithful friend to call a wanderer home.

verseByVerse.quote: But exhort one another every day, as long as it is called “today,” that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Exhort one another. Here is the remedy, and it is not what a modern reader expects. He does not say: examine yourselves, or pray harder. The prescription is other people, talking to you, daily. A hardening heart is precisely the organ that cannot diagnose itself: the condition feels normal from inside. That is why the remedy has to come from someone else’s mouth.

Called alongside. The verb is parakaleite, from the same root as the word by which John records Jesus naming the Holy Spirit the Helper (John 14:16): to call alongside. It covers encouraging, urging, comforting and admonishing at once. It is not nagging and it is not flattery. And it is one another: every believer to every other, not just pastors to people.

The word of Christ between brothers. What the daily encouragement carries is not general cheerfulness but Christ: letting the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another (Colossians 3:16). Sin deceives by keeping a heart from looking at him; a brother answers by turning it back to him, to his cross, his promises and his return. Exhortation in Hebrews is always, in the end, another way of saying consider Jesus (3:1).

Every day. The frequency is not weekly. It does not describe a congregation that meets on Sunday and is otherwise unknown to one another. Isolated Christians are vulnerable, as a coal taken out of the fire goes grey on the hearth.

As long as it is called today. There is a stretch of time called today, and it will not always be called that, both because life is short and because Christ will return.

The deceitfulness of sin. “Hardened” is passive: hardened by sin. “Deceitfulness” (apatē) is trickery, and that is sin’s method. It does not present itself as sin; it presents itself as reasonable, or deserved, or temporary, or nobody’s business. Few people harden deliberately. They are talked into it, and the voice doing the talking is their own. That is why the counter-voice has to be somebody else’s, and daily: because the deceiving is.

What does daily exhortation look like in a busy life? It is smaller and more ordinary than it sounds. A text in the morning with a verse that helped you. A question over coffee: how are you doing with the Lord? A word of thanks to someone for their faithfulness. A gentle question when a friend says something that worries you. Praying aloud with someone before you part. It does not need to be long or eloquent; it needs to be regular and real. And it works both ways: let others into your life enough that they can say a hard thing to you. If no one ever does, ask someone to.

What if I have no Christian friends near me? Then begin by making one, because this verse assumes you need it. Join a small group or a midweek meeting; ask an older believer if you can meet regularly; invite someone from church for a meal. If you are housebound or far from other believers, use a phone call or a message. Ask your pastor to help connect you. Isolation is not a neutral condition for a Christian; it is a dangerous one, and God has given you his people precisely so that you would not have to keep yourself alone.

For worship. God did not save us to be solitary. When a friend’s word stops you on the edge of a sin, that is the Good Shepherd using a sheep to turn a sheep. How kind of God, to keep us not only by his own hand but by each other’s.

verseByVerse.quote: For we have come to share in Christ, if indeed we hold our original confidence firm to the end. As it is said, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the rebellion.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we have come to share in Christ. The tense is the Greek perfect: something that happened and stands. We have become partners (metochoi, as at 3:1 and 6:4), and remain so. What belongs to Christ is shared with you: his righteousness is credited to your account (2 Corinthians 5:21), his Father has become your Father (John 20:17), and you will share his inheritance as a fellow heir (Romans 8:17).

If indeed we hold firm. He does not say we shall share in Christ if we hold on, as though the future were in the balance. He says we have become partakers, if indeed we hold on. Holding on is the proof of having become. The evidence runs backwards.

Our original confidence. Literally the beginning of our assurance, our first conviction: the boldness they had when newly converted, before the property was confiscated and the neighbours turned (10:32–34). And firm to the end (mechri telous) is what makes it costly: not firm while it was exciting, but to the end of life or to Christ’s return.

But do these warnings not imply that a true believer could be lost? Arminian Christians (those who believe a true Christian can finally fall away) read them so: the if is a real condition, and a true believer who does not hold fast will lose what he had; they point to 3:12, 6:4–6 and 10:26–29. The warnings are certainly real, and nobody should treat them as idle. But the grammar here, we have come to share if we hold firm, makes holding on the evidence of a share already given, not the means of keeping it. The same letter says that Christ always lives to make intercession for those who draw near through him (7:25), and it ends its sternest warning by saying, we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls (10:39). Those who shrink back show that they never had the share. Those who truly have it are kept, and one of the ways they are kept is by hearing warnings like this and heeding them.

As it is said. He quoted it eight verses earlier (v. 7), and will again (4:7). This is a preacher who has found the sentence he needs and will not let his congregation put it down.

Can I be sure now that I will hold firm to the end? Yes, and the ground of that certainty is not your strength but Christ’s. He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Philippians 1:6); you are guarded by God’s power through faith (1 Peter 1:5). Assurance looks first to Christ and his promises, then to the Spirit’s witness, and then to the fruit of a changed life (2 Peter 1:10). If you are trusting Christ today and want to go on trusting him, you have every reason to expect that you will, because he is the one holding on. Your part is to keep looking to him one day at a time; his part is to bring you to the end.

On a Tuesday. Remember the beginning: what you believed when you first trusted Christ, or what first made him precious to you. The confidence may be quieter now, but it is probably still there. Holding firm rarely looks heroic. It looks like opening your Bible on a morning when you feel nothing, confessing the same sin again, going to church when you would rather not. Perseverance is made of ordinary days.

verseByVerse.quote: For who were those who heard and yet rebelled? Was it not all those who left Egypt led by Moses? And with whom was he provoked for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness? And to whom did he swear that they would not enter his rest, but to those who were disobedient?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For who were those who heard and yet rebelled? Three questions, each answered by another question, drawn from Numbers 14, and the writer is cross-examining the psalm. “Heard”: they heard God’s voice. “Rebelled” (parepikranan): provoked, embittered.

Was it not all those who left Egypt led by Moses? The first question is the devastating one, and it is designed to remove an escape route. A reader might comfort himself that the wilderness generation were outsiders, half-hearted, never really in. The writer forecloses it. These were the people who came out of Egypt: the redeemed ones, the ones who kept Passover, walked through the sea on dry ground and sang on the far shore. They had experienced God’s great salvation. “All those” is a broad sweep. Caleb and Joshua did go in, but they were the rare exceptions, and the point stands: the people who rebelled were the people who had been rescued, and they had religious credentials few generations have ever matched. Privilege did not protect them. The readers were in a similar position: they had heard the gospel and seen God’s work.

And with whom was he provoked for forty years? Forty years of patience and provocation. God did not lose his temper at the first complaint. He bore with them for four decades, and they provoked him for four decades.

Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness? The phrase is from Numbers 14:29, 32, and it is grim. “Bodies” (kōla) is limbs, corpses. Their corpses dropped in the desert, one funeral after another for forty years, until the whole generation was in the sand. They did not die at once and they did not die dramatically. They simply never arrived.

And to whom did he swear that they would not enter his rest, but to those who were disobedient? The word matters, because it introduces the letter’s definition. “Disobedient” (apeithēsasin) is literally unpersuadable, those who refused to be persuaded. And that ties the third answer to the first two: they heard, they saw, and they were not persuaded. Disobedience and unbelief are two sides of the same coin (v. 19). Unbelief shows itself in disobedience; disobedience flows from unbelief.

Closing every gap. Together the three questions close every gap between that generation and this congregation. Hearing is not enough; being rescued from Egypt is not enough. Paul makes the same point: these things happened as examples for us (1 Corinthians 10:1–11).

Led out by Moses. Moses led them out, and could not lead them in; he died on Mount Nebo looking at the land (Deuteronomy 34:4). Even Joshua did not give them the rest God meant (4:8). The letter’s answer is a leader of a different kind: the founder of salvation who has already gone through death into glory and is bringing many sons with him (2:10), and who will lose none the Father has given him (John 6:39). Israel’s journey ended in graves. The church’s road ends at home, because its leader is the Son.

Were all who died in the wilderness lost for ever? Not necessarily. Moses himself was kept out of the land, yet he appears with Christ in glory on the mountain (Matthew 17:3), so being shut out of Canaan was not the same as being shut out of heaven. But Paul says that with most of them God was not pleased (1 Corinthians 10:5), and the writer uses their fate as a picture of final loss: they heard God’s voice, saw his works and would not believe. We are not told the eternal state of each one. Whatever became of each of them, the warning to us is about eternity.

I grew up in church and have seen God do good things. Is that not enough? It is a great gift, and it is not enough on its own. The wilderness generation had one of the greatest religious upbringings in history and still did not believe. A Christian home, baptism, years of sermons and even real answers to prayer are not the same as trusting Christ yourself, today. They are meant to lead you to that trust. So do not lean on your background; lean on him. Ask yourself not, have I been near the things of God? but, do I believe God’s promise in Christ, and am I following him now?

verseByVerse.quote: So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So we see. The chapter ends on a single word, and it is not the one we would have chosen.

That they were unable to enter. It does not mean they tried to enter and were physically prevented; at Kadesh they refused to go in, and when they changed their minds and attacked in their own strength, they were routed (Numbers 14:39–45). The inability is moral. Unbelief makes entering impossible, because entering was always a matter of trusting the God who promised.

Because of unbelief. Not because of idolatry, though they made a calf; not because of grumbling, though the wilderness narratives are full of it. The writer traces them to a root: a failure to take God at his word. The calf and the complaining were symptoms: how long will they not believe in me, in spite of all the signs that I have done among them? (Numbers 14:11). Unbelief is the sin behind all sins.

Impeccable credentials. The going back these readers were pressed toward would look like piety: the temple, the sacrifices, the ancestral faith. The last generation to walk away from a promise did it with impeccable religious credentials, and it killed them.

The mercy in where the chapter stops. Unbelief is the reason they did not enter, which means belief is the way in, and no one is too far gone to exercise it. Now God’s word has come in a Son. The one who says, come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matthew 11:28), is the Lord of the wilderness made flesh, and the door unbelief closed on a generation he holds open to anyone who trusts him.

Where does faith come from, if I cannot make myself believe? From God, through his word. Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ (Romans 10:17), and it is the gift of God (Ephesians 2:8). You cannot squeeze it out of yourself by effort, but you can put yourself where God gives it: under the preaching of the gospel, in the pages of Scripture, among believing people, and on your knees asking for it. Look at the promises and at the one who made them. Faith grows not by staring at your faith but by looking at Christ. And the smallest true faith, faith like a mustard seed, rests on the same strong Saviour as the greatest.

4.title: A Rest That Remains: The Throne of Grace
4.overview:
The rest God promised was not fully given under Joshua; otherwise, why would God say through David, centuries later, “Today, if you hear his voice”? So the rest remains. And it is not a land or a day, but a share in God’s own Sabbath rest: the rest of finished work. To enter it is to stop working to justify ourselves and trust what Christ has finished.

The chapter ends with a sword and an invitation. God’s word lays us bare; and then: since we have a great high priest who sympathises with our weakness, let us draw near with confidence to the throne of grace.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — There Remains a Sabbath Rest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer finishes his sermon on Psalm 95 by asking what God’s rest is. Setting Genesis 2:2 beside it, he shows that the rest is God’s own, open since creation, and still offered after Joshua. Believers enter it now by faith and will enter it fully at the end.
verseByVerse.theology:
A Rest That Remains

Psalm 95 still says today centuries after Joshua, so the land was never the rest itself. What remains is a Sabbath rest: ceasing from our own works as God did from his.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The wilderness generation heard good news, and it did not benefit them because it was not united with faith.

Now: Strive to enter that rest. Trusting God is harder work than being busy for him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, while the promise of entering his rest still stands, let us fear lest any of you should seem to have failed to reach it. For good news came to us just as to them, but the message they heard did not benefit them, because they were not united by faith with those who listened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Hebrews 4 continues the warning of chapter 3 and explains what God’s rest really is. The promise of entering it still stands; the wilderness generation heard good news too, but without faith it did them no good (vv. 1–2). The rest is God’s own rest, begun on the seventh day (vv. 3–5), and since Psalm 95, written long after Joshua, still offers it today, Joshua cannot have given the final rest (vv. 6–8). So there remains a Sabbath rest for God’s people, and we must strive to enter it (vv. 9–11). God’s word exposes the heart (vv. 12–13). But we have a great high priest who sympathises with our weakness, so we draw near with confidence to the throne of grace (vv. 14–16).

The promise still stands. That is the foundation of the whole chapter, and it is a mercy. The last generation forfeited it; the promise did not lapse with them. God’s offer outlived the people who refused it, and it has outlived every generation since.

Let us fear. “Fear” (phobēthōmen) is not the fear of a God who might turn on us without warning; the same chapter ends by sending its readers boldly to a throne of grace. It is the fear appropriate to standing near something enormous and being capable of walking past it (Philippians 2:12; 1 Peter 1:17). And again it is let us, not you must. The preacher stands inside his own warning.

Should seem to have failed. The phrasing is unexpectedly gentle: not lest any of you fail, but lest any should seem (dokē: appear, be found) to have failed. The writer will not pronounce on who is in and who is out, and still leaves the warning its full weight. “Failed to reach” means to fall short, to come too late, like a traveller who arrives after the city gates have closed for the night.

Good news came to us. That sentence should stop a reader, because it says the wilderness generation had good news preached to them (euēngelismenoi, we have had the gospel preached). Not the same details, but the same thing in substance: a promise from God about a rest they had not seen, to be received by trusting him. They heard the promise of the land. We have heard the greater good news of Christ. The God of the exodus and the God of the cross deal with people the same way: he promises, and calls them to believe.

Not united by faith. The word (synkekerasmenous) means mixed together, blended. Some manuscripts read it as the message not being combined with faith in the hearers; others as the hearers not being united in faith with those who truly listened, Joshua and Caleb. The KJV, not being mixed with faith in them that heard it, follows the first. Either way, the message was heard and not absorbed. Food that is not eaten does not nourish, however good the meal.

Why the same sermon does different things. What makes preaching profitable is not the eloquence of the preacher or the accuracy of the content, both of which the wilderness generation had in Moses. It is whether faith mixes with what is heard. The same sermon profits one person and does nothing to the man beside him. And what faith takes hold of is a person. The Westminster Shorter Catechism (question 86) says that faith in Jesus Christ receives and rests upon him alone for salvation, as he is offered to us in the gospel. Rest is the very word of this chapter: faith mixed with the word is a sinner leaning his whole weight on Christ, and that leaning is already the beginning of rest.

How do I mix the word with faith when I hear it? By taking it as God speaking to you, and answering him. Before the sermon or the reading, ask the Spirit to open your heart. While you listen, listen for a promise to trust, a command to obey, a warning to heed, or a glimpse of Christ to adore. Afterwards, do not just evaluate how good it was; say to God, I believe this, and tell him what you will do about it. Talk about it with someone over lunch. Faith is not a feeling that comes over you during a good sermon; it is the act of leaning your weight on what God has said.

verseByVerse.quote: For we who have believed enter that rest, as he has said, “As I swore in my wrath, ’They shall not enter my rest,’” although his works were finished from the foundation of the world. For he has somewhere spoken of the seventh day in this way: “And God rested on the seventh day from all his works.” And again in this passage he said, “They shall not enter my rest.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
We who have believed enter. Present tense: where they did not mix the word with faith, these have, and the entering is happening now. They enter now, in part: rest from the burden of earning salvation, peace with God, rest of conscience (Matthew 11:28–29; Romans 5:1). And they will enter it fully in glory. The rest is both present and future.

The oath again. The negative proves the positive: God did not swear that nobody would enter; he swore that those would not.

Finished from the foundation of the world. The point is about timing. God speaks in the psalm of my rest, and his own rest has existed since the seventh day. So the rest in question is not something God started providing at Sinai or in Canaan. It is God’s own rest, and he invites his people to share it.

The seventh day. Genesis 2:2 supplies the definition. God rested (katepausen, ceased) not because he was tired, for he does not faint or grow weary (Isaiah 40:28), but because his work was complete: the settled satisfaction of a maker who has finished and found it very good.

The day with no evening. Every other day of creation ends with the refrain, and there was evening and there was morning. The seventh day has no such close. Many readers have seen in that silence a picture of what the writer argues from Psalm 95: God’s rest has no end, and it has been waiting for guests since the world began.

Two texts side by side. Putting Genesis 2:2 and Psalm 95:11 together, the rest Israel failed to enter was God’s own Sabbath rest, of which Canaan was only a picture. If the rest has existed since creation, and a whole generation missed it, then the rest is still there and someone else may enter. That is what verse 6 will say: a doctrine of present opportunity drawn from two old texts.

A second finished work. The rest believers enter now stands on another finished work. On the cross the Son cried, It is finished (John 19:30), and then sat down at the right hand of God because nothing remained to add to his sacrifice (1:3; 10:12). That is why the rest can be entered today. The rest of creation was God’s delight in a world made good; the rest of redemption is his delight in sinners made clean.

What is this rest like now, if I have believed? It is the rest of a forgiven person who no longer has to prove himself to God. Your standing is settled, so you do not need to earn his favour each morning or fear losing it each evening. It is rest of conscience: guilt answered by the blood of Christ. It is rest from the restless search for meaning, because you have found the one you were made for. It does not mean an easy life; these readers were suffering. But underneath the trouble there is a floor that does not move. Augustine put it in a prayer: you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.

On a Tuesday. Watch today for the places where you are still working for God’s approval: the anxious overwork in ministry, the guilt after a poor quiet time, the feeling that he must be disappointed in you. Stop at that moment and say: I have believed, and I am entering his rest. Then do the thing in front of you as a child at home, not as a servant on probation.

verseByVerse.quote: Since therefore it remains for some to enter it, and those who formerly received the good news failed to enter because of disobedience, again he appoints a certain day, “Today,” saying through David so long afterward, in the words already quoted, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.” For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It remains for some to enter. The rest was not abolished when the wilderness generation forfeited it; a vacancy was created. The failure of one generation did not cancel God’s plan.

Because of disobedience. The word is the one from 3:18: unpersuadable. Not believing God is not obeying him, because his word came as a promise to be trusted.

Saying through David so long afterward. The writer’s decisive card is a point about dates. Psalm 95 is attributed to David in the Greek translation (the Hebrew gives it no title). David lived centuries after Joshua, and in it God is still saying today, still holding a rest open. If the promise of rest had been fully realised in Canaan, why would David still be offering it?

If Joshua had given them rest. Joshua did give them rest, in the ordinary sense: the LORD gave them rest on every side (Joshua 21:44–45). And the writer says: evidently that was not it. A man farming his own field in Judah under David was, on any ordinary reading, in the rest, and God tells him not to harden his heart today, lest he fail to enter.

Joshua and Jesus. In Greek, Joshua and Jesus are the same name (Iēsous), meaning the LORD saves. The first readers would have heard it at once, and that is why the KJV, rendering the Greek name directly, reads if Jesus had given them rest; the man meant is Joshua. The first Joshua brought Israel into an earthly land, and they still needed a rest. The greater Joshua, Jesus, brings his people into God’s eternal rest. The land was never the thing itself. It was a picture, and possessing it did not settle the question. That is precisely what the readers of this letter needed to hear, since what they were being drawn back to was the whole apparatus of land, temple and ancestral religion: the very things that had never given anybody final rest.

Is the promised rest the same as heaven? It includes heaven, but it is larger than a place you go when you die. It begins now, when you trust Christ and cease from trying to save yourself (v. 3). It continues through this life as peace with God in the middle of trouble. It comes to its fullness when Christ returns and his people enter the new creation, the true promised land, where there is no more death or mourning or pain (Revelation 21:4). Canaan pictured it; heaven anticipates it; the new heavens and new earth complete it. The rest is finally not a location but a sharing in God’s own joy, wherever he is.

On a Tuesday. Ask what you are expecting to give you rest: the next holiday, retirement, a paid-off mortgage, a settled family, a better church. None of these is wrong; each is a Canaan, real and good and not the thing itself. Enjoy them as gifts, and stop asking them to be your rest. Tell Jesus, the greater Joshua, that you are looking to him for what no land can give.

verseByVerse.quote: So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God, for whoever has entered God’s rest has also rested from his works as God did from his.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A Sabbath rest. Throughout, the writer has said katapausis, rest. Here, once, he reaches for sabbatismos, a Sabbath celebration, a word found nowhere else in the Greek Bible. What remains is not merely relief but a festive rest. On the seventh day God looked at a finished world and enjoyed it. The rest held out to us is a share in that enjoyment: to stand before God with nothing left to prove, like a guest at a feast he has prepared, not a worker waiting to be paid (Revelation 19:9). And it is there now, still waiting, still to come in its fullness, for all who believe.

Rested from his works. To enter this rest is to stop working, in the way God stopped: because the work was finished, and there was nothing left to add to it. Applied to a person, that is the end of religious self-effort and the beginning of rest in Christ’s finished work. To the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness (Romans 4:5). It may also refer to the final rest: blessed are the dead who die in the Lord, that they may rest from their labours (Revelation 14:13). Both are true.

Why going back was a refusal to rest. Going back to the sacrifices meant going back to a system where the work was never finished and no priest ever sat down. It would have felt like devotion. It was, in the terms of this chapter, a refusal to rest.

Where Christians differ: is the weekly Sabbath still binding on Christians? Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists hold that the seventh-day Sabbath is still binding. Many in the Reformed and Puritan tradition, following the Westminster Confession, hold that the Sabbath commandment continues as a creation ordinance (Genesis 2:3), transferred to Sunday as the Christian Sabbath, a day of holy rest from ordinary work. Others see the Sabbath as wholly fulfilled in Christ, with no special day required. This commentary’s view: the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, our true rest (Matthew 11:28–12:8; Hebrews 4:9–10), and Christians are not bound to the Old Testament Sabbath regulations. A weekly rhythm of rest is a wise and kind gift, and the early church gathered on the first day of the week, the Lord’s Day, to celebrate Christ’s resurrection (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10). So Christians gladly set Sunday apart for worship, fellowship and rest, out of joy and wisdom, not as a binding law with rules about work or a means of earning favour, and no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5; Colossians 2:16–17). Many godly brothers, with the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, hold that the fourth commandment carries over to Sunday as the Christian Sabbath (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8), and their view deserves real respect.

What it does not mean. Resting from works as a means of salvation frees us for good works as fruit of salvation (Ephesians 2:8–10).

How do I rest from my works when I am naturally a striver? Begin by noticing what you are trying to prove, and to whom. Strivers often carry a quiet belief that God’s love is in proportion to their output. Answer it with the gospel every day: Christ has finished the work, and you are accepted in him, not on your performance. Then let that truth shape your week. Keep the Lord’s Day as a gift: worship, rest, enjoy people, leave the unfinished work unfinished, and discover that the world, and God, carry on without you. Good works will still flow, but from rest rather than toward it, which makes them gladder and lighter.

For worship. God finished his work and rested, and invited his people to rest with him. Then the Son did the work they could not do, cried that it was finished, lay in a tomb through the Sabbath, and rose on the first day of a new week. Since then his people have gathered on that day to celebrate a rest they did not earn.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us therefore strive to enter that rest, so that no one may fall by the same sort of disobedience.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Strive to enter. Work hard at resting. The verb (spoudasōmen) means to be diligent, to hurry, and its object is the rest. The paradox is not a contradiction, and verse 10 has already resolved it. The works rested from are works of self-establishment. The striving commanded is the effort of trusting: to keep believing, to resist hardening, to hold fast (3:6, 14), when everything in the circumstances argues against it.

Harder than being busy. It is far easier to be busy for God than to believe him. Resting on a promise, when the property has been confiscated and the neighbours have turned, is not passive at all. It has to be fought for.

The same sort of disobedience. “Fall” echoes the bodies that fell in the wilderness (3:17), and “same sort” is literally the same example, the same shape of failure (1 Corinthians 10:6, 11). And note the singular once more, no one, as at 3:12 and 4:1.

A failure of nerve. The wilderness generation stood at the border of a good land, heard of giants and walled cities, and judged it too dangerous. Their disobedience was not a wild plunge into sin but a failure of nerve at the edge of a promise, the danger many Christians are actually in.

In the flow. With verse 11 the sermon on Psalm 95 that began at 3:7 ends, closing as it opened with concern for every single hearer (3:12). Verses 12–13 give the reason for the effort, and 4:14 turns to the high priest who makes it possible.

The one who went in first. Israel stood at the border and would not go in. The letter’s answer is a forerunner who did. Jesus has passed through the heavens (4:14) and entered behind the curtain as a forerunner on our behalf (6:19–20). The striving commanded here is not the effort of finding a way into God’s rest alone. It is the effort of following someone who has already arrived and who always lives to intercede for those still on the road (7:25). Faith strives toward a rest that its Saviour already occupies.

If God keeps me, why must I strive? Because God keeps you by making you strive. Perseverance is God’s work in you and your work at the same time: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure (Philippians 2:12–13). Your effort does not compete with his grace; it is the form his grace takes in you. A ship crossing the sea is carried by the wind, and the sailors still trim the sails all night. If you find a desire in yourself to keep going with Christ, that desire is his gift, and the warning is his way of strengthening it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–16 — Laid Bare, and Invited In
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two verses about God’s searching word leave the reader exposed, and the next three answer with the high priest. These verses turn the letter to its central subject, the priesthood of Jesus.
verseByVerse.theology:
Why the Exposure Comes First

The word lays us bare, and only then does the writer say, “since then we have a great high priest”. The one who sees through us is the one who sympathises with us.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Drawing near was once the privilege of priests alone.

Now: Come to the throne of grace with confidence: mercy for what lies behind, grace for what lies ahead, help that arrives when it is needed.

verseByVerse.quote: For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and of spirit, of joints and of marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the word of God. The for explains why we must strive (v. 11): God’s word sees through every pretence. The writer has just spent eleven verses proving that a psalm of David still says today to people a thousand years later. “The word of God” is here especially the warnings of Psalm 95 just quoted, and all Scripture.

Is living and active. “Living” (zōn): alive, because it comes from the living God (3:12). It keeps speaking. “Active” (energēs, from which we get energetic) means effective, at work: it convicts, converts, comforts and sanctifies. It goes out from God’s mouth and does not return empty (Isaiah 55:10–11); it is like a hammer that breaks the rock in pieces (Jeremiah 23:29).

Sharper than any two-edged sword. The sword here (machaira) is not the great battle blade but the short one used for close combat, the surgeon’s and the assassin’s instrument, and the word Paul uses for the sword of the Spirit (Ephesians 6:17). “Two-edged” is literally two-mouthed, a fine touch in a passage about a word that speaks.

Soul and spirit, joints and marrow. The writer is not offering a psychology here. He is piling up pairs of things that cannot ordinarily be got between. Where does soul end and spirit begin? Where exactly does a joint stop and the marrow start? Nobody can find the seam. This word can.

Thoughts and intentions. The adjective is kritikos, able to judge, to sift, to pass verdict; our word critical. And the two objects are exact. Thoughts (enthymēseis): what passes through the mind, reflections, ideas. Intentions (ennoiai): the purposes underneath, the motives, what we are actually after. That second one is the sting. Thoughts can be reported honestly; motives are harder, because the mind is expert at supplying respectable reasons for what it wanted anyway. The word of God is here described as the instrument that gets between the stated reason and the real one. We do not judge Scripture; it judges us.

The sword from his mouth. That is exactly what this congregation needed. They were, presumably, telling themselves that returning to the old ways was a matter of conscience, or family, or prudence, and here is a word that can divide the reason from the motive. It is the word God has spoken in his Son (1:2), and the New Testament puts this sword in Christ’s own mouth: John saw the risen Lord with a sharp two-edged sword coming from his mouth (Revelation 1:16). In the Gospels he knew what was in man (John 2:25), and he still went looking for Peter after the denial (John 21:15–19). His word cuts to the heart of the matter, and it cuts for our good.

Where Christians differ: are soul and spirit two different parts of a person? Some teach a threefold view of human nature (body, soul and spirit as three distinct parts), using this verse and 1 Thessalonians 5:23. This commentary’s view: Scripture generally uses soul and spirit interchangeably for the immaterial part of a person (Luke 1:46–47; John 12:27 and 13:21; Matthew 10:28). The body-and-soul view (dichotomy) fits the overall biblical teaching best. This verse does not teach that soul and spirit are separate components; like joints and marrow, it pictures the word cutting to the very core of a person. Faithful Christians hold the threefold view too, and nothing in the gospel hangs on the difference.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Scripture works like magic apart from the Spirit, who uses the word.

Why does the Bible sometimes feel dead to me, if it is living? Because the problem is usually on the receiving end, not the sending end. A living word can meet a dull heart, a hurried reading or a mind full of noise. Sometimes it is a season of dryness God uses to deepen trust that does not depend on feelings. Keep reading anyway, slowly, and pray before you start: open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law (Psalm 119:18). Read aloud; read a whole book through; read with others; memorise a verse and turn it over through the day. The word is still at work even when you do not feel it, as seed in the ground is alive before anything shows.

For worship. God’s word is alive because he is alive, and it still does what it did when it said let there be light. It lays us open as the priest’s knife laid the sacrifice bare (v. 13), not to destroy but to heal. And when it has laid us open, it carries us straight to a high priest who was already wounded for everything the blade has found (Isaiah 53:5).

verseByVerse.quote: And no creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No creature is hidden. The subject shifts from the word to the one who speaks it, and the shift is the point: to be read by the word is to be seen by God. Nothing in all creation escapes his knowledge (Psalm 139:1–16).

Naked and exposed. Two words, and both are vivid. “Naked” (gymna) is bare, uncovered, and it carries the whole biblical weight of the word. The first thing sin produced was the impulse to cover up and hide among the trees of the garden. Every religious system since has been in some measure an elaborate rearrangement of fig leaves. The second word, tetrachēlismena, is rarer and harder. It comes from the word for neck, and its uses point several ways. It was used of a wrestler’s hold that seizes the throat and forces the opponent’s face upward so that he cannot look away, of a sacrificial animal whose neck was drawn back to expose the throat for the knife, and of a criminal forced to lift his face to the judge. Every picture says the same thing: there is no averting the eyes.

To whom we must give account. Literally with whom is our word (pros hon hēmin ho logos), playing on word in verse 12. God’s word judges us, and we must give our word, our account, to him. And the one before whom we stand is the Son: the Father has given all judgment to him (John 5:22; 2 Corinthians 5:10).

Stripped in order to be clothed. The chapter would be unbearable if it stopped here. A word that divides motive from motive, a God from whom nothing is hidden, and an account to be rendered. Any honest person reading verses 12 and 13 should feel exposed, and is meant to. That is why the writer goes straight on: since then we have a great high priest (4:14). He has stripped his readers deliberately, in order to tell them who is standing at the throne. The one who will judge is the same one who intercedes.

Does God see the things I have done in secret, even the shameful ones? Yes, every one of them, and he saw them before you did them. That is terrifying if you are hiding from him, and it is the deepest relief if you belong to Christ. You are not going to be found out; you have been fully known all along, and he loved you and sent his Son anyway (Romans 5:8). So stop spending your strength on concealment. Bring the secret to him by name in confession; he already knows it, and you do not need to soften it. Where it is wise, tell a mature believer too (James 5:16). What is brought into the light with God is covered by the blood of Christ (1 John 1:7–9).

Is a God who sees everything not just a cosmic surveillance camera? No. A camera records and does not care. The God of this verse sees in order to judge, and also in order to save. Our dread of being seen is really a dread of being seen and rejected, which is why we spend so much effort managing what other people know about us. The gospel offers what no camera can: to be completely known and still loved. Hagar, alone and runaway in the desert, called the LORD a God of seeing, and it was a comfort to her, not a threat (Genesis 16:13). For those who hide from him, his gaze is judgment. For those who come to Christ, it is the look of a Father who knew the worst and sent his Son anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: Since then we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus, the Son of God, let us hold fast our confession. For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A great high priest. The pivot of the letter comes immediately after its most exposing sentences. Naked, laid bare, accountable, and we have a priest. Aaron was the high priest; Jesus is the great high priest. The main theme of chapters 4 to 10 begins here.

In the flow. At 2:17 and 3:1 Jesus was first called a merciful and faithful high priest; now the warning is finished, and the writer returns to the priest. Almost the same words come back at 10:19–23, so these verses and those are the two bookends of the letter’s central teaching about Christ.

Passed through the heavens. “Passed through” (dielēlythota) is perfect tense: he has gone through, and the result stands. The picture is the Day of Atonement, when the high priest passed through the courts and the curtain into the Most Holy Place, once a year, with blood (Leviticus 16). Jesus has passed through the heavens themselves into the very presence of God (9:24), at his ascension. The tabernacle was a copy; Christ entered the reality.

Jesus, the Son of God. Both names are needed: Jesus, the man from Nazareth who was hungry and tired and wept; Son of God, the one whom angels worship. Truly human to represent us, truly divine to make his sacrifice infinitely effective.

Hold fast. The confession is the one named at 3:1, which they are under pressure to unsay. The order matters: not hold fast, and then you will have a priest; but we have a great high priest, so hold fast.

Able to sympathize. The double negative is there because the writer knows what his readers are afraid of. A priest who has passed through the heavens sounds magnificent and remote; the very grandeur of verse 14 might make a struggling person feel he could not possibly understand. So the writer denies it before it can be said out loud. “Sympathise” (sympathēsai) is to suffer with, to feel together with; our word sympathy. Not pity from above, which is what a superior offers an inferior, but feeling with. “Weaknesses” (astheneiai) are frailties, infirmities, limitations: not only sins, but the whole fragility of being human.

Tempted in every respect. The perfect tense: tested, and he still knows it from experience. Jesus faced every kind of temptation humans face: to doubt God, to take shortcuts, to avoid suffering, to seek glory, to give up. Not every circumstance, but every type, at full force.

Yet without sin. “Without sin” (chōris hamartias): there is the exception promised at 2:17. He never sinned, in thought, word or deed (7:26; 2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:22; 1 John 3:5). It is often misheard as limiting his sympathy, as though the sinless could not understand sinners. The opposite is true. The man who yields to a temptation never discovers how strong it was, because he stopped the pressure early. Only the one who holds out to the end feels its full weight. He is not less qualified to sympathise for never having fallen. He is the only person who has ever felt the whole force of what we surrender to. And he held out for us: his unbroken obedience is the righteousness counted to those who fail (2 Corinthians 5:21).

Where Christians differ: could Jesus have sinned? This commentary’s view: the Son of God could not sin, yet his temptations were real, because his human nature genuinely felt their pull; his inability to sin does not lessen his sympathy but makes his help sure. (See Matthew 4:1 for the fuller answer.)

Did Jesus face temptations like mine, sexual temptation, despair, addiction? He faced every kind of temptation common to human beings, though not every circumstance: he was never married, never old, never addicted. He knew the pull of hunger, of comfort and of pride, as the temptations in the wilderness show (Matthew 4:1–11), and he knew loneliness, betrayal and the desire to escape suffering in Gethsemane. There was one difference. Our temptations often rise from desires already disordered within us (James 1:14); his came from outside, never from a sinful heart. He felt them in full; he never fed them. So whatever form your temptation takes, you can bring it to him without shame. He will not be shocked, and he knows the way through.

Does his sympathy mean he excuses my sin? No. He sympathises with your weakness, not with your sin; he feels with you in the struggle, and he is on your side against the sin. That is why his sympathy is so strong a help. A friend who excuses you leaves you where you are; a friend who understands and also hates what is destroying you will help you fight it. Jesus is both merciful and faithful (2:17). Come to him expecting tenderness, and expecting him to lead you out.

For worship. He has passed through the heavens, and he has not forgotten what it is to be weak. The eyes that see every heart once wept at a friend’s grave; the one who upholds the universe once sat down tired by a well (John 4:6). He took his human nature with him into glory, and wears it still. In heaven there is a man who feels for us, and he is God.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Draw near. Everything in the letter so far has been building to this sentence, and everything after it will be building on it. “Draw near” (proserchōmetha) is present tense: keep coming. It is priestly language (Leviticus 9:7; 21:17). In the tabernacle it is what priests do, and what nobody else may do. The ordinary Israelite stood at a distance; only the high priest could approach God’s presence, once a year, with blood, and the penalty for approaching wrongly was death. That the whole congregation is now told to draw near, at any time, is a revolution stated in two words.

With confidence. “Confidence” (parrēsia) was originally the right of a free citizen to speak openly in the assembly, the opposite of the slave’s silence. We are to come with our mouths open: not arrogance, but freedom to come without fear, because of our high priest (10:19–22).

Exposed, and invited closer. Three verses earlier everything was laid bare. The natural response to being exposed is to cover up and withdraw. The writer says: precisely because you are seen through, come closer. There is nothing left to hide, which turns out to be a liberty rather than a terror.

To the throne of grace. It is a throne: not an altar, not a bench, not a counter. Real authority sits on it, God’s royal seat, and a throne is the last place a guilty man would ordinarily approach. For sinners, God’s throne would be a throne of judgment. But because of our high priest, it is a throne of grace (tō thronō tēs charitos), where grace is dispensed, which is a combination the ancient world rarely imagined: power that gives rather than power that takes. Behind the phrase stands the mercy seat, the lid of the ark of the covenant, God’s throne in the Most Holy Place, where he said he would meet with his people (Exodus 25:22). It was a throne with blood on it.

Mercy and grace. The two are distinct, and both are wanted. Mercy (eleos) is not getting what we deserve: pity, forgiveness for our failures and sins. It looks backward. Grace is getting what we do not deserve: strength for what comes next. It looks forward. A person who comes to this throne needs pardon for what is behind and power for what is ahead, and both are on offer at the same seat. “In time of need” (eukairon) is one word, meaning well-timed, at the right moment: grace that arrives exactly when needed. And “help” (boētheia) comes from the same root as the verb at 2:18, where he is able to help: the word means aid brought to someone who calls for it. It is not stockpiled in advance; it arrives when it is needed, which means we keep coming.

What it does not mean. We need no saints, priests or Mary to approach for us; Christ is our only and sufficient high priest (1 Timothy 2:5).

How can I come boldly when I have just sinned again? By remembering that your confidence was never in your record. You do not come because you have done well this week; you come because your high priest has passed through the heavens with his own blood, and he is the reason the throne is a throne of grace. The moment after a sin is exactly the time of need this verse is talking about. Do not wait until you feel worthy, or punish yourself first to earn the right to pray. Come at once, name the sin, receive the mercy, and ask for the grace to do differently next time. The longer you stay away, the harder you will find it to come.

What if I do not know what to pray? Come anyway, and say so. You can bring a groan, a single sentence, or a name. The Spirit helps us in our weakness and intercedes for us when we do not know what to pray for as we ought (Romans 8:26), and the high priest at the throne already knows your need better than you do. Use the Psalms when you have no words; pray the Lord’s Prayer slowly; tell God plainly that you are tired and need help. Boldness is not eloquence. It is coming in.

For worship. In the old tabernacle one man, once a year, went trembling through the curtain with blood. Now the high priest has gone through the heavens with his own blood, and the King of the universe has opened his court to beggars, and tells them to come boldly. Mercy for everything behind us, grace for everything ahead, because Jesus the Son of God is there, and he is ours.

hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.”<sup>8</sup>For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on.<sup>9</sup>So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the
