people of God,<sup>10</sup>for whoever has entered God’s rest has also rested from his works as God did from his.<sup>11</sup>Let us therefore strive to enter that rest, so that no one may fall by the same sort of disobedience.<sup>12</sup>For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and of spirit, of joints and of marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart.<sup>13</sup>And no creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account.<sup>14</sup>Since then we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus, the Son of God, let us hold fast our confession.<sup>15</sup>For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin.<sup>16</sup>Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.

5.title: The Qualifications of the Perfect Priest
5.overview:
Chapter 5 opens the letter’s central theme: Jesus as a priest after the order of Melchizedek. The writer first sets out what every true high priest must be: chosen from among men, able to deal gently with the weak, and called by God rather than self-appointed. Jesus meets every qualification, without the flaw of needing to offer for his own sins.

Psalm 110:4 opens an argument that runs to chapter 7. Between the qualifications and that argument stands Gethsemane: the Son praying in anguish, heard, and learning obedience through suffering. Then, abruptly, the writer stops to rebuke his readers for their dull hearing.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer sets out the marks of a high priest (vv. 1–4) and then shows that Christ has them, in reverse order: his call by God (vv. 5–6), his share in human weakness (vv. 7–8), and the salvation he brings (vv. 9–10). Where Aaron’s weakness meant sins of his own, Christ’s meant tears, prayer and obedience.
verseByVerse.theology:
Appointed, Not Self-Chosen

Christ shares our weakness and was called by God, and is named a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In the days of his flesh he prayed with loud cries and tears, and was heard.

Now: An answer that does not come in the form we asked for is not proof that we were unheard.

verseByVerse.quote: For every high priest chosen from among men is appointed to act on behalf of men in relation to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins. He can deal gently with the ignorant and wayward, since he himself is beset with weakness. Because of this he is obligated to offer sacrifice for his own sins just as he does for those of the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Hebrews 5 sets out what qualifies a high priest and shows that Jesus meets every qualification, and more. A high priest is taken from among men, deals gently with the ignorant and wayward because he shares their weakness, and is called by God, as Aaron was (vv. 1–4). God called Christ Son and priest forever in the order of Melchizedek (vv. 5–6). In the days of his flesh he prayed with loud cries and tears, learned obedience through suffering, and became the source of eternal salvation (vv. 7–10). Then the writer pauses: his readers have become dull of hearing (vv. 11–14).

What a high priest is. Having called Jesus a great high priest (4:14), the writer now sets out what a high priest is. In Israel he was the descendant of Aaron who alone, once a year on the Day of Atonement, went behind the curtain into the Most Holy Place with blood. Everything the readers had loved about the temple came to its point in that one man on that one day.

Chosen from among men. The first qualification: he is taken from among human beings (ex anthrōpōn lambanomenos). He must be one of the people he represents. That is not a detail. A representative who does not share the condition of those he stands for cannot stand for them, and it is why chapter 2 insisted that the Son had to be made like his brothers in every respect (2:14–17). An angel could not be our priest. Neither could God in his bare deity. The one who would stand for us had to have our flesh.

On behalf of men. The second: his whole business is Godward (ta pros ton theon, as at 2:17). A prophet faces the people with a word from God; a priest faces God with people on his hands. And his work is to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins. A priest without an offering is not a priest at all, which is why the letter will soon ask what this priest offers (8:3; 9:14).

Deal gently. The third qualification, and the one the writer dwells on. The word for dealing gently, metriopathein, is rare and precise: to moderate one’s feelings, to take the measured path between two failures. A priest must not be indifferent to sin, and he must not be enraged by it. Both extremes disqualify a man for the work. One shrugs and leaves the sinner in his sin; the other explodes and drives him away from the altar. Anyone who has gone to a minister with something shameful knows how rare the middle way is, and how much it matters that the man on the other side of the desk neither flinches nor pretends it does not matter.

The ignorant and the wayward. He deals gently with particular people: those who sin without knowing (agnoousin) and those who wander off (planōmenois), like sheep that drift. Not the defiant. The law made provision for sins of ignorance and weakness, but none for the high-handed sin of a man who despised the word of the LORD with his eyes open (Numbers 15:27–31). The writer keeps that boundary in view, and it will surface again at 6:4–6 and 10:26. The gentleness of a priest is for the stumbling, not for the scornful.

Beset with weakness. What makes the gentleness possible is stated flatly. The verb perikeitai means to be surrounded by, to have something lying round you; it is used of a chain hung round a prisoner (Acts 28:20), and here it is weakness worn like a garment. A man who knows his own frailty from the inside cannot be contemptuous of anyone else’s. Harshness toward people who fail usually grows from forgetting our own failures, because the self-righteous heart needs others to look worse so that it can feel safe.

For his own sins. Here the qualification shows its flaw: what makes him sympathetic makes him compromised. On the Day of Atonement Aaron had first to offer a bull for himself and his house, and only then for the people (Leviticus 16:6, 11). That is the gap Christ fills. He shares our weakness but not our sin (4:15); he needs no sacrifice for himself (7:27).

Where Christians differ: are Christian ministers priests? Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches call their clergy priests, who offer the sacrifice of the Mass (the Catholic name for the Lord’s Supper; the Orthodox speak of the Divine Liturgy) on behalf of the people. Many in those churches love Christ sincerely, and the disagreement is about what his once-for-all sacrifice leaves to be done. This commentary’s view: The New Testament never calls Christian ministers priests (hiereis) in this sense. Jesus is the one and only high priest of the new covenant, whose sacrifice was offered once for all (7:27; 9:25–28; 10:10–14). There is no further sacrifice for sin to offer. All believers together are a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices of praise and good works (1 Peter 2:5, 9; Hebrews 13:15–16). Ministers are elders and shepherds, not sacrificing priests. The Lord’s Supper is a remembrance and spiritual feeding on Christ, not a re-offering of him.

How can a sinless Christ really understand my weakness? Because weakness and sin are not the same thing. Weakness is hunger, tiredness, grief, fear, being tempted, being misunderstood, feeling the pull of an easier road. Jesus knew every one of these; he was hungry in the desert, weary at the well, troubled in the garden. Sin is giving way. And the one who never gives way feels temptation’s full force, because he has not let it off by yielding. The man who resists a storm all night knows its strength better than the one who goes indoors after ten minutes. So when you bring him your weakness, you are not explaining it to a stranger. You are bringing it to the one person who has carried it all the way to the end.

On a Tuesday. Who is the person you find it hardest to be patient with when he fails? Measured feeling is a priestly quality, now asked of every believer (1 Peter 2:9): neither shrug nor explode. And when you are the one who has fallen, notice where you go: away from God until you feel better, or straight to the high priest whose office exists for people in exactly your state.

verseByVerse.quote: And no one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron was.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one takes this honor. The fourth qualification is appointment. The high priesthood was an honour (timē), but not one to be grabbed. It cannot be applied for or earned. It is given.

Called by God, as Aaron was. God chose Aaron and his sons (Exodus 28:1), and when the tribes challenged it, he settled the matter with a sign (Numbers 17). It was plainly not Aaron’s by merit: this was the man who made the golden calf. The priesthood rested from the beginning on the choice of God, not on the worth of the man.

Scripture keeps this boundary with severity. Korah and his company were swallowed by the ground (Numbers 16); Saul lost his kingdom for offering the sacrifice himself (1 Samuel 13:8–14); King Uzziah went into the temple to burn incense and came out a leper (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). The severity is not arbitrary. If a man could appoint himself to represent others before God, the sinner’s hope would be only as good as the priest’s opinion of himself.

The setting. There is an immediate relevance here that the first readers would have felt. By the first century the high priesthood had become notoriously political. Herod and then the Roman governors appointed and deposed high priests at will, and the office was bought, traded and passed around within a few powerful families; Annas and Caiaphas, who handed Jesus over, belonged to one of them (John 18:13). A congregation being tempted back toward the temple system was being tempted toward a priesthood that had plainly taken the honour for itself. The writer goes back past all of it to the ideal: God’s calling.

The staff that budded overnight. The sign by which God settled Aaron’s call is worth setting beside Christ. A cut, dead stick was laid before the LORD, and in the morning it had budded, blossomed and borne ripe almonds: life out of deadness was God’s own seal on the priest he had chosen (Numbers 17:8). Hebrews remembers that staff, kept in the ark (9:4), and it rests the priesthood of Jesus on the same kind of seal raised to its height. He is priest by the power of an indestructible life (7:16), and he was declared to be the Son of God in power by his resurrection from the dead (Romans 1:4). Jesus did not take the honour for himself. The Father gave it, and proved he had given it by an empty tomb.

How does a man know whether God is calling him to be a pastor? Not usually by a voice or a vision, and Scripture never asks for one. Look for three things together. An inward desire that is about serving Christ’s people rather than being seen (1 Timothy 3:1). The character Paul lists, which is mostly ordinary godliness that others can verify: faithful in marriage, self-controlled, hospitable, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money, managing his home well (1 Timothy 3:2–7; Titus 1:5–9). And the ability to teach, recognised and confirmed by the elders and congregation who know him, not merely asserted by himself. The call of God normally comes through the church’s judgment, which is the opposite of taking the honour for oneself.

On a Tuesday. Notice where you are pushing for recognition at church, at work or in your family: the credit you quietly steer toward yourself, the resentment when someone else is asked. Let God do the exalting (1 Peter 5:6). The person who has to appoint himself is always anxious about his position. The person God has placed can afford to be content.

verseByVerse.quote: So also Christ did not exalt himself to be made a high priest, but was appointed by him who said to him, “You are my Son, today I have begotten you”; as he says also in another place, “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ did not exalt himself. The qualification of verse 4 is met by the one person who could have claimed the office on his own account. The Son through whom the world was made (1:2) waited to be given it, as he did not count equality with God a thing to be grasped (Philippians 2:6): it is my Father who glorifies me (John 8:54).

You are my Son. Then two quotations, the two halves of the appointment. The first, Psalm 2:7 (already at 1:5), establishes the relationship. Before office, there is sonship: the one who brings us to God is himself at home with God.

A priest forever. The second is Psalm 110:4, the verse this letter will spend three chapters on. Psalm 110 has already been quoted at 1:13 for its first verse, where the LORD tells David’s Lord to sit at his right hand. Now the writer takes its fourth verse, and the entire letter turns on it. Here is a psalm that Jesus himself read as speaking of the Messiah (Mark 12:35–37), in which God swears that the coming king will be a priest. That was constitutionally impossible in Israel, since kings came from Judah and priests from Levi, and the two lines never crossed.

Unless the priesthood in question is not Levitical. Hence Melchizedek, who appears in three verses of Genesis (Genesis 14:18–20) and nowhere else in the Old Testament except this psalm. “Forever” no Levitical priest could be, since they all died. And “after the order of” means of the rank or kind of Melchizedek: a different line, older than Levi and independent of him.

Who was Melchizedek? He was king of Salem (probably the old name for Jerusalem; compare Psalm 76:2) and priest of God Most High in Abraham’s day. When Abraham returned from rescuing Lot, Melchizedek met him with bread and wine, blessed him, and received a tenth of the spoils (Genesis 14:18–20). He was not descended from Levi or Aaron, who did not yet exist; his priesthood was of a different and earlier kind, and he was both king and priest at once. Chapter 7 will explain at length why that matters. For now, the point is simple: God promised a priest who would also be king, and who would never die.

The writer stops. He names Melchizedek here and does not return to him until 6:20, because he has judged that his readers are in no condition yet to take the argument in.

Does “today I have begotten you” mean the Son had a beginning? No. The psalm was first spoken over David’s son on the day he was crowned, the day God publicly owned the king as his son. Paul, preaching in Acts, applied the “today” to the day God raised and enthroned Jesus (Acts 13:33): the day the eternal Son was publicly installed as the messianic king and priest. It is a coronation word, not a birth certificate. Hebrews has already said that the Son made the worlds and is the exact imprint of God’s nature (1:2–3); he had no beginning, and the church confessed it at Nicaea as begotten, not made.

verseByVerse.quote: In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the days of his flesh. The years when the Son lived in a body that could tire and bleed and die. Those days are over; he is risen and seated. But what happened in them is the ground of everything this priest is for us.

In the flow. Verses 5–10 show that Christ meets the marks of verses 1–4, in reverse order: his call (vv. 5–6), his share in our weakness (vv. 7–8). But where Aaron’s weakness meant sins of his own, Christ’s meant tears, prayer and obedience.

Prayers and supplications. “Offered up” is the priestly word of verse 1: his prayers were part of his priestly offering. And “supplications” (hiketērias) was used of the suppliant who came holding an olive branch wrapped in wool, the sign of a man pleading for his life.

With loud cries and tears. The loud cries (kraugēs ischyras) are strong crying, a word used of a shout, not a murmur; and there were tears (dakryōn). Most likely the writer means the agony in Gethsemane, where Jesus said his soul was very sorrowful, even to death, where his sweat became like great drops of blood, and where he prayed three times for the cup to pass (Matthew 26:36–46; Luke 22:39–46). Perhaps he includes the cries from the cross (Mark 15:34, 37). Luke 22:43–44, with the angel and the sweat like drops of blood, is missing from some early manuscripts, though many others include it, so most modern Bibles keep it with a note. None of the Gospels records tears in the garden. The writer either knows something about that night that the Gospels do not tell us, or he is drawing out what they imply. Either way, the Son of God did not face the cup with serene detachment. His human anguish was real and deep.

Why did he pray like that? Because the cup was not merely death. Many brave men have died calmly. What Jesus faced was the wrath of God against sin, poured out on the one who would bear it for others (Isaiah 53:10; Mark 14:36). His holy human soul recoiled from it as no sinful soul ever could, because he knew the Father’s love perfectly and was about to be forsaken. The loud cries are the measure of what our salvation cost.

Able to save him from death. The Father could have rescued him from dying. The Greek can also be read as save him out of death (ek thanatou): bring him through death and out the other side, in resurrection.

He was heard. Here is the difficulty every reader feels: he was heard, and he died. What does it mean that the prayer was answered? The answer lies in the shape of the prayer itself, which was conditional: if it be possible, let this cup pass; nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done (Luke 22:42). A prayer that ends in that way is answered when the Father’s will is done, and it was. He was strengthened in the garden (Luke 22:43), carried through death, and raised out of it on the third day. He was heard, not by escaping death, but by triumphing over it. And the word for reverence (eulabeia) means godly fear, a holy caution: the disposition of a son who wants above everything not to displease his Father. He was heard because of that, not because of the volume of the crying.

Why would the Son of God need to pray at all? Because he was truly man as well as truly God, and a true man depends on God and speaks to him. Jesus prayed through the night before choosing the twelve, rose early to pray, prayed at his baptism and on the mountain. He did not pray as an act for the disciples’ benefit. In his human nature he lived by faith in his Father, as we must, and in the garden that dependence was tested to the uttermost. His prayers are part of the obedience by which he saved us.

Is it wrong for me to cry out to God in anguish, or to ask him to take something away? No. The sinless Son did both. Loud cries and tears are not a failure of faith; they are faith speaking honestly to the only one who can help. The Psalms are full of them. What made Jesus’ prayer holy was not calm, but submission: he asked plainly for what he wanted, and then he put the Father’s will above his own. You may ask God to heal, to rescue, to spare, with all your heart. Then learn to add his words: nevertheless, not my will, but yours.

Is this not a Father forcing his Son to suffer? No. The Son was not an unwilling victim pushed to the cross. Father and Son are one God with one saving purpose, and the Son came gladly to do his Father’s will (John 4:34). Jesus said that no one takes his life from him; he lays it down of his own accord (John 10:18). The cries in the garden show how terrible the cost was, not that he was coerced: not my will, but yours, is the free choice of a Son who loves his Father and his people. The cross is not one person punishing another for his own satisfaction. It is the triune God himself bearing the cost of saving sinners, in the person of the Son.

On a Tuesday. The Son of God prayed with shouting and tears, did not get what he asked for in the form he asked for it, and was heard. So unanswered prayer is not evidence of being unheard. Bring the request again, with tears if they come, and leave the form of the answer with him. A no that ends in resurrection is a better answer than a yes that ends anywhere else.
verseByVerse.note: Most likely a reference to Jesus’ agony in Gethsemane.

verseByVerse.quote: Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered. And being made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey him, being designated by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Although he was a son. One might think sonship would exempt him from suffering. It did not; in this letter it is the path along which the Son leads many sons to glory (2:10).

He learned obedience. The Greek is wordplay: emathen, he learned, and epathen, he suffered; the proverb was familiar in Greek: suffering teaches. “He learned obedience” needs care, because it cannot mean he moved from disobedience to obedience. He was never disobedient; he was always perfectly willing. What he learned was obedience by experience: the difference between a man who has always intended to be loyal and the same man after loyalty has cost him everything. He knew what obedience was; in the garden and on the cross he came to know what it weighs. His obedience was tested, proved and completed as he became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:8). And it was obedience in our place. We never obey perfectly, not even on our best days; he did, and by the one man’s obedience the many are made righteous (Romans 5:19).

Made perfect. The word of 2:10: brought to completion, made fully fit for an office. Not moral improvement, since he had no flaw. Through suffering and obedience he was fully equipped as Saviour and High Priest.

The source of eternal salvation. The word for source (aitios) is the word for cause: not a means to salvation but its author. And eternal, set against the temporary: an annually repeated sacrifice produced an annually repeated forgiveness; the salvation Christ causes lasts forever (9:12).

To all who obey him. It is a striking way to describe Christians: not those who believe, which is what we might expect, but those who obey (hypakouousin, literally those who listen and respond). The two are not alternatives in this letter. The wilderness generation’s failure was called disobedience in one verse and unbelief in the next (3:18–19; 4:6). Paul speaks the same way of the obedience of faith (Romans 1:5; 16:26), and John sets believing in the Son against not obeying the Son (John 3:36). Faith that does not eventually move the feet was never the thing Hebrews means by faith.

The symmetry. He learned obedience through suffering; he became the source of salvation to those who obey. The road the Son walked is the road his people walk, and his Spirit now walks it in us.

Designated by God. God publicly hailed him high priest in the words of Psalm 110:4. The writer is now ready to explain it, except that he has looked at his congregation and decided they cannot yet take it in.

What it does not mean. “All who obey him” does not mean salvation is earned by obedience. The obedience in view is trusting and following Christ, the fruit and expression of faith.

Am I among those who obey him, when my obedience is so patchy? The verse describes the direction of a life, not a flawless record. Those who obey him are those who have bowed to him as Lord, who listen to his word and want to do it, who fight sin and confess it when they fall, and who keep coming back to him. Your obedience will be imperfect all your life (1 John 1:8–9). What marks a believer is not that he never fails but that he does not make peace with failing, and that he runs to Christ, not away from him. If you grieve over your disobedience and long to please him, that grief and that longing are themselves the work of his Spirit in you. And remember whose obedience saves you. It is his, offered perfectly in your place.

Does suffering make me holier automatically? No. Suffering is a tool in a Father’s hand (12:5–11), but it does not work by itself; the same trial that softens one man hardens another. It trains those who receive it from God and keep trusting him in it. Jesus learned obedience through suffering because he kept obeying while he suffered. That is the opening for us: in pain, keep doing the next right thing, keep praying, keep trusting, and the suffering will not be wasted.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before going on to Melchizedek, the writer turns to his hearers. The trouble is not the subject but their ears, and the cure is not more information but practice.
verseByVerse.theology:
What Maturity Actually Is

Maturity is not a store of information but a trained faculty: discernment exercised by constant practice until it can tell good from evil.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The readers had become dull of hearing; they had not always been so.

Now: When Scripture seems dry, ask whether the dullness is in the passage or in the hearer.

verseByVerse.quote: About this we have much to say, and it is hard to explain, since you have become dull of hearing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
About this we have much to say. The writer is standing at the door of his central argument, and he stops, turns to his congregation, and tells them why he is not going on yet. There is a great deal more about Melchizedek, and he intends to say it (7:1–28). But first he must deal with the ears that will hear it.

In the flow. From here to the end of chapter 6 the writer steps aside, but the step aside is part of the argument: rebuke (5:11–14), call to go on (6:1–3), warning (6:4–8), encouragement (6:9–12), and God’s oath (6:13–20). At 6:20 Melchizedek returns.

Hard to explain. The fault is not located where we would expect. The word dysermēneutos means hard to interpret, hard to put into words, and the reason given is not that the subject is obscure. It is since you have become dull of hearing. The difficulty is in the audience. That is a bold thing for any preacher to say, and he says it without malice. He has called these people holy brothers (3:1) and will call them beloved (6:9). He is not writing them off; he is telling them the truth about why the sermon is stalling.

Dull of hearing. “Dull” is nōthroi: sluggish, slow, torpid. The word could be used of a numb limb or a lazy animal, and it comes back at 6:12, translated sluggish. It is the opposite of the alertness the letter has been urging since 2:1. And the decisive word is “become” (gegonate, a perfect tense: you have become, and you are now). They were not always like this. There was a time when these people were sharp, when they took the word in eagerly, when they stood their ground publicly and lost property for it; the writer will remind them of exactly that at 10:32–34. They have become dull, which means the condition was acquired, gradually, and probably without their noticing.

How it happens. That is the drift of 2:1 showing up in the ears. Few people decide to stop hearing. Often the truth had begun to demand change or suffering, and the easiest way to avoid a demand is not to hear it clearly.

The ear that was never dull. Set these sluggish hearers beside the priest the writer has just described. The Greek word for obedience (hypakoē) is built on the verb to hear, and Jesus learned obedience (5:8): his whole life was hearing his Father and doing what he heard. Isaiah gives the Servant’s own testimony: morning by morning the Lord GOD wakens his ear to hear as one who is taught, and he is not rebellious; he gives his back to those who strike him (Isaiah 50:4–6). That is Gethsemane and the cross, the listening Son going wherever the word led him. Our ears grow dull; his never did, and our salvation rests on that perfect hearing. He is also the word these readers had stopped attending to, for God has spoken to us by his Son (1:2).

How can I tell whether I have become dull of hearing? Look for the signs. Sermons wash over you and by Sunday lunch you cannot say what the text was. You know the answers but they no longer surprise or humble you. You read the Bible, if at all, to tick it off. You find yourself drawn to teaching that entertains or confirms what you already think, and impatient with anything that requires effort or change. And you have not acted on the last thing God clearly showed you. That last sign is usually the root: the ear grows dull when the will has stopped obeying. The remedy begins not with more information but with doing the last thing you heard, and then asking God, honestly, to open your ears again (Psalm 119:18).

On a Tuesday. Something as ordinary as preparation can change how you hear. Reading on Saturday the passage that will be preached, and praying over it for a few minutes, turns the sermon into a conversation already begun.

For worship. How patient our God is with slow hearers. He could have closed the book on a congregation that had stopped listening; instead he stopped his greatest argument to win them back to it. Christ has far more to say to us than we have ever taken in, and he opens our ears, because he means us to hear every word.

verseByVerse.quote: For though by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to teach you again the basic principles of the oracles of God. You need milk, not solid food, for everyone who lives on milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, since he is a child.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By this time you ought to be teachers. The rebuke is not that they know little but that they have not moved. These were not new converts; they should have been instructing others, and instead they need the alphabet again.

The normal expectation. Not that everyone should hold office (James 3:1), but that the ordinary path of a believer runs from being taught to being able to explain: a parent explaining the gospel to a child, a friend opening a passage over coffee, an older woman training a younger (Titus 2:3–5).

The basic principles. “Basic principles” is ta stoicheia tēs archēs, the elements of the beginning, the ABC. The “oracles of God” are his revealed word. Chapter 6 will list the first things (6:1–2).

Milk, not solid food. Paul uses the same image (1 Corinthians 3:1–2), and Peter tells new believers to long for pure spiritual milk (1 Peter 2:2). Milk is exactly right, for an infant. It becomes a problem only when a person is still on it years later.

Milk and solid food are both Christ. The oracles of God, in this letter, have one climax: in these last days God has spoken to us by his Son (1:2). The ABC these readers keep relearning is the first word about Christ (6:1), and the solid food the writer longs to serve them is more of Christ: his priesthood after the order of Melchizedek. Growing up in the faith is never growing past him into something more advanced. It is going deeper into the one in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Colossians 2:3). The infant and the mature are fed at the same table, and the food is the same person.

Unskilled in the word of righteousness. “Unskilled” (apeiros) is literally without experience, not having handled the thing. The “word of righteousness” may mean the teaching about how God makes sinners righteous, or the skill of using God’s word to tell right from wrong; probably the latter, given verse 14. Spiritual infancy is natural at the start; it is a problem when it lasts too long.

Knowledge that is never used. This reframes the whole rebuke. The writer is not complaining that his readers have not read enough. He is saying that knowledge which is never exercised does not mature anybody. A man can sit under good teaching for decades and remain an infant, because hearing without doing produces nothing (James 1:22–25). Maturity, as verse 14 says, comes by practice. And knowledge can become an idol of its own. Knowing the right answers can make a person feel safe with God while keeping him at arm’s length, which is a very religious way of not listening.

Does this verse condemn me if I am not a natural teacher? It is not asking you to become a preacher, or to be good at public speaking. It asks whether you have grown enough to help someone else understand and follow Christ. Can you explain, simply, who Jesus is and why he died? Can you point a struggling friend to a promise, or show your child where a truth is found? If not yet, that is not a reason for shame but a direction for growth. Start where you are: learn one passage well enough to explain it, and then explain it to one person. Teaching in this sense is mostly the overflow of a believer who has been feeding well.

verseByVerse.quote: But solid food is for the mature, for those who have their powers of discernment trained by constant practice to distinguish good from evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Solid food is for the mature. “Mature” (teleioi) is grown-up, related to the word for Christ being made perfect in verse 9. Maturity is the goal of the whole Christian life (Ephesians 4:13).

Powers of discernment trained. “Powers of discernment” (aisthētēria) is literally the faculties or organs of perception, the same word used of the physical senses. The writer is describing moral and spiritual judgment as a sense: something that perceives directly, the way a tongue tastes, like a trained palate that knows good food from bad without consulting a chart. “Trained” is gegymnasmena, the gymnasium word, from which we get gymnastics. It means exercised, put through a training regime, as an athlete trains a body, and the perfect tense means trained and now in condition.

By constant practice. One word, hexis, habit, a state produced by repetition. Not by a crisis or a conference. By habit.

To distinguish good from evil. Not only moral good and evil, but true and false teaching. The readers needed to discern that the old covenant, though good, had been surpassed, and that turning back would be turning away from Christ.

The measure of the mature. The standard is the stature of the fullness of Christ (Ephesians 4:13). Tempted in the wilderness, he told good from evil at once and answered every lie with Scripture (Matthew 4:1–10). Christian maturity is the mind of Christ formed in his people (1 Corinthians 2:16), until his instincts become theirs.

A definition of maturity. Maturity is not the accumulation of doctrine but a trained faculty. Solid food is withheld from these readers not because they are unintelligent, but because the faculty that would digest it has not been exercised.

The comfort in it. There is comfort here as well as rebuke. If maturity came by intellect, most Christians would be excluded from it. It comes by practice, which is available to everybody. The ordinary believer who has spent thirty years making small decisions in the fear of God has a trained palate, whatever he can or cannot explain. The grandmother who has never read a theology book but can smell false teaching at fifty paces is mature in exactly this sense. And the writer’s next words, at the head of chapter 6, are let us go on. He does not leave them where they are.

How do I actually train my discernment? The same way an athlete trains: small, regular, real exercises. Read Scripture daily, and ask of each passage what it shows you about God and what it asks of you. When you face a decision, even a small one about words, money, time or entertainment, stop and ask what God’s word says, and then act on the answer. Notice afterwards whether it was right. Listen to teaching with an open Bible and test it (Acts 17:11). Spend time with mature believers and watch how they judge things. Confess quickly when you get it wrong. Over years, what began as slow deliberate thinking becomes instinct.

Is discernment the same as being critical? No. Some people mistake suspicion for discernment and spend their lives finding fault with sermons and other Christians. The discernment of this verse distinguishes good from evil, which means it recognises and delights in the good as quickly as it detects the evil. A mature palate does not only spit out what is bad; it relishes what is good. True discernment makes a person humbler, more thankful and more careful with his own heart, not sharper with everyone else’s.

5.text: <sup>1</sup>For every high priest chosen from among men is appointed to act on behalf of men in relation to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins.<sup>2</sup>He can deal gently with the ignorant and wayward, since he himself is beset with weakness.<sup>3</sup>Because of this he is obligated to offer sacrifice for his own sins just as he does for those of the people.<sup>4</sup>And no one takes this honor for himself, but only when called by God, just as Aaron was.<sup>5</sup>So also Christ did not exalt himself to be made a high priest, but was appointed by him who said to him, “You are my Son, today I have begotten you”;<sup>6</sup>as he says also in another place, “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.”<sup>7</sup>In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence.<sup>8</sup>Although he was a son, he learned obedience through what he suffered.<sup>9</sup>And being made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey him,<sup>10</sup>being designated by God a high priest after the order of Melchizedek.<sup>11</sup>About this we have much to say, and it is hard to explain, since you have become dull of hearing.<sup>12</sup>For though by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to teach you again the basic principles of the oracles of God. You need milk, not solid food,<sup>13</sup>for everyone who lives on milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, since he is a child.<sup>14</sup>But solid food is for the mature, for those who have their powers of discernment trained by constant practice to distinguish good from evil.

6.title: Press On to Maturity: The Anchor of the Soul
6.overview:
Chapter 6 holds one of the letter’s most debated passages and one of its most encouraging. It begins with a call to maturity: build on the foundations, do not keep relaying them. Then comes the severest warning (vv. 4–8): those who have seen the full light of the gospel and then deliberately turn away cannot be restored to repentance.

At once the writer turns to his confidence about his readers, grounded in God, who will not forget their love. And the chapter ends with hope as an anchor for the soul, lodged behind the curtain where Jesus has gone ahead as forerunner.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Hardest Warning, and the Confidence After It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The section moves in three steps: a call to build on the foundation rather than relay it (vv. 1–3), the warning of verses 4–8 with its picture of two fields, and the writer’s confidence in his readers, with a call to earnest hope (vv. 9–12).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Passage Set Out Honestly

Sincere Christians read verses 4–6 differently. The list describes what was received and seen, not what saves; and five verses later the writer calls his readers beloved and speaks of things that belong to salvation.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Two fields drink the same rain; the crop shows the soil.

Now: The warning is not addressed to the anxious. God is not unjust so as to overlook love shown in serving the saints.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let us leave the elementary doctrine of Christ and go on to maturity, not laying again a foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith toward God, and of instruction about washings, the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. And this we will do if God permits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Hebrews 6 holds together one of the letter’s most solemn warnings and one of its strongest assurances. It calls the readers on from the foundations to maturity (vv. 1–3). Then comes the warning: those who have tasted the heavenly gift and the powers of the age to come, and then fall away, cannot be restored to repentance; they are like land that drinks the rain and bears only thorns (vv. 4–8). Yet the writer is sure of better things in his readers (vv. 9–12). The chapter ends with God’s oath to Abraham and a hope that is a sure and steady anchor of the soul, fixed behind the curtain where Jesus has gone as our forerunner (vv. 13–20).

Let us leave the elementary doctrine. “Leave” sounds alarming until the metaphor is seen. The image is a building: not laying again a foundation. You do not abandon a foundation by building on it. You abandon it by digging it up every few years to check it is still there. That is what these readers were doing: endlessly returning to the basics, and never getting a wall up.

In the flow. The therefore is surprising. He has just said they need milk (5:12), and now he says, let us go on. Standing still is not safe for these people (vv. 4–8), so he gives them solid food, Christ’s priesthood (chapter 7), and trusts God to make them able to take it in (v. 3).

Go on to maturity. The verb (pherōmetha) is passive: let us be carried along, the word for a ship running before the wind, and Peter’s word for the prophets carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1:21). Growth is something we press into and something God does to us at the same time. And it is let us: the preacher is not standing on the finished storey calling down.

Not laying again a foundation. Then six items, probably in three pairs. The first pair is conversion: repentance from dead works and faith toward God, the two sides of one turning, away from and toward. Dead works are deeds that lead to death or come from spiritual death: sinful deeds, and perhaps also religious works done to earn God’s favour (9:14).

Washings and the laying on of hands. The second pair is initiation. “Washings” (baptismōn) is plural, and it is the ordinary word for ceremonial cleansings rather than the usual term for Christian baptism (9:10; Mark 7:4). That suggests teaching Jewish converts how Christian baptism differed from the washings they had known all their lives, and from John’s baptism (Acts 19:1–5). The many washings of the old covenant gave way to the one Christian washing, given to those who have turned from dead works and come to faith. The laying on of hands was used in the New Testament to bless, to heal, to commission for service (Acts 6:6; 13:3; 1 Timothy 4:14), and in the apostles’ ministry as the moment the Spirit was given (Acts 8:17; 19:6).

The resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. The third pair is the last things: the bodily resurrection of all people (John 5:28–29) and God’s everlasting judgment (9:27). These were among the first things a convert was taught.

Nothing peculiar to Christ. Here is the striking thing about the list: there is almost nothing in it that is distinctively Christian. Every item could have been taught in a synagogue. Repentance, faith in God, ceremonial washing, laying on of hands, resurrection, judgment: a devout Pharisee would have affirmed the lot. His readers were stalled precisely where Judaism and Christianity overlap. They had never moved on to what is peculiar to Christ, his priesthood, his sacrifice, his finished work, and that is exactly why going back looked so easy. If you have not yet built anything above the shared foundation, stepping off it costs you nothing you can see. That is the quiet danger of respectable religion. A person can believe in God, repentance and judgment and still have no use for a priest, because the heart would much rather manage its own standing with God than owe everything to someone else.

And this we will do if God permits. Progress in understanding is not simply a matter of resolve; it is granted. It also prepares for what follows, where the writer describes people for whom God does not permit renewal (vv. 4–6).

Does “washings” here teach anything about how to baptise? Not directly; the verse is about instruction, not method. But it fits the wider teaching of the New Testament that baptism belongs at the beginning of the Christian life, alongside repentance and faith. The order of the first pair matters: those who have turned from dead works and trusted God are the ones who are washed. That is why this commentary, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, holds believer’s baptism, while gladly honouring paedobaptist brothers who read the covenant signs differently and who love the same Saviour. Whichever view a Christian holds, the point of the verse stands: baptism is foundation, not a place to camp.

Does the laying on of hands still give the Spirit today? The Spirit is given to every believer at conversion, through faith in Christ, not through anyone’s hands (Romans 8:9; Galatians 3:2). In Acts the Spirit sometimes came at the laying on of apostolic hands, as the gospel crossed new boundaries and the church’s foundation was being laid (Acts 8:14–17; 19:6). That belonged to the apostolic foundation and is not repeated: those moments marked the gospel’s first crossing to new peoples, and Acts does not present them as a pattern for every believer. Many Pentecostal and charismatic brothers pray with laying on of hands for a fresh filling of the Spirit, and they mean to honour him; this commentary differs from them gladly as from fellow believers. What continues is the laying on of hands with prayer to set apart elders and missionaries for their work (Acts 13:3; 1 Timothy 4:14), a sign of the church’s blessing and recognition, not a channel of power.

On a Tuesday. Notice where you keep digging up the foundation: the assurance you re-examine every week without ever resting on it. Stand on what God has laid, and build: go deeper into his priesthood, his once-for-all sacrifice, his intercession for you now.

verseByVerse.quote: For it is impossible, in the case of those who have once been enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift, and have shared in the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the goodness of the word of God and the powers of the age to come,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it is impossible. The most disputed sentence in the letter. “Impossible” (adynaton) stands in the emphatic position: not difficult, but impossible, the word used of God’s inability to lie (v. 18) and of the blood of bulls taking away sins (10:4). Its object does not arrive until verse 6: impossible to restore them again to repentance. Everything between describes the people in view.

In the flow. The for gives the reason for verses 1–3: there is no safe standing still. This is the third and sharpest so far of the letter’s five warnings, and it is followed at once by the writer’s confidence about his readers (6:9) and by the anchor behind the curtain (6:19–20). The warning and the assurance belong to one sermon.

A word first to the anxious reader. If these verses frighten you, the fear itself is good news. The people described here are not worried about Christ; they have turned their backs on him and do not want him back. A believer who loves Christ and still falls into the same sin, who hates it, fights it and grieves over it, is not falling away: that struggle is the Spirit’s work in him, the Spirit and the flesh at war (Galatians 5:17; Romans 7:22–25). Depression, numbness and dark seasons of doubt are not apostasy either. Hold that as you read on, and remember how this chapter ends: with a hope anchored behind the curtain, where Jesus has gone for you (6:19–20).

Once been enlightened. “Once” (hapax) is once for all. Light has fallen on them: they heard and understood the gospel (10:32). Some early Christian writers used “enlightened” as a name for baptism.

Tasted the heavenly gift. Some have tried to soften “tasted” into a sip, but at 2:9 Jesus tasted death for everyone, and he did not sample it. The word means real experience of the blessing that comes from heaven, within the life of the church.

Shared in the Holy Spirit. The word is the one used at 3:1 and 3:14. They had participated in the Spirit’s work in the community, his convicting power, his gifts and blessings, as Judas shared in the apostles’ ministry and was sent out to heal with the rest (Matthew 10:1–8).

The goodness of the word and the powers of the age to come. They have found Scripture good, perhaps with joy, like the seed on rocky ground that springs up quickly and has no root (Matthew 13:20–21). And they have seen the miracles of 2:4, the foretaste of the age to come.

A formidable description. Whatever the passage finally means, these people were not obviously never involved at all. They had been inside, near the fire, warmed by it.

The crowd that ate the bread and left. The Gospels show such people around Jesus himself. In John 6 a crowd had eaten the bread he multiplied, seen his signs and heard his words, and followed him across the lake. He told them plainly that they were seeking him for the loaves, not for himself, and that he was the bread of life come down from heaven (John 6:26, 35). When his words grew hard, many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him (John 6:66). They had tasted his gifts and his powers, and refused him. Whatever exactly the heavenly gift is, every gift of heaven comes in Christ, and the dividing line runs between those who have received his benefits and those who have received him.

Where Christians differ: are these true believers? This is one of the most debated passages in Scripture. Four main views: (1) these are genuine believers who lose their salvation (the Arminian view, held by many earnest Christians, that a true believer can finally fall away); (2) these are genuine believers, but the warning is hypothetical, describing what would happen if they could fall away, which they cannot; (3) these are genuine believers who lose rewards, not salvation; (4) these are people who have experienced the blessings of the gospel community without being truly regenerated, and whose falling away shows they were never truly saved. The first view has a difficulty inside the letter itself, which says Christ is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them (7:25); and by this reading the loss would be irreversible, which few who take the view actually teach. The second fits the theology but reads thinly against the urgency of the warning, and the third cannot do justice to burning (v. 8) or to 10:26–31. This commentary’s view: The fourth view best fits the passage and the whole of Scripture. Every phrase in verses 4–5 describes real experiences that can be had without regeneration: being enlightened (understanding the gospel), tasting (experiencing without fully receiving), sharing in the Spirit’s work (as Judas and Balaam did), tasting the word with joy (like the rocky soil). The passage does not use words like justified, born again, saved or sanctified of these people. In verse 9 the author distinguishes them from those who have “things that belong to salvation.” And the land illustration (vv. 7–8) shows the difference: the same rain falls on two kinds of ground, but the fruit reveals the nature of the soil. Scripture elsewhere teaches that those whom God saves he keeps (John 10:28–29; Romans 8:29–30; Philippians 1:6). The warning is real: such people exist, and God uses this warning to stir true believers to persevere.

How can someone share in the Holy Spirit and not be saved? Because the Spirit works in more ways than regeneration. He convicts the world of sin (John 16:8), he gives gifts and power in the church, and he moves on people who hear the word, so that they are stirred, sobered and attracted. Balaam prophesied when the Spirit of God came upon him, and died among the enemies of God’s people (Numbers 24:2; 31:8). Saul had the Spirit come on him and ended consulting a medium (1 Samuel 10:10; 28:7). Judas preached and healed. Jesus warned of many who would say on the last day that they had prophesied and done mighty works in his name, to whom he would say, I never knew you (Matthew 7:22–23). Being near the Spirit’s work is not the same as being born of him. Regeneration, the word used in the verdict above, means exactly that new birth: the Spirit giving new life to a heart that was dead, so that the person truly turns to Christ and goes on trusting him (John 3:3–8; Ezekiel 36:26).

Then how can I know I am not one of these? Not by the size of your experiences, since these people had large ones, but by what the Spirit produces over time. Do you trust Christ himself, not your experiences, for your acceptance with God? Do you love him and want to please him? Do you hate your sin and fight it, and confess it when you fall? Do you love other Christians and serve them (v. 10; 1 John 3:14)? Do you keep coming back to his word, even when it is hard? These are the things that belong to salvation, and they are usually clearer to others than to the anxious person himself. If you find even a weak longing for Christ in you, rest on his promise and not on your feelings: whoever comes to me I will never cast out (John 6:37).

For worship. How rich the goodness of God is, that he pours light and tastes of heaven even on those who finally reject him. And how much richer his grace to his own, who are given not only the taste but the feast, not only the Spirit’s nearness but his indwelling for ever. We rest on Christ, who never lets go of anyone the Father has given him.

verseByVerse.quote: and then have fallen away, to restore them again to repentance, since they are crucifying once again the Son of God to their own harm and holding him up to contempt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then have fallen away. The word (parapesontas) is to fall aside, to defect. It is not stumbling into sin but the deliberate abandonment warned of since 3:12: for these readers, renouncing Christ and returning to the old system to escape persecution, publicly and for good.

To restore them again to repentance. “Again” implies they had shown repentance once, outwardly at least. They have rejected the only means of forgiveness: Christ’s sacrifice. There is no other (10:26). A drowning man who pushes away the one rope thrown to him has refused the only rescue there is.

Crucifying once again the Son of God. The verb (anastaurountas) means to crucify again, or to crucify up, on a cross. By rejecting Christ, they side with those who crucified him and declare that he deserved it. And both participles are present and continuous. Most translations, the ESV among them, take them as giving the reason: since they are crucifying him again. Some read them as meaning while: as long as they go on doing this, and on that reading a person in the act of publicly repudiating Christ cannot at the same time be repenting of it. Either way, the impossibility lies in their settled rejection of the only sacrifice there is. And it is “to their own harm” (heautois, for themselves, to their loss): Christ cannot be crucified again in fact, but they crucify him for themselves, and the ruin is theirs.

Holding him up to contempt. The word is a public one, making a public example of someone. These are people who have said, before witnesses, that the crucified man was rightly crucified.

The pastoral force is the same. Whichever reading one holds, the warning is not addressed to the anxious. A person terrified that this describes him is displaying precisely the softness of heart the passage says is absent. The people in view are not agonising. They have walked out (1 John 2:19).

What about the Christian who has really wandered? This verse does not describe him. A believer may fall into serious sin and stay away for a season, cold, ashamed and defensive. Peter denied Christ three times with curses, and Jesus had prayed that his faith would not fail: when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers (Luke 22:32). David committed adultery and murder, and wrote Psalm 51. The warning is against final apostasy, not against backsliding. Whoever wants to come back to Christ may come, and the church is to restore him in a spirit of gentleness (Galatians 6:1). The door is not shut on anyone who knocks.

If true believers cannot finally fall away, why warn them? Because the warnings are one of the means God uses to keep them. God promises to preserve his people, and he does it not by switching off their wills but by speaking to them: by promises that draw and warnings that alarm. A sign at a cliff edge saying danger is not pointless because it works. The elect do persevere (John 10:28–29; Philippians 1:6), and they persevere partly because passages like this one make them flee to Christ. The warning is sincere, the danger it describes is real for those who are near the church but not in Christ, and for true believers it is a fence God has built on the path.

Is this the same as the unforgivable sin? They are closely related. Jesus spoke of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (Mark 3:28–30): deliberately calling the Spirit’s plain work in Christ the work of the devil, against the light. Hebrews 6 and 10 describe the same settled, knowing, public rejection of Christ after seeing his truth. Neither is a sin someone commits by accident or in a moment of weakness, and neither is a sin committed by a person who wants forgiveness. Any sin that is repented of is forgiven, because the blood of Jesus cleanses from all sin (1 John 1:7).

Should a church refuse to receive back someone who left the faith and now returns? No. The church cannot read hearts, and this verse is not a rule for church discipline. It describes from God’s side what happens to the hardened, not a policy for the elders. If someone who had walked away returns professing repentance, the church should receive him with joy, as the father received the prodigal (Luke 15:20–24), test the fruit patiently, and welcome him to the Lord’s Table when it is evident. That he has come back at all suggests he was not the person this verse describes.
verseByVerse.note: Christians have read this warning in different ways; all agree it is a real warning against turning away from Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: For land that has drunk the rain that often falls on it, and produces a crop useful to those for whose sake it is cultivated, receives a blessing from God. But if it bears thorns and thistles, it is worthless and near to being cursed, and its end is to be burned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Land that has drunk the rain. The picture explains more than the argument does. The rain is the same on both fields, and the ground has genuinely absorbed it: “drunk” corresponds to the tasting and sharing of verses 4 and 5. The rain is God’s repeated blessing: the gospel preached again and again, the Spirit’s work, the fellowship of believers.

A useful crop. Good land responds to the rain with fruit: by their fruits you will recognise them (Matthew 7:16–20).

Receives a blessing from God. Fruitful land is blessed further, as the vinedresser prunes the fruitful branch so that it bears more (John 15:2).

Fruit that comes from the Son. Jesus taught the same lesson: whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing (John 15:5). The harvest God blesses is not produced by the soil’s own strength. It grows out of union with Christ.

Thorns and thistles. The exact phrase of the curse in Eden (Genesis 3:17–18). The unfruitful ground is doing what cursed ground does.

Near to being cursed. The writer is careful here. He does not say the field is cursed but near to a curse (kataras engys). Near is not yet. As long as a field is only near, there is time for something else to come up, and the whole letter is written to make that happen.

Its end is to be burned. A picture of final judgment (10:27; John 15:6). The fruit shows the soil; the soil determines the end.

How do you tell the fields apart? The parable answers the pastoral question the previous verses raise. If both fields look identical while the rain is falling, how does anyone know? By the crop. Not by the intensity of the experience, not by how much was tasted, but by what is growing now, which is precisely what the writer turns to next, when he points to his readers’ love shown in serving the saints (v. 10).

What fruit am I looking for, and what if mine looks small? The fruit Scripture means is mostly ordinary: trust in Christ that keeps returning to him, love for God’s people, hatred of sin and a fight against it, honesty, kindness, patience under trial, joy in God’s word, the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23). It grows slowly and is rarely spectacular. A small crop is still a crop; thorns are not small wheat. And remember who makes good soil. The new heart is God’s gift (Ezekiel 36:26), and the vinedresser does not neglect his vineyard. If you see little fruit, do not despair; ask him to work, stay under the rain of his word, and look again in a year.

For worship. The rain is God’s, and it falls often on fields that do not deserve a drop, and on his own people he does more: he takes out the stone and makes the soil itself new. The thorns and thistles were the curse of Eden, and Christ wore them on his head so that the ground of his people’s hearts could be blessed.

verseByVerse.quote: Though we speak in this way, yet in your case, beloved, we feel sure of better things—things that belong to salvation. For God is not unjust so as to overlook your work and the love that you have shown for his name in serving the saints, as you still do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Beloved. The writer has just written one of the hardest paragraphs in the letter, and he knows how it will land on a congregation that loves him. “Beloved” (agapētoi) is the only time in the letter he uses that word, and he uses it here. Whatever the warning was for, it was not to tell these people he had given up on them. “Feel sure” (pepeismetha) is a perfect tense: we have been persuaded, and we are convinced. He is not being polite. He has just described people who fall away, and he says: that is not you, and I am confident of it.

Better things, because a better Christ. “Better things” (ta kreissona) is the letter’s key word, and in Hebrews it nearly always points to Christ and what he brings: a Son better than the angels (1:4), a better hope by which we draw near (7:19), a better covenant with Jesus as its guarantor (7:22), better sacrifices (9:23), sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (12:24). So when the writer is sure of better things in his readers, he is not praising their superior character. He is saying that they belong to the better Priest, and that the things which accompany salvation in them are the overflow of their share in him (3:14).

Things that belong to salvation. Some things always go with genuine salvation, and they are exactly what is missing from the list in verses 4–5. The experiences of verses 4–5 can happen without salvation; the fruit described in verse 10 accompanies it.

God is not unjust. Then the ground of his confidence, and it is not what we might expect. The evidence is the crop. The parable asked how you tell one field from another, and the writer now points at what is growing in this one. “Unjust” (adikos): God is faithful to his promises, and he will not forget the fruit of faith. This does not mean God owes them. It is not that their service has earned salvation; it is that a God who had produced such fruit and then discarded the field would be acting unjustly toward his own work. He will acknowledge it, down to a cup of cold water (Matthew 10:42; 25:34–40). None of that service was flawless, and it did not need to be: through Jesus Christ the imperfect offerings of his children are acceptable to God (1 Peter 2:5), because his obedience was whole.

Serving the saints. “For his name” (eis to onoma autou) means for God’s sake: they loved his people because they were his. And the verb comes twice, as a past and a present: having served (diakonēsantes) and still serving (diakonountes). They had cared for persecuted believers, visited prisoners and accepted the plundering of their property (10:32–34), and they were still doing it. They may be dull of hearing and stalled in understanding, and they are still looking after people. That is fruit, and he treats it as decisive. Love for fellow believers is a mark of genuine faith: we know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers (1 John 3:14).

If he is so sure of them, why did he warn them? Because confidence about a congregation and warnings to a congregation work together. He is sure of the body as a whole, from what he sees, and he knows that any one person in it might be quietly slipping (v. 11). He is also sure that true believers respond to warnings, and his warning is part of how God will keep them. A doctor can be confident that a patient will recover and still tell him firmly to finish the medicine. The confidence is not instead of the instruction; it rests on the expectation that the instruction will be taken.

The comfort of the double negative. There is comfort here for anyone whose service has gone unnoticed. The meals taken to a sick house, the years of unremarkable faithfulness to awkward people, the hospital visit nobody thanked you for, the prayers for a church that never knew who was praying: God is not unjust so as to overlook it. He may be the only one who has not.

On a Tuesday. Look for the fruit in someone else this week, and tell them, as the writer named what God was doing in his readers. And if some act of love has dropped away since an earlier, keener season, a visit, a meal, a regular prayer for a struggling believer, pick it up again for his name.

verseByVerse.quote: And we desire each one of you to show the same earnestness to have the full assurance of hope until the end, so that you may not be sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each one of you. “Each one” is the individual concern again, as at 3:12 and 4:1. He will not let confidence about the body become a blanket that covers someone quietly slipping. He asks them to apply to their hope the diligence (spoudē) they already apply to their neighbours.

Full assurance of hope. The word (plērophoria) means a mind filled to the brim with confidence. Assurance is here something to be pursued, a state a Christian may grow into, and it is not presumption but a fruit of faith (10:22; 2 Peter 1:10).

So that you may not be sluggish. The word is nōthroi, as at 5:11. Sluggish ears and sluggish lives are the same condition, and the remedy for both is the same earnestness.

Imitators. Against the dullness, examples: real people who waited and received. “Imitators” (mimētai) is the word Paul uses when he says, be imitators of me, as I am of Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1). Here the letter turns a corner that will not be completed until chapter 11, where the long line of the faithful passes before us. And “faith and patience” is the pairing that runs to the end of the letter. Patience (makrothymia) is long-temperedness, the endurance that keeps going when the promise is slow. Faith takes God at his word; patience keeps taking him at it for years.

The last name on the list. The line of the faithful that begins here with Abraham ends with Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross (12:2). And he is more than an example, because the promises the faithful inherit are inherited in him, the heir of all things (1:2).

What had run out. Not information, and not zeal at the start. What had run out was the long, unglamorous willingness to keep believing a promise that had not yet arrived.

Can a Christian really be sure he is saved, or is that arrogant? He can, and it is not arrogance, because the confidence rests on God, not on himself. Hebrews wants every believer to have full assurance. It rests first on God’s promises in Christ, which cannot fail (vv. 17–18); it is confirmed by the Spirit’s witness that we are God’s children (Romans 8:16) and by the fruit he produces in us (v. 10). The Westminster Confession says that true believers may be infallibly assured, though they may wait long and struggle for it, and that it may be shaken and then revived (Westminster 18.3–4; 1689 18.3–4). Assurance is humble certainty: I am sure, not because I am strong, but because he is faithful.

How do I grow in assurance? Look mostly at Christ and his promises, not mostly at yourself. Read and trust the promises made to all who come to him (John 6:37; 10:28). Use the means of grace: the preached word, the Lord’s Supper, prayer, the fellowship of other believers. Obey in the small things, because disobedience clouds assurance and obedience clears it. Deal quickly with known sin. Serve others, as these readers did. And when you are low, remember that assurance is not the ground of your salvation. A believer with weak assurance is as safe as one with strong assurance, because both are held by the same hand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–20 — Two Unchangeable Things, and an Anchor Behind the Curtain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Abraham is the example of faith and patience, and God’s oath to him is the ground of the believer’s confidence. The section ends with the anchor behind the curtain and brings the writer back to Melchizedek.
verseByVerse.theology:
An Anchor That Goes Upward

God confirmed his promise with an oath so that we might have strong encouragement. Our hope is anchored behind the curtain, where Jesus has gone ahead of us as forerunner.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Abraham waited twenty-five years for Isaac, not always steadily, and obtained the promise.

Now: We are those who have fled for refuge. The storm and the anchorage are in different places.

verseByVerse.quote: For when God made a promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater by whom to swear, he swore by himself, saying, “Surely I will bless you and multiply you.” And thus Abraham, having patiently waited, obtained the promise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A promise to Abraham. Here is the example promised in verse 12: the father of the nation becomes the pattern of waiting. God promised him descendants, land and blessing for all nations (Genesis 12:1–3).

He swore by himself. The occasion is Genesis 22, on the mountain, immediately after Abraham had raised the knife over Isaac: the point at which the promise looked most impossible and the man had proved he would trust God with it anyway. It is the only place in Genesis where we hear God swear an oath to Abraham: by myself I have sworn, declares the LORD (Genesis 22:16). The logic of an oath is that you invoke something greater than yourself as surety. God has no such thing available. So he swore (ōmosen) by himself, which means the guarantee of the promise is his own existence: for it to fail he would have to cease to be God.

Surely I will bless you. From Genesis 22:17, compressed. Behind it lies a doubled Hebrew expression, literally blessing I will bless you, which underlines the certainty.

The oath sworn over a son. The setting of the oath is no accident. God swore it on the mountain where Abraham had received his son back from the knife and a ram had died in his place, and the oath itself names an offspring in whom all the nations of the earth will be blessed (Genesis 22:13–18). Paul says that offspring is finally one person, Christ (Galatians 3:16). And the New Testament reads the scene as a shadow of a greater giving: Abraham’s son was spared, but God did not spare his own Son, and gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32). The promise sworn over Isaac was kept at Calvary.

Having patiently waited. Everything hangs on the middle phrase (makrothymēsas, having been patient). Put the years against it. Abraham was seventy-five when the promise was first made and a hundred when Isaac was born (Genesis 12:4; 21:5). Twenty-five years, most of them with no evidence whatever, and through a stretch in which he twice passed off his wife as his sister to save his own skin, took Hagar to arrange the heir himself, and laughed when God repeated the promise (Genesis 12; 16; 17:17; 20). The waiting was not serene. It was long and it was patchy, and Hebrews still calls it patience.

The comfort in a patchy patience. What the New Testament commends in Abraham is not that he never wobbled; it is that he was still there at the end, because God was still there.

Obtained, and not yet. At 11:13 the writer will say, these all died in faith, not having received the things promised. Abraham received Isaac, the first fulfilment, not the city or the blessing to all peoples. The promise was kept and not yet finished, which is exactly our position.

How do I wait when God seems to be doing nothing? Abraham’s story answers in three ways. First, remember what God has said, not what you have assumed he would do; Abraham held a promise, not a timetable. Second, keep obeying in the meantime. Abraham kept building altars, kept moving when told, kept praying, and the waiting years were full of ordinary faithfulness. Third, do not try to force the outcome; Hagar was the fruit of impatience, and it brought grief for generations. Waiting on God is not passivity but steady trust that goes on doing the next right thing while the promise ripens.

verseByVerse.quote: For people swear by something greater than themselves, and in all their disputes an oath is final for confirmation. So when God desired to show more convincingly to the heirs of the promise the unchangeable character of his purpose, he guaranteed it with an oath, so that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Something greater than themselves. Human beings are not reliably truthful, so an oath calls something greater to witness, and the matter is closed.

To the heirs of the promise. This is astonishing. God’s bare word is already as reliable as anything in the universe; an oath cannot make him more truthful. The oath adds nothing to God and everything to our confidence, and he swore it for that reason alone. And the beneficiaries are named: the heirs of the promise. The oath sworn on a mountain to one old man is described as made for everyone who would ever inherit it, Abraham and all who share his faith (Galatians 3:29). That includes the congregation hearing this letter, and it includes anyone reading it now.

The unchangeable character of his purpose. “Unchangeable” was used in legal documents of a will that cannot be altered. God’s saving plan cannot change: the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable (Romans 11:29).

He guaranteed it with an oath. The verb (emesiteusen) is literally he mediated, he stood in the middle as guarantor. God made himself the guarantor of his own promise, standing between himself and us, as it were, to pledge that he would keep it. God, that is, put his own name up as the security, so that his promise is as safe as he is. And the pledge did not stay abstract. By another sworn word, You are a priest forever (Psalm 110:4), God made Jesus the guarantor of a better covenant (7:20–22), so that the guarantee given to Abraham now stands in a living person at his right hand.

Two unchangeable things. His word, and his word sworn, because God cannot lie (Titus 1:2). And “impossible” is the word that opened verse 4. The letter’s two impossibilities face each other: it is impossible to restore an apostate, and it is impossible for God to lie. The second is the one to build on.

We who have fled for refuge. The phrase (hoi kataphygontes) is drawn from the cities of refuge (Numbers 35; Joshua 20), where a man who had killed accidentally ran for his life to a walled town, pursued by the avenger of blood. He was safe inside and dead outside, and the running was undignified and absolutely necessary. That is the writer’s picture of a Christian: not a seeker weighing options but a man running for his life to God in Christ, the only place that will hold him.

Strong encouragement. The hope set before us is eternal salvation in God’s presence, like the prize at the end of a race (12:1–2). God swore an oath so that frightened people would keep their grip.

What does fleeing for refuge look like for me? It means coming to Christ as your only safety from God’s just judgment against your sin, and it means coming back to him whenever guilt or fear pursues you. The manslayer did not argue with the avenger or try to prove his innocence on the road; he ran. So when your conscience accuses you, do not try to settle the matter by your own record. Go to Christ in prayer, plead his blood, and rest inside the walls. You do not flee once and then live outside. You live in the city.

But what if my grip on the hope is weak? Then look again at what God has done to strengthen it. He gave two unchangeable things for exactly that reason: for people whose grip was failing. Your safety does not depend on the strength of your hold but on the strength of the city. The manslayer was safe because he was inside, not because he was brave. Hold fast as well as you can, and when you cannot, remember that the one who swore the oath holds you (John 10:29).

For worship. God has given us his word and his oath, and swore it to people running for their lives. In Israel the manslayer could go home only when the high priest died (Numbers 35:25, 28). Our High Priest has died, and the avenger has no claim left; and he lives for ever, so the freedom he won can never be revoked.

verseByVerse.quote: We have this as a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, a hope that enters into the inner place behind the curtain, where Jesus has gone as a forerunner on our behalf, having become a high priest forever after the order of Melchizedek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A sure and steadfast anchor. Early Christians carved the anchor in the catacombs as a symbol of hope. Sure: it will not slip. Steadfast: it will not shift under strain. A bad anchor fails either by breaking or by dragging, and this one does neither.

Behind the curtain. Then the writer does something unusual with the metaphor. An anchor goes down. This one goes up and in. The curtain is the veil of the Most Holy Place (Exodus 26:31–33; Leviticus 16:2, 12), the barrier no one crossed but the high priest, once a year, with blood, where God’s presence dwelt. That is where the anchor is lodged. Not in circumstances, not in the believer’s own steadiness, not even in the visible church. The cable runs out of this world altogether and is made fast inside the sanctuary of God, where nothing can move it.

The storm and the anchorage. A ship in heavy weather is held by ground it cannot see, and the state of the sea has no bearing on the holding. For a congregation whose property had been seized, that is the entire point.
