A forerunner. The metaphor changes again. “Forerunner” (prodromos) is one who runs ahead. The word was used of scouts sent ahead of an army, and preachers have often pictured a small boat carrying a ship’s anchor ahead into a harbour too shallow for the ship, fixing it so the ship could be pulled in, though there is little ancient evidence for the practice. Either way, a forerunner is not merely someone who has arrived; he is someone who goes first so that others follow. The high priest of old went behind the curtain alone and came out again, and nobody followed him. This one went in and stayed, and the rope is attached to us (10:19–20). And he went “on our behalf” (hyper hēmōn): as our representative, so that where he is, we shall be.

A high priest forever. Psalm 110:4 returns for the third time, bringing the writer back to 5:10. His congregation is warned, reassured, anchored and ready, and chapter 7 begins the argument he broke off.

What if I feel no hope at all? Then this verse is for you more than for anyone. The anchor does not depend on the feeling of the sailor. In the worst storm the deck heaves, the crew is frightened and nobody on board feels secure, and the ship holds, because the anchor is fixed somewhere the storm cannot reach. Your hope is not your feeling of hopefulness; it is Christ, alive in God’s presence for you. On days when you feel nothing, tell yourself where he is and what he is doing: he is there, he is your forerunner, and he always lives to intercede for you (7:25).

On a Tuesday. When the bad news comes this week, what do you reach for: your plans, your savings, the approval of the people around you? Every one of those is in the sea. When you feel yourself drifting, pray one sentence that names where your anchor is: Lord Jesus, you are in heaven for me.
verseByVerse.note: The high priest passed behind the curtain into the Most Holy Place once a year, on the Day of Atonement.

7.title: The Order of Melchizedek: A Priest Forever
7.overview:
From two short Old Testament passages, Genesis 14:17–20 and Psalm 110:4, the writer shows that Jesus’ priesthood is greater than Levi’s and replaces it.

The first half (vv. 1–10) reads Genesis: Melchizedek, king and priest in one, received Abraham’s tithe and blessed him. The second half (vv. 11–28) reads the psalm: a priest of a different order, sworn in by oath, who never dies. Every step leads to one sentence: he is able to save to the uttermost.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Melchizedek, and What Abraham Did
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer works through the names, the silence, the tithe and the blessing of Genesis 14 to show that this priest was greater than Abraham and so greater than Levi.
verseByVerse.theology:
Reading the Silence of Scripture

Genesis gives Melchizedek no genealogy, and the writer reads the silence as a portrait of a priesthood that does not rest on descent. Abraham tithed to him and was blessed by him: the lesser by the greater.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Levi, still in Abraham's loins, paid tithes to Melchizedek.

Now: Righteousness comes first, then peace; there is no peace with God that bypasses righteousness.

verseByVerse.quote: For this Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of the Most High God, met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, and to him Abraham apportioned a tenth part of everything. He is first, by translation of his name, king of righteousness, and then he is also king of Salem, that is, king of peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Hebrews 7 is the heart of the letter’s argument that Jesus is a better priest than the priests of Israel. Melchizedek, king of righteousness and king of peace, with no recorded genealogy, birth or death, pictures a priest who continues forever (vv. 1–3). He is greater than Abraham, and so than Levi (vv. 4–10). Psalm 110’s promise of another priest means the Levitical priesthood could not perfect, and a change of priesthood means a change of law (vv. 11–14). Jesus is priest by the power of an indestructible life, sworn in by God’s oath, the guarantor of a better covenant (vv. 15–22). He lives forever, so he is able to save to the uttermost those who come to God through him (vv. 23–25). Holy and exalted, he offered himself once for all (vv. 26–28).

The argument resumes. The argument broken off at 5:11 resumes, and everything now turns on a man who appears in three verses of Genesis (14:18–20) and one line of one psalm (110:4). Chapter 6 ended with Jesus entering behind the curtain as a high priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek (6:20), and chapter 7 explains what that title means.

King of Salem, priest of the Most High God. The episode is Genesis 14. Salem was probably the early name of Jerusalem (Psalm 76:2), the city where David would one day reign and where the temple would stand. And “priest of the Most High God” (El Elyon in Genesis) is the arresting phrase. This is centuries before Sinai, before Levi is born, before there is any Israelite priesthood at all, and here is a king in Canaan who is already a priest of the true God, the creator of heaven and earth, outside the line of Abraham. Abraham recognises him as such. A priest and king in one person, as Christ is.

Met Abraham. Abraham had just rescued Lot by defeating four kings (Genesis 14:1–17), and on the way home a stranger comes out with bread and wine, blesses him in the name of God Most High, receives a tenth of the spoil, and vanishes from the narrative.

A tenth part. That detail will carry the argument of verses 4–10. Abraham, the man to whom the promises were made, handed over a tithe, and a tithe is what you give to a superior.

King of righteousness. The writer works on the names, reading them as the text’s own authors read names, as carrying significance. Malki-tsedeq is king of righteousness. Christ is the righteous King of whom the prophets spoke, the branch of David who would be called the LORD is our righteousness (Jeremiah 23:5–6).

King of peace. Salem is shalem, related to shalom, peace. Christ is the Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6), who makes peace between God and sinners and himself is our peace (Ephesians 2:14). And the writer presses the order: first, and then. Righteousness first, then peace. That is not decoration but the shape of the gospel, and the order cannot be reversed. There is no peace with God that does not come by way of righteousness: righteousness and peace kiss each other (Psalm 85:10), and since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God (Romans 5:1). That is why the cross was necessary, and why a merely merciful God who waived the problem of sin would have given us neither. The reason is simple: God cannot make peace with sinners by looking the other way, because a holy Judge does not pretend wrong was never done. So the wrong had to be put right first: Christ bore its penalty and gives his own righteousness to all who trust him (2 Corinthians 5:21). To be justified is exactly that, to be declared right with God on the ground of what Christ has done, and peace follows as the fruit.

Where Christians differ: are believers required to tithe? Some teach that the tithe, a tenth of income, is binding on Christians, since Abraham tithed before the law of Moses, Jacob vowed a tenth (Genesis 28:22), and Jesus told the Pharisees not to neglect the tithe (Matthew 23:23). Others answer that Abraham’s tenth is recorded as a single gift from the spoils, not a rule; that the tithes the law commanded belonged to the Levitical system that this chapter says has changed (v. 12); and that Jesus was speaking to men still under that law. This commentary’s view: Abraham’s tithe was a voluntary act of honour on a single occasion. The New Testament does not command a fixed percentage. It teaches generous, regular, proportional, cheerful giving (1 Corinthians 16:2; 2 Corinthians 8:1–15; 9:6–7). A tenth is a good starting guide for many, but Christians under grace should often give more, not less, and never under compulsion.

How did Melchizedek know the true God, outside Abraham’s family? Genesis does not tell us, and we should not invent an answer. What we know is that the knowledge of God had not yet died out everywhere after the flood, and that God is free to make himself known where he will. Melchizedek is one of a few such figures, like Jethro the priest of Midian later on. His existence is a quiet sign that the God of Abraham was never a tribal deity. He is God Most High, possessor of heaven and earth, and the blessing to all nations was always his intention.

Was the bread and wine a kind of Lord’s Supper? Not in the sense of a sacrifice. Genesis says Melchizedek brought out bread and wine to a tired army returning from battle; it was hospitality and refreshment, and Hebrews, which makes so much of every detail, never mentions the bread and wine at all. Christians have long seen in it a beautiful foreshadowing of the table where Christ, our priest-king, feeds his people. But it gives no support to the idea that the Supper is an offering of Christ’s body by a priest. The writer’s whole point in this chapter is that Christ offered himself once for all (v. 27).

verseByVerse.quote: He is without father or mother or genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but resembling the Son of God he continues a priest forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without father or mother. This verse has been read as meaning Melchizedek was a supernatural being, an angel or an appearance of the pre-incarnate Christ. What the writer is actually doing is reading the silence of Scripture, and it was a recognised way of arguing that his readers would have followed easily. The three words are apatōr, without father, amētōr, without mother, and agenealogētos, without genealogy. Genesis is a book of genealogies. It tells you who fathered whom, how long they lived and when they died, for chapter after chapter. Melchizedek walks into the narrative with none of it. No father, no mother, no ancestry, no birth, no death.

Why the silence matters. For a priest that absence is extraordinary, because the Levitical priesthood was entirely a matter of documentation: after the exile men who could not produce the records were excluded from the priesthood (Ezra 2:61–63). Melchizedek has no papers whatever, and is a priest of the Most High God.

Neither beginning of days nor end of life. The writer takes the silence as deliberate: a portrait drawn with the genealogy left out, to sketch a priesthood that does not depend on descent and does not end with a funeral.

Resembling the Son of God. “Resembling” (aphōmoiōmenos) is made like, made to resemble. The direction of the comparison matters, and it is easy to get backwards. The writer does not say Christ is like Melchizedek. He says Melchizedek was made to resemble the Son of God. The eternal reality came first; the man in Genesis is the sketch. The Son truly has no beginning or end; Melchizedek only appears that way in the record.

He continues a priest forever. True of Melchizedek only in the sense that the text never records him stopping. True of Christ absolutely, and that is the point of the whole chapter.

In the flow. Verse 3 lays down the two threads the chapter will pull: no genealogy (vv. 11–17, a priesthood resting on who he is) and no end of life (vv. 16, 23–25, a priest who lives for ever and so can save for ever).

Where Christians differ: was Melchizedek Christ himself? Some believe Melchizedek was a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ (a Christophany), or an angel. This commentary’s view: Melchizedek was most likely a real, historical human king and priest, whose recorded life God arranged to foreshadow Christ. The text says he was made like the Son of God, which would be odd if he were the Son: a thing does not resemble itself. He is a type, a living prophecy, not the reality itself. His lack of recorded genealogy is the point, not a claim that he literally had no parents.

Is it fair to build an argument on what Scripture does not say? Yes, when the silence is part of the shape God gave the text. The writer is not saying that Melchizedek had no parents; he is saying that God, who inspired Genesis, chose to present him without them, in a book where almost everyone else gets a genealogy, and then named him in a psalm about an eternal priest. And the writer never rests his case on silence alone. His foundation is the plain statement of Psalm 110:4, sworn by God. The silence of Genesis illustrates what the psalm declares.

On a Tuesday. Your standing with God does not depend on your pedigree either. Some Christians feel second-class because they did not grow up in church; others quietly rely on their Christian background. Neither counts in the priesthood of Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Genesis records no parents, birth or death for Melchizedek. The writer draws out the meaning of that silence, not a claim that Melchizedek had no parents.

verseByVerse.quote: See how great this man was to whom Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth of the spoils! And those descendants of Levi who receive the priestly office have a commandment in the law to take tithes from the people, that is, from their brothers, though these also are descended from Abraham. But this man who does not have his descent from them received tithes from Abraham and blessed him who had the promises. It is beyond dispute that the inferior is blessed by the superior.
verseByVerse.commentary:
See how great this man was. “How great” asks for a measurement. The argument builds on two customs the readers understood perfectly: who pays tithes to whom, and who blesses whom.

The patriarch. Not simply Abraham, but the patriarch, the greatest name a Jewish reader possessed, and the spoils are literally the top of the heap, the choicest part.

The descendants of Levi. Under the law of Moses, the Levites received tithes from their own relatives, the other tribes, by a written command (Numbers 18:21–26).

Not descended from them. Melchizedek was not a Levite and had no legal warrant to collect, and the man who paid him was Abraham himself. It was given, not levied.

Blessed him who had the promises. The second and stronger argument. Abraham, the bearer of the blessing for all the families of the earth (Genesis 12:2–3), received a blessing from a stranger.

Beyond dispute. “Beyond dispute” is literally without any contradiction (chōris pasēs antilogias). The writer states it as a self-evident social fact, and in that world it was. In a formal blessing, blessing runs downhill: father to son, as Isaac blessed Jacob and Jacob blessed his sons (Genesis 27; 48–49); priest to people, as Aaron blessed Israel (Numbers 6:22–27); king to subject. So Abraham, who was carrying the promise, the father of the nation, the man in whom all families of the earth would be blessed, put himself in the lower position twice in a single meeting, and Genesis records it without comment. The writer’s readers had been reading that chapter all their lives and may never have noticed what it implied.

Why does it matter to me who was greater than whom? Because the readers were tempted to go back to the Levitical priests as if they were the real thing. The writer shows from their own Scriptures that before Levi was born, Abraham himself bowed to a greater priest. If Abraham honoured the shadow, how much more should we honour the reality? Every argument in this chapter is designed to make you see that leaving Christ for anything else, however old and venerable, is trading the greater for the lesser. And it means that the blessing you receive from Christ is a blessing from above, from the greatest, with all of God’s authority behind it.

verseByVerse.quote: In the one case tithes are received by mortal men, but in the other case, by one of whom it is testified that he lives. One might even say that Levi himself, who receives tithes, paid tithes through Abraham, for he was still in the loins of his ancestor when Melchizedek met him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mortal men. “Mortal” is literally dying men. The Levitical priesthood was a relay: Aaron died on Mount Hor, Eleazar took the robes, and so on for well over a thousand years. The system was designed around mortality.

It is testified that he lives. Not who lives, but of whom it is testified that he lives: Genesis records no death, and Psalm 110 says, You are a priest forever. This points to Christ, who truly lives forever (v. 16).

One might even say. The writer knows he is pressing hard, and offers this as a way of seeing the thing, not a knock-down proof.

In the loins of his ancestor. In the Hebrew way of reckoning, a descendant is present in his ancestor and acts in him. The whole Levitical priesthood bowed to Melchizedek when Abraham did.

Representation is the logic of the Bible. That way of thinking is not a curiosity. It is the logic of the whole Bible. It is why the sin of one man could involve a race, and why the obedience of one man can make many righteous (Romans 5:12–19). A modern reader who finds representative solidarity strange will find most of the doctrine of salvation strange, since it all runs on the same principle. So the conclusion stands: the tribe that would one day collect Israel’s tithes had already, in its ancestor, paid them to somebody else. The Levitical priesthood acknowledged a greater priesthood before it existed, and Genesis 14 has been sitting in the Torah, the five books of Moses, all along saying so.

Is it fair that I should be counted in someone else? It can feel unfair when the head is Adam, whose sin brought death to all. But the same principle is the only reason anyone is saved. If God did not deal with people through a representative, Christ could not have stood in our place, his death could not count as ours, and his righteousness could not be credited to us. No one complains that it is unfair to be counted righteous in Christ. The question that matters is not whether we are represented, because everyone is, but by whom: Adam or Christ.

On a Tuesday. The man who represented an Israelite before God would one day be carried out. Think about whom you lean on spiritually: a pastor, a parent, a gifted friend. Thank God for them, and let them point you past themselves to the one representative who will never be carried out.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–28 — A Priest Forever, and the Change That Follows
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the writer turns to Psalm 110:4 and draws out its words one by one: another priest, of a different order, for ever, sworn by oath. Together they bring the reader to the priest who saves completely, always intercedes, and offered himself once for all.
verseByVerse.theology:
Change the Priesthood and the Law Must Follow

The law rested on the Levitical priesthood, and God has replaced that priesthood by oath with a priest who holds office by the power of an indestructible life.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The former priests were many, because death stopped each one.

Now: He is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to intercede for them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if perfection had been attainable through the Levitical priesthood (for under it the people received the law), what further need would there have been for another priest to arise after the order of Melchizedek, rather than one named after the order of Aaron? For when there is a change in the priesthood, there is necessarily a change in the law as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If perfection had been attainable. Now the argument turns from Genesis to the psalm, and the question is put with real force. “Perfection” (teleiōsis) means completion, the bringing of a thing to its intended goal: the same root as made perfect in 2:10 and 5:9, and a keyword of the letter. Perfection here means bringing people fully into God’s presence, with sins dealt with completely and consciences cleansed (9:9; 10:1, 14). The question is not whether the Levitical priesthood was good, but whether it could finish anything. It could not.

Under it the people received the law. The law established the priesthood, and the priesthood administered the law. They stand or fall together.

What further need would there have been for another priest to arise after the order of Melchizedek? The logic is simple. Psalm 110 was written by David, centuries into the Levitical system, and in it God announces a priest of a different order. You do not announce a replacement for something that is working. If the Levitical priesthood had been sufficient, why would God promise a new priest of a different kind? The very existence of the promise is evidence that the arrangement it replaces was not final.

Rather than one named after the order of Aaron? The new priest is not in Aaron’s line. God did not promise a better Aaron, a reformed Levitical priesthood with holier men in it. He promised a different order altogether.

A change in the law. “Change” is transfer, the word used of moving something elsewhere. Since the law of Moses was tied to the Levitical priesthood, a new priesthood means the whole Mosaic covenant arrangement, with its sacrifices, priesthood and ceremonies, changes.

What it meant for the first readers. They were being drawn back to the temple, the sacrifices, the food laws and the calendar, and told that these were God’s own commands. The writer agrees that they were. But the whole structure was attached to a priesthood, God himself has changed the priesthood, and the law therefore cannot stand as it did. Not that the law was bad, but that its foundation has been replaced by the God who laid it, and a building does not outlive its foundation.

Does this mean the Ten Commandments are abolished? No. The law that changes is the law bound up with the priesthood: the sacrifices, the temple, the purity rules and the calendar. Reformed Christians have long distinguished the ceremonial law, fulfilled in Christ and set aside; the civil law, given to Israel as a nation; and the moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments, which still shows believers how to love God and neighbour (Matthew 5:17–19; Romans 13:8–10). Some Christians prefer to say that the whole law of Moses has given way to the law of Christ; but they agree that its moral demands come to us again in the New Testament, and the new covenant writes God’s law on the heart (8:10). What changes is not God’s standard but the way to him.

Should Christians keep the Old Testament food laws and festivals, then? Not as a duty before God. Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19), and Paul calls the festivals, new moons and food rules a shadow of the things to come, whose substance belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16–17). A Christian may eat or abstain, and may find it instructive to learn about Passover or the Day of Atonement, because they point so clearly to Christ. What he must not do is treat them as necessary for acceptance with God or as a mark of a superior holiness. That was exactly the pull these readers felt, and the writer says it means going back to a priesthood God has retired.

On a Tuesday. Old-covenant instincts survive in much of our religion: the feeling that a bad week puts you outside until you have made up for it. Keep God’s commandments gladly, as his child, and come to him through Christ alone, today, as you are.

verseByVerse.quote: For the one of whom these things are spoken belonged to another tribe, from which no one has ever served at the altar. For it is evident that our Lord was descended from Judah, and in connection with that tribe Moses said nothing about priests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Another tribe. Under the law, priesthood was a matter of tribe, and the boundary was absolute. Jesus was not from Levi.

No one has served at the altar. No man from Judah was ever appointed to the altar, and when King Uzziah presumed to burn incense in the temple, he was struck with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26:16–21).

Descended from Judah. The word “evident” (prodēlon) means clearly known, obvious. It is common knowledge, not a claim requiring proof. The genealogies were public (Matthew 1:1–16; Luke 3:23–33), and the expectation had always been that the deliverer would come from Judah and from David: the sceptre shall not depart from Judah (Genesis 49:10), and he is the Lion of the tribe of Judah (Revelation 5:5). And the word for “descended” (anatetalken) is lovely: it is used of the sun rising and of a shoot springing up. The prophets used both pictures of the Messiah, the sunrise from on high (Luke 1:78) and the branch from Jesse’s stump (Isaiah 11:1).

The two requirements collide. The Messiah had to be from Judah, because the promise said so. A priest had to be from Levi, because the law said so. And Psalm 110 says the Messiah will be a priest.

Moses said nothing. Again the argument runs on a silence. There was no provision, because the priesthood being announced was never going to run through the law at all.

The objection conceded. Anyone defending the old arrangement could say, correctly, that Jesus had no right to the Levitical priesthood. The writer concedes it: Jesus holds a different office, established by an oath the law knew nothing about.

Why did God arrange it so that the Messiah would come from the wrong tribe for priesthood? So that no one could mistake Christ’s priesthood for a continuation of the old one. If Jesus had been a Levite, his ministry could have been read as the best chapter of the old system. By bringing him from Judah, God made it plain that something new had come: a king who is also a priest, uniting in one person the two offices that Israel had always kept apart. The kings of Israel could rule but not atone; the priests could atone in shadow but not rule. Christ does both, perfectly and for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: This becomes even more evident when another priest arises in the likeness of Melchizedek, who has become a priest, not on the basis of a legal requirement concerning bodily descent, but by the power of an indestructible life. For it is witnessed of him, “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Another priest. The change becomes clearer still in the kind of priest promised. “Another” (heteros) means another of a different kind: not a successor but a different species of priest.

Not by bodily descent. Literally a law of a fleshly commandment: a rule about physical pedigree. Not character, devotion or gifts, but birth. A godly Israelite from the wrong tribe could not serve; an indifferent one from the right family could.

An indestructible life. Against that stands “the power of an indestructible life”, and power (dynamis) is the word for the mighty works of 2:4. The word akatalytos means undissolvable, incapable of being broken up or destroyed; it is related to the word for taking down a tent or pulling down a building (2 Corinthians 5:1). Not merely a life that happens to go on, but one that cannot be ended, and the resurrection is behind the phrase. Death did its worst and could not dissolve it. As Peter preached at Pentecost, death could not keep its hold on him (Acts 2:24). His priesthood is based not on genealogy but on who he is and on his victory over death.

Two qualifications side by side. One priesthood rests on records of ancestry that can be lost, as they were after the exile (Ezra 2:61–62). The other is guaranteed by an empty tomb.

It is witnessed of him. Everything hangs on “forever”: only someone with an indestructible life could be a priest forever. He needs no successor and cannot be replaced by a better one.

What difference does an indestructible life make to me? It means your priest cannot be taken from you. Every human helper you have can be lost: by death, distance, illness, failure or simply their own limits. Christ cannot. His care for you does not depend on his health, his mood or his circumstances, and it will not be interrupted by any crisis in your life or in the world. It also means his life is the guarantee of yours. Because I live, you also will live, he said (John 14:19). The life that could not be dissolved is the life he shares with everyone united to him.

What should this mean for how churches choose leaders? It is a warning against choosing people for pedigree. The old priesthood ran on bloodline; the new people of God are not to be led on the basis of family, wealth, education or connections, but on character and gifts given by the Spirit (1 Timothy 3:1–7). A pastor’s son is not thereby fit to be a pastor, and a convert from a broken home is not thereby disqualified. The church that follows a priest qualified by an indestructible life should look for leaders marked by his life in them.

For worship. Men tried to destroy our High Priest’s life with nails and a spear and sealed it in a tomb, and on the third day it broke every bond. That same life is now spent, without pause, in priestly care for us. Every other priest’s ministry ended at a funeral; his goes on from an empty tomb for ever.

verseByVerse.quote: For on the one hand, a former commandment is set aside because of its weakness and uselessness (for the law made nothing perfect); but on the other hand, a better hope is introduced, through which we draw near to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A former commandment is set aside. “Set aside” (athetēsis) was a legal term for annulling a decree. These are strong words about God’s own law, and they must be read exactly: the writer is not saying the law was a mistake or evil.

Because of its weakness and uselessness. “Weakness” (asthenes) is powerlessness; “uselessness” (anōpheles) is unprofitableness. These are judgments about capacity for a particular purpose. Not that the law was bad, but that it was weak for this purpose: it could not achieve full cleansing and access to God. The law was perfectly effective at what it was given to do. It exposed sin, regulated a nation and pointed forward. It was useless for making anybody perfect, which it never claimed to do. A thermometer is useless for heating a room, and the fault is not in the thermometer. And the weakness lay in the flesh it worked through: what the law, weakened by the flesh, could not do, God did by sending his own Son (Romans 8:3).

The law made nothing perfect. Not nobody: nothing. The law pointed to perfection but could not provide it (10:1); it was a guardian until Christ came (Galatians 3:24).

A better hope. “Better” is the letter’s signature word: a better priest, covenant, promises, sacrifices, country. The better hope is the new covenant hope in Christ, ushered in like a new heir brought into a house.

We draw near. And then the purpose clause, which is where the whole chapter has been going. That is the point of all of it: the genealogies, the tithes, the tribes, the oath. Not to win an argument about priesthood but to get people into the presence of God. The old system existed to manage distance: curtains, courts, and a single man admitted once a year. The new one exists to remove it, so that every believer can draw near (4:16; 10:19–22). “Draw near” (engizomen) is the letter’s word for what a Christian actually does, and everything else is scaffolding around it. Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you (James 4:8). And this exposes a quiet idol of religious people: we can come to love the scaffolding, the routines and the sense of being in the right place, more than the God it was built to bring us to.

If the law made nothing perfect, why did God give it? Because it was never meant to make perfect. It was given to show sin for what it is (Romans 3:20; 7:7), to restrain evil, to set Israel apart, and above all to point forward: every sacrifice, every washing, every feast and every priest was a picture of Christ. Like scaffolding round a building, it was essential until the building stood, and then it came down. The law did not fail; it did its work, which was to lead us to Christ, so that we might be justified by faith (Galatians 3:24).

What does drawing near to God actually look like? It is the whole life of faith gathered into a single act: coming to God, through Christ, with nothing in your hands. You draw near when you pray, speaking to God as Father in Jesus’ name; when you confess sin and receive his forgiveness; when you hear his word with faith; when you come to the Lord’s Table; when you worship with his people. And you draw near without the old fear, because the way is open. You do not need a priest, a holy place, a special mood or a good week. You need Christ, and in him you have everything.

On a Tuesday. Much of our praying is errands: things to get done, people to ask about, a list to get through. Those are good, and the throne invites them. But drawing near also means simply coming to be with God, through Christ, with no performance, no record of good deeds and no promise to do better: Father, I come in Jesus’ name, and then staying a while. The curtain is open, and you are welcome.

verseByVerse.quote: And it was not without an oath. For those who formerly became priests were made such without an oath, but this one was made a priest with an oath by the one who said to him: “The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind, ’You are a priest forever.’” This makes Jesus the guarantor of a better covenant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not without an oath. The argument about Abraham in chapter 6 now applies to the priesthood. God does not swear because his plain word could be doubted, but because we are slow to believe it; the oath is his kindness to weak faith (6:17).

Made priests without an oath. Aaron and his sons were appointed by command (Exodus 28–29). God legislated the Levitical priesthood; he never once swore to it.

With an oath. Psalm 110:4 again, now with the clause previously left out: God swears, and will not reverse the decision.

Will not change his mind. The KJV adds after the order of Melchisedec here, following later manuscripts; the earliest stop at for ever. An arrangement made by command can be amended by a later command. An arrangement established by the oath of God cannot be. Christ’s priesthood is irrevocable.

The guarantor. The word is engyos, a legal and commercial term used only here in the New Testament: a surety, the person who stands behind an obligation with his own property and his own person. If the debtor fails, the guarantor pays. Judah offered himself to his father in exactly this way for Benjamin: I will be a pledge of his safety; from my hand you shall require him (Genesis 43:9), and when the moment came he offered to become a slave in the boy’s place (Genesis 44:32–33). Jesus personally guarantees that the new covenant will be fulfilled. He stands surety for his people: he pledges that their debts are paid and that God’s promises to them will be kept.

Why a guarantor matters. A covenant has two parties, and covenants fail because one of them does, which is exactly what happened to the first one: they did not continue in my covenant (8:9). Jesus is not the covenant’s administrator or its witness. He is the surety, and he stands behind it with himself. That means the new covenant cannot fail on our side, because our side has a guarantor who has already paid. The word names one of the strongest securities a first-century reader knew: not a document but a person. And “better covenant” (kreittonos diathēkēs) is the first mention of covenant in Hebrews; chapter 8 will develop it as the new covenant of Jeremiah 31.

What is a covenant? A covenant is a binding relationship God establishes with promises, sealed in a solemn way, and more than a contract. The new covenant, established in Christ’s blood (Luke 22:20), Christ both makes by his death and guarantees by his life. (See 1 Corinthians 11:25 for the fuller answer.)

On a Tuesday. When your failures make you wonder whether God will finally give up on you, remember that the new covenant does not rest on your keeping it but on Christ’s guaranteeing it. Say it to yourself in the words of this verse: Jesus is the guarantor. Then, because you are secure and his Spirit is in you, take up the obedience you have been avoiding. A child who knows his place in the family is safe obeys from love, not from fear of being sent away.

For worship. The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind. Judah pledged himself for one brother and was never required to pay; the Son of God stood surety for a great multitude, and everything was required of him, and he paid it with his own blood. There is no security in the universe stronger than that.

verseByVerse.quote: The former priests were many in number, because they were prevented by death from continuing in office, but he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever. Consequently, he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many in number. Josephus, the first-century Jewish historian, counted eighty-three high priests from Aaron to AD 70: eighty-three funerals, one after another.

Prevented by death. Death kept interrupting. Aaron died on Mount Hor, and his son was dressed in his garments (Numbers 20:23–29). Every priest’s intercession ended at death.

Permanently. The word (aparabaton) can mean non-transferable. He has no successor, because he never dies.

To the uttermost. And everything in the chapter now cashes out in a single sentence. “Able” (dynatai) is has power. “To the uttermost” (eis to panteles) can mean completely or forever, and the ambiguity is a gift: both are true. He saves entirely, leaving nothing unfinished, and he saves permanently, without expiry. Nothing in a person is beyond its reach and no stretch of time is outside it. There is no sinner too far gone, no sin too great, no time too long.

Those who draw near to God through him. The only qualification named. Not those who understand, or who have never failed. Those who come, and keep coming, through Christ alone (John 14:6).

He always lives to intercede. And there is the ground, and the place to rest. What is Christ doing now? Hebrews answers: he is praying for his people, and he never stops. “Always lives” is pantote zōn; “make intercession” (entynchanein) is to plead, intervene, appeal on behalf of. Christ’s intercession is not begging an unwilling Father, but his presence before the Father as the one whose sacrifice has been accepted, continually presenting his finished work on behalf of his people and asking for all they need (Romans 8:34; 1 John 2:1). His intercession guarantees their perseverance: he prayed for Peter that his faith would not fail (Luke 22:32), and he prays for all his own (John 17:9, 15, 20, 24). This is the perseverance of the saints: those God has truly brought to himself he keeps trusting him to the end. They may stumble badly, as Peter did, but they will not finally fall away, because the one who began a good work in them will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6).

At three in the morning. At three in the morning, when a Christian is too tired or too ashamed to pray for himself, there is somebody at the right hand of God who is praying for him and has not paused. The salvation reaches to the uttermost because the interceding does.

Do Christians, then, need human priests? No. If Christ holds his priesthood permanently and offered himself once for all (v. 27), no other mediator is needed and no sacrifice is to be repeated. Scripture knows only one go-between for us before God: the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). Every believer draws near to God through him (4:16; 10:19–22), and the whole church is a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9). Pastors are shepherds and teachers, not priests. We may and should ask one another to pray for us, but no believer needs anyone except Christ to stand between him and God.

If Jesus is praying for me, do I still need to pray? Yes, and his praying is the reason your prayers count. You pray in his name, which means your prayers rise to the Father carried by his intercession, made acceptable by his blood. His intercession does not make yours unnecessary any more than a father’s love makes a child’s requests unnecessary. And on the days when you cannot find words, both he and the Spirit pray for you (Romans 8:26–27, 34). You are never praying alone.

Can I be beyond his saving? Not if you come to God through him. The verse names no limit except coming. Whatever you have done, however long you have been away, however many times you have fallen in the same place, the word is uttermost. The only person beyond his saving is the one who will not come. If you are coming, or want to come, you are exactly the person this verse is about.

verseByVerse.quote: For it was indeed fitting that we should have such a high priest, holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens. He has no need, like those high priests, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people, since he did this once for all when he offered up himself. For the law appoints men in their weakness as high priests, but the word of the oath, which came later than the law, appoints a Son who has been made perfect forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Such a high priest. “Fitting” is the word of 2:10: it suited the character of God to provide him. Five descriptions follow, moving outward from his character to his location.

Holy, innocent, unstained. The first word (hosios) is not the usual one for holiness but a term for devout, pious, wholly given to God; it describes his Godward disposition. The second is literally without evil (akakos): guileless, harmless, containing no malice toward people. The third is undefiled (amiantos), untouched by any pollution. The high priest had to avoid ritual defilement, and could not even go near a dead body, not even his own father’s (Leviticus 21:10–15). Jesus was free from all moral defilement. He touched lepers and the dead, and instead of being defiled by them, he made them clean.

Separated from sinners. This requires care, because it can be read to contradict everything the Gospels show. “Separated” (kechōrismenos) is a perfect tense: set apart, and remaining so. The man who was called a friend of tax collectors and sinners, who ate with them (Luke 15:2), is not being described as aloof. The separation is moral and, since the ascension, positional. He was among sinners without becoming one, utterly different from them in character, and is now exalted beyond their reach to harm him.

Exalted above the heavens. Raised to the highest place (4:14; Ephesians 4:10). The old high priest went through a curtain; this one has passed through the heavens and sits above them.

No need to offer sacrifices daily. Priests offered morning and evening (Exodus 29:38–42), and the high priest yearly. The repetition proved their inadequacy (10:1–4, 11).

First for his own sins. As in 5:3. Jesus had no sins of his own.

Once for all. “Once for all” (ephapax) is once, finally, never to be repeated: a single, unrepeatable, completely sufficient act (9:12, 26, 28; 10:10). It is one of the letter’s great words, and it will dominate chapters 9 and 10. And the last words are where the chapter arrives. Every other priest offered something else: a bull, a goat, a lamb. This one had nothing to bring but himself, and brought it. This is the first explicit statement in Hebrews that Christ’s sacrifice was his own self. Priest and sacrifice in the same person, something no priest of Israel had ever been or could be.

A Son made perfect. The chapter closes on its two contrasts: weak men against a Son, and a temporary command against a later oath. Psalm 110 came centuries after the law of Moses, and God does not swear to things he means to revise. “Made perfect” is a perfect tense, as in 2:10 and 5:9: fully qualified, forever.

In the flow. The whole chapter is gathered up here, and the next three are opened: the sanctuary where he serves (chapter 8) and the once-for-all offering of himself (chapters 9 and 10). 8:1 will call this the main point.

Where Christians differ: is Christ’s sacrifice re-presented in the Mass? Roman Catholic teaching holds that the Mass (the Catholic celebration of the Lord’s Supper) is the same sacrifice of Calvary made present again in an unbloody manner, offered for the living and the dead. Catholics mean by this to honour Christ’s one sacrifice, not to add to it, and the disagreement should be stated with care. This commentary’s view: Hebrews insists that Christ offered himself “once for all,” and that unlike the old priests he has no need to offer repeatedly (7:27; 9:25–28; 10:10–18). Where there is forgiveness, there is no longer any offering for sin (10:18). The Supper is a memorial of Christ’s one sacrifice and more than a memorial: by faith and through the Spirit believers truly feed on Christ, spiritually, not physically (1 Corinthians 10:16; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 30.7; the Westminster Confession 29.7). It is not a repeated sacrifice or a re-offering of it.

Why does a sinless Son need to be made perfect? Because perfect here does not mean morally improved but completed for a task. Jesus was always without sin. But to be our high priest he had to become man, live a life of obedience, suffer, die, rise and ascend. When all of that was done, he was made perfect: fully and finally qualified, having finished everything a priest must do for sinners. A fully trained surgeon who has completed the operation has not become a better man; he has done the work. Christ has done it, and his qualification will never lapse.

If he offered himself once for all, what does that mean when I fail again? It means there is no new sacrifice to be made for you, and none needed. When you confess sin, you are not asking Christ to be offered again; you are resting on the offering already made, which covers your past, present and future sins. Repentance is real and necessary, but it is not payment. The payment was once, and it was enough. Come back to the cross not to add to it but to receive from it again what it has already accomplished.

On a Tuesday. We often try to offer something more for our sins: an extra effort at religion, a period of feeling bad, a promise to God that we will make up for it. Every one of those is a small attempt at a daily sacrifice. Stop offering. Confess, thank him that the offering is finished, and then go and serve him out of gratitude rather than debt. The Supper you take on Sunday is a remembrance of a finished work, not a top-up.

He is first, by translation of his name, king of righteousness, and then he is also king of Salem, that is, king of peace.<sup>3</sup>He is without father or mother or genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but resembling the Son of God he continues a priest forever.<sup>4</sup>See how great this man was to whom Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth of the spoils!<sup>5</sup>And those descendants of Levi who receive the priestly office have a commandment in the law to take tithes from the people, that is, from their brothers, though these also are descended from Abraham.<sup>6</sup>But this man who does not have his descent from them received tithes from Abraham and blessed him who had the promises.<sup>7</sup>It is beyond dispute that the inferior is blessed by the superior.<sup>8</sup>In the one case tithes are received by mortal men, but in the other case, by one of whom it is testified that he lives.<sup>9</sup>One might even say that Levi himself, who receives tithes, paid tithes through Abraham,<sup>10</sup>for he was still in the loins of his ancestor when Melchizedek met him.<sup>11</sup>Now if perfection had been attainable through the Levitical priesthood (for under it the people received the law), what further need would there have been for another priest to arise after the order of Melchizedek, rather than one named after the order of Aaron?<sup>12</sup>For when there is a change in the priesthood, there is necessarily a change in the law as well.<sup>13</sup>For the one of whom these things are spoken belonged to another tribe, from which no one has ever served at the altar.<sup>14</sup>For it is evident that our Lord was descended from Judah, and in connection with that tribe Moses said nothing about priests.<sup>15</sup>This becomes even more evident when another priest arises in the likeness of Melchizedek,<sup>16</sup>who has become a priest, not on the basis of a legal requirement concerning bodily descent, but by the power of an indestructible life.<sup>17</sup>For it is witnessed of him, “You are a priest forever, after the order of Melchizedek.”<sup>18</sup>For on the one hand, a former commandment is set aside because of its weakness and uselessness<sup>19</sup>(for the law made nothing perfect); but on the other hand, a better hope is introduced, through which we draw near to God.<sup>20</sup>And it was not without an oath. For those who formerly became priests were made such without an oath,<sup>21</sup>but this one was made a priest with an oath by the one who said to him: “The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind, ’You are a priest forever.’”<sup>22</sup>This makes Jesus the guarantor of a better covenant.<sup>23</sup>The former priests were many in number, because they were prevented by death from continuing in office,<sup>24</sup>but he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever.<sup>25</sup>Consequently, he is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to make intercession for them.<sup>26</sup>For it was indeed fitting that we should have such a high priest, holy, innocent, unstained, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens.<sup>27</sup>He has no need, like those high priests, to offer sacrifices daily, first for his own sins and then for those of the people, since he did this once for all when he offered up himself.<sup>28</sup>For the law appoints men in their weakness as high priests, but the word of the oath, which came later than the law, appoints a Son who has been made perfect forever.

8.title: A Better Covenant: Written on the Heart
8.overview:
Chapter 8 caps the argument about priesthood: a better Priest ministers in a better sanctuary under a better covenant. The “main point” (v. 1) is that our high priest is seated at God’s right hand, serving in the true tent, of which the tabernacle Moses built was a copy and shadow (Exodus 25:40).

The better covenant is then proved from Jeremiah 31:31–34, quoted in full. It promised a new covenant in which God himself undertakes to change hearts and forgive. By calling it new, God made the old one old, and the readers have nothing to go back to.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — A Minister in the True Tent
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer sums up seven chapters in one point: the high priest we have, and where he serves. The earthly tent was a copy of a heavenly original, and verse 6 ties Christ’s better ministry to the better covenant that the rest of the chapter explains.
verseByVerse.theology:
Copy, Shadow, and the Pattern on the Mountain

The earthly tent was a copy of what Moses was shown. Christ ministers in the true tent, and the covenant he mediates is better because it rests on better promises.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Readers grieving the loss of the temple had not been shut out of the sanctuary.

Now: They had been let into the one the sanctuary pictured, where their high priest is seated.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the point in what we are saying is this: we have such a high priest, one who is seated at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven, a minister in the holy places, in the true tent that the Lord set up, not man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Hebrews 8 sums up the argument so far and introduces the new covenant. We have a high priest seated at God’s right hand, serving in the true sanctuary (vv. 1–2). On earth he would not be a priest at all, for the Levitical priests serve there in a copy and shadow of the heavenly sanctuary (vv. 3–5). His ministry is as much better as the covenant he mediates (v. 6). God promised through Jeremiah a new covenant: his laws written on their hearts, all knowing him, and their sins remembered no more (vv. 7–12). By calling it new, he has made the first one old (v. 13). The readers have not lost the temple; they have been given what the temple was always about.

The point. The word (kephalaion) means the chief thing, and also the sum of an account, the total at the bottom of the column. After seven chapters of argument, here is the bottom line.

We have such a high priest. We have: possession, present tense, belonging to the frightened congregation hearing this read. Why would they return to the old priesthood, when they already have this one?

Seated at the right hand. The seated posture (ekathisen) has been in the letter since 1:3, and by now the reader knows what it signifies: his work is finished (10:12). The Levitical priests stood daily at a work that never ended (10:11). And the seat is at the right hand of the throne, the place of supreme authority, Psalm 110:1 again. This priest is not waiting on the throne’s pleasure; he shares its authority. And the Majesty is a reverent way of naming God himself, the holy one whose glory once filled the tent so that even Moses could not go in (Exodus 40:34–35). The man who sits at his right hand is not tolerated in that light; he belongs there.

A minister in the holy places. The word is leitourgos, from which we get liturgy: someone performing priestly service for others. The one who sits on the throne is enthroned and still at work for us.

The true tent. There is a real sanctuary, and it is not in Jerusalem. “True” (alēthinos) does not mean genuine as against fraudulent; the tabernacle was not a fake. It means original as against derivative. Moses built a good copy. The Lord himself pitched this tent, not human hands (9:11, 24).

The answer to their grief. For readers grieving the loss of access to the temple, perhaps shut out by their own families for following Jesus, this is a large answer. You have not been shut out of the sanctuary. You have been let into the one it was a picture of, and there is a man of your own flesh and blood sitting in it.

If my high priest is in heaven, is he far away from me? No. He is far above, but not far off. Being in heaven means he is in the place of all power and all access, not in a distant room out of earshot. He sympathises with our weaknesses (4:15), he intercedes for us always (7:25), and by his Spirit he is with his people to the end of the age (Matthew 28:20). His being in heaven is the guarantee that our prayers reach the throne, because the one who presents them is sitting at the Father’s right hand. A high priest on earth could only get as close as a curtain. Ours is inside.

verseByVerse.quote: For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices; thus it is necessary for this priest also to have something to offer. Now if he were on earth, he would not be a priest at all, since there are priests who offer gifts according to the law. They serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things. For when Moses was about to erect the tent, he was instructed by God, saying, “See that you make everything according to the pattern that was shown you on the mountain.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Something to offer. A priest without an offering is a contradiction. The answer was given at 7:27, he offered up himself, and chapters 9 and 10 will work it out: a single offering, made once (9:14).

If he were on earth. A startling admission: under the earthly arrangement Jesus has no standing whatever, since he was from Judah (7:13–14). His sacrifice was made on earth, at the cross; but he entered heaven with it and serves there.

Priests who offer gifts. “There are” is present tense: the temple was still standing, which suggests the letter was written before AD 70.

A copy and shadow. Two words, and both are careful. A copy (hypodeigma) is a sketch, an outline, a model of something real. A shadow (skia) is cast by a body: it has the shape and none of the substance, and it proves the body exists (10:1; Colossians 2:17). Neither word means false. A shadow is genuinely there and genuinely tells you something. But nobody mistakes a shadow for the man, and nobody prefers it once the man has walked into the room. The tabernacle and its ritual were God-given sketches of heavenly realities, pointing to Christ.

The pattern on the mountain. Then the proof, from Moses himself. “Instructed” (kechrēmatistai) is a word for an oracle, and the oracle was Exodus 25:40: see that you make everything according to the pattern that was shown you on the mountain. The writer’s use of it is telling. The “pattern” is typos, a model, a design, the word from which we get type. God did not simply hand Moses a set of measurements; he showed him something on Mount Sinai and told him to reproduce it. That means the tabernacle was, by its own founding charter, a copy, and the original was not on earth. This is not the writer imposing a Greek idea of shadows and forms on Scripture. It is the plainest reading of what God said when the tent was commissioned. Everything in it had to be exact, because it was a picture of something greater. And that reframes the readers’ whole crisis. They thought they were leaving the real thing for something less tangible, and they had it exactly backwards: the incense, the lampstand, the altar and the veil were the sketch, and Christ is the substance.

Where Christians differ: will the temple and its sacrifices be restored? Some dispensationalists (Christians who see a distinct future programme for national Israel, including a literal thousand-year reign of Christ on earth) expect a rebuilt temple in Jerusalem with renewed animal sacrifices during that millennium, often as memorials. They hold this out of a sincere wish to take prophecies such as Ezekiel 40–48 literally, and they too insist that nothing could add to Christ’s sacrifice. This commentary’s view: Hebrews teaches that the earthly sanctuary and its sacrifices were shadows, now fulfilled and made obsolete in Christ (v. 13; 10:1–18). To return to them would be to go back from the reality to the shadow, the very thing the letter warns against. The true temple now is Christ himself and his people (John 2:19–21; Ephesians 2:19–22), and the future hope is the new creation where God and the Lamb are the temple (Revelation 21:22).

How far should I look for Christ in the details of the tabernacle? Far enough to follow the New Testament, and carefully beyond it. Hebrews itself shows the main lines: the priest, the sacrifices, the altar, the curtain, the Most Holy Place, the blood, the ark (9:1–14). John sees Jesus as the one who tabernacled among us (John 1:14), and the curtain tore when he died (Matthew 27:51). Those lines are sure. But the writer himself refuses to go into every detail (9:5), and readers who find a hidden meaning in every peg and thread are usually inventing it. Hold the big picture firmly: the whole tent says that God dwells with his people, but only through a priest and a sacrifice, and Christ is both.

Is it wrong to have beautiful church buildings, or to call the worship room a sanctuary? No, provided we know what they are and are not. A church building is not a temple where God is more present than elsewhere, and no place on earth is holy ground in the old covenant sense; the church is the people, not the bricks (1 Corinthians 3:16; 1 Peter 2:5). A beautiful, well-kept building can serve worship and be an act of care. But if a building, a style of music or a particular ritual starts to feel necessary for meeting God, we have drifted back toward the shadows. The true sanctuary is in heaven, and we enter it by faith wherever we gather.

For worship. The God who showed Moses the pattern on the mountain had his Son in mind all along. Every curtain and lampstand was his sketch of the coming one, and when the Son came, the shadows bowed and gave way. He is the tent where God dwells with men, the priest who enters, and the offering he brings.

verseByVerse.quote: But as it is, Christ has obtained a ministry that is as much more excellent than the old as the covenant he mediates is better, since it is enacted on better promises.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But as it is. The phrase turns from what would be true on earth to what is actually the case. “More excellent” is the word used of his name in 1:4, and again the writer ties greatness to something the reader can weigh.

The covenant he mediates. A “covenant” (diathēkē) is a binding arrangement, initiated by God, in which he commits himself to his people and they to him. And “mediates” introduces a word that will matter for the rest of the letter: mesitēs, mediator, go-between (1 Timothy 2:5). A mediator stands between two parties who cannot deal directly. Moses was the mediator of the first covenant (Galatians 3:19), standing on the mountain between a holy God and a terrified people who begged Moses to speak to them instead, lest they die (Exodus 20:19). Christ mediates the new (9:15; 12:24). “Better” (kreittōn) again.

Two mediators. Moses pleaded, even asking to be blotted out of God’s book for the people’s sake (Exodus 32:32), but he could not pay for their sin, and the arrangement failed anyway. This mediator is also the guarantor (7:22) and the sacrifice (7:27). He does not merely convey the covenant; he pays for it.

Better promises. “Enacted” is legally established. The better promises are those of verses 10–12: an inward law, a personal relationship with God, knowledge of God among all his people, and complete forgiveness. The old covenant’s promises were conditional on Israel’s obedience, which failed. The new are guaranteed by Christ (7:22).

The verbs have changed hands. The new covenant is not better because its rules are easier. It is better because of what God undertakes to do in it. The Sinai covenant said: if you keep my statutes, you shall live (Leviticus 18:5). The new one says: I will put my laws in their minds, I will be merciful, I will remember their sins no more.

In the flow. Everything pivots on verse 6: verses 1–5 showed where Christ serves; verses 7–13 prove from Jeremiah that his covenant is better. Covenant is the word that will carry chapters 8 to 10.

Were Old Testament believers saved in a different way from us? No. Everyone who has ever been saved has been saved by grace through faith in the promised Saviour. Abraham believed God and it was counted to him as righteousness (Genesis 15:6; Romans 4:3), and David rejoiced in the forgiveness of sins (Romans 4:6–8). The faithful of Israel looked forward through the sacrifices and promises to the Christ who was to come, as we look back to the Christ who has come. What differs is the administration: shadows then, substance now; promise then, fulfilment now (the Westminster Confession 7.5–6). Chapter 11 will parade the Old Testament believers as our examples of faith, not as people who were saved by a different route.

On a Tuesday. A good deal of Christian life can run on if: if I pray more, if I stop this habit, if I serve better, then God will accept me. Those are the grammar of the old covenant. Take one of the new covenant promises, I will remember their sins no more, and live this week on God’s I will instead of your own if. Obedience will follow, not as the price of acceptance but as its fruit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — The New Covenant Promised by Jeremiah
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer frames Jeremiah’s words with two short comments: the promise of a new covenant shows the first was not final (vv. 7–8), and the word new marks the old as passing (v. 13). Between them stand the four promises of the new covenant.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Verbs Have Changed Hands

In Jeremiah's promise God says “I will”: the law written on the heart, knowledge of God for all, and sins remembered no more.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: God found fault with the people, not with the covenant.

Now: God does not forget; he has resolved never to act toward his people on the basis of their sins.

verseByVerse.quote: For if that first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no occasion to look for a second. For he finds fault with them when he says: “Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord, when I will establish a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt. For they did not continue in my covenant, and so I showed no concern for them, declares the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If the first covenant had been faultless. The argument used of the priesthood at 7:11: God does not announce a new covenant while the old one is doing everything required.

He finds fault with them. Then a crucial qualification. “Finds fault” (memphomenos) is blames, and the blame falls on them: not with it, but with the people. The defect was not in the covenant but in those who were party to it. Paul says the same at more length: the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good (Romans 7:12), and what it could not do was because it was weakened by the flesh (Romans 8:3). A perfect law given to imperfect people cannot produce righteousness, and the failure is not the law’s. The old covenant had no power to change hearts.

The days are coming. Then the quotation begins, and it is usually reckoned the longest citation of the Old Testament anywhere in the New. It runs from here to verse 12: Jeremiah 31:31–34, all four verses, quoted in full. The writer wants the whole passage in front of his readers, because his case is that the Old Testament itself announced the passing of the old arrangement. And Jeremiah spoke these words early in the sixth century BC, as judgment closed in and exile loomed, when the first covenant was most visibly collapsing because of Judah’s covenant-breaking. It is hope announced at the point of maximum ruin.

A new covenant. “New” (kainē) is new in quality: not another edition of the old but a different kind, and entirely God’s initiative.

Israel and Judah. The whole of God’s people, divided after Solomon, gathered again under one covenant. Jesus took the cup and called it the new covenant in his blood (Luke 22:20), and Paul calls himself a minister of a new covenant (2 Corinthians 3:6).

By the hand. The image is tender: the exodus as leading a child by the hand. When Israel was a child, I loved him, God says through Hosea (Hosea 11:1–4).

They did not continue. Israel broke the covenant again and again, beginning with the golden calf at the foot of the very mountain (Exodus 32). The new covenant is constructed so that it cannot fail in the same way.

A partner who did continue. The first covenant broke on the side of the people. The new one needed a partner on the human side who would not break, and God provided him. Israel was called God’s son and failed in the wilderness (Hosea 11:1); Jesus, the true Son, went into the wilderness and did not fail (Matthew 2:15; 4:1–11). Through Isaiah God says of his Servant that he will give him as a covenant for the people (Isaiah 42:6). The new covenant will not fail as the old did, because at its centre stands one Israelite who kept faith all the way to the cross, and he stands surety for his people’s side of it (7:22).

I showed no concern. So the Greek translation of Jeremiah; the Hebrew reads though I was their husband. Either way, the hand that had led them out of Egypt let them go into Babylon.

Who is this covenant for? The promise is made to the house of Israel and the house of Judah, and dispensational Christians hold that it will be fulfilled to the nation of Israel in the future, while the church shares only in some of its blessings. But Hebrews quotes it to explain what Christ has already done for its readers. He is the mediator of this better covenant now (v. 6; 9:15); the Holy Spirit bears witness to it now (10:15–17); believers have already come to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant (12:24). The more likely reading is that the new covenant is fulfilled in Christ and his people, Jew and Gentile together. Its promises are already ours, though their fullness, when all shall know the Lord, waits for his return. Christians who agree on all this still differ over how to read Paul’s hope that all Israel will be saved (Romans 11:26–27): some expect a great turning of the Jewish people to Christ before the end, others read all Israel as the whole number of God’s elect, Jew and Gentile. On either view, there is one covenant, one Mediator and one people, and every Jew who comes to Christ comes home to promises first made to his fathers.

On a Tuesday. If your life feels like a collapsing covenant, a broken marriage, a pattern of failure you cannot escape, notice when God spoke these words: at the point of ruin, to people who had brought the ruin on themselves. Do not wait until things improve to look for his promise.
verseByVerse.note: The longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament runs from v. 8 to v. 12.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws into their minds, and write them on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And they shall not teach, each one his neighbor and each one his brother, saying, ’Know the Lord,’ for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the covenant. Now the four promises. Count the times God says I will.

On their hearts. The first promise: inward transformation. Under the old covenant the law was written on tablets of stone (Exodus 31:18) and stood outside the people, telling them what to do. The new one is written inside them. The content does not change. It is the same law; God does not say he will give a different or easier one. What changes is its location. The problem was never the standard; it was that the standard was external to people who did not want it. The remedy is not a lower demand but a new heart that wants what the law commands: I will give you a new heart, and I will put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes (Ezekiel 36:26–27; 2 Corinthians 3:3). This is regeneration, which means new birth: the Spirit of God giving life to a heart that was dead toward him, so that it now loves what it once resisted (John 3:3–8). The law is not abolished but taken inside.

A different kind of obedience. That is what makes obedience under the new covenant a different kind of thing. It is not compliance with a rule imposed from outside but the expression of something now written inward, which is why the New Testament can say that his commandments are not burdensome (1 John 5:3) without lowering any of them. A child who loves music does not experience practice the way a child forced to the piano does, though the scales are the same. It also answers the suspicion that God’s commands are a cage. To a new heart they are the shape of its freedom: I will walk in a wide place, for I have sought your precepts (Psalm 119:45).

The first heart with the law written on it. Before God wrote his law on any of his people’s hearts, there was one heart where it was already written. The psalm Hebrews puts in the mouth of Christ as he comes into the world (Hebrews 10:5–7) goes on: I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart (Psalm 40:8). Jesus is the first man in whom the new covenant’s promise was simply true, and he writes it in his people by giving them his Spirit (2 Corinthians 3:3). The knowledge of God that every member shares comes through him too: no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him (Matthew 11:27).

Their God, my people. The second promise: relationship. This covenant formula runs through the whole Bible, to the new creation, where the voice from the throne says exactly this (Genesis 17:7; Revelation 21:3). It is the sentence God keeps saying, and everything else is machinery for making it true.

They shall not teach. The third promise. The New Testament plainly commands teaching (5:12), so the promise is not that instruction ceases. Under the old covenant, people were born into the community and then had to be urged to know the Lord; many never did.

They shall all know me. “Know” (eidēsousin) is not just knowledge about God but personal, saving knowledge: this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent (John 17:3). Under the old arrangement you could be born into the nation and live your whole life inside it without knowing God at all, which is precisely the tragedy of the wilderness generation. Under the new, everyone in it knows him. There are no second-hand members. And from the least to the greatest abolishes the tiers: no inner circle with access and an outer ring who take it on trust, no mediating priestly class; every believer has direct access.

Where Christians differ: who belongs to the new covenant? Paedobaptists (those, such as Presbyterians and Anglicans, who baptise the infants of believers) see the new covenant, like the old, as including believers and their children, and so baptise infants as covenant members. This commentary’s view: One of the key differences between the old and new covenants is that all members of the new covenant know the Lord personally, from the least to the greatest, and have the law written on their hearts. The old covenant community was mixed, including many who did not know God; the new covenant community, properly understood, consists of those who have been regenerated. This is why baptism, the sign of the new covenant, belongs to those who profess faith. This credobaptist conclusion is held charitably toward paedobaptist brothers, who agree that only the regenerate are truly saved but understand the visible covenant community differently.

Do the Ten Commandments still bind the Christian, then? Yes, as the moral law God writes on the heart, though not as the terms of a covenant by which we earn life. What becomes obsolete (v. 13) is the Mosaic administration: its priesthood, sacrifices and temple, and the civil law of Israel as a nation. Some Christians speak instead of the law of Christ replacing the law of Moses; the practical result is close, since the moral substance of the commandments is repeated in the New Testament. The fourth commandment is where views differ most. Many Reformed Christians, with the Westminster and 1689 Confessions, hold that the Sabbath continues as the Lord’s Day, moved to the first day of the week in honour of the resurrection (Westminster 21.7–8; 1689 22.7–8). Others hold that the Sabbath rest is fulfilled in the rest Christ gives (4:9–10; Colossians 2:16–17), while still gladly gathering on the Lord’s Day. This commentary holds that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ, and that the Lord’s Day is his gift, gladly set apart for worship, fellowship and rest rather than kept as a law of rules, and that no one may bind another’s conscience about it (Romans 14:5), while honouring those who hold the Westminster and 1689 view. Both agree that God’s people need worship and rest, and that Christ is the true rest.

How do I know God has written his law on my heart? Not by never sinning, but by what you love and what grieves you. Do you want to please God, even when you fail? Do you find that sin which once felt natural now troubles you? Do you love God’s word and want to understand it, even when it rebukes you? Do you know God, not only facts about him, so that you speak to him as your Father? These are the marks of a new heart. A person under the old covenant alone felt the law as a weight outside him; a person with the law written within feels it as a description of what he longs to be. If that longing is in you, God put it there.

On a Tuesday. Choose one commandment you obey grudgingly, perhaps truthfulness at work or honouring a difficult parent, and pray the promise over it: Lord, write this one on my heart. Then obey, and watch for the change from duty to desire; meanwhile your halting obedience is accepted for the sake of the one in whose heart that law was always written.

verseByVerse.quote: For I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will be merciful. The fourth promise, and the foundation of the others: complete forgiveness. The little word at the front carries the weight of everything before it. For: this is the reason the others are possible. Law written on hearts, God as their God, everyone knowing him: none of it can happen while the sin question is open. Forgiveness is not the last of the promises but the foundation of them. And “merciful” (hileōs) means propitious, gracious, and it is related to the word for propitiation (2:17). God will be favourable toward his people because their sins have been atoned for. A propitiation is an offering that removes God’s just anger against sin by taking it in the sinner’s place, and Christ is that offering (Romans 3:25; 1 John 2:2). Mercy here is not God deciding that sin does not matter; it is God satisfied that sin has been paid for. The “iniquities” (adikiai) are their wrongs, their unrighteous deeds.

Remember no more. A strong double negative: I will certainly never again remember. It does not mean God is forgetful; a God who could lose track of the past would be a smaller God, not a kinder one.

What remembering means. To remember, in Hebrew usage, is not chiefly a mental act but an act of engagement. When God remembered Noah, he acted for him and the waters subsided (Genesis 8:1); when the thief asked Jesus to remember him, he was asking to be acted for (Luke 23:42). So not to remember sins is not to have mislaid the record. It is a settled determination never to act toward the sinner on the basis of it: never to hold sins against his people, never to bring them up again, never to punish them. He has removed our transgressions as far as the east is from the west, and cast all our sins into the depths of the sea (Psalm 103:12; Isaiah 43:25; Micah 7:19). That is stronger than forgetting, not weaker. A God who had forgotten might be reminded. This is a God who knows exactly what was done and has decided, on grounds outside the sinner altogether, never to bring it up.

The reversal. This reverses the old arrangement at its most painful point. Under the law, the annual Day of Atonement was a reminder of sins year by year (10:3); every one said, in effect, here we are again. The new covenant’s promise is the exact opposite: sins completely and permanently forgiven (10:17–18). For a congregation being drawn back to that calendar, this verse is the writer’s most personal argument. They were considering returning to a system whose annual centrepiece existed to bring their sins to mind, and leaving a covenant in which God has undertaken never to raise them.

Sins forgotten, a Saviour remembered. On the night Jesus inaugurated this covenant, he took the cup, poured out for the forgiveness of sins, and said, do this in remembrance of me (Matthew 26:28; Luke 22:19–20). God remembers their sins no more, and his people remember Christ.
