What it does not mean. It does not mean believers never face the consequences of sin or God’s discipline (12:5–11). It means the guilt and condemnation are gone forever.

If God remembers my sins no more, why can I not stop remembering them? Because memory and conscience are not the same as God’s verdict. You may remember a sin for the rest of your life, and Satan, the accuser, will gladly remind you. But the question is not whether you remember it but whether God holds it against you, and he has said he will not. When an old sin rises, do not argue with the memory or try to make up for it. Answer it with the promise: God has said he will remember it no more, because Christ has paid for it. Let the memory become an occasion for thanks rather than shame (1 John 1:9; Romans 8:1).

Does this mean I must forgive and forget when others sin against me? Forgive, yes, freely and from the heart, as God in Christ forgave you (Ephesians 4:32). Forgetting in the sense of losing the memory is not possible, and God does not ask it. What he asks is what he does: that you decide not to hold the wrong against the person, not to keep bringing it up, not to take revenge. That does not mean pretending nothing happened, or trusting someone who has not changed, or staying exposed to abuse; forgiveness and safety are different questions, and a victim of abuse should seek protection and help. But in your heart, release the debt to God, as he has released yours.

For worship. The record of debt is not lost; it is nailed to the cross and cancelled (Colossians 2:14). Where once a priest went in every year with blood that reminded God and the people of their sins, now a high priest sits at the right hand of the Majesty, and the subject is closed. Who is a God like this, pardoning iniquity and delighting in steadfast love (Micah 7:18)?

verseByVerse.quote: In speaking of a new covenant, he makes the first one obsolete. And what is becoming obsolete and growing old is ready to vanish away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He makes the first one obsolete. You cannot call something new without implying that something else is old. When God spoke of a new covenant, six centuries before Christ, he already marked the old one as old.

Growing old. The words are used of clothing worn thin and of a person ageing: a garment fraying at the seams, a body bending with age.

Ready to vanish away. When this was written the sacrifices were still being offered daily. In AD 70 the Romans destroyed the temple, and the sacrificial system stopped and has never resumed.

Arguing from a text. The writer may not have known exactly what was coming; he is arguing from a text, not a newspaper. But any of his readers who lived another decade watched the argument confirmed in the most literal way. And there is pastoral force in his tense. The old covenant has not vanished; it is growing old, near to disappearing. The temple was busy and the smoke went up every morning, and it looked permanent. He tells them what they are looking at: an institution in its last days, kept going by habit, with the reality it pictured already seated at the right hand of God. Going back to it would be stepping onto a floor about to give way.

In the flow. Verse 13 closes the case that Christ mediates a better covenant, and opens chapter 9, which walks through the old tent piece by piece. There is nothing to go back to but a covenant God himself has called old.

What it does not mean. The Old Testament Scriptures are not obsolete; they testify to Christ. What is obsolete is the old covenant as a system.

Does this chapter give any ground for contempt toward Jewish people? None at all. The writer was almost certainly Jewish, writing to Jewish believers. The new covenant was promised in Israel’s own Scriptures, to Israel, by Israel’s God, and its mediator is a son of David from the tribe of Judah. Saying that the old covenant has given way to the new is not saying that Jews are worse than Gentiles; the fault Jeremiah found was in human hearts, and every Gentile heart has the same disease. Paul, who taught the same truth, said he had great sorrow and unceasing anguish for his people (Romans 9:1–3). The right response is not pride but love and prayer, and a glad offer of the Messiah to the people from whom he came.

Are there old-covenant habits that Christians fall into? Yes, often without noticing. Treating the minister as a priest who must stand between us and God. Treating a building as holier than a kitchen table. Measuring ourselves by external rules while our hearts stay cold. Feeling that God keeps a running tally and that each Sunday restarts the account. Believing that our standing depends on our performance this week. Each of these is a kind of going back to the temple. The new covenant answer is the same each time: Christ is our priest, the law is written on our hearts by the Spirit, our sins are remembered no more, and we know God ourselves.

8.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the point in what we are saying is this: we have such a high priest, one who is seated at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven,<sup>2</sup>a minister in the holy places, in the true tent that the Lord set up, not man.<sup>3</sup>For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices; thus it is necessary for this priest also to have something to offer.<sup>4</sup>Now if he were on earth, he would not be a priest at all, since there are priests who offer gifts according to the law.<sup>5</sup>They serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things. For when Moses was about to erect the tent, he was instructed by God, saying, “See that you make everything according to the pattern that was shown you on the mountain.”<sup>6</sup>But as it is, Christ has obtained a ministry that is as much more excellent than the old as the covenant he mediates is better, since it is enacted on better promises.<sup>7</sup>For if that first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no occasion to look for a second.<sup>8</sup>For he finds fault with them when he says: “Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord, when I will establish a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah,<sup>9</sup>not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt. For they did not continue in my covenant, and so I showed no concern for them, declares the Lord.<sup>10</sup>For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws into their minds, and write them on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.<sup>11</sup>And they shall not teach, each one his neighbor and each one his brother, saying, ’Know the Lord,’ for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest.<sup>12</sup>For I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more.”<sup>13</sup>In speaking of a new covenant, he makes the first one obsolete. And what is becoming obsolete and growing old is ready to vanish away.

9.title: The Blood of Christ: Once for All Into the Holy Place
9.overview:
Chapter 9 is the heart of Hebrews’ teaching on atonement. The tabernacle’s design was itself a sermon about access to God: priests in the outer room daily, the high priest alone in the inner room once a year, never without blood. By this the Spirit was saying that the way in was not yet open.

Christ entered heaven itself, once for all, with his own blood, securing an eternal redemption and cleansing the conscience to serve the living God. He will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to save those who wait for him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Closed Door, and the Blood That Opened It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer walks his readers through the first covenant’s sanctuary and shows what its restrictions taught: the way into God’s presence was not yet open, and its sacrifices could not cleanse the conscience. Then he sets Christ against it point by point: a greater tent, his own blood, once for all, and a conscience made clean to serve the living God.
verseByVerse.theology:
Architecture That Preached

By the tabernacle's design the Holy Spirit was saying not yet: one man, one day a year, never without blood. Its sacrifices could not perfect the conscience; the blood of Christ does.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The ark held manna, Aaron's staff and the tablets, with the mercy seat over them.

Now: A cleansed conscience is set free from dead works to serve the living God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now even the first covenant had regulations for worship and an earthly place of holiness. For a tent was prepared, the first section, in which were the lampstand and the table and the bread of the Presence. It is called the Holy Place. Behind the second curtain was a second section called the Most Holy Place, having the golden altar of incense and the ark of the covenant covered on all sides with gold, in which was a golden urn holding the manna, and Aaron’s staff that budded, and the tablets of the covenant. Above it were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat. Of these things we cannot now speak in detail.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Hebrews 9 sets the worship of the old covenant beside the work of Christ. The tabernacle’s rooms and rites showed that the way into God’s presence was not yet open and that its sacrifices could not cleanse the conscience (vv. 1–10). Christ entered the true sanctuary once for all with his own blood (vv. 11–14); his death puts the new covenant into force, as a death puts a will into force (vv. 15–22); and he will appear a second time to save those who wait for him (vv. 23–28). It is a chapter about a closed door, and about the blood that opened it.

A tour of the building. Chapter 8 ended by calling the first covenant obsolete (8:13), and chapter 9 opens with those very words, then takes the readers round its sanctuary. Nobody in his congregation would have thought the old worship shabby; many were tempted to go back to it precisely because it was so beautiful, so ancient and so plainly given by God. So he does not sneer at it. He walks them through it, room by room, until they can see what it was for: it was always a picture, and the one it pictured has come.

Regulations for worship. Both terms are respectful. “Regulations” (dikaiōmata) are requirements God himself laid down; nobody invented this worship. “Worship” (latreia) is priestly service, the work of approaching God. The adjective “earthly” (kosmikon, belonging to this world) is the only hint of limitation, and it is doing all the work. The sanctuary was holy, and it was made of the same materials as the world it stood in: acacia wood, goat hair, linen and gold, a copy and shadow of the heavenly one (8:5).

A tent was prepared. The writer always speaks of the tent (skēnē), the portable sanctuary built in the wilderness (Exodus 25–40), and never of Herod’s temple that stood in Jerusalem as he wrote. He goes back to the pattern God showed Moses on the mountain, to the original, because the meaning lies there and not in whatever later kings added to it. The first section, the Holy Place (Hagia), was about thirty feet long and fifteen wide. Ordinary priests served in it daily, and it was as near to God as any of them would come.

The lampstand and the table. The outer room held three things. The lampstand (lychnia) was the golden menorah with its seven lamps, beaten out of a single piece of gold, its cups shaped like almond blossoms (Exodus 25:31–40). It burned continually, because the tent had no windows: the only light in the house of God was the light God commanded. The table, overlaid with gold, carried the bread of the Presence, twelve loaves set out fresh every Sabbath, one for each tribe (Leviticus 24:5–9). Every week the whole nation lay before the face of God, as if the tribes were his guests at table. Jesus said, I am the light of the world (John 8:12), and I am the bread of life (John 6:35). The furniture was preaching him for centuries before he arrived.

Behind the second curtain. There were two curtains, one at the entrance of the tent and one dividing the two rooms (Exodus 26:31–33). The curtains were the point of the architecture: barriers, in a building designed to teach people how far away they were. The inner room, the Holy of Holies (Hagia Hagiōn), was a perfect cube, about fifteen feet in every direction, dark, silent and empty of everything except the ark. It was the place on earth where the glory of God was pleased to dwell above the mercy seat, and almost nobody had ever seen it. When John describes the new Jerusalem, the city is a cube too (Revelation 21:16). The whole redeemed world becomes the Most Holy Place.

Having the golden altar of incense. This detail has puzzled readers, because the altar of incense actually stood in the Holy Place, just in front of the curtain (Exodus 30:1–6). But the writer says the Most Holy Place had it, not that it stood inside. It stood directly before the mercy seat, its coals and incense were carried inside by the high priest on the Day of Atonement so that the cloud of incense covered the mercy seat (Leviticus 16:12–13), and 1 Kings 6:22 likewise speaks of the altar that belonged to the inner sanctuary. It belonged to the inner room in function. Some take the word (thymiatērion) to mean the golden censer the high priest carried in, as the KJV does. Either is reasonable, and nothing turns on it.

The ark of the covenant. The ark (kibōtos, a chest) was a wooden box about four feet long, overlaid inside and out with gold (Exodus 25:10–22). It was the most sacred object in Israel, and quite simply a box with things in it.

Manna, staff and tablets. The three objects are a small sermon in themselves. The manna was bread from heaven, given to people who grumbled about the food (Exodus 16:32–34). Aaron’s staff was a dead stick that flowered overnight, to settle a rebellion against the priesthood God had chosen (Numbers 17:1–11). The tablets were the law, which they had broken before Moses got down the mountain (Exodus 32:19; Deuteronomy 10:1–5). So the holiest box in the world held three memorials of Israel’s failure: complaint, rebellion and disobedience, kept in gold in the presence of God. And each also pointed to Christ: the true bread from heaven (John 6:32–33), the chosen priest who came back from death to life, and the one man who kept the law written on those tablets from his heart.

But 1 Kings says there was nothing in the ark except the tablets. It does: in Solomon’s day there was nothing in the ark except the two tablets of stone (1 Kings 8:9). But the writer is describing the tabernacle of Moses’ day, when the urn of manna and Aaron’s staff were laid up with the ark before the testimony (Exodus 16:34; Numbers 17:10). By Solomon’s time, centuries later and after the ark had been captured by the Philistines and moved from place to place, only the tablets remained. The two passages most likely describe two different moments, and so they do not clash.

The cherubim of glory. Two golden cherubim stood on the lid of the ark, facing each other, with their wings spread over it (Exodus 25:18–22). They are called cherubim of glory because the glory of God was pleased to dwell between them: there I will meet with you, God told Moses, and from above the mercy seat I will speak with you (Exodus 25:22; Numbers 7:89). The lid itself was the mercy seat (hilastērion), the place of atonement, where the high priest sprinkled blood once a year (Leviticus 16:14–15). Paul uses exactly this word of Christ: God put him forward as a propitiation by his blood (Romans 3:25). Christ is the mercy seat, the place where the wrath of God is turned away and God meets sinners in peace.

The picture on the lid. Take the arrangement as a whole. Inside the box lay the record of the people’s rebellion: the broken law, the grumbling, the revolt. Above the box hovered the glory of a holy God. And between them, exactly between them, lay the lid where blood was sprinkled. God did not look down on the broken law directly. He looked at it through the blood. That is the whole gospel in gold and wood: the record of sin is real and is not thrown away, the holiness of God is real and is not lowered, and between them, covering the one from the other, is the blood of a sacrifice.

Of these things we cannot now speak in detail. The preacher pulls himself up. His argument is not about furniture but about the one day in the year when the high priest went behind the curtain, and what that day meant.

Why does a Christian need to know about a tent that no longer exists? Because God built it to teach the gospel before the gospel arrived, and the New Testament explains Christ in its terms. Words like mercy seat, veil, high priest, atonement, sprinkled blood and access only make sense against this building. When Jesus’ death tore the temple curtain from top to bottom (Mark 15:38), the event means something only if you know what the curtain was for. Reading Exodus 25–40 and Leviticus 16 with this chapter open beside them is one of the surest ways to grow in understanding the cross. The tabernacle is not a puzzle for specialists; it is a picture book God drew for his children.

On a Tuesday. Most of us carry a private record of our failures, and take it out when we are tired or ashamed. The tabernacle does not tell you to pretend the record is not there. It tells you where to put it: under the mercy seat, under the blood. When a remembered sin accuses you, do not argue that it was not so bad, and do not try to bury it under a better week. Name it to God, and say that Christ is your mercy seat, and that God now looks at it through his blood.

verseByVerse.quote: These preparations having thus been made, the priests go regularly into the first section, performing their ritual duties, but into the second only the high priest goes, and he but once a year, and not without taking blood, which he offers for himself and for the unintentional sins of the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests go regularly. Now the writer moves from the architecture to what happened in it, and every detail makes one point about access. He uses the present tense throughout. Most likely the temple services were still going on as he wrote, with the smoke still going up in Jerusalem, though writers sometimes described the old rites in the present tense even after they had ended. “Regularly” (dia pantos) means continually. Priests entered the Holy Place every day, morning and evening, to trim the lamps and burn incense, and every Sabbath to change the bread (Exodus 27:20–21; 30:7–8).

Performing their ritual duties. Literally, completing their services (tas latreias epitelountes), and the next day the duties were all waiting again: always being completed and never complete. No seat for the priest appears among its furnishings: he stood at his service day after day (10:11).

Only the high priest, once a year. Now the restrictions pile up. Only the high priest: one man out of a nation. And only once a year, on the Day of Atonement, Yom Kippur, the tenth day of the seventh month (Leviticus 16:29–34; 23:26–32). Even then he went in more than once, with the incense and with the blood, but only on that one day out of three hundred and sixty-five.

And not without taking blood. Never without blood. No man walked into the presence of God on his own merits, not even the holiest man in Israel. Without a death, no approach was possible.

For himself and for the people. First for himself, a bull (Leviticus 16:11), because the man doing the representing was himself part of the problem. Then for the people, a goat (16:15). Four limitations in a single sentence, and their combined effect is arithmetic: for some fourteen centuries, access to the presence of God amounted to one man, on one day, with a basin of blood, having first dealt with his own sin.

The sins it did not reach. “Unintentional sins” (agnoēmata) are sins of ignorance and error. The sacrifices of the law were given for sins of weakness and ignorance (5:2; Numbers 15:22–29). For the high-handed sin, done with a raised fist in defiance of God, the law named no offering at all (Numbers 15:30–31), though it did provide for some wilful wrongs that were confessed and repaid (Leviticus 6:1–7). The Day of Atonement did cleanse the people from all their sins before the LORD (Leviticus 16:21, 30), but that cleansing was ceremonial, and the writer will soon say that no animal’s blood could ever truly take a sin away (10:4). So on the most solemn day in the calendar, the sins that troubled a man most, the ones he chose with his eyes open, still lay on his conscience when he went home. David knew it. After Bathsheba and Uriah he wrote: you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it (Psalm 51:16). There was no animal for what he had done. He could only throw himself on the mercy of God.

A high priest with no bull of his own. The writer describes the old system until his readers feel its shape, a closed door, and then sets Christ against every line of it. Aaron had to bring a bull for himself before he could do anything for anyone else; Christ is holy, innocent and unstained, and has no need to offer first for his own sins (7:26–27). Aaron represented the people while sharing their guilt; Christ represents them while bearing it. Aaron went in once a year and came out to die like his fathers; Christ went in once for all and lives for ever to intercede (7:24–25). The one man, the one day and the basin of blood were a portrait drawn in outline, and Jesus is the face that fills it.

Is there forgiveness for a sin I committed knowing it was wrong? Yes. This is exactly the sin the old sacrifices could not reach, and exactly the sin Christ came to deal with. Peter denied Jesus with full knowledge, three times, with curses, and was restored on the shore (John 21:15–19). If you have sinned with your eyes open, do not try to reclassify it as a weakness so that it will feel forgivable. Call it what it was, confess it to God, and trust the blood that was shed for precisely that. The very fact that it grieves you is a sign that the Spirit is at work in you, not that you are beyond reach.

On a Tuesday. A faithful Israelite lived and died without ever coming nearer to God than a curtain. Tonight you will pray, perhaps briefly and tiredly, and come straight into the presence of God through Christ, without a bull, a goat or a priest between you. Before you speak to him, remember the curtain, and thank him that you may come in.

verseByVerse.quote: By this the Holy Spirit indicates that the way into the holy places is not yet opened as long as the first section is still standing (which is symbolic for the present age). According to this arrangement, gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot perfect the conscience of the worshiper, but deal only with food and drink and various washings, regulations for the body imposed until the time of reformation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By this the Holy Spirit indicates. “Indicates” (dēlountos) means makes clear, shows. The design did not merely happen to suggest something: the Spirit who gave Moses the pattern was speaking through the architecture. The curtains, the restrictions and the single day were a sermon in cloth and gold, preached silently for centuries.

Not yet opened. And the message of the sermon was two words: not yet. “Way” (hodos) is a road. The road into the true presence of God was not open. Every priest who walked into the Holy Place and stopped at the second curtain was preaching it. When Jesus died, the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom (Matthew 27:51; Mark 15:38). Torn from the top: God did it, not men. And this letter will soon tell us that we now have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain (10:19–20).

Still standing. “First section” (prōtē skēnē, first tent) here probably means the whole first tabernacle arrangement. As long as that order had standing, its very existence said the way was shut. It was “symbolic” (parabolē, a parable) for the time then present, its meaning hidden in plain sight until the one it pictured came.

Cannot perfect the conscience. Then the verdict, and it is the heart of the chapter. “Perfect” (teleiōsai) means bring to completion, bring to the goal. “Conscience” (syneidēsis) is the inner moral awareness of guilt, the knowledge we carry about ourselves. Not that the sacrifices did nothing: they did what they were given to do. What they could not do was reach the conscience. A man could bring his goat, watch it die, see the blood applied, walk home ceremonially clean, and still know perfectly well what he had done (10:1–4).

A description you can check from the inside. Religious observance can leave a person outwardly regular and inwardly unrelieved: you can attend, give, sing and serve and still lie awake with the thing you did. The old system was designed so that the ache would remain until something could answer it. The modern versions seldom involve goats. The churchgoer who trusts his attendance and the unbeliever who trusts that he is at least a decent person are both offering something that cannot reach the conscience, and the same blood is offered to both.

Until the time of reformation. Food laws (Leviticus 11), drink offerings and rules about drink (Numbers 6:3), ritual washings (Leviticus 15; Numbers 19): outward things, “regulations for the body” (dikaiōmata sarkos), “imposed” (epikeimena) like a load; Peter called the law a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear (Acts 15:10). “Until the time of reformation” (mechri kairou diorthōseōs) means until the time of setting things straight, a word medical writers used of setting a broken limb. The old arrangement had an expiry date written into it from the beginning, and in Christ that time has come.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that believers under the old covenant had no forgiveness. They were truly forgiven, through faith in God’s promise, looking forward to what the sacrifices pointed to (11:39–40; Romans 3:25; 4:6–8). Abraham was justified by faith; David knew the blessedness of the man whose sin is covered. But the sacrifices themselves could not give the clear and settled conscience that Christ’s finished work now gives. The saints of old were forgiven, and longed for what we have been shown.

Do the food laws and washings apply to Christians today? No. They were regulations for the body, imposed until the time of reformation, and that time has come. Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19), and Peter was told not to call common what God has cleansed (Acts 10:15). The moral law, summarised in the Ten Commandments, still shows us how to love God and our neighbour; but the ceremonial laws, the diet, the washings, the sacrifices, were shadows, and the substance belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16–17; the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, 19.3). A Christian may keep any diet he likes for health or conscience, but no food and no washing brings him nearer to God.

Why do I still feel guilty after I have prayed and gone to church? Because religious activity cannot do what only Christ’s blood does, and sometimes we are leaning on the activity. Ask what you are trusting: the fact that you prayed, or the one you prayed to. A clean conscience comes from looking at the finished sacrifice, not at the quality of your devotion. Sometimes, too, guilt lingers because a specific sin has not actually been confessed, or a wrong done to someone has not been put right; then the remedy is to do that. And sometimes the conscience is simply oversensitive and needs to be taught by Scripture. In each case the answer is the same: bring it to Christ, and believe what God says about his blood.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Christ appeared as a high priest of the good things that have come, then through the greater and more perfect tent (not made with hands, that is, not of this creation) he entered once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The good things that have come. After ten verses of curtains and restrictions, the sentence breaks like a door opening. “The good things that have come” (tōn genomenōn agathōn) are the blessings of the new covenant, already present: real forgiveness, access to God, a clean conscience. Many manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read good things to come (mellontōn), as in 10:1, and the difference is small: the good things have arrived in Christ and will be fully enjoyed when he returns. Either way, the man who brings them is already here.

The greater and more perfect tent. “Greater” (meizonos) and “more perfect” (teleioteras). The sanctuary Christ passed through is the heavenly reality the tabernacle copied. It is greater because it is God’s own dwelling, and more perfect because it actually does what the earthly one could only picture: it brings a man into the presence of God.

Not made with hands. “Not made with hands” sets human shrines against God’s reality (Acts 7:48; Mark 14:58), and “not of this creation” puts it outside the whole order of made things. The sanctuary he passed through is not a building at all. It is heaven, the presence of God himself (v. 24).

Once for all. There is the word again, ephapax, once for all, as in 7:27, and set against verse 7 it is the whole argument. The high priest went in once a year, every year, and came out again, and next year he had to go back. This one went in once in all history, at his ascension, and did not need to go again (v. 24). He sat down (1:3; 10:12).

By means of his own blood. Every high priest in history walked behind that curtain carrying blood that was not his. The animal had died in his place, and the man was, in the most literal sense, handling somebody else’s death. This priest brought his own, which means he had already been the victim before he was the officiant. Blood signifies life given up in death (Leviticus 17:11), and this was the blood of the sinless Son of God (Acts 20:28).

An eternal redemption. “Redemption” (lytrōsis) is release by ransom, as of captives and slaves. “Eternal” is the letter’s standing contrast with the annual: not a release renewed each autumn, but one that never expires. And “having obtained” is a finished achievement.

A redemption actually secured. Christ obtained not a possible redemption, offered to all and secured for none, but an actual redemption, obtained and secured for those for whom he died. When a ransom is paid, the captive goes free. The death of Christ did not make salvation merely possible; it accomplished it, and it will be applied by the Spirit to every one of those for whom it was paid (John 6:37–39; 10:11, 27–29). That is why the redemption is eternal: nothing in the redeemed can undo what the Redeemer has done. This is what Reformed Christians call definite or particular redemption, taken up again at verse 28, and the same Christ is freely held out to everyone.

What it does not mean. “By means of his own blood” does not mean that Christ literally carried a vessel of blood into heaven, as some have imagined. It means he entered by virtue of a death already accomplished, on the strength of his own life laid down, rather than an animal’s. Nor does it mean that his work in heaven completes an unfinished sacrifice. The sacrifice was finished on the cross, as he himself said: it is finished (John 19:30). In heaven he appears for us on the ground of what was done, and intercedes for us (7:25), but he never offers again.

Does eternal redemption mean I can never be lost? Yes, if you belong to Christ. A redemption that could be lost would not be eternal; it would last only as long as the redeemed held on. But the ransom was paid by Christ and accepted by the Father, and the one who redeemed you keeps you (John 10:28–29; Romans 8:33–39). That does not make sin unimportant. The redeemed are given a new heart and will persevere in faith and holiness, though with falls along the way; Hebrews itself warns sharply against drifting, because warnings are one of the means God uses to keep his people. But your security rests on what he secured, not on how firmly you hold him.

verseByVerse.quote: For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the sprinkling of defiled persons with the ashes of a heifer, sanctify for the purification of the flesh, how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if the blood of goats and bulls. The argument is from lesser to greater, and it begins by conceding that the old sacrifices worked. The blood of goats and bulls was shed on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16).

The ashes of a heifer. The ashes of the red heifer (Numbers 19) were the remedy for corpse-defilement. A spotless red heifer was burned outside the camp, with cedar wood, hyssop and scarlet yarn, and its ashes were kept and mixed with water and sprinkled on anyone who had touched a dead body. Death defiled; and in a world full of death, everyone needed the water sooner or later.

The purification of the flesh. And it worked. “Sanctify” (hagiazei) is to make holy, and the rite really did restore ritual purity, so that a man could take part in worship again. But mark what it achieved: purification of the flesh (tēs sarkos katharotēta), outward, bodily cleanness. It made a man ceremonially clean and fit to come back into the camp. It did not touch him.

How much more. “How much more” (posō mallon) is the argument from the shadow to the reality. If the shadow worked outwardly, how much more will the substance work inwardly. Three things are said about this offering.

Through the eternal Spirit. First, “through the eternal Spirit” (dia pneumatos aiōniou). Most likely this is the Holy Spirit, who anointed and empowered Christ throughout his ministry (Luke 4:18; Acts 10:38) and in his self-offering. The whole Trinity is in the sentence: the Son offers himself, through the Spirit, to the Father. Calvary was not the Father doing something to an unwilling Son, nor the Son persuading a reluctant Father, but the one God acting together to save. Second, he offered himself, and the reflexive is the difference between this and every sacrifice before it. No animal ever volunteered. They were led, held and killed. This victim walked to it (John 10:17–18), and the letter has already shown him praying with loud cries and tears about doing so (5:7). He was both priest and sacrifice.

Without blemish to God. Third, “without blemish” (amōmos), the technical requirement for a sacrificial animal (Leviticus 22:20–22), applied here to a moral life. Every lamb was inspected for defects. This one was inspected by enemies who wanted a charge and could not find one; by Pilate, who found no guilt in him; by a dying thief, who said this man has done nothing wrong; and by the Father, who was well pleased (1 Peter 1:19; 2:22; Luke 23:4, 41).

Purify our conscience from dead works. Here is the answer to verse 9: not the flesh but the conscience, the thing that goes on accusing after the ritual is complete. “Purify” (kathariei) is to cleanse. “Dead works” (nekra erga), as in 6:1, are works that lead to death: our sins, and perhaps also the religious works done to earn God’s favour. Just as touching a corpse defiled a man under the law of the red heifer, so dead works defile the conscience. We have all been handling death. The blood of Christ is the water that cleanses from it.

To serve the living God. The contrast is exact and faintly shocking: dead works, living God. “Serve” (latreuein) is to worship, to serve as a priest. The purpose of cleansing is not merely relief but service. A conscience that has not been cleansed produces religion: activity performed to settle a debt, which never settles it. A cleansed conscience is released into service, which is a different thing altogether, and can only be done by someone who has stopped paying.

How do I know my conscience has been cleansed, when I still remember what I did? Cleansing is not forgetting. Paul never forgot that he had persecuted the church (1 Timothy 1:13–15), but he remembered it as a forgiven man, and it made him wonder at grace rather than sink under guilt. A cleansed conscience is one that no longer accuses you before God, because it has accepted God’s verdict on the blood of Christ. The memory may still bring sorrow, and it may make you humble and gentle with others; but when it starts to say that you are condemned, answer it with this verse. God has accepted the offering, and your guilt is gone.

What is the difference between serving to pay and serving because you are free? The work may look the same from outside, and the difference is in the heart. The man who serves to pay is anxious, keeps score, resents interruptions, and is crushed when he fails, because his standing depends on it. The man who serves because he is free works hard too, but gladly; he can rest without guilt, fail without despair, and rejoice when someone else gets the credit. If your service feels like an unpaid debt, you have probably slipped back into dead works. Go back to the blood, and let your service begin again from there.

For worship. The ashes of a heifer could make a man clean enough to come back into the camp. The blood of Christ makes a sinner clean enough to come into the presence of the living God. The whole Godhead bent down to wash the conscience of people who had been handling death all their lives, and having washed us, he does not send us away. He takes us into his service, priests of the living God, working not for our pardon but from it.
verseByVerse.note: The ashes of a red heifer were mixed with water to cleanse anyone defiled by touching a corpse.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–28 — A Death That Reaches Backward, and a Return Without Sin
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Why did it have to be a death? The writer answers from the double sense of one word, covenant and will: a will takes effect only when its maker dies. Sinai itself was ratified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness. Christ was offered once to put away sin, and will appear a second time to save his waiting people.
verseByVerse.theology:
How the Old Testament Saints Were Saved

Christ's death redeems from transgressions committed under the first covenant. There is one way of salvation, looked forward to and looked back on.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: At Sinai the book and the people were sprinkled with the blood of the covenant.

Now: Christ will appear a second time, not to deal with sin, but to save those eagerly waiting for him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, since a death has occurred that redeems them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The mediator of a new covenant. “Therefore” (dia touto): because his blood cleanses the conscience (v. 14). A “mediator” (mesitēs) stands between two parties to bring them together, and the “new covenant” (diathēkē kainē) is the one God promised through Jeremiah, in which he writes his law on the heart and remembers sins no more (Jeremiah 31:31–34; 8:8–12). Christ is not a go-between who carries messages. He is the one in whose blood the covenant is made.

Those who are called. “Those who are called” (hoi keklēmenoi) is a perfect participle: those who have been called and remain called. Not those who volunteered, but those whom God has effectually called (3:1; Romans 8:28–30), that is, by a call that does what it says. The gospel invitation goes out to all, but in his own people the Spirit makes it a summons that wakes the dead, as the voice of Jesus brought Lazarus out of the tomb (John 11:43–44). And “inheritance” (klēronomia) is family language: the Son was appointed heir of all things (1:2), and what is his by right becomes theirs by gift. It is not the land of Canaan, which Israel lost, but eternal life, the new creation, God himself: an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled and unfading, kept in heaven (1 Peter 1:4).

A death has occurred. “A death” is Christ’s death, and it “redeems” (apolytrōsis): release by ransom. The inheritance comes to the heirs only because a death has taken place. And the death reaches backward. It deals with sins committed before it happened: the transgressions of people who lived and died under the old arrangement, whose sacrifices could not perfect the conscience. That answers a question every thoughtful reader of the Old Testament eventually asks. If the blood of bulls and goats could not take away sins (10:4), on what basis were Abraham, Moses and David forgiven? The answer here is that they were forgiven on exactly the same basis as we are, and the payment was made afterwards.

Credit against a payment God intended to make. Paul says the same: God in his divine forbearance had passed over former sins, and showed his righteousness at the cross, so that he might be just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Romans 3:25–26). So there are not two ways of salvation in Scripture, an older one by law and a newer one by grace. There is one, and everyone who has ever been saved has been saved by the same death, some looking forward to it without knowing its name, and some looking back.

How do I know if I am one of the called? Not by trying to look into God’s secret decrees, but by looking at Christ. Those whom God calls, he brings to faith in his Son, and the evidence of the call is that you have come to Christ and are trusting him (John 6:37, 44). If you are trusting Christ, however weakly, you were called; nobody comes unless the Father draws him. If you are not sure you are trusting him, the answer is not to wait for a sign but to come to him now, for he has promised that whoever comes to him he will never cast out. The call of God is heard in the invitation of the gospel.

Were Old Testament believers saved by keeping the law? No. They were saved by grace through faith, exactly as we are (Romans 4:1–8; Galatians 3:6–9). Their sacrifices were God’s appointed way for them to express faith and repentance, and they pointed to the coming sacrifice, but the sacrifices were not the ground of their forgiveness. The ground was the death this verse describes, which God had already determined and which reached back to them. Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness; and the righteousness counted to him was the righteousness of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: For where a will is involved, the death of the one who made it must be established. For a will takes effect only at death, since it is not in force as long as the one who made it is alive. Therefore not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For where a will is involved. The writer is playing on a word. The Greek diathēkē means both covenant and testament: a legal arrangement, and specifically a last will. In everyday Greek it usually meant a will. He has been using it in the first sense for two chapters, and here he turns it to the second. An inheritance (v. 15) comes through a will, and a will requires a death.

The death must be established. A will takes effect only at death: “takes effect” (bebaia) means valid, binding, in force. A will is a real document the day it is signed, and it does nothing whatever until that one event. Christ is the mediator, and there is a promised eternal inheritance, and the testator had to die before anybody could receive anything.

The cross as the reading of a will. That puts the cross in an unexpected light. It was not only a sacrifice offered and a penalty borne, though it was both. It was also the death that made a will operative, the moment at which an estate long promised became actually available to the heirs. In every other case the testator is dead when the will is read, and has no further say. This testator rose on the third day, and he is himself the executor of his own will. He sees to it personally that every heir receives what was left to him.

Not even the first covenant. “Inaugurated” (enkekainistai) means dedicated, ratified, put into effect. The writer swings back to the other sense of the word, and the Sinai covenant was ratified with blood (v. 19; Exodus 24:3–8). In ancient covenant-making a sacrificial death often sealed the agreement (Genesis 15:9–18; Jeremiah 34:18–20). So the two meanings of the word are held together by a single fact: whichever way you read diathēkē, somebody has to die before it operates.

Where translations differ. Some translators keep covenant throughout verses 16–17, reading them of a covenant ratified by a representative death, the animal standing for the covenant-maker. The ESV takes them as a testament, and the logic of verse 17 favours that, because the sentence about a document not being in force while its maker lives fits a will exactly. Both readings land in the same place: the covenant God made with his people could not come into force without the death of Christ.

If a will can be changed, can God change his mind about me? No. A human will can be altered while the testator lives, but this one came into force by his death, and the testator who rose does not revoke it. The terms are fixed in his blood, and he lives to see that they are carried out (7:25). God’s promises in Christ are yes and amen (2 Corinthians 1:20). The will names its heirs as those who are called and who trust the Son, and if you are trusting him, you are named.

For worship. The Son is the heir of all things, and he wrote into his will people who had nothing to bring and every reason to be left out: rebels, debtors and strangers to the covenant. To make them his heirs he did what no rich man ever does for a beggar. He died, so that what was his by right could become theirs by gift, and the estate he left is not a portion of his goods but all of them, and himself with them.
verseByVerse.note: The Greek word for “covenant” can also mean a “will,” and the writer uses both senses.

verseByVerse.quote: For when every commandment of the law had been declared by Moses to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people, saying, “This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you.” And in the same way he sprinkled with the blood both the tent and all the vessels used in worship. Indeed, under the law almost everything is purified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Declared to all the people. The scene is Exodus 24, the ratification of the covenant at Sinai, and the writer wants the blood in his readers’ eyes. Moses first read the Book of the Covenant to the people, and they promised to obey (Exodus 24:3–7). Nobody was bound to something they had not heard.

Scarlet wool and hyssop. Hyssop was a small bushy plant used as a brush. It appears at the Passover, where it painted the blood on the doorposts (Exodus 12:22); in the cleansing of lepers (Leviticus 14:4–7); in David’s prayer, purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean (Psalm 51:7); and at the cross, where a sponge of sour wine was lifted to Jesus on a hyssop branch (John 19:29).

Both the book and the people. Exodus 24:6–8 mentions the altar and the people. The writer adds the book, and the water, scarlet wool and hyssop, which Exodus 24 does not mention. He draws them from the law’s other cleansing rites (Leviticus 14:4–7; Numbers 19:6, 18), and perhaps from Jewish tradition, to make one picture of covenant cleansing. He adds nothing that contradicts Exodus. Picture it: a nation standing in the open, and blood flicked over them and over the scroll of the law, marking document and people as bound together.

The blood of the covenant. These words from Exodus 24:8 had been heard again in an upper room, from a man holding a cup: this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many (Mark 14:24; Matthew 26:28), the new covenant in my blood (Luke 22:20). Jesus was quoting Sinai deliberately, and every time the church takes the cup it hears Moses at the foot of the mountain and Christ on the night he was betrayed saying the same thing.

The tent and all the vessels. The tabernacle and its furnishings were consecrated with oil, and the altar with blood (Exodus 40:9–11; Leviticus 8:15, 19). Exodus does not mention blood on the tent itself; the writer may be drawing on a tradition his readers knew, and his point is plain either way. Nothing used in the worship of a holy God by sinful people could be used without being cleansed first.

Almost everything. The “almost” (schedon) is a careful touch. Some things were purified by water or by fire (Numbers 31:22–24), and there was an exception for the very poor, who could bring flour for a sin offering (Leviticus 5:11–13). But blood was the main means, and the exceptions prove the rule by their rarity.

Without the shedding of blood. “Shedding of blood” (haimatekchysia) is a word perhaps coined by the writer himself: blood-pouring. “Forgiveness” (aphesis) is release, cancellation. Sin deserves death (Romans 6:23), and forgiveness comes only when a substitute dies in the sinner’s place, life given for life (Leviticus 17:11). This is penal substitution, which the whole sacrificial system taught: Christ bearing the penalty of our sin in our place. He was pierced for our transgressions (Isaiah 53:5), and God made him to be sin who knew no sin (2 Corinthians 5:21).

A sentence many modern readers resist. It should not be softened, and it should be understood. The point is not that God is appeased by suffering, which is the pagan idea of an angry deity bribed with blood. It is that sin is not a debt that can be waived by a stroke of the pen without something being false. A God who simply overlooked evil would not be kind; he would be indifferent to the people it destroyed. A judge who lets the man who abused a child walk free because he is a forgiving sort of person is not merciful but corrupt. Forgiveness is never free. It is free to the one forgiven and costly to the one who forgives, and the cross is what that costs when the wrong is against God. And God in love provided the death himself, in his Son (Romans 5:8; 1 John 4:10): the one who demanded the blood is the one who gave it.

Why does the Lord’s Supper use wine for blood? Because Jesus deliberately took the covenant words of Sinai and applied them to his own death, and he gave the cup as the sign of it. The wine does not become blood; it is a sign and pledge of the blood once shed, and by faith those who drink it truly feed on Christ and the benefits of his death, spiritually and not physically (1 Corinthians 10:16; 11:25–26; the 1689 London Baptist Confession 30.7; the Westminster Confession 29.7). It is not a repeated sacrifice, since this chapter insists there is only one. It is a meal of remembrance and communion at which the covenant is renewed in the hearts of God’s people. Come to it as a forgiven sinner, examining yourself, not as someone trying to make yourself worthy.

On a Tuesday. When someone wrongs you, forgiveness turns out to cost something. You cannot simply say it did not matter; it did. To forgive is to absorb the cost yourself rather than make the other person pay it: the lost money, the hurt reputation, the pain you carry and refuse to repay. That is a small picture of what God did. So when you find it hard to forgive, look at the cross, where your own debt was absorbed, and ask the Spirit who has poured God’s love into your heart (Romans 5:5) to make you able.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be purified with these rites, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. For Christ has entered, not into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf. Nor was it to offer himself repeatedly, as the high priest enters the holy places every year with blood not his own, for then he would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world. But as it is, he has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The copies of the heavenly things. “Copies” (hypodeigmata), as in 8:5, are sketches or patterns, and the copy needed cleansing with animal blood.

The heavenly things themselves. The sentence has puzzled readers: why would heavenly things need purifying? Not because heaven itself is defiled. The likeliest sense is that access for sinners to the heavenly sanctuary had to be opened by blood, as the tabernacle’s use required its dedication. And the people of God are themselves his true dwelling, the house he lives in (3:6), and they needed cleansing. “Better sacrifices” is plural as a general category, matching the plural of the old rites, but it means Christ’s single sacrifice, offered once (vv. 25–26).

Into heaven itself. Earthly shrines are only copies (antitypa, corresponding figures) of the real. Christ entered not a heavenly building but heaven itself, the very presence of God.

On our behalf. “Now”: at this very moment. “Appear” (emphanisthēnai) is to show oneself before someone’s face. The high priest went behind the curtain representing the tribes, with their names cut into stones on his shoulders and on the breastpiece over his heart (Exodus 28:9–12, 29). This one went into the presence of God carrying us, and he is there now (7:25; Romans 8:34; 1 John 2:1).

Not repeatedly. If Christ’s offering worked the way the old ones did, it would need renewing, and since sin has been in the world from the beginning, he would have been dying over and over since Eden. A sacrifice that has to be repeated is a sacrifice that did not work.

At the end of the ages. This is his first coming, and “the end of the ages” (synteleia tōn aiōnōn), the consummation, the completion of the ages, is where the New Testament always locates the cross (1:2): not in the middle of history but at its climax.

To put away sin. “Put away” (athetēsis) is a strong word: to abolish, to set aside, to annul. It is the word used of setting aside the former commandment (7:18). Sin was not merely covered, as the old rites covered it, but abolished, its guilt cancelled and its power broken, “by the sacrifice of himself”.

What it does not mean. Christ’s appearing for us mean that the Father is reluctant and must be talked round. It was the Father who sent him (John 3:16), and Christ appears before a Father who loves us as he loves the Son (John 16:26–27; 17:23).

What is Christ doing in heaven now? He is appearing for you. He is not repeating his sacrifice, which is finished; he is presenting himself, the one whose sacrifice was accepted, as the ground on which you are received. He intercedes for his people, praying for them as he prayed for Peter (Luke 22:32; Romans 8:34). He rules all things for the church (Ephesians 1:20–22). And he is preparing a place (John 14:2–3). When you pray, you are not approaching a stranger; you are coming to a Father before whom your Saviour is already standing, with your name on his heart.

Does the Roman Catholic Mass repeat Christ’s sacrifice? Roman Catholic teaching calls the Mass a true and propitiatory sacrifice, the same sacrifice as Calvary offered in an unbloody manner, and denies that it is a new or different one. But this verse rules out any continuing offering of Christ for sin. He does not offer himself repeatedly; he appeared once for all to put away sin. The Lord’s Supper is a remembrance of that one sacrifice and a communion in it, not a re-presentation of the victim to God for propitiation (the 1689 London Baptist Confession 30.2; the Westminster Confession 29.2). Hebrews returns to this again and again (7:27; 10:10–14, 18): where there is forgiveness, there is no longer any offering for sin.

verseByVerse.quote: And just as it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment, so Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Appointed to die once. Two facts, stated without argument. “Appointed” (apokeitai) means laid up, reserved, destined. Death is not an accident of biology but an appointment kept, God’s appointment because of sin (Genesis 3:19; Romans 5:12). And “once” (hapax) rules out any scheme of repeated lives (those Jesus raised, like Lazarus, were brought back to this life and died again, which is not reincarnation), and sets the pattern the next verse needs: one death, then the reckoning.

After that comes judgment. Something follows death. “Judgment” (krisis): every person faces the judgment of God. At death the soul goes immediately into conscious existence, the believer to be with Christ (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8), the unbeliever to punishment (Luke 16:22–26); at Christ’s return all will be raised and judged (John 5:28–29; Revelation 20:11–15).

Where Christians differ: is there a second chance after death, or a purgatory? Some teach that those who never heard the gospel will have an opportunity to believe after death. Roman Catholic teaching holds that many believers must pass through purgatory to be purified before heaven. Others teach soul sleep, unconsciousness until the resurrection, or annihilation of the wicked. Such views are often held out of real compassion, or a sincere reading of hard texts. This commentary’s view: this verse is clear: death, then judgment. Death is followed by judgment, not by a further opportunity, and our eternal destiny is fixed at death (Luke 16:26). Believers enter conscious joy with Christ immediately (Luke 23:43; Philippians 1:23). There is no purgatory, because by a single offering Christ has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (10:14), and that leaves nothing to be paid afterward. Believers too will stand before God, but for them the verdict was given at the cross; what remains is the review of their lives for reward (2 Corinthians 5:10), not a sentence to be served. Unbelievers face conscious punishment, eternal and real (Matthew 25:46; Revelation 14:11). The time to respond to the gospel is now (3:13; 2 Corinthians 6:2).

To bear the sins of many. “So Christ”: he follows the human pattern exactly. Offered once (hapax prosenechtheis), corresponding to the one death of every person; and then what comes after. But his death was for others. “To bear the sins” (anenenkein hamartias, to carry up sins) is Isaiah’s verb: he bore the sin of many (Isaiah 53:12). Not to sympathise with sinners but to shoulder what they owed, bearing their penalty in his body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24).

Does many mean that Christ bore the sins of only some? The word comes from Isaiah 53:12, where it sets the one servant against the great number he saves, and Jesus used it of his own death, a ransom for many (Mark 10:45). Many Christians take it to mean simply that his death was for the multitude. Reformed Christians take it to mean that he actually bore the sins of a definite people, all who will be saved, the many sons he brings to glory (2:10). The second is the more likely, since to bear sin is to carry it away, and those whose sins he carried will never have to bear them (compare 2:9). This is the Reformed teaching often called definite atonement, and faithful Christians differ over it without doubting each other’s love for the cross. Either way, many is not few, and the invitation is to all: no one who comes to him will find that he was not included.

Will appear a second time. Here the parallel turns: what follows his death is not judgment for him, for he has been judged already, in our place. “Appear” (ophthēsetai) means will be seen: his second coming will be visible. And the picture is from the Day of Atonement. No one was allowed in the tent while the high priest made atonement (Leviticus 16:17), and the people waited outside. He went in under warning, so that he would not die (Leviticus 16:2, 13), and when he came out again alive, it showed that the offering had been accepted, and the waiting could turn to joy. So Christ will come out from heaven, to the joy of his people.

Not to deal with sin. Literally “without sin” (chōris hamartias): not to bear sin again. For anyone afraid of the second coming, the sin business is finished. He is not returning to reopen the file, to weigh his people again, or to see whether the first visit took. That work was completed at his first coming, and he sat down.

Eagerly waiting. “Save” (eis sōtērian, for salvation) means the final and full salvation of his people, including the resurrection of their bodies (Romans 8:23; Philippians 3:20–21). “Eagerly waiting” (apekdechomenois) is a mark of true believers (Titus 2:13; 2 Timothy 4:8). That is the description of a Christian this chapter ends on, after all the blood and curtains and ashes: someone standing at the window, looking down the road, waiting for a man who has already dealt with everything that could have made the waiting frightening.

What it does not mean. “Appear a second time” does not mean there will be a secret coming before his visible return. Scripture speaks of one future return, visible and glorious, at which he gathers his people and judges the world (Matthew 24:30–31; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). Many sincere Christians have been taught to expect a secret rapture before a time of tribulation; this commentary reads the gathering of believers and the visible return as one event, because the same passages place them together, but the hope we share is the same: he is coming for his own.

Will Christians be judged at the last day? Yes, but not to decide whether they are saved. Every person will stand before God, and the lives of believers will be opened (2 Corinthians 5:10; Romans 14:10–12). But the question of their guilt was settled at the cross, where Christ bore their sins, and there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:1). What remains is a Father’s public acknowledgement of his children, and the reward of what was done in his name, even a cup of cold water (Matthew 10:42). That should make us serious about how we live, and not afraid of the day.

What happens to my believing loved ones who have died? They are with Christ, consciously, now. To be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8), and Paul calls it far better (Philippians 1:23). They are not asleep in the sense of being unconscious, nor in purgatory, nor wandering; they are with him, at rest and in joy, waiting with us for the resurrection of the body. When Christ appears the second time, he will bring them with him (1 Thessalonians 4:14), and their bodies will be raised and made like his. You may grieve, and you should; but you grieve as one who has hope.

In the flow. Three times in a few lines the writer says Christ appears: once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin (v. 26), now in the presence of God for us (v. 24), and a second time to save (v. 28). Past, present and future are all held by the one sacrifice.

For worship. Every one of us has an appointment we cannot cancel: death, and then the judgment. Christ kept that appointment for us. He died once, and the judgment that should have followed our death fell on him, as he bore the sins of many. So for his people the order of the verse is changed: after death comes not the judgment but the Judge, the one who was judged in their place. He who came the first time carrying their sins will come the second time without them, bringing nothing but salvation.

parallels.desc: he bore the sin of many

9.text: <sup>1</sup>Now even the first covenant had regulations for worship and an earthly place of holiness.<sup>2</sup>For a tent was prepared, the first section, in which were the lampstand and the table and the bread of the Presence. It is called the Holy Place.<sup>3</sup>Behind the second curtain was a second section called the Most Holy Place,<sup>4</sup>having the golden altar of incense and the ark of the covenant covered on all sides with gold, in which was a golden urn holding the manna, and Aaron’s staff that budded, and the tablets of the covenant.<sup>5</sup>Above it were the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy seat. Of these things we cannot now speak in detail.<sup>6</sup>These preparations having thus been made, the priests go regularly into the first section, performing their ritual duties,<sup>7</sup>but into the second only the high priest goes, and he but once a year, and not without taking blood, which he offers for himself and for the unintentional sins of the people.<sup>8</sup>By this the Holy Spirit indicates that the way into the holy places is not yet opened as long as the first section is still standing<sup>9</sup>(which is symbolic for the present age). According to this arrangement, gifts and sacrifices are offered that cannot perfect the conscience of the worshiper,<sup>10</sup>but deal only with food and drink and various washings, regulations for the body imposed until the time of reformation.<sup>11</sup>But when Christ appeared as a high priest of the good things that have come, then through the greater and more perfect tent (not made with hands, that is, not of this creation)<sup>12</sup>he entered once for all into the holy places, not by means of the blood of goats and calves but by means of his own blood, thus securing an eternal redemption.<sup>13</sup>For if the blood of goats and bulls, and the sprinkling of defiled persons with the ashes of a heifer, sanctify for the purification of the flesh,<sup>14</sup>how much more will the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God.<sup>15</sup>Therefore he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance, since a death has occurred that redeems them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant.<sup>16</sup>For where a will is involved, the death of the one who made it must be established.<sup>17</sup>For a will takes effect only at death, since it is not in force as long as the one who made it is alive.<sup>18</sup>Therefore not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood.<sup>19</sup>For when every commandment of the law had been declared by Moses to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled both the book itself and all the people,<sup>20</sup>saying, “This is the blood of the covenant that God commanded for you.”<sup>21</sup>And in the same way he sprinkled with the blood both the tent and all the vessels used in worship.<sup>22</sup>Indeed, under the law almost everything is purified with blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins.<sup>23</sup>Thus it was necessary for the copies of the heavenly things to be purified with these rites, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these.<sup>24</sup>For Christ has entered, not into holy places made with hands, which are copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf.<sup>25</sup>Nor was it to offer himself repeatedly, as the high priest enters the holy places every year with blood not his own,<sup>26</sup>for then he would have had to suffer repeatedly since the foundation of the world. But as it is, he has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.<sup>27</sup>And just as it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment,<sup>28</sup>so Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, not to deal with sin but to save those who are eagerly waiting for him.

10.title: Once for All: The New and Living Way
10.overview:
Chapter 10 concludes the letter’s central argument on priesthood, covenant and sacrifice. The law’s yearly sacrifices are set against Christ’s single offering, with Psalm 40 as the key: the Son came to do God’s will, and by that will we have been sanctified once for all.

Then the teaching becomes appeal (vv. 19–39): draw near, hold fast, stir one another up. A severe warning against turning from the only sacrifice (vv. 26–31) is followed at once by encouragement to endure, for the coming one will come.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — One Sacrifice, and a Priest Who Sat Down
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The writer gathers up his argument. Yearly sacrifices confessed that they had not finished the work; Psalm 40 shows what replaces them: a willing Son in a prepared body. The priests stood daily; Christ offered one sacrifice and sat down, and the promise of Jeremiah settles it: where God remembers sins no more, no further offering remains.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Tenses in One Sentence

By a single offering Christ has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified. Where sins are forgiven, there is no longer any offering for sin.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The yearly sacrifices were a reminder of sins, and their repetition confessed that they had not finished the work.

Now: Standing before God does not wait on our progress; our progress flows from a finished offering.

verseByVerse.quote: For since the law has but a shadow of the good things to come instead of the true form of these realities, it can never, by the same sacrifices that are continually offered every year, make perfect those who draw near. Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered, since the worshipers, having once been cleansed, would no longer have any consciousness of sins?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Hebrews 10 completes the argument about Christ’s sacrifice and turns it into urgent appeal. The yearly sacrifices could never take sins away (vv. 1–4); Christ came, as Psalm 40 foretold, to do God’s will in the body prepared for him (vv. 5–10); the priests stand daily, but he offered one sacrifice and sat down, and where sins are forgiven no further offering remains (vv. 11–18). So let us draw near, hold fast and stir one another up (vv. 19–25). For those who deliberately turn from that sacrifice, none remains, only judgment (vv. 26–31); yet do not throw away your confidence, for the coming one will come (vv. 32–39). It is the chapter of the priest who sat down.

In the flow. Verses 1–18 conclude the argument about priesthood and sacrifice begun at 7:1, gathering up the shadow (8:5), the sacrifice repeated year after year (9:7, 25), and the conscience the old rites could not reach (9:9, 14). From verse 19 the teaching becomes appeal.

A shadow of the good things. The shadow image returns from 8:5. A shadow (skia) shows the outline of something real but is not the thing itself. It tells you a body is there, roughly what shape; it does not show you the face. “The good things to come” are the blessings of the new covenant in Christ (9:11): real forgiveness, open access, a cleansed conscience.

The true form. “True form” (eikōn) is the image, the actual likeness, the very substance. The contrast is not between a shadow and nothing, but between a shadow and the thing that casts it. The law had the shadow; Christ is the body that cast it (Colossians 2:17).

It can never make perfect. “Never” (oudepote): the writer is not describing a system that worked imperfectly, but one that could not, in principle, finish the job. “Continually” (eis to diēnekes) means perpetually; “every year” is the Day of Atonement; and “make perfect” (teleiōsai), as in 7:19 and 9:9, means to bring to the goal, full cleansing and access to God.

Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered? Then a piece of plain reasoning that any worshipper could have done for himself. The repetition is the evidence. A medicine that cures is not taken for ever. If the Day of Atonement had actually dealt with the matter, there would have been no need for another one the following autumn. The fact that the calendar came round again every year was itself a confession that nothing had been concluded.

No longer any consciousness of sins. The test is an experiential one. “Having once been cleansed” (hapax kekatharismenous) means cleansed once for all. “Consciousness of sins” (syneidēsis hamartiōn) is a conscience of sins, the sense of guilt. A sacrifice that had truly worked would leave a person without a nagging sense of guilt before God: not because he had become forgetful or hardened, but because the thing had been settled.

The same accusation, year after year. Put that plainly to any religious system, including the ones people build for themselves inside Christianity. If a person is still trying to quiet the same accusation this year that he was trying to quiet last year, the method is not working, and the repetition is the proof. Penance that has to be done again, a vow renewed every January, a frantic burst of devotion after every fall: these are the Day of Atonement come round again.

Should a Christian ever feel guilty? Yes, when he sins; that is the conscience working as God made it, and the Spirit uses it to bring us back (2 Corinthians 7:10). What this verse rules out is the guilt that stays after a sin has been confessed and forgiven, as if the matter were still open before God. That guilt is not humility; it is unbelief about the sacrifice. The answer to it is not to do something more, but to believe what God says: the sin is cleansed, once for all. Feel sorrow for sin, confess it, turn from it, and then let it go, because God has.

verseByVerse.quote: But in these sacrifices there is a reminder of sins every year. For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A reminder of sins. The Day of Atonement is usually thought of as the day sins were dealt with; the writer says its actual effect was to bring them to mind (anamnēsis, remembrance). The high priest lays both hands on the head of the live goat and confesses over it all the iniquities of the people, and the goat is led away into the wilderness (Leviticus 16:21). The whole nation stands and hears its sins recited. That is not an annual clearing of the books. It is an annual reading of them aloud, and a devout Israelite grew old hearing it, while the new covenant promises that God will remember sins no more (8:12; 10:17).

The other remembrance. Jesus used the same word, anamnēsis, of the Lord’s Supper: do this in remembrance of me (Luke 22:19; 1 Corinthians 11:24–25). The old ritual remembered sins; the new remembers the Saviour who removed them.

It is impossible. “Impossible” (adynaton) is the same absolute word as 6:4 and 6:18. Not inadequate, not partial: it cannot be done, and it never could. “Take away” (aphairein) means remove, lift off. The mechanism was never capable of the result.

Why an animal cannot do it. Sin is a personal and moral matter between a creature and his Maker, and an animal is neither a person nor a moral agent. It has consented to nothing, it is not of the same nature as the sinner, and it is not of infinite worth. Only the sacrifice of a sinless man, who is also God, could take away sin: a man, to stand in the place of men; sinless, to have no debt of his own; God, to give the offering infinite value.

So what were the sacrifices for? Everything the letter has said supplies the answer. They were the shadow, teaching a nation over many centuries that sin costs life, that God provides the victim, and that somebody innocent dies in the place of somebody guilty. They were a language being taught, so that when the reality came there would be words to describe it. When John the Baptist pointed at Jesus and said, Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29), the Jews in earshot could hardly miss the echo, because God had spent centuries teaching them the word lamb.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that Old Testament believers were not truly forgiven. They were, by grace through faith, on the credit of the sacrifice Christ would offer (9:15; Romans 3:25), not by the animals.

How should I remember my sins at the Lord’s Supper? Remember them truly, but remember them as forgiven. Paul tells us to examine ourselves before we eat (1 Corinthians 11:28), and that means honest confession of what is wrong and a turning from it. But the Supper is not the Day of Atonement, where sins are read out and left hanging. It is a remembrance of Christ, who bore them. So look at your sins only long enough to see them laid on him, and then look at him. Come to the table not because you are worthy, but because you need him and he has invited you.

For worship. Year after year the goat went out into the wilderness, and the people knew it would have to go again. Then the Lamb of God went out of the city carrying their sins to a cross, and they did not come back. He has not asked us to forget what we were. He has given us something better to remember.

verseByVerse.quote: Consequently, when Christ came into the world, he said, “Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body have you prepared for me; in burnt offerings and sin offerings you have taken no pleasure. Then I said, ’Behold, I have come to do your will, O God, as it is written of me in the scroll of the book.’”
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Christ came into the world. The writer puts Psalm 40 on the lips of the incarnate Son at the moment of his coming. David wrote the words, but the writer hears the psalm as the Son’s own words to the Father about why he came.

Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired. This is easy to misread. “Sacrifices” (thysia) are animal sacrifices and “offerings” (prosphora) grain offerings. God commanded them; he cannot be renouncing his own institution. The prophets use the same idiom: to obey is better than sacrifice (1 Samuel 15:22); I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice (Hosea 6:6; Psalm 51:16–17; Micah 6:6–8). The meaning is comparative: not these for their own sake, but something they were pointing toward. What God desired was obedience from the heart.

A body prepared. The Hebrew of Psalm 40:6 reads, literally, ears you have dug for me, an odd phrase, probably meaning ears opened to hear and obey. The Greek translation the writer uses reads a body you have prepared for me. The two are not at odds. An ear is the organ of obedience, and the Greek translators probably took the part for the whole: God prepared a whole person for obedience. Under the Spirit’s guidance the writer uses the Greek because it points precisely to the incarnation. God did not want a body brought to the altar. He prepared one, and it walked there (v. 10).

Burnt offerings and sin offerings. “Burnt offerings” (holokautōmata, offerings wholly burnt) and “sin offerings” (peri hamartias) were the main categories of Levitical sacrifice. God took no pleasure in them as ends in themselves.
