I have come to do your will. That is the sentence the writer will build on. No bargaining, no conditions, no mention of the cost. Just arrival and willingness (idou hēkō, behold, I have come). His whole life was devoted to doing the Father’s will: my food is to do the will of him who sent me (John 4:34; 6:38). And it ended in a garden where the same will was spoken in agony: not as I will, but as you will (Matthew 26:39, 42). Luke adds that his sweat became like great drops of blood (Luke 22:44), though some early manuscripts lack that verse.

The scroll of the book. The “scroll of the book” (kephalis bibliou) is the roll of Scripture, which testifies of Christ (Luke 24:27, 44; John 5:39). The incarnation was not a rescue plan improvised after things went wrong. It was in the book.

A will saying yes. If bulls and goats cannot take away sins, what can? The answer is not a better animal. It is a will: a human will, in a prepared body, saying yes. What God wanted from the beginning was a human being who would give himself wholly to him, and in the whole history of the race there had never been one. So God prepared one.

Did Jesus know from the beginning that he had come to die? Yes. The psalm puts these words in his mouth as he came into the world, and the Gospels show him speaking of his death long before it came (Mark 8:31; 10:45; John 10:17–18). As a true man he grew in wisdom (Luke 2:52), and his human understanding of his mission deepened through Scripture and prayer. But the Son did not stumble onto the cross. He came to do the Father’s will, and the cross was at the centre of that will from the start. That is why his death was an offering and not an accident.

On a Tuesday. It is easy for religion to become offerings rather than obedience: the hymn you sing on Sunday while nursing a grudge, the money given while refusing to forgive, the Bible reading done while the plain command you read is set aside. God does not want the offering instead of you. He wants you. Before you do any religious duty today, say to God the words of this psalm about one specific thing: here I am, I have come to do your will. You will not do it perfectly; nobody but Christ ever has. He did, and by his obedience you are counted righteous (Romans 5:19), so your halting yes is accepted for his sake, and the Spirit who wrote his law on your heart (v. 16) makes it real.
verseByVerse.note: “A body have you prepared for me” follows the Greek Old Testament; the Hebrew of Ps 40:6 reads “you have given me an open ear.”

verseByVerse.quote: When he said above, “You have neither desired nor taken pleasure in sacrifices and offerings and burnt offerings and sin offerings” (these are offered according to the law), then he added, “Behold, I have come to do your will.” He does away with the first in order to establish the second. And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he said above. The writer now takes his own quotation apart, as the New Testament reads the Old. He divides the psalm into two statements and puts them in order. First a negative: God did not desire sacrifices and offerings. Then a positive: behold, I have come to do your will.

Offered according to the law. All four kinds of sacrifice gather the whole system into one phrase, and then a remarkable parenthesis: these are offered according to the law. The psalm’s rejection of sacrifices applies to the very offerings the law required. God, through David, in the middle of the old covenant, signalled that the law’s sacrifices were not his final desire.

He does away with the first. The order is not accidental: the second replaces the first. “Does away with” (anairei) is a strong verb: to take up and remove, to abolish. And “establish” (stēsē) is its opposite: to make stand. The first is the sacrificial system; the second is Christ’s obedience to God’s will.

By that will. The summit of the chapter. “By that will” (en hō thelēmati): the will of God, his saving purpose, which the Son came to do. What sanctifies us is not our willing but his. And “we have been sanctified” (hēgiasmenoi) should stop any reader who has spent years anxious about his own progress. It is the Greek perfect: completed, with the result standing. Here sanctification means being set apart, consecrated to God, made fit for his presence, a definitive, once-for-all act (as in 1 Corinthians 6:11), not the ongoing process of growth in holiness.

The offering of the body. The “offering” (prosphora) is of the “body” (sōma) prepared for him (v. 5), and it was made “once for all” (ephapax), the word the whole letter has been driving toward. The body God prepared in the womb of Mary was given on the cross, and the will that said I have come said it finished.

Two kinds of holiness, in the right order. The letter is not confusing definitive sanctification with the daily business of becoming holy: verse 14 will speak of those who are being sanctified in the same breath. Both are true, and the order matters enormously. A Christian is set apart definitively by what Christ did, and is then progressively made to match it. The second is a lifetime’s work. The first is finished.

If I am already sanctified, why do I still struggle with sin? Because you have been set apart for God, but you have not yet been made completely like him. Think of a bride on her wedding day: she is fully and truly married, though she will spend a lifetime learning what that means. Your struggle is not evidence that you are not his; often it is evidence that you are, since the unconverted do not fight sin as an enemy (Galatians 5:17). The struggle is the outworking of what was done once. Fight on from the position Christ has given you, not toward it.

verseByVerse.quote: And every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God, waiting from that time until his enemies should be made a footstool for his feet. For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every priest stands. One word, prepared since 1:3: “stands” (hestēken). The furniture of the tabernacle is listed in detail in Exodus, and no seat for the priests appears in the list, as if a priest whose work was finished were a contradiction in terms. They stood, every day, for some fourteen centuries, from Aaron to the writer’s own day.

The same sacrifices. “Repeatedly” (pollakis, many times); “the same”: endless repetition of identical sacrifices. “Take away” (perielein) means strip off, remove entirely.

He sat down. One sacrifice (mian), effective for ever. There is the contrast, and it is made entirely with a posture. Sitting signals completion: they stand, he sits; they offer repeatedly, he offered once. And he sits at the right hand of God, the place of honour and of rule, which no Levitical priest ever approached.

Waiting. Psalm 110:1 once more (1:13). He is seated and he is waiting, which tells you where we are in the story. The work of atonement is over; the subduing of enemies is not, and the letter’s readers were feeling the difference. “Waiting” (ekdechomenos) is not idle. He reigns while the Father subdues his enemies, through the advance of the gospel now and finally at his return (1 Corinthians 15:24–28).

Perfected for all time. Two tenses in one sentence, and holding them together is the whole Christian life. “Perfected” (teteleiōken) is a perfect tense: done, complete, and it remains complete, and “for all time” removes any question of expiry. “Being sanctified” (tous hagiazomenous) is present and continuous: unfinished, still in progress this morning. In God’s sight, on the basis of one offering, they are already finished: complete, accepted, cleansed before him. In their own experience they are halfway through and struggling. Our standing is perfect; our condition is improving; and the one guarantees the other. Get them the wrong way round and the Christian life becomes unbearable: a person who thinks his standing depends on his progress will never rest.

Where Christians differ: can a believer lose what Christ’s sacrifice achieved? Some teach that a believer’s perfected standing can be forfeited, through serious sin or through ceasing to believe. This is the Arminian view (that saving grace can in the end be resisted and lost), held by many earnest Christians who want the letter’s warnings taken seriously. This commentary’s view: this verse says Christ has perfected his people for all time by a single offering. What is perfect for all time cannot be undone. Christ’s death did not merely make salvation possible; it actually and permanently perfected those for whom it was made, guaranteeing their sanctification and final glory (Romans 8:30). This is the ground of both definite atonement (that Christ died to save a particular people and surely saves them) and the perseverance of the saints (that all who truly believe will be kept to the end).

How can I be perfect and still be such a mess? Because the perfection is in Christ’s offering, not in your performance. God looks at you through the single sacrifice and sees you complete, as a man is counted fully paid once his debt is cleared, even if his house is still untidy. At the same time the Spirit is at work in you, so that the mess is being cleaned up, slowly and really. The two belong together: you are being sanctified because you have been perfected, not in order to be. When you see your mess, do not doubt your standing; thank God for it, and ask him to go on making you what he has declared you to be.

On a Tuesday. Picture where Christ is as you go about your day: seated. Not pacing, not anxious, not still working to make up for your failures. Then let that change how you work. Much Christian activity is done standing, as if the work of acceptance were never finished. Do your duties today seated, so to speak: from rest, not toward it. When you fail, remember that the one who perfected you is sitting at the right hand of God, and his work does not wobble when yours does.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Holy Spirit also bears witness to us; for after saying, “This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws on their hearts, and write them on their minds,” then he adds, “I will remember their sins and their lawless deeds no more.” Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Holy Spirit also bears witness. Present tense again, as at 3:7: the Jeremiah passage of chapter 8 returns, shortened, as testimony the Spirit gives now, to us, today.

This is the covenant. The writer quotes only two clauses of Jeremiah 31:33–34. He leaves out the promise that all shall know the Lord, and the covenant formula about being their God. He takes the law written on hearts, and the sins remembered no more. The purpose arrives in verse 18.

Laws on their hearts. The new covenant does not abolish God’s law; it writes it inside. What was once on stone, outside a man and accusing him, is now in the heart, changing him. This does not mean that a Christian no longer needs the Bible; it means that he now wants what it commands: he finds himself loving the ways of God he once resented, because God has given him a new heart and put his Spirit within him (Ezekiel 36:26–27). It is the very thing Psalm 40, just quoted, says of Christ: I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart (Psalm 40:8).

Remember no more. The climax of the new covenant (8:12): complete, permanent forgiveness. And now the writer draws an inference he did not draw in chapter 8.

No longer any offering. If God has undertaken never to bring up a person’s sins again, then there is nothing left for a sacrifice to do. An offering exists to deal with an outstanding matter. Where the matter is closed, the offering is not merely unnecessary; it is unintelligible. This is the conclusion of the whole argument from 7:1: since sins are fully forgiven, no further sacrifice is needed or possible.

Why going back made no sense. That is the decisive argument against what his readers were contemplating. Going back to the temple would not be a harmless supplement or a matter of ancestral loyalty. It would be to keep offering for sins that God has said he will not remember, which is to imply that the promise is not true.

No offering for sin in the church. The verse also settles a question that has divided Christians. If there is no longer any offering for sin, then whatever the church does when it gathers, it is not offering a sacrifice for sin. The New Testament knows sacrifices of praise and of doing good (13:15–16), and calls a Christian’s body a living sacrifice (Romans 12:1). It knows no repeatable offering for sin, and this verse is why. The Lord’s Supper is a remembrance of the one sacrifice and a communion in it, not a further offering of it (see 9:25–26). With that the great doctrinal argument of the letter is complete. From verse 19 the writer turns, with a therefore, to what his readers must do about it.

How can an all-knowing God forget my sins? He does not suffer a lapse of memory; the God who knows all things knows what you did. To remember sins no more is covenant language: he will never again bring them up against you, never act toward you on the basis of them, never hold them over you. It is like a judge who has acquitted a man and will not try him again for the same charge. So when your own heart or the accuser brings up a forgiven sin, you may answer that God himself has promised not to. If he will not hold it against you, you need not hold it against yourself.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–39 — Let Us Draw Near, Hold Fast, and Consider One Another
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With a therefore, the teaching turns to appeal. Because the way is open and the priest is ours, draw near, hold fast and stir one another up, and do not stop meeting. Then the solemn warning: for one who knowingly turns from Christ’s sacrifice, no other remains. But he reminds his readers of the courage they once showed, and ends sure that they are not of those who shrink back.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Curtain Is His Flesh

The way into the holy places has been opened through the curtain, his flesh. So draw near, hold fast because he who promised is faithful, and stir one another up.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: These believers had once joyfully accepted the plundering of their property.

Now: The warning of verses 26–31 is aimed at deliberate repudiation of Christ, not at a struggling believer; and it ends in assurance: we are not of those who shrink back.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh, and since we have a great priest over the house of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, brothers. And the letter turns from teaching to application. Everything from 4:14 to 10:18, the priest, the covenant, the sanctuary and the sacrifice, now becomes the ground of three exhortations. And he calls them brothers: the warnings that follow are spoken inside a family.

Confidence to enter. The word is parrēsia, as at 4:16: boldness, freedom, the free citizen’s right to speak openly in the assembly. And the place is the one the whole letter has been circling: the room behind the curtain. What only the high priest could do once a year, every believer may now do at any time.

By the blood of Jesus. That is the only ground offered. Not by sincerity, not by improvement, not by a life that has earned an audience. By his blood, his sacrifice. And note the name: Jesus, the human name, the name of the man who bled.

The new and living way. “New” (prosphatos) means fresh, recent. The way into God’s presence was opened by a recent death, and it never grows old. And “living” (zōsa): not a dead ritual path but a way that is alive, because it is a person. I am the way, Jesus said (John 14:6). He opened the road (enekainisen, inaugurated, as at 9:18) and walked it first.

Through his flesh. The curtain (katapetasma) was the barrier that kept people out, and the writer says the curtain is his flesh: the way in was opened by the tearing of it. When his body was broken on the cross, the temple veil was torn from top to bottom (Mark 15:38), and the Gospels record it as an act done from above rather than below.

A beautiful barrier. The curtain was beautiful: blue and purple and scarlet, of fine twined linen, worked with cherubim (Exodus 26:31). The barrier was magnificent, and it had to be destroyed. So it was with the flesh of Christ: the most beautiful human life ever lived, and it had to be torn so that we could come in.

A great priest. The second ground: not only an open way but a man standing at the end of it who belongs to us. “Great priest” (hierea megan) is a Hebrew way of saying high priest. “Over the house” recalls 3:6, where Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son, and we are that house.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we approach God casually. We come with confidence because of Christ, but still with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire (12:28–29). Boldness is not swagger. It is the freedom of a child who knows he will be received.

What does confidence before God actually feel like? It is not a feeling of being good enough; it is the settled knowledge that you will be welcomed, because of Jesus’ blood. You may come to prayer feeling dull, ashamed or unsure of what to say, and still come with confidence, because your confidence is not in your state but in the way Christ opened. A child who has broken something still runs to his father, not because he is proud of himself, but because he knows his father. That is the confidence of this verse.

For worship. For centuries one man passed the curtain once a year, and came out again. Now a whole family walks through it every day, because the Son of God let his own flesh be torn to make the way. He did not show us the road and leave us to find it. He is the road, and he stands at the end of it, waiting for his brothers and sisters to come in.

verseByVerse.quote: let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us draw near. The first of three exhortations (vv. 22, 23, 24): draw near, hold fast, consider one another; faith, hope and love, in that order. “Draw near” (proserchōmetha), as in 4:16, is the priestly word, now commanded of everybody. Four qualifications follow: two about the person coming, two about what has been done to him.

With a true heart. A genuine one (alēthinos), without pretence, not hypocritical or divided (Isaiah 29:13). God is not interested in a performance at the throne.

In full assurance of faith. The same phrase as 6:11 (plērophoria), complete conviction: not certainty about oneself, which nobody has, but about the ground just described, the blood, the way, the priest.

Sprinkled clean. Then the second pair, both passive and perfect: things done to us, and remaining done. “Sprinkled” (rerantismenoi): the image is the sprinkling of blood that consecrated priests at their ordination (Exodus 29:21; Leviticus 8:30), and the people at the covenant’s ratification (9:19). The target is the conscience again, the thing 9:9 said the old sacrifices could not reach. What accuses a man on the inside has been dealt with, and that is why he can come with a true heart rather than a defended one.

Washed with pure water. Priests were also washed at their ordination (Exodus 29:4; 30:19–21), and God promised through Ezekiel: I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean (Ezekiel 36:25). Most interpreters see here a reference to Christian baptism, the outward sign of the inward cleansing named in the same breath (Acts 22:16; 1 Corinthians 6:11; Titus 3:5; 1 Peter 3:21). Some read it as purely figurative, but the pairing looks deliberate: inward cleansing and outward sign, the whole person made fit.

No requirement of worthiness. Among the four there is no requirement of worthiness, no interval of preparation, no measure of progress. Every qualification is either an attitude of honesty or something Christ has already done, which is exactly the point, because a throne you must qualify for is not a throne of grace.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that baptism cleanses the conscience by itself. Even if baptism is in view, the water does not do the cleansing. The heart is sprinkled clean by Christ’s blood, received by faith; baptism is the public sign of that cleansing, given to those who have drawn near in faith. That is one reason this commentary, with the 1689 London Baptist Confession, holds to the baptism of believers, while honouring paedobaptist brothers (those who baptise the infants of believers, seeing baptism as the covenant sign that replaced circumcision) who read the covenant signs differently and who love the same Saviour. A reader baptised as a baby should hear this as a family difference, not a slight on his faith.

What if I do not feel full assurance? Then come anyway, and come honestly. Full assurance of faith is assurance about Christ, not a constant feeling about yourself. Feelings of doubt are common in true believers, and Scripture is full of them (Psalm 42; Mark 9:24). The way to grow in assurance is not to stay away until you feel sure, but to draw near and look at the ground: the blood, the way, the priest. Assurance grows as faith looks at Christ, and it often comes while you are praying rather than before. Bring your doubts with you to the throne of grace; they are safer there than anywhere else.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hold fast the confession. The second exhortation, aimed most directly at these readers. “Hold fast” (katechōmen) means grip, retain, do not let go, as in 3:6, 14 and 4:14. “The confession” (homologia) is the word from 3:1 and 4:14: what they had said publicly, probably at baptism, and were under pressure to unsay. In a hostile city a confession is not a private opinion; it is the thing that got their property confiscated. And “of our hope” is our confident expectation of glory.

Without wavering. A single word (aklinē), meaning not leaning, not tilting: something that stays upright under pressure rather than swaying between two positions.

He who promised is faithful. One short clause carries the whole weight, and the logic is not the one we would supply. He does not say hold on because you are strong, or because you have held on so far, or because giving up would be shameful. The ground of our holding is his faithfulness (pistos). He will keep every promise (6:13–18; 11:11; 1 Corinthians 1:9; 1 Thessalonians 5:24). Our grip may be weak, but his is not.

Perseverance and determination. That is the difference between Christian perseverance and mere determination. A man gritting his teeth is relying on his grip, and grips fail. A man holding fast because the promiser is faithful is relying on something outside himself, and the holding on is a response to reliability rather than a substitute for it. And what is held is the confession of our hope: not our feelings, which come and go, but something not yet in hand.

The good confession before Pilate. Their confession has a history older than their baptism. Paul tells Timothy to hold to his confession in the presence of Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession (1 Timothy 6:12–13), using the same word. Standing alone, bound, before the power of Rome, Jesus did not waver: he said he was a king and that he had come to bear witness to the truth (John 18:37), and it cost him his life. Every Christian who holds fast under pressure is holding to what Jesus held to first, and is held by the one who did not let go.

The answer to drift. A congregation slipping away (2:1) is not usually losing an argument; it is losing its grip in the dark. The writer does not give them a new argument. He points at the character of the one who made the promise.

How do I hold fast when my faith feels weak? By looking away from your faith to the one who promised. Weak faith holding a strong Saviour is safe; strong faith in a weak saviour is not. In practice, holding fast means keeping on with the ordinary means: reading and hearing God’s word, praying even when it feels empty, gathering with God’s people, coming to the Lord’s Supper, and saying again what you believe. You will not always feel strong. You are not asked to. You are asked to keep your grip on a promise made by someone who has never broken one.

verseByVerse.quote: And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day drawing near.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consider how to stir up. The third exhortation turns outward, to each other. “Consider” (katanoōmen) is the verb of 3:1, where it was applied to Jesus: helping a particular person forward needs the same attention as contemplating Christ.

Provoke one another. “Stir up” is startling. The noun is paroxysmos, from which we get paroxysm; it means a sharp provoking, an irritation. It is the word Luke uses of the bitter quarrel between Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15:39). So the instruction is to provoke one another, and the only thing that redeems it is the object.

To love and good works. Provoke, yes, but to love and good works: love that shows itself in practical deeds. Some friction between Christians is entirely legitimate: the friend who will not let you settle, whose example makes your comfort uncomfortable, whose generosity shames your caution, and who asks the question you were hoping nobody would ask.

Not neglecting to meet together. Here is the first concrete symptom the letter names: the drift of 2:1 and the dullness of 5:11 show in people who had stopped coming. “Neglecting” (enkataleipontes) means forsaking, abandoning, deserting. “Meet together” (episynagōgē) is assembling, gathering. And it is called a habit (ethos): not a decision or a repudiation but a pattern, which is exactly how drifting works. The verse names no day, but from the beginning the church met on the first day of the week, the Lord’s Day (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10). Christians differ over whether it is a Sabbath kept by rule; this commentary believes the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), and that no one may bind another’s conscience about the day (Romans 14:5).

The reasons would have been good ones. Meeting was dangerous; assembling with Christians marked you out in a city that had already plundered their property. Others may have been drifting, or quietly returning to the synagogue. The writer names it anyway, because you cannot stir up one another, or be stirred, from a distance. Today the reasons are usually softer: tiredness, sport, a busy week, or the wish to believe without being known. But a heart that wants Christ without his people is wanting a Saviour on its own terms, and the one who calls them his brothers (2:11) does not offer himself on those terms.

The Son who sings in the assembly. This letter has already put on the lips of Jesus the words of Psalm 22: I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise (2:12). The risen Son stands among his gathered brothers leading the praise of his Father. And the word for meeting together is the one Paul uses of the last great gathering, our being gathered together to him at his coming (2 Thessalonians 2:1). Every gathering of his people is a small and early form of the one he will call when he comes.

But encouraging one another. “Encouraging” (parakalountes) means exhorting, urging, coming alongside, as in 3:13, where the writer told them to exhort one another every day, as long as it is called today. It is not flattery but putting courage into someone.

The Day drawing near. “The Day” is the day of Christ’s return and judgment (1 Corinthians 3:13; 1 Thessalonians 5:2, 4), and every passing day brings it closer (engizousan, drawing near). It may also include the approaching destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, a foretaste of the final judgment that some of the first readers would live to see. The instinct under pressure is to withdraw and go quiet. The letter says the opposite: the nearer the Day and the harder the times, the more of this, not less.

Does watching a service online fulfil this command? The word is about gathering, being together in one place, and the stirring up it describes needs people who are present to each other. For the sick, the housebound and those cut off by persecution, a livestream is a real mercy, and no one should be made to feel guilty for what they cannot help. But for those who can come, watching is not meeting, and a settled habit of staying away is exactly the drift this verse warns against.

What if my church is difficult, or I have been hurt there? Then take the hurt seriously, and do not take it out on Christ’s body by leaving it altogether. Some churches are unsafe, and if you or your children have been abused or controlled, you must get away and get help; God never asks anyone to stay under abuse. But most of the time the difficulty is ordinary: awkward people, dull sermons, a slight that still stings. Talk to someone you trust, go to the person who hurt you if you can (Matthew 18:15), and if you must move, move to another faithful church, not to no church. Every church is full of sinners; that is who it is for.

On a Tuesday. Choose one specific person in your church and one specific way to spur them on to love and good works this week: a message telling them what you saw God doing in them, an invitation to serve alongside you, a question about how they are really doing.

For worship. The Son of God did not save a scattered crowd of individuals. He loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25). So the awkward brother in the next row and the weary sister by the door are people he died for, given to us to provoke to love, to encourage and to carry, and not one of them will be missing when he calls them home.

verseByVerse.quote: For if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, but a fearful expectation of judgment, and a fury of fire that will consume the adversaries.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the flow. The “for” of verse 26 gives the reason for the urgency of verses 23–25: neglecting to meet was the first step of a drift, and this is where that road ends. Like the earlier warnings, it rests on the teaching just given: Christ’s sacrifice is the only one, so to reject it leaves none. And verses 32–39 turn at once to encouragement.

Sinning deliberately. The fourth warning, to be read with the same care as chapter 6. The preacher includes himself in the “we”. “Deliberately” (hekousiōs, willingly, wilfully) stands first in the Greek sentence, in the emphatic position. And the phrase is a technical one. The law distinguished sins committed unintentionally, for which sacrifice was provided (Leviticus 4), from sin done with a high hand, in open defiance, for which the law named no offering and the sinner was cut off (Numbers 15:27–31). His readers would have recognised the category. “Go on sinning” (hamartanontōn) is a present participle: continuing, persisting. Not a fall but a settled course.

The knowledge of the truth. Full knowledge (epignōsis): not the sin of the ignorant or the deceived, but of those who had understood and confessed the gospel. Rejecting known truth is more serious than rejecting what one has never understood.

The sin in view. Put those together and the sin in view is specific: the informed, deliberate, persistent repudiation of Christ by someone who knows exactly what he is walking away from. In context it is apostasy, the opposite of holding fast (v. 23), and verse 29 will describe it in the plainest terms: trampling the Son of God underfoot. It is not occasional sins of weakness, which all believers commit (1 John 1:8–10). Nor is it the besetting sin a believer hates and keeps falling into and keeps fighting: a sin can be loved and hated at once, and the fight itself is the Spirit’s work (Romans 7:15–25; Galatians 5:17). Nor is it a season of depression, grief or spiritual dryness in which faith feels faint. The person in view has stopped fighting and walked away.

No longer remains a sacrifice. The logic of verse 18 runs the other way. There is one sacrifice, offered once, and a person who rejects it has not exhausted a supply; he has refused the only one there is, and there is no second provision behind it.

A fury of fire. “Fury of fire” (pyros zēlos) is literally a zeal of fire, a fiery jealousy, and the language is Isaiah’s (Isaiah 26:11): God’s holy zeal against those who oppose him. And the word for adversaries (hypenantioi, opponents) makes the point: this is what awaits enemies, not stumbling sons. Apostates join the enemies of God (Philippians 3:18).

What it does not mean. It does not mean a believer who falls into serious sin is lost for ever. David committed adultery and murder, and was restored (Psalm 51). Peter denied Christ, and was restored. The warning is against a deliberate, persistent rejection of Christ. And “consume” does not mean annihilation; Scripture describes the punishment of the wicked as conscious and eternal (Matthew 25:46; Mark 9:48; Revelation 14:11). Fire that consumes describes the destructive, ruinous character of judgment, not the end of the person who suffers it.

Am I lost if I have sinned deliberately since becoming a Christian? No, not if you still want Christ. Every believer sins knowingly at times; that is what makes David and Peter such comfort. The sin of this verse is not a deliberate act of sin but a deliberate abandonment of the Saviour: turning your back on his sacrifice and treating it with contempt. The very fact that you are troubled, and want to be forgiven, shows that you have not done that, because the apostate does not grieve over his rejection of Christ; he despises it. Come back to the sacrifice that still remains for you, confess your sin, and believe the promise of 1 John 1:9.

Why does the warning say “we” if true believers cannot fall away? Because the writer speaks to the whole church as it appears, which includes true believers and some who only profess, and he cannot see hearts. And because warnings are one of the means God uses to keep his true people. A true believer hears the warning and is driven closer to Christ; that is how perseverance works. The guardrail on a mountain road does not imply that cars regularly go over; it is the reason they do not. God has promised to keep his own (v. 39; John 10:28), and he keeps them partly by warnings like this one.

For worship. The severity of this warning is the measure of the sacrifice’s worth. If there were many ways back to God, rejecting one would not matter much. But there is only one, and it cost the blood of the Son of God. And that same sacrifice still stands today, sufficient for every sinner who comes to it, however deliberately he has sinned. The door that is shut to the one who tramples it is wide open to the one who knocks.

verseByVerse.quote: Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the evidence of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has profaned the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and has outraged the Spirit of grace? For we know him who said, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay.” And again, “The Lord will judge his people.” It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Set aside the law of Moses. The argument runs from lesser to greater, as at 2:2–3. The law is Deuteronomy 17:2–7, and the offence in view there is idolatry, going and serving other gods. “Set aside” (athetēsas) means rejected, nullified. Deliberate rejection of the covenant brought the death penalty, and the safeguard was the testimony of witnesses.

How much worse. The writer puts it as a question and invites his readers to do the arithmetic themselves. If rejecting the shadow was so serious, how much more rejecting the substance?

Trampled underfoot. Three descriptions escalate. “Trampled underfoot” (katapatēsas) is to treat with contempt. Instead of honouring the Son whom God exalted to his right hand, seated above the angels with his enemies under his feet (1:13), the apostate treats him as dirt beneath his own.

By which he was sanctified. “Profaned” (koinon hēgēsamenos) is to reckon something holy as ordinary, treating Christ’s blood as if it were the blood of a common criminal. “By which he was sanctified” (en hō hēgiasthē) is the hardest phrase in the passage, since it appears to describe the apostate as sanctified by the blood.

A hard phrase. The views are set out below; the reading that fits best is that he was outwardly set apart as part of the covenant community without inward regeneration, as all Israel was sprinkled with covenant blood at Sinai (9:19–20) though many were unbelievers. He is like the field in 6:7–8 that drank the same rain as the fruitful one and bore thorns.

The Spirit of grace. “Outraged” (enybrisas) is to treat with insolent contempt. “The Spirit of grace” is the Holy Spirit, who brings God’s grace and had worked among them (6:4). There is an echo here of the unforgivable sin of blasphemy against the Spirit (Mark 3:28–29). To insult the one whose whole work is grace is to cut oneself off from grace. Those who fear they have committed it show by their fear that they have not, for the hardened do not grieve over it.

Vengeance is mine. Two quotations from the Song of Moses: God himself will judge (Deuteronomy 32:35; Romans 12:19), and, sharper, he will judge his people (32:36). Belonging to the covenant community is not a shelter from God’s judgment; it is the reason judgment begins there (1 Peter 4:17).

The hands of the living God. To fall into his hands is to fall under his direct judgment, with no mediator. Living is the key word. An idol cannot see, act or judge; this God does all three, and his holiness is not an idea to be managed but a person to be met, for our God is a consuming fire (12:29). The phrase cuts both ways. To fall away is to fall away from the living God (3:12), and there is nowhere to fall except into his hands. David once chose to fall into the hands of the LORD, for his mercy is great (2 Samuel 24:14). The same hands are the only refuge and the only danger, and which they are depends entirely on how a man comes. For those who come through Christ, they are a Father’s hands.

A word to the frightened. These verses are meant to stop someone walking away, not to torment someone trying to come home. If you read them and tremble because you love Christ and fear you have failed him, that trembling is a sign of life: the person described treats the Son’s blood as common, and you are treating it as precious. A troubled conscience, a sin you still battle, a dark season of the mind: none of these is trampling the Son of God. The hands of the living God are fearful only to those who refuse his Son. To everyone who runs to Christ they are open, and he has promised never to cast out anyone who comes (John 6:37).

Where Christians differ: does this verse show that the sanctified can be lost? Christians answer in three main ways. Arminians (who hold that saving grace can be resisted) believe that a real believer can turn away and be lost; they are brothers who take the warning with deep seriousness, and they point to the strong words here: he was sanctified by the blood. Some take the warning as hypothetical, describing what would happen if a believer fell away, though God will not let it happen. Others hold that the writer describes someone who belonged to the covenant community, knew the truth and shared its privileges, but never truly trusted Christ, and at last walked away (6:4–8). This commentary’s view: sanctified in Hebrews can refer to the outward consecration of covenant membership, as when the whole people of Israel was sprinkled with covenant blood. The apostate had been outwardly identified with the new covenant community, baptised and sharing its life, and so in an outward sense set apart by the covenant blood, without inward renewal. Those whom Christ has perfected for all time by his single offering (v. 14) cannot be lost. Verse 39 makes the distinction: there are those who shrink back and are destroyed, and those who have faith and are saved. The letter rests its readers’ perseverance on Christ, who is able to save to the uttermost (7:25). God keeps his own, and warnings like this one are among the means he uses to do it.

How can a God of love speak like this? Because love is not the same as indifference. A father who is never angry at what destroys his children does not love them more; he cares less. God’s anger is his holiness standing against everything that ruins the people he made, never an outburst. And look at who the warning is aimed at: not sinners who come for mercy, but people who have known the mercy and trampled it. The same God who speaks these words gave his Son to bear that very wrath for everyone who comes to him (Romans 5:9; 1 Thessalonians 1:10). The cross is the proof that he does not delight in judgment, and the only safe place to stand when you think about it.

How can I tell the difference between a true believer and someone only outwardly sanctified? Often, in this life, you cannot tell with certainty about someone else, and you are not asked to. Both may be baptised, attend, and know the truth. The difference shows over time: true faith goes on trusting Christ, loves him, and comes back to him after falling, while a merely outward profession eventually treats him as common and walks away. For yourself, the question is not whether you have been baptised or how long you have attended, but whether you are trusting Christ now and want him. If you do, you are not the person of this verse. Look to him, not to your record.

Can someone who has walked away from Christ ever come back? Yes, if they come back. Many who drifted, even for years, have returned, and their return showed that they were his all along, like the prodigal son, who was a son in the far country. Only God knows who has finally hardened himself, and the warning describes the end of that road, not every person who has wandered on it. So pray for those you love who have walked away, and keep the door open. If you are the one who walked away and you want to return, the fact that you want to is God drawing you. Come.

On a Tuesday. Treat the blood of Christ as holy today. It can become common in our thinking: a careless joke about the cross, the Lord’s Supper taken absent-mindedly, an assumption that grace means God does not mind. Repent of that, and let the fear of God drive you not from him but into his hands as a child.

verseByVerse.quote: But recall the former days when, after you were enlightened, you endured a hard struggle with sufferings, sometimes being publicly exposed to reproach and affliction, and sometimes being partners with those so treated. For you had compassion on those in prison, and you joyfully accepted the plundering of your property, since you knew that you yourselves had a better possession and an abiding one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Recall the former days. The tone changes completely. Having brought them to the edge, the writer reminds them who they are, as in 6:9–12, and tells us what had actually happened to them.

After you were enlightened. “Enlightened” (phōtisthentes), as in 6:4: when they first came to faith, when the light of the gospel broke on them. The suffering came after the light: becoming Christians is what brought it on them.

A hard struggle. The word for struggle (athlēsis) gives us athlete: a great contest, fought in public. If the readers lived in Rome, as 13:24 may suggest, it was possibly the trouble under the emperor Claudius, who expelled Jews from Rome around AD 49, partly because of disturbances over one Chrestus (probably Christ), according to the Roman historian Suetonius (Acts 18:2).

Publicly exposed. The verb (theatrizomenoi) is a theatre word: made a spectacle of, put on a stage. Mocked in public, in a culture where honour and shame were the currency of a life. Paul used the same picture of the apostles: we have become a spectacle to the world (1 Corinthians 4:9).

The reproach was his before it was theirs. The word for reproach (oneidismos) is one this letter keeps for Christ. Moses considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt (11:26), and the readers are told at the end to go to Jesus outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured, since he suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people through his own blood (13:12–13). So the mockery they met in the streets was the shame he carried first, when he was mocked, spat on and crucified in public, now falling on those who bore his name. To be shamed for Christ is to be found standing where he stood.

Partners. “Partners” (koinōnoi) are sharers, and that took its own courage. It is one thing to be dragged out yourself; it is another to walk over and stand beside somebody who has been, sharing their shame, when you could have stayed indoors.

Compassion on those in prison. “Had compassion” (synepathēsate) is to suffer with, the same word used of Christ in 4:15, who is able to sympathise with our weaknesses. Roman prisoners depended on friends for food and care, and visiting one meant identifying yourself publicly with his crime (13:3; Matthew 25:36). These people went.

Joyfully accepted. Not merely endured: joyfully accepted, while their houses were being emptied, perhaps by neighbours or a mob, with little hope of redress. It is what Jesus said would happen: blessed are you when others revile you and persecute you; rejoice and be glad (Matthew 5:11–12), and what the apostles did, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name (Acts 5:41).

A better possession. Not by stoicism, or by pretending the loss was small, but by knowing they owned something the mob could not reach and could not carry. “Abiding” (menousan) is the letter’s word for what lasts, set against everything that wears out like a garment (1:11). Their real treasure was in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal (Matthew 6:19–21; 1 Peter 1:4). Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, add in heaven; the earliest do not, and the meaning is the same.

Be what you already were. These people had once made that calculation under real pressure and come out singing. The writer is not asking them to become something new. He is asking them to be what they already were. Memory is one of God’s gifts for perseverance: the grace that carried you once is evidence that it will carry you again.

How can anyone be joyful when they are being robbed? Not by being glad about the loss itself, which is still a real wrong, but by being more glad about something else. The joy came from what they knew: they had a better and lasting possession. A man who has just inherited a fortune can lose his wallet with a smile. That is the joy here. It is not natural cheerfulness, and it does not deny grief; it is the fruit of a heart that has put its treasure in heaven. Such joy grows by setting your mind on what you have in Christ long before the loss comes.

Should Christians resist injustice, or just accept it joyfully? Both have their place. Paul appealed to his rights as a Roman citizen when that served the gospel (Acts 16:37; 22:25; 25:11), and Christians may rightly use lawful means to protect themselves, their families and the weak. But when the only way to keep your goods is to deny Christ, or when there is no remedy, you let them go, and you can do it with joy. The question is not whether you may seek justice, but whether your heart is free to lose everything and still have Christ.

On a Tuesday. These believers fed and visited the imprisoned, and Christians are still in prison for their faith today. This week visit, write to or pray by name for one of them, as if you were in the cell beside them (13:3), and give something you own towards their help, since Christ is your better and abiding possession.

For worship. The God who gave these believers their light also gave them their joy, with their houses emptied, by showing them a possession no mob can carry: Christ himself. He was stripped of his own clothes at the cross, and soldiers gambled for them, so that we might be given riches that last.
verseByVerse.note: Possibly the persecution under the emperor Claudius, who expelled Jews from Rome about AD 49.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not throw away your confidence, which has a great reward. For you have need of endurance, so that when you have done the will of God you may receive what is promised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not throw away. Not do not lose it, as though it might slip out of a pocket. To throw away (apobalēte) is an act: you do it on purpose, as a soldier might throw away his shield to run faster. And “confidence” (parrēsia) is the same word as verse 19, 3:6 and 4:16: the boldness to speak, the freedom to come. What they are in danger of discarding is not a mood but their access. There is a version of quietness that looks like humility and is actually the shield going over the wall.

A great reward. The writer is not embarrassed by the motive. Reward language runs through this letter (11:6, 26), and it is never treated as a lower motive. God rewards persevering faith, and he wants us to want the reward.

Need of endurance. Not need of better arguments, or clearer teaching, or a fresh experience. Endurance (hypomonē): remaining under a weight without buckling (12:1–3; James 1:3–4). That is the writer’s diagnosis after ten chapters of theology, and it is a humbling one for anyone who assumes that people leave the faith because they have run out of reasons. These readers had the reasons. What they were short of was staying power.

Done the will of God. Doing comes first and receiving after: not because the promise is earned, but because it lies at the end of a road that must actually be walked. What is promised is the eternal inheritance (9:15). Endurance is not waiting; it is continuing to obey while nothing visible changes.

The will he did first. The phrase has already appeared on the lips of the Son: behold, I have come to do your will, O God (v. 7), and by that will we have been sanctified (v. 10). The will these weary believers must keep doing is the will Christ has already done for them, to the cross and through it. They are not asked to win by their endurance what he won by his. They are asked to walk the road that his obedience has made safe, behind the one who endured the cross and is now seated at the right hand of the throne (12:2).

Is it wrong to serve God for a reward? No, provided the reward is God himself and what he gives, not a lever for getting something else from him. Moses looked to the reward (11:26), and Jesus endured the cross for the joy set before him (12:2). God made us to want joy, and he is the greatest joy. What would be wrong is serving him only for earthly payment, or thinking the reward is wages we have earned. It is a Father’s gift to his children, out of all proportion to anything they did, and it is meant to strengthen us to keep going.

What if I am worn out and do not think I can keep going? Then you are exactly the person this verse was written for. These readers were tired too. Endurance is not the absence of weariness; it is continuing under it, one day at a time, and it is given by God as you look to Christ (12:2–3). Do the next faithful thing, not the whole of the rest of your life. Get rest if you need rest, ask for help, and tell God honestly that you are weak. He gives power to the faint (Isaiah 40:29–31), and he has promised that the one who began a good work in you will bring it to completion (Philippians 1:6).

verseByVerse.quote: For, “Yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay; but my righteous one shall live by faith, and if he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet a little while. The writer quotes Habakkuk, the prophet of waiting, whose book opens with the complaint: O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear? (Habakkuk 1:2). The answer he received was that the vision awaits its appointed time; if it seems slow, wait for it (Habakkuk 2:3). The words blend Isaiah 26:20 and Habakkuk 2:3–4 in the Greek translation, whose a little while (mikron hoson hoson) doubles itself to press the shortness of the wait.

The coming one. Where Habakkuk’s Hebrew speaks of the vision coming, the Greek text the writer follows speaks of a person: “the coming one” (ho erchomenos), a title for the Messiah (Matthew 11:3). The writer applies it to Christ’s return. The promise has a face. “Will not delay” (ou chronisei): it may seem slow, but it will come at the right time (2 Peter 3:8–9).

Shall live by faith. It is the sentence that changed Luther’s life, and Paul quotes it at key points in two letters (Romans 1:17; Galatians 3:11). Hebrews uses it differently. Paul takes it to answer the question how a man is justified: by faith, not works. Hebrews takes it to answer how a man keeps going: by faith, not sight. The emphasis falls on live: the righteous man does not merely begin by faith; he lives by it, and chapter 11 is about to illustrate what that looks like over a lifetime.

If he shrinks back. The verb (hyposteilētai) was used of furling a sail and of a soldier shrinking from danger (compare Acts 20:27). Faith goes forward when it cannot see; shrinking back is what faith looks like when it fails. The wilderness generation shrank back at the border of a good land. “My soul has no pleasure in him” (ouk eudokei) is a restrained way of saying something severe, and its restraint is characteristic of Scripture at its most serious. It is not rage. It is the withdrawal of delight, which from God is worse.

Textual note. The writer reverses the order of Habakkuk’s two clauses in the Greek translation, so that my righteous one becomes the subject of if he shrinks back. This makes clear that the warning is addressed to those who profess to be God’s people. The KJV’s if any man draw back adds words not in the Greek, which says simply if he shrinks back.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the coming of Christ was expected within a few years only, and that the writer was mistaken. A little while is God’s perspective; from his view, the whole age between the comings is brief, and a thousand years are as one day (2 Peter 3:8). Every generation lives in the last hour, and every believer’s waiting is short compared with the eternity that follows.

Why does it feel as if Christ is taking so long? Because we measure time by our lifetimes, and God measures it by his purpose. Peter answers the question directly: the Lord is not slow as some count slowness, but patient, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance (2 Peter 3:9). Every day of delay is a day in which more of his people are being gathered in. Meanwhile the righteous live by faith: they go on trusting and obeying in the gap, as Habakkuk did. And for each of us, the waiting ends at death, when we go to be with him, which can never be more than a little while away.

verseByVerse.quote: But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not of those who shrink back. The chapter of the letter’s most frightening warning ends with the writer putting himself and his readers firmly on the right side of it. “Are not of those” is a statement of category, not of achievement: not we have performed better, but we belong to a different kind.

Preserve their souls. “Destroyed” (eis apōleian) is perdition, eternal ruin (Philippians 1:28; 3:19; 2 Thessalonians 1:9). Set against it is “preserve their souls” (eis peripoiēsin psychēs): literally the gaining, keeping or possessing of the soul, an idiom for coming through alive.

How the warnings work. The writer describes the danger in the strongest terms available, and then tells his readers he does not believe it applies to them, the same pattern as chapter 6, where the severest warning in the letter is followed at once by we feel sure of better things (6:9). Warning and assurance are not alternatives. The warning is one of the means by which the assurance turns out to be true.

Defined by faith. The two categories are defined by one thing only: faith. Not endurance, though he has just demanded it; not good works, though he has commended theirs. That is why Hebrews 11 follows: the writer defines faith, and then spends forty verses producing a crowd of people who had it, so that a struggling congregation could see what the word looks like when it is worn by real men and women over a lifetime. And the crowd ends not with one of them but with Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith (12:1–2). Faith preserves the soul because of where it looks: away from itself, to the one who ran the race first and finished it.

How can I be sure I am one of those who have faith? Look first at Christ, and then at the evidence. Are you trusting him, and him alone, for your acceptance with God? That is faith, however weak it feels. Then look for the signs that faith is alive: you still come back to him after you fall, you want to be holy even when you are not, you love his people, and you cannot let him go. These are not the grounds of your salvation, but they are its fruit. If you find them in yourself, take this verse as spoken to you: you are not of those who shrink back.

For worship. Faith is the whole difference between those who are lost and those who are saved, and faith is God’s gift. The God who has just shown us the fire stoops to say of trembling believers, you are not of those. Our souls are preserved because they are held, and the one who holds them laid down his life for them (John 6:39).

10.text: <sup>1</sup>For since the law has but a shadow of the good things to come instead of the true form of these realities, it can never, by the same sacrifices that are continually offered every year, make perfect those who draw near.<sup>2</sup>Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered, since the worshipers, having once been cleansed, would no longer have any consciousness of sins?<sup>3</sup>But in these sacrifices there is a reminder of sins every year.<sup>4</sup>For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.<sup>5</sup>Consequently, when Christ came into the world, he said, “Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but a body have you prepared for me;<sup>6</sup>in burnt offerings and sin offerings you have taken no pleasure.<sup>7</sup>Then I said, ’Behold, I have come to do your will, O God, as it is written of me in the scroll of the book.’”<sup>8</sup>When he said above, “You have neither desired nor taken pleasure in sacrifices and offerings and burnt offerings and sin offerings” (these are offered according to the law),<sup>9</sup>then he added, “Behold, I have come to do your will.” He does away with the first in order to establish the second.<sup>10</sup>And by that will we have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.<sup>11</sup>And every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins.<sup>12</sup>But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God,<sup>13</sup>waiting from that time until his enemies should be made a footstool for his feet.<sup>14</sup>For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.<sup>15</sup>And the Holy Spirit also bears witness to us; for after saying,<sup>16</sup>“This is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws on their hearts, and write them on their minds,”<sup>17</sup>then he adds, “I will remember their sins and their lawless deeds no more.”<sup>18</sup>Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin.<sup>19</sup>Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Jesus,<sup>20</sup>by the new and living way that he opened for us through the curtain, that is, through his flesh,<sup>21</sup>and since we have a great priest over the house of God,<sup>22</sup>let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water.<sup>23</sup>Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for he who promised is faithful.<sup>24</sup>And let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works,<sup>25</sup>not neglecting to meet together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another, and all the more as you see the Day drawing near.<sup>26</sup>For if we go on sinning deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins,<sup>27</sup>but a fearful expectation of judgment, and a fury of fire that will consume the adversaries.<sup>28</sup>Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the evidence of two or three witnesses.<sup>29</sup>How much worse punishment, do you think, will be deserved by the one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has profaned the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and has outraged the Spirit of grace?<sup>30</sup>For we know him who said, “Vengeance is mine; I will repay.” And again, “The Lord will judge his people.”<sup>31</sup>It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.<sup>32</sup>But recall the former days when, after you were enlightened, you endured a hard struggle with sufferings,<sup>33</sup>sometimes being publicly exposed to reproach and affliction, and sometimes being partners with those so treated.<sup>34</sup>For you had compassion on those in prison, and you joyfully accepted the plundering of your property, since you knew that you yourselves had a better possession and an abiding one.<sup>35</sup>Therefore do not throw away your confidence, which has a great reward.<sup>36</sup>For you have need of endurance, so that when you have done the will of God you may receive what is promised.<sup>37</sup>For, “Yet a little while, and the coming one will come and will not delay;<sup>38</sup>but my righteous one shall live by faith, and if he shrinks back, my soul has no pleasure in him.”<sup>39</sup>But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.

11.title: By Faith: The Great Cloud of Witnesses
11.overview:
Ten chapters have argued that Jesus is better. Chapter 11 shows what it looks like to live on that: a gallery of people who took God at his word about things they could not see, and acted on it.

The gallery is honest. Its members are often inconsistent (Sarah laughed, Jacob deceived, Samson was a disgrace), and its outcomes are opposite: some shut lions’ mouths, some were sawn in two. All are commended, and none received what was promised. The chapter ends by saying why: God was keeping something better, so that they and we would be made perfect together.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — By Faith: Title Deeds and Tents
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faith takes hold of what is promised and not yet seen, and without it no one can please God. The gallery opens with creation, Abel, Enoch and Noah, and then dwells on Abraham and his family: strangers in the land of promise, looking for a city God is building, and dying still trusting.
verseByVerse.theology:
Faith as a Title Deed

Faith gives the things hoped for a footing in the present, because it rests on the reliability of the one who promised. Everyone in this gallery is commended for something they did that made no sense apart from God's word.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob lived in tents in the land of promise and died without receiving it.

Now: God is not ashamed to be called the God of people who are visibly waiting for a better country.

verseByVerse.quote: Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen. For by it the people of old received their commendation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Hebrews 11 is the great chapter on faith, answering the call of 10:38–39 to live by faith and not shrink back. Faith is assurance of what we hope for and conviction of what we cannot see (vv. 1–3). Then comes the gallery: Abel, Enoch and Noah (vv. 4–7); Abraham and Sarah, strangers looking for God’s city (vv. 8–22); Moses, the Red Sea, Jericho and Rahab (vv. 23–31); judges, kings, prophets and martyrs, of whom the world was not worthy (vv. 32–38). None received what was promised, for God had planned something better, that they should be made perfect together with us (vv. 39–40).

Now faith is. It is not quite a definition: the writer says less what faith is in the abstract than what it does toward the future and the unseen. That was exactly these readers’ difficulty: they could see the hostile neighbours and the plundered houses (10:32–34); they could not see what they had been promised.

The assurance of things hoped for. “Assurance” is hypostasis, literally that which stands under, a foundation; the same word is used at 1:3 of the very being of God. In some papyri it is used in property documents for something like a title deed, the paper that establishes a claim to something you do not yet hold. A man with the title deed to a house he has never seen owns it, and behaves accordingly. Faith is the title deed to what God has promised: the city, the inheritance, the resurrection, the return of Christ.

The conviction of things not seen. “Conviction” is elenchos, a word from the law courts: proof, evidence, the demonstration that settles a case. Faith functions as evidence of what cannot be seen: God himself, heaven, Christ at the right hand of God, and the events still to come (2 Corinthians 4:18; 5:7).

Resting on the promiser. Both words guard against the idea that faith is believing without grounds. Its ground is not the strength of the believing but the reliability of the promiser (10:23).

The unseen one at the centre. What, above all, does faith see that the eye cannot? We do not yet see everything in subjection to man, the letter says, but we see Jesus, crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death (2:8–9). He is the hidden centre of every hope in this chapter: the offspring promised to Abraham, the reproach Moses chose (11:26), the something better the whole gallery died waiting for (11:39–40). And the chapter runs straight on into looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith (12:2). Every portrait in this gallery is painted with its face turned toward him.

The people of old. “Received their commendation” (emartyrēthēsan) means they were witnessed to, a word that recurs through the chapter (vv. 4, 5, 39): God himself bears witness, in Scripture, that they pleased him.

How is faith different from positive thinking? Positive thinking trusts that things will turn out well because you expect them to; faith trusts that God will do what he has said because he has said it. Positive thinking is about outcomes you choose; faith is about promises God has made, and it can be just as confident when the outcome looks bad, because it is not resting on the outcome. Abraham, as this chapter will show, expected his son to die and still trusted God. Positive thinking would have been useless on Mount Moriah. Faith was not.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By faith we understand. The first example is not a person but something every reader already believes. “By faith” will open each example like a drumbeat. And faith is paired with understanding (nooumen, perceive with the mind): not a substitute for knowing, but the means by which something is genuinely known.

By the word of God. “Universe” (tous aiōnas) is the ages, all of space and time, as in 1:2, “framed” by God’s spoken word, as Genesis tells it: God said, and it was (Genesis 1:3; Psalm 33:6, 9).

How long did God take? The verse teaches that God made the world out of nothing, by speaking. It does not say how long he took. That question belongs to Genesis itself, and this commentary reads the days there as six ordinary days: Genesis numbers them and marks each with evening and morning, and the fourth commandment builds our week on them: in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them (Exodus 20:11). Other Christians who hold to the full authority of Scripture read the days differently, as long ages, as a literary framework, or as analogical days, often because they weigh the evidence for an old earth or the literary pattern of the chapter, and Reformed Christians have differed on this without dividing. In any reading the point of this verse stands: the world exists because God spoke.

Not made out of things visible. The visible world does not have a visible origin: trace it back and you arrive not at earlier stuff but at a word. Strictly, the verse says that the visible did not come from anything visible; read with the rest of Scripture, that means God created from nothing, ex nihilo, by his word alone, for he calls into existence the things that do not exist (Romans 4:17; Colossians 1:16). This was a radical claim against Greek philosophy, which generally held that matter was eternal and that a god at best shaped it.

Through whom he made the ages. Hebrews has already named the Word by which the ages were framed: the Son, through whom God created the world, and who upholds the universe by the word of his power (1:2–3). So faith in creation is faith not in an impersonal command but in a Person, the Saviour who made purification for sins and sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high.

Why start with creation? Because the chapter is about acting on the strength of what cannot be seen, and creation is the first and largest instance. Nobody watched it happen. There were no witnesses, and there is no possibility of any. Every person who believes the world was made does so on the strength of testimony rather than observation. So the writer establishes at the outset that this is not a strange way to hold anything. His readers already order their whole understanding of reality around an event none of them saw, and he is about to ask them to keep ordering their lives around a promise they cannot see either. The first lesson of faith is that the God who made everything from nothing can be trusted to keep every promise.

Does science contradict this verse? No honest science contradicts it, because science studies the visible world, and this verse is about where the visible world came from. Science can describe how things work and trace them back a long way, but it cannot see behind the beginning, and it cannot tell you why there is something rather than nothing. Christians should welcome the study of creation, much of which was pioneered by believers who wanted to think God’s thoughts after him. Where particular theories conflict with what God has plainly said, the theories are human and changeable, and God’s word stands. Faithful Christians still differ over how some findings fit with Genesis, and those questions can be held with patience and humility.

On a Tuesday. Look at something made today: the sky, a tree, your own hand. It was not there, and then God spoke, and it was. Set the worry you are carrying next to that fact, and tell him in a sentence that the God who made something out of nothing is not short of resources for it.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Abel offered to God a more acceptable sacrifice than Cain, through which he was commended as righteous, God commending him by accepting his gifts. And through his faith, though he died, he still speaks. By faith Enoch was taken up so that he should not see death, and he was not found, because God had taken him. Now before he was taken he was commended as having pleased God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A more acceptable sacrifice. Genesis records that Abel’s offering was accepted and Cain’s refused without saying why (Genesis 4:3–5). The writer supplies the reason: faith. It was not merely that Abel’s was an animal and Cain’s was grain, for the law later commanded both. Abel brought the firstborn of his flock and their fat portions, the best (Genesis 4:4), from a heart right with God; Cain’s heart was wrong, as his murder of Abel showed (1 John 3:12).

The same act is not the same act. Two men brought what they had, and God saw what was underneath it. Two people may sing the same hymn, give the same amount and kneel in the same pew, and God sees one offering and not the other. Cain shows the heart of religion used as a bargain: when God did not accept his offering, he was not humbled but angry, and the anger turned on the brother God had accepted (Genesis 4:5–8). Religion that tries to earn God’s favour always resents grace shown to someone else.

Commended as righteous. “Commended” (emartyrēthē) means testified to, and God himself bore the witness by accepting Abel’s gifts. Abel is the first person in the Bible’s story to be called righteous, as Jesus called him (Matthew 23:35; compare 1 John 3:12), and God declared him so on the ground of faith. To be declared righteous is to be counted in the right before God the Judge and accepted by him; the New Testament calls it justification, and from Abel on it has come by faith (Romans 4:5).

He still speaks. In Genesis it is Abel’s blood that cries out from the ground (Genesis 4:10); here it is his faith that goes on speaking. Nearly everyone in this chapter in it is dead, and every one of them is still talking.

A better word than Abel’s. Abel’s voice is not the last word. Believers have come to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (12:24). Abel’s blood cried out against the one who shed it. Jesus, the Righteous One, was handed over by the leaders of his own people, and his blood does not call for vengeance. It pleads for pardon; Luke records the prayer: Father, forgive them (Luke 23:34), a verse missing from some early manuscripts but widely received as genuine. Abel’s faith still speaks of a God who accepts sinners by faith; Christ’s blood is the reason he can.

Enoch was taken up. The shortest biography in Genesis: Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him (Genesis 5:24). In a chapter whose refrain is he died, he died, he died, one man has no death recorded. God took him directly to himself, as he later took Elijah (2 Kings 2:11). He was not found, as the Greek of Genesis 5:24 puts it, as if people looked for him and he had gone on ahead.

Having pleased God. The Greek Old Testament renders walked with God as pleased God (euarestēkenai tō theō), which is where the writer gets the phrase, and it leads straight into verse 6. To walk with God is to please him, and to please him requires faith.

Opposite outcomes, both commended. Set the two men side by side. Abel died young and violently; Enoch did not die at all. Faith produced opposite outcomes in the first two examples, and both are commended. Anyone reading this chapter as a list of what faith gets you has been warned in the first two entries of the gallery.

What does it mean to walk with God? It means living each day in his company, as two people walk together on a road, going the same way, talking as they go. In practice it is ordinary: speaking to him through the day, listening to his word, keeping in step with what he wants, turning back quickly when you wander off. Enoch did it for three hundred years while raising sons and daughters (Genesis 5:22), so it is not a life withdrawn from the world. The question is not whether you have had dramatic experiences, but whether you are going his way and keeping him company.

verseByVerse.quote: And without faith it is impossible to please him, for whoever would draw near to God must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Impossible to please him. “Impossible” (adynaton) is the letter’s absolute again (6:4, 18; 10:4). Faithless obedience is not inferior; it cannot please him at all. A person may live decently and give generously, and none of it pleases God if it is not done in faith. Whatever does not proceed from faith is sin (Romans 14:23).

In the flow. Verse 6 is the principle under the whole gallery. It explains why Enoch pleased God (v. 5), and answers 10:38, where God has no pleasure in one who shrinks back.

Why it has to be so. To do good without trusting God is to treat him as somebody to be managed rather than believed, and no relationship can be pleased by a partner who does not take the other at his word. A husband who brings his wife flowers every week but does not believe a word she says has not pleased her.

Whoever would draw near. “Draw near” is the letter’s key verb for approaching God (4:16; 7:25; 10:22). The two things anyone drawing near must believe are strikingly modest.

Must believe that he exists. Not a developed doctrine of God: that he is there, the living God, not an idea or a force. This is the most basic element of faith. But even demons believe that, and shudder (James 2:19); saving faith goes further.

He rewards those who seek him. That he is worth approaching: that the seeking is not into an empty room. God is not indifferent, distant or stingy; he responds to those who seek him and gives them himself and his blessings (Jeremiah 29:13; Matthew 7:7–8).

The harder of the two. A great many people believe God exists and behave as though seeking him were pointless. The practical atheism of the half-believing is not a denial of God’s existence but a settled expectation that nothing will come of approaching him. Hebrews says faith is precisely the confidence that something will.

Reward without apology. The reward language needs no apology. It runs through the chapter: Moses was looking to the reward (v. 26), the patriarchs to a city (v. 10). Seeking God for what he gives is only mercenary if what he gives is something other than himself. It is not. Fear not, Abram, I am your shield; your reward shall be very great (Genesis 15:1).

Drawing near through a priest. Who may draw near to a God this holy? Under the old covenant only the high priest, once a year and never without blood (9:7).
