The letter answers with a person: Jesus is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him (7:25), and has opened a new and living way through his own flesh (10:19–22). Pleasing faith rests on what he did.

What about those who have never heard? This verse does not say that a vague belief in God is enough: the faith that pleases God draws near through Christ (7:25), and the God who rewards seekers sends them the message, as he sent Peter to Cornelius (Acts 10). The answer is not to speculate about them but to go to them. (See Matthew 7:13–14 for the fuller answer.)

Can my good deeds before I believed please God? Not in the sense this verse means. They may be good for others, and God in his kindness restrains evil and uses even the deeds of unbelievers. But they are not done in faith, from love for God, for his glory, and so they cannot make a person acceptable to him (the Westminster Confession and the 1689 London Baptist Confession, 16.7). That is humbling, and it is freeing. You do not have to bring a record to God. You come with empty hands, trusting Christ, and from then on even your small and imperfect works are pleasing to him, because they are offered through his Son (13:21; 1 Peter 2:5).

For worship. God is not hiding to make himself hard to find. He is there, and he is good, and the reward is himself. And he has done more than wait: he has come looking for us in his Son, and drawn us to seek him by his Spirit. No one has ever sought the living God in vain.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Noah, being warned by God concerning events as yet unseen, in reverent fear constructed an ark for the saving of his household. By this he condemned the world and became an heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Events as yet unseen. “Events as yet unseen” were a flood of judgment such as had never happened (Genesis 6:13–17). Noah was told about something for which there was no evidence whatever, and perhaps about a kind of rain he had never watched fall.

In reverent fear. One word (eulabētheis), holy fear, the same disposition credited to Christ at 5:7. Noah took God seriously, which is the whole of his commendation.

For the saving of his household. Here faith becomes visible: not a private conviction but a very large wooden object, probably built over years in full view of neighbours who had every reason to think him mad. And it was for the saving of his household: one man’s obedience carried seven others through (Genesis 7:1; 1 Peter 3:20). Not one person in this gallery is commended for holding an opinion. Every one is commended for something they did that made no sense apart from a word from God.

He condemned the world. Not by preaching at it, though Peter calls him a herald of righteousness (2 Peter 2:5). By building. A man taking God at his word in public passes a verdict on everyone who has heard the same word and done nothing, not by criticising them but simply by acting as though it were true.

An heir of the righteousness. The phrase (tēs kata pistin dikaiosynēs) is Paul’s (Romans 4; Philippians 3:9), and it is placed on a man who lived before Abraham, before the law and before circumcision. Noah found favour in the eyes of the LORD (Genesis 6:8): grace came first, and God declared him righteous (Genesis 7:1). Righteousness by faith is how it has always worked. The word heir explains it: an heir does not earn his inheritance; he receives it because of whose he is. Noah’s right standing with God was not wages for building the ark but a gift he received by trusting God’s word, the same gift every believer receives in Christ (Romans 4:4–5).

One man’s obedience, a household saved. The shape of Noah’s story is the shape of the gospel: one man, moved by reverent fear, did what God said, and those who belonged to him were carried through the judgment with him. Hebrews uses the same word of Jesus, heard because of his reverence (5:7–9), and calls the church his house (3:6). Noah’s obedience saved his family from drowning; Christ’s obedience to the point of death carries his whole household through the judgment of God itself (Romans 5:19).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Noah was saved by building the ark. He was saved by faith in God’s word, which showed itself in building the ark. Faith and obedience are inseparable but distinct: the obedience was the shape his faith took, not the ground of his acceptance.

What if my family thinks my faith is foolish? Noah’s neighbours certainly did, and God did not ask him to win the argument; he asked him to keep building. Live faithfully, kindly and consistently, without preaching at people who are not listening, and without hiding what you believe. Your steady obedience is itself a testimony, and God often uses it over years. Bring each member of your family before God. And remember that Noah’s faith was for the saving of his household; God has often been pleased to bring families to himself through one member who believed first.

On a Tuesday. Is God calling you to obey him in something that looks foolish to others: giving generously when money is tight, gladly setting Sunday apart for worship when everyone else is busy, refusing to cut a corner at work, staying faithful in a hard marriage? Do it by faith, as Noah did. Your obedience will be patchy, as Noah’s was after the flood (Genesis 9:20–21); Christ’s was not, and his is counted as yours.

For worship. God warned the world through a man with a hammer, year after year, while his patience waited (1 Peter 3:20). When the flood came, he shut the door himself (Genesis 7:16), and the ark rode on the very waters of judgment that drowned the world. So it is with all who are in Christ: the judgment broke over him, and those inside are carried through it, shut in by God’s own hand.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance. And he went out, not knowing where he was going. By faith he went to live in the land of promise, as in a foreign land, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, heirs with him of the same promise. For he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham obeyed. Abraham receives more attention than anyone else in the chapter (vv. 8–19), and his first act is obedience. “Called” (kaloumenos) is a present participle: the obedience began before the call had finished ringing (Genesis 12:1–4). The place was Canaan, promised to him and his descendants as an inheritance (Genesis 12:7; 15:18–21).

Not knowing where. The order is the point: he obeyed first and found out afterwards. A man of seventy-five, having already left Ur, left his father’s household for an unnamed destination, with no map and no way of verifying anything he had been told (Genesis 12:1–4). Security in that culture was land and kin, and he left both.

As in a foreign land. He arrived, and he was still a stranger, a resident alien (parōkēsen). The land was promised to him, and the only part of it he ever owned was a grave: a field with a cave, bought to bury his wife in (Genesis 23:17–20).

Living in tents. He lived in a tent for a hundred years in the country God had given him (Genesis 12:8; 26:25; 33:18–19). The son and the grandson inherited the promise and the tent together, and none of the three saw it kept.

The city that has foundations. The explanation is in the contrast between a tent, pegs and cloth moved every season, and a city with foundations, the part of a building that does not move. The city is the heavenly Jerusalem (12:22; 13:14), which John saw with twelve foundations (Revelation 21:2, 10–14). Abraham could live in the temporary because he was expecting the permanent: a word to readers whose houses had been emptied, about a man who never had a house and did not mind.

Whose designer and builder is God. “Designer” (technitēs) and “builder” (dēmiourgos) are an architect’s and a craftsman’s words: God himself designed and built it. Abraham never saw the city; he did know who was building it.

Outside the camp, toward the city. Hebrews makes Abraham’s tent-life the shape of every Christian life. Jesus suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people through his own blood, so let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured, for here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come (13:12–14). Abraham left Ur for a city he never saw; believers leave the comfort of the camp to follow a Saviour who went out ahead of them, and the road leads to the same city.

How do I know if God is calling me to go somewhere? God does not usually speak to us as he spoke to Abraham, in a direct word naming a journey. He guides us now through his written word, through wisdom, prayer, the counsel of mature Christians, and the circumstances he opens and closes. So the question is less what has God secretly decided, and more what does faithfulness require: what would serve Christ, love my family, and use my gifts well. Then act, even without seeing the whole road. Abraham’s faith was not knowing where; it was knowing who.

On a Tuesday. Jesus has gone ahead of you as a forerunner (6:20), so hold your earthly home and plans loosely. Let that shape one decision this week: how much you spend on the house compared with how much you give, or whether a career move serves Christ or only yourself. And if you are unsettled, moving, or without a home, take heart from Abraham: living in a tent is not a sign that God has forgotten you.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive, even when she was past the age, since she considered him faithful who had promised. Therefore from one man, and him as good as dead, were born descendants as many as the stars of heaven and as many as the innumerable grains of sand by the seashore.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sarah herself. Even Sarah. She laughed when she overheard the promise and then denied laughing (Genesis 18:12–15), and she had earlier arranged a substitute in Hagar rather than wait (Genesis 16:1–2). That is the old temptation of an impatient heart: when God seems slow, take control and make the promise happen yourself. Her faith was not straightforward, and Hebrews still says: by faith. God commends a faith not perfect, but real.

Who received the power. The phrase “power to conceive” (dynamin eis katabolēn spermatos) is literally power for the laying down of seed, and the expression usually refers to the father’s part. So some take this verse as applying to Abraham, with Sarah as a secondary subject: by faith Abraham, together with Sarah, received power to become a father. Either way, both shared in the miracle by faith.

She considered him faithful. Sarah was ninety and had always been barren (Genesis 11:30; 17:17), and faith looked past that to the one who had spoken. It is the same phrase as 10:23: he who promised is faithful (pistos). Faith in this chapter is repeatedly a judgment about the character of the promiser rather than a feeling about the promise.

As good as dead. “As good as dead” (nenekrōmenou) is deadened, and Paul uses the phrase too (Romans 4:19). A hundred-year-old body and a ninety-year-old womb, and the writer softens neither. Faith here is not optimism about the possible: the situation was humanly closed.

As many as the stars. The images are God’s own from the Genesis promises (Genesis 15:5; 22:17; 32:12), given to a childless man taken outside one night and told to look up. From one man as good as dead, a nation, and through Christ, children of Abraham from every nation: if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s offspring (Galatians 3:7, 29). The readers of this letter were the sand, hearing about the night their ancestor was told to count the stars.

From a body as good as dead to an empty tomb. Paul reads this moment as a picture of saving faith: Abraham did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, as good as dead, or the barrenness of Sarah’s womb, and the words counted to him as righteousness were written for us also, who believe in him who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord (Romans 4:19–24). The God who brought Isaac out of a deadened body is the God who brought Jesus out of a sealed grave. Faith in both cases trusts the God who gives life to the dead (Romans 4:17).

Is my faith real if it is mixed with doubt and failure? Very often, yes. Sarah’s was, and Hebrews commends it. The question is not whether your faith is pure, but whether it is resting on God. A trembling hand holding a rope is as safe as a steady one, because the rope does the holding. Bring your doubts to God honestly, as the father did who said, I believe; help my unbelief (Mark 9:24), and keep looking at God’s faithfulness rather than at your own feelings. Faith grows by being fed on God’s promises and tested in hard places, and God is patient with it.

On a Tuesday. What seems dead in your life: a marriage gone cold, a child far from God, a sin you cannot seem to break? Do not pretend it is not dead. Bring it to God as it is, and tell him that you consider him faithful who has promised. If your sorrow is childlessness, remember that God made Sarah a particular promise; he does not promise every couple a child, and a long grief is no sign of weak faith. What he does promise is himself.

verseByVerse.quote: These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar, and having acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth. For people who speak thus make it clear that they are seeking a homeland. If they had been thinking of that land from which they had gone out, they would have had opportunity to return. But as it is, they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These all died in faith. The writer pauses to say what all of them had in common, and it is not what a modern reader expects: they died still trusting.

In the flow. Verses 13–16 interrupt the roll-call to state the chapter’s theme plainly: faith lives and dies on promises not yet received (vv. 39–40). These all most naturally means the patriarchs and their families (v. 9), since Enoch, for one, did not die.

Not having received the things promised. Against any account of faith that measures it by results: every one of them died without getting it: the land, the nation, the Messiah, the heavenly city. Abraham got Isaac and a burial cave. Yet they did not die without salvation. They were saved as we are, by faith in God’s promise of the Christ who was to come, and his death covers their sins too (9:15).

Greeted from afar. Picture travellers sighting a country from the deck of a ship and waving at a shore they will not reach on this voyage. They saw it, were glad, and did not land. Jesus said that Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day; he saw it and was glad (John 8:56).

Strangers and exiles. “Exiles” (parepidēmoi) are temporary residents. That is Abraham’s own description of himself when he came to buy the burial cave: I am a sojourner and foreigner among you (Genesis 23:4). Believers are pilgrims in this world (1 Peter 1:1; 2:11).

Seeking a homeland. A man who calls himself a stranger has told you he belongs somewhere else (patris, fatherland).

Opportunity to return. Verse 15 closes the obvious escape. Ur was still there, and the road ran both ways. They did not go back, because their hearts were set on something else. Their homesickness was not for anywhere they had left.

A better country. “Desire” (oregontai) is to stretch out for. They longed for heaven, God’s country, the new creation: our citizenship is in heaven (Philippians 3:20).

God is not ashamed. “Not ashamed” (ouk epaischynetai): as Jesus is not ashamed to call us brothers (2:11). God calls himself the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (Exodus 3:6), three men who lived in tents and died holding nothing, and Jesus used that title to prove the resurrection: he is not God of the dead, but of the living (Matthew 22:32). People visibly waiting for another country do not embarrass him. It is those who have settled here who make the title awkward.

He has prepared a city. “Prepared” (hētoimasen): God has already made it ready (John 14:2–3; Revelation 21:2). Their hope is not a fantasy: he has actually built the thing.

Is it wrong to enjoy life here and want things to go well? No. God gives us richly all things to enjoy (1 Timothy 6:17), and a pilgrim may delight in a good meal, a happy marriage, a beautiful place and work well done. What this passage warns against is settling: treating this world as home, so that we would not really mind if Christ never came. The test is what you long for most, and what you could lose without losing everything. Enjoy the inns on the road with thanks; just do not mistake them for the destination.

Does God feel ashamed of me when I fail? Not if you belong to him. This verse says God is not ashamed to be called the God of people like Jacob, who was a schemer and a liar for much of his life. What made the difference was not their performance but their faith, which looked to his promise and away from this world. Christ, too, is not ashamed to call his people brothers (2:11). The shame of your sin was borne by him at the cross, where he despised the shame (12:2). You may feel ashamed of yourself; God, in Christ, is not ashamed of you.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac, and he who had received the promises was in the act of offering up his only son, of whom it was said, “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.” He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he was tested. Genesis 22, one of the hardest chapters in the Old Testament, is taken as the summit of Abraham’s faith. God tested him (Genesis 22:1), not to tempt him to sin, but to prove his faith. “Offered up” (prosenēnochen) is a perfect tense: as good as offered. In intention and obedience the sacrifice was complete, though God stopped his hand.

His only son. “Only son” (monogenēs) means unique. Abraham had Ishmael too, but Isaac was the unique son of promise: take your son, your only son Isaac, whom you love (Genesis 22:2).

Through Isaac. From Genesis 21:12. The promised line ran through Isaac; everything God had promised depended on this boy. He was the promise, in a body, and God told Abraham to kill him. So the test was not merely whether Abraham loved God more than his son, terrible as that is. He had to obey God’s command while still holding God’s promise, when the two seemed to cancel each other out, and leave it to God to make them fit.

Able even to raise him. “Considered” (logisamenos) is a reckoning word: he worked it out. The promise runs through Isaac; God does not lie; God has commanded Isaac’s death; therefore if Isaac dies, God will raise him. No one had ever been raised from the dead; Abraham inferred the resurrection from the character of God alone. Genesis records the conclusion in his words to the servants: I and the boy will go over there and worship and come again to you (Genesis 22:5). He said we.

Figuratively speaking. In a figure (parabolē), Isaac was as good as dead and came back down the mountain alive, a picture of resurrection. The whole episode is a picture: a father, an only son, wood carried up a hill by the son, and a substitute provided by God. Abraham named the place The LORD will provide, and some two thousand years later, on a hill in the same region (if Moriah is the temple hill, as 2 Chronicles 3:1 suggests), he did. The greater Father did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32; John 3:16), and received him back from the dead, not figuratively but in reality.

How could God command a father to sacrifice his son? He never intended it to be carried out. It was a test (Genesis 22:1), and God stopped Abraham’s hand: do not lay your hand on the boy (Genesis 22:12). The same God forbade child sacrifice in the plainest terms (Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31; Jeremiah 7:31). The story is unique, and it points beyond itself: God spared Abraham’s son and did not spare his own. It gives no one warrant to harm anyone in God’s name. And if you have lost a child, this chapter does not ask you to see that loss as a test you passed or failed; the God of Moriah is the Father who gave up his own Son, and he is near to the broken-hearted (Psalm 34:18).

What should I do when God seems to contradict his own promises? Do what Abraham did: reason from who God is. When circumstances seem to say that God has forgotten you, or that his word cannot be true, hold on to the fixed points: God does not lie, God is good, and God can raise the dead. Then obey what you know, even when you cannot see how it will work out. Abraham did not know about the ram when he climbed the mountain. He knew God. Many believers have found that the provision came only at the last moment, and only on the mountain.

For worship. Isaac asked the question on the way up the mountain: where is the lamb? And his father answered better than he knew: God will provide for himself the lamb (Genesis 22:7–8). On Moriah the son was spared and a ram died in his place. At Golgotha there was no ram caught in a thicket, because the Son was the Lamb, and the Father who stopped Abraham’s hand did not stop his own. The LORD has provided.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Isaac invoked future blessings on Jacob and Esau. By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, bowing in worship over the head of his staff. By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus of the Israelites and gave directions concerning his bones.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaac invoked future blessings. Three men in three verses, all dying men acting in faith about a future they will not see (Genesis 27:27–40). Isaac was blind, deceived by his wife and younger son, and meant the blessing for Esau. When he discovered the deception he trembled very violently, and then said of Jacob: yes, and he shall be blessed (Genesis 27:33). Hebrews commends that moment: Isaac saw that God’s purpose had gone through his own mistake, and did not try to undo it.

Jacob, when dying. Another old man whose eyes had failed, and another blessing that went against the expected order. Jacob blessed Ephraim and Manasseh, and deliberately gave the greater blessing to the younger, over Joseph’s objection (Genesis 48:14–19). The man who had stolen a blessing by deceit gives one away, at the end, by the same principle he had once tried to force.

Over the head of his staff. An old man too weak to stand unsupported, leaning on a staff, as he had once crossed the Jordan with nothing but a staff (Genesis 32:10), worshipping.

Staff or bed? The word follows the Greek Old Testament of Genesis 47:31. The Hebrew, with different vowels, reads bed. The Hebrew consonants for bed (mittah) and staff (matteh) are the same, and the vowels were added much later; the Greek translators read them as staff. Both readings picture a dying old man bowing in worship, and neither changes the point.

Joseph made mention. Joseph was the second man in Egypt, with a palace, a title and a family established in the best land of the country. Nothing in his circumstances suggested that his descendants would ever leave, and the exodus was centuries away. Yet he spoke of God bringing Israel out: God will surely visit you (Genesis 50:24).

Concerning his bones. He made Israel swear to carry his bones to Canaan (Genesis 50:25). His faith took the form of a funeral instruction: a set of bones in a box, sitting in Egypt for centuries as a standing statement that this was not home. And they kept the promise. Moses took the bones (Exodus 13:19), the box travelled forty years in the wilderness, and they were buried at Shechem after the conquest (Joshua 24:32), over four hundred years later.

The future the blessings were about. Not merely more children and land. Isaac gave Jacob lordship over his brothers and nations bowing down to him (Genesis 27:29), and from Jacob’s deathbed came the promise that the sceptre would not depart from Judah, and to him would be the obedience of the peoples (Genesis 49:10). This letter names the one it meant: our Lord was descended from Judah (7:14), the offspring in whom all nations would be blessed (Genesis 22:18; Galatians 3:16).

How should a Christian face death? As these men did: still trusting, still worshipping, and still thinking about the future of God’s people. Death is an enemy, and it is right to grieve and even to fear the dying. But for a believer it is not the end of the story; it is the doorway to being with Christ, and the body will be raised. Practically, that means putting your affairs in order, speaking blessings and the gospel to your family, forgiving and asking forgiveness, and telling those you leave behind where your hope is. A deathbed can be one of the most powerful pulpits there is.

For worship. God kept his promises across centuries, through blind fathers, scheming sons and a coffin in Egypt. Not one word of his failed. And the greatest grave in the story is the one outside Jerusalem, which held the Son of Judah for three days and then could not hold him. Because that tomb is empty, the graves of his people are like Joseph’s coffin: a standing statement that this is not home, waiting for the morning when he calls them out.
verseByVerse.note: “Staff” follows the Greek Old Testament of Gen 47:31; the Hebrew text as later pointed reads “bed”; the consonants are the same.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–40 — The Turn: Some Were Tortured
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses chooses the reproach of Christ over Egypt’s treasures, Israel crosses the sea, Jericho falls and Rahab is spared. Then the names come too fast to tell: some were rescued by faith, and others were tortured and killed by faith. None received the promise in full, because God had planned something better that includes us.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Chapter Turns Over Mid-Verse

In verse 35 faith that raised the dead becomes faith that was tortured to death: the same faith, opposite outcomes, both commended. Of such people the world was not worthy.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David and Samuel were far from consistent, and they are in the roll.

Now: All these died waiting for what the church now has; apart from us they are not made perfect.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful, and they were not afraid of the king’s edict. By faith Moses, when he was grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin. He considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking to the reward.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hidden by his parents. The first act of faith in the Moses section belongs to his parents, Amram and Jochebed (Exodus 6:20), defying a royal edict with a baby in a basket. Pharaoh had ordered every Hebrew baby boy to be thrown into the Nile (Exodus 1:22), and they hid Moses at great risk (Exodus 2:1–3).

The child was beautiful. “Beautiful” (asteios) is the word of Exodus 2:2 and Acts 7:20, where Stephen says he was beautiful in God’s sight. Perhaps they sensed that God had a special purpose for this one.

The king’s edict. Faith overcame fear of the most powerful ruler on earth. The midwives made the same calculation (Exodus 1:17).

When he was grown up. Grown up, at about forty (Acts 7:23), he renounced it all. Whatever his exact standing, he was raised in the royal household of the greatest power on earth, with its education, wealth and prospects. He walked away from it to identify with his people (Exodus 2:11–12).

Choosing rather. He weighed two options and took one. He chose solidarity with despised slaves over the palace.

The fleeting pleasures of sin. The pleasures were real: the writer does not pretend Egypt was miserable. But they were fleeting (proskairos), temporary, lasting a season. Set against them was mistreatment, which was also real, and permanent company with the people of God. It is not asceticism but arithmetic about duration. For Moses, staying in the palace would have been sin, because it meant denying God’s people and God’s call.

The reproach of Christ. A startling phrase, since Moses lived some fourteen centuries earlier. Reproach is disgrace: being sneered at, shamed and pushed to the edge for belonging to someone. It most likely means the reproach borne by God’s anointed people, and so by the Anointed One with whom they are identified, the same disgrace in a different century (Psalm 89:50–51). Moses identified with the people through whom the Messiah would come, and looked ahead to him (John 5:46). “Greater wealth” is a commercial word: reproach for Christ was the better asset, and the readers were facing that reproach themselves (10:33; 13:13).

Looking to the reward. “Looking” (apeblepen) is fixing the eyes on, and it is verse 6 again. He was not being noble. He was looking at a figure the Egyptians could not see, and he weighed the eternal against the temporary and chose wisely (2 Corinthians 4:17–18).

What it does not mean. It does not mean wealth or high position is sinful in itself. Joseph and Daniel served faithfully in pagan courts. For Moses, remaining meant disobeying God’s call. The question is always: what does faithfulness require of me here?

Is it right to disobey the government? Christians are to submit to governing authorities and honour them, because God has appointed them (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17). But when the state commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands, we must obey God rather than men, as Moses’ parents, the midwives, Daniel and the apostles did. Such disobedience should be open, peaceful and limited to the point of conflict, and we should be willing to bear the consequences, as they were. It is not a licence to rebel whenever we dislike a law.

Why are the pleasures of sin called pleasures? Because they are. Sin rarely tempts us with misery; it offers something sweet, and the Bible is honest about it. The problem is not that sin is never enjoyable, but that its enjoyment is short and its cost is long, and it takes what belongs to God. The way to resist is not to pretend sin is dull, but to set against it a greater pleasure: at your right hand are pleasures forevermore (Psalm 16:11). Moses gave up the palace because he had seen something better.

On a Tuesday. Watch this week for the places where you are embarrassed to be identified with God’s people, the unimpressive church, the awkward believer. Christ was not ashamed to stand with you; stand with them.

verseByVerse.quote: By faith he left Egypt, not being afraid of the anger of the king, for he endured as seeing him who is invisible. By faith he kept the Passover and sprinkled the blood, so that the Destroyer of the firstborn might not touch them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He left Egypt. Exodus says Moses fled to Midian because he was afraid (Exodus 2:14–15). The likeliest reading is that this verse refers to the exodus itself (Exodus 12:31–42), when he led Israel out in defiance of Pharaoh; the writer follows the order of events, and the Passover comes next. Others take it as the flight to Midian, read as a decision of faith rather than mere panic. Either way, Hebrews is not rewriting history; it is characterising a man.

Seeing him who is invisible. The paradox is deliberate. Seeing the invisible (ton aoraton hōs horōn): God is invisible (1 Timothy 1:17), yet Moses lived as though he saw him. If the visible was made out of what cannot be seen (v. 3), the invisible is the more solid, and a man who reckons with it is being realistic. “Endured” (ekarterēsen) is held out, remained under weight (10:36). That is what the seeing produced: not a mystical experience, but forty years of staying put.

He kept the Passover. The Passover (Exodus 12) was a new ritual, never done before. A lamb killed, and its blood painted on the doorposts of every Israelite house, and every firstborn son in the country would live or die that night on the strength of it. Moses had only the word of God that blood on a doorframe would protect anyone.

The Destroyer of the firstborn. “Destroyer” (ho olothreuōn) is the one who destroys: the angel of death, or the Lord himself acting in judgment (Exodus 12:23). And the Israelites were not exempt by nationality. The angel passed over houses with blood on them, and only those, which is the letter’s whole argument in a single night’s history: not who you are descended from, but whether the blood has been applied. And the Passover lamb pointed to Christ, our Passover lamb, who has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7; John 1:29), whose blood protects us from judgment.

Was it not cruel of God to strike the firstborn of Egypt? It was judgment, not cruelty, and it did not come without warning. Egypt had thrown Israel’s baby boys into the Nile (Exodus 1:22), and God had told Pharaoh beforehand that Israel was his firstborn son, and that if Pharaoh would not let him go, Pharaoh’s own firstborn would die (Exodus 4:22–23). Nine plagues came first, each a call to repent. The holy God is the Judge of all the earth, and he owes no sinner a long life. What is astonishing is not that he judged, but that on the same night he provided a shelter from his own judgment: the blood of a lamb. The real question is not why God judges, but why he spares anyone at all, and the answer is the blood. This remains one of Scripture’s hardest pages, and it is right to feel its weight; the little ones who died that night were in the hands of the Judge of all the earth, who will do what is right (Genesis 18:25).

How can I see someone who is invisible? Not with the eyes, but by trusting what God has shown of himself in his word and in his Son. Jesus is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1:15); whoever has seen him has seen the Father (John 14:9). So you see the invisible God by looking at Christ in the Scriptures, until his reality becomes more weighty to you than what you can see around you. Practically, that means time in the Gospels, prayer that speaks to him as present, and remembering through the day that he is there. The more real he is to you, the smaller everything else becomes.

For worship. On the night in Egypt every house lost its firstborn except the houses marked with blood. At the cross the order was reversed. God’s own Firstborn (1:6) was not passed over: judgment fell on him so that it could pass over us, and every firstborn sheltered by that blood is enrolled in heaven for ever (12:23).

verseByVerse.quote: By faith the people crossed the Red Sea as on dry land, but the Egyptians, when they attempted to do the same, were drowned. By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days. By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient, because she had given a friendly welcome to the spies.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Red Sea. “The people” is Israel collectively, hemmed in between the sea and Pharaoh’s army, going forward at God’s command (Exodus 14:13–22). Their faith was weak: they had complained bitterly only hours before that Moses had brought them out to die in the wilderness (Exodus 14:10–12). Yet they obeyed, and walked through.

When the Egyptians attempted. The same water, the same seabed, the same walls on either hand, and two entirely different outcomes (Exodus 14:23–28). What saved Israel was not the act of walking but God, received by faith, exactly as with Abel’s sacrifice in verse 4.

The walls of Jericho. Joshua 6: no siege engines, only marching, trumpets and a shout, as God commanded. Faith here takes the form of doing something visibly absurd for a week, an army walking in silence round a fortified city, watched from the battlements. Nothing happened on days one to six. Faith often looks foolish for a while before it looks like anything at all.

Rahab the prostitute. The writer keeps the description, and the placing is deliberate: immediately after Moses stands a Canaanite woman of that trade, commended on the same terms. “Disobedient” (apeithēsasin) describes the people of Jericho, who knew of God’s works, had heard of the Red Sea and were melting with fear, but did not believe (Joshua 2:9–11).

A friendly welcome. Literally with peace (met’ eirēnēs): she hid the spies and confessed faith in Israel’s God. She had heard what happened at the Red Sea and drew a conclusion the rest of her city refused: the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath (Joshua 2:11). She had less evidence than anyone in Israel and believed more than most of them. James also commends her faith shown in action (James 2:25).

Where Christians differ: did God approve Rahab’s lie? Rahab lied to the king’s men to protect the spies (Joshua 2:4–6). Some hold that deceiving those bent on murder is not the false witness the ninth commandment forbids, and point to the Hebrew midwives, with whom God dealt well (Exodus 1:19–20). Others, with Augustine and Calvin, hold that the lie was a sin, forgiven like the rest of her past, and that God honoured her faith in spite of it. This commentary’s view: Scripture commends Rahab for her faith, shown in her welcome of the spies and her protection of God’s people; Hebrews and James hold up her faith, not her words, as the pattern. But deceiving those bent on murder is not the lie the ninth commandment forbids: she owed no truth to men coming to kill God’s servants, and those who hid Jews from the Gestapo stood where she stood. That narrow case is no licence for ordinary lying, which remains sin (Colossians 3:9).

Written into the line of the Saviour. Rahab’s story does not end at Jericho. Matthew names her in the genealogy of Jesus: Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab (Matthew 1:5). The woman spared when her city fell became part of Israel, by Matthew’s list the great-great-grandmother of David, and an ancestor of the Messiah. The Son of God came through a family line that included a Canaanite prostitute, and Matthew records him telling the religious leaders that tax collectors and prostitutes were going into the kingdom of God before them, because they believed (Matthew 21:31–32).

Can God really use someone with my past? Look at the names in this verse. A people who had grumbled their way to the shore of the Red Sea; a Canaanite prostitute who lied to protect strangers. God did not choose them because they were respectable, and he does not wait for us to be. Whatever you have done, if you trust Christ, your past is forgiven, and God delights to show his grace by using people the world would have written off. That does not mean the consequences of sin always vanish, or that you should not make amends where you can. But your history is not the end of your story; Rahab’s certainly was not.

verseByVerse.quote: And what more shall I say? For time would fail me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, of David and Samuel and the prophets— who through faith conquered kingdoms, enforced justice, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the power of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, were made strong out of weakness, became mighty in war, put foreign armies to flight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And what more shall I say? For time would fail me to tell of. The preacher looks at his material and stops trying to cover it all. It was a common device in ancient speeches, and a skilful one: the sense of an endless supply is stronger than another twenty examples would be. Then he speeds up.

Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah. Not the names we would have chosen (Judges 4–16). Gideon defeated the Midianites with three hundred men (Judges 7), but demanded two signs with a fleece first, and later made an ephod that became an idol (Judges 8:27). Barak defeated Sisera (Judges 4), but would not go unless Deborah came with him. Samson’s life was a catalogue of appetite and folly, yet at the end he called on God and brought down the Philistine temple (Judges 16:28–30). Jephthah defeated the Ammonites (Judges 11) and made a rash vow with terrible consequences.

Of David and Samuel and the prophets. David, the king after God’s own heart, who also committed adultery and murder. Samuel, the last judge and first great prophet, whose sons took bribes. The prophets: Elijah, Elisha, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel and others.

What the roll is measuring. Not one of them is a model of consistency, and his readers knew those stories far better than we do. He puts them in the roll anyway, which tells you what it measures: not achievement or character, but the bare fact of having taken God at his word, in the middle of lives that were often a mess.

Conquered kingdoms. The achievements, rattled off at speed. Joshua, the judges and David conquered kingdoms (2 Samuel 8). Enforced justice is literally worked righteousness (eirgasanto dikaiosynēn): judges and kings like Samuel and David who ruled justly (1 Samuel 12:3–5; 2 Samuel 8:15). And they received specific promises and fulfilments from God: not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made had failed (Joshua 21:45).

Does obtained promises contradict verse 39? No. These men received particular promises in their lifetimes: victories, deliverances, sons. What none of them received was what was promised in the full sense, the coming of Christ and the city God has prepared. God kept his smaller promises along the way, and every one of them was a pledge of the great one.

Lions, fire and sword. Daniel in the lions’ den (Daniel 6:22), and perhaps Samson and David, who killed lions (Judges 14:6; 1 Samuel 17:34–37); Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the furnace (Daniel 3:23–27), where a fourth figure walked with them in the flames; David escaping Saul (1 Samuel 19–27), Elijah fleeing Jezebel (1 Kings 19), and Jeremiah protected from those who sought his life (Jeremiah 26:24).

Were made strong out of weakness. The pattern of nearly every name: not strong men who stayed strong, but weak men made strong, a passive verb that locates the strength elsewhere. Gideon, the least in his father’s house (Judges 6:15); Samson, blind and shackled at the end (Judges 16:28); Hezekiah, raised from his sickbed (Isaiah 38). My power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9).

Mighty in war. Jonathan and his armour-bearer (1 Samuel 14), David, Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles 20). The list ends at its most triumphant, and the very next words in the chapter are women received back their dead, and then the whole thing turns over.

The Son these deliverers waited for. Every office on this list was a partial sketch of the Son (1:1–2). The judges and kings worked righteousness unevenly and briefly; of the Son God says that the sceptre of uprightness is the sceptre of his kingdom, for he has loved righteousness and hated wickedness (1:8–9). Gideon, Samson and David saved Israel for a generation, and died. The Son conquered by dying, and sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high, a Deliverer who never needs replacing (1:3; 7:24–25).

Why does God put such flawed people in the hall of faith? Because the chapter is about faith, and faith is trust in God, not confidence in oneself. If the list were made of flawless people, none of us could hope to be on it. God includes Samson and Jephthah to show that he works through the faith of sinners, and to give hope to everyone who knows his own failures. But the honesty of Scripture cuts both ways: their sins brought real harm, to themselves and others. God’s grace in using them is not permission to imitate their folly. It is an invitation to trust the same God.

On a Tuesday. Name your weakness to God today, specifically: fear, lack of ability, a past failure, a body that no longer works as it did. Then take one step in the thing he has given you to do, asking his Spirit, who raised Jesus from the dead (Romans 8:11), to make you strong out of weakness. And if what he has given you seems to achieve nothing, a prayer unanswered or a class that will not listen, you may be on the fourth day of seven at Jericho. Keep walking.
verseByVerse.note: Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah are from Judges; the lions’ mouths recall Daniel, and the fire recalls his three friends.

verseByVerse.quote: Women received back their dead by resurrection. Some were tortured, refusing to accept release, so that they might rise again to a better life. Others suffered mocking and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment. They were stoned, they were sawn in two, they were killed with the sword. They went about in skins of sheep and goats, destitute, afflicted, mistreated— of whom the world was not worthy—wandering about in deserts and mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Women received back their dead by resurrection. A dead child handed back alive: the widow of Zarephath, whose son Elijah raised (1 Kings 17:17–24), and the Shunammite woman, whose son Elisha raised (2 Kings 4:18–37).

Refusing to accept release. The turn mid-verse is the hinge of the chapter: faith does not always bring deliverance. The word for tortured (etympanisthēsan) probably refers to being beaten to death on a rack or frame shaped like a drum. They were offered a way out by renouncing their faith, and would not take it. This probably refers to the martyrs under the Syrian king Antiochus IV Epiphanes around 167 BC, recorded in 2 Maccabees 6–7, which the readers probably knew: the old scribe Eleazar, and a mother and her seven sons, tortured to death rather than eat pork and deny the law of God.

A better life. The Greek is literally a better resurrection (kreittonos anastaseōs), the same word as the first clause. Some got their dead back by resurrection; some died for it. The identical faith produced both, and theirs was better than being restored to mortal life like the sons of the widows, who would one day die again. They looked to the final resurrection to eternal life.

Mocking and flogging. Jeremiah was beaten, put in the stocks, imprisoned and lowered into a muddy cistern (Jeremiah 20:2; 37:15; 38:6); Micaiah was imprisoned and fed on bread and water (1 Kings 22:27).

Sawn in two. Zechariah the son of Jehoiada was stoned in the court of the house of the LORD (2 Chronicles 24:20–22; Matthew 23:35). Jewish tradition says the prophet Isaiah was sawn in two under King Manasseh, a tradition recorded in a later writing called the Ascension of Isaiah. Prophets were killed by Jezebel and Ahab (1 Kings 19:10), and Uriah the prophet was struck down by King Jehoiakim (Jeremiah 26:23).

Skins of sheep and goats. This is the prophet’s uniform, Elijah’s garment of hair (2 Kings 1:8), a picture of the men God sent to Israel living like vagrants in the country they were sent to. “Mistreated” (kakouchoumenoi) is the word of verse 25: they chose the lot Moses chose.

Of whom the world was not worthy. In the middle of the squalor comes the great reversal of the chapter. The world looked at these people in their goatskins, sleeping in caves, and reckoned them worthless, not fit to live. God’s verdict is that the world was not good enough for them.

Dens and caves. Elijah in the wilderness (1 Kings 19); the prophets whom Obadiah hid by fifties in a cave and fed with bread and water (1 Kings 18:4, 13); the faithful of the Maccabean period hiding in caves (1 Maccabees 2:29–38; 2 Maccabees 6:11).

The paragraph they most needed. A congregation whose property had been plundered could look at the first half of the list and wonder why their faith had produced no such deliverance. The second half says: it produced these people too, and God is not ashamed of them either.

The last name in the line. The list of sufferers does not stop at the caves. A few sentences later the writer names one more: Jesus, who endured the cross, despising the shame, and endured from sinners such hostility against himself (12:2–3). He is the sum of this paragraph. Matthew records that he could have asked for more than twelve legions of angels and did not (Matthew 26:53): he refused release. He suffered outside the gate (13:12). And because the God of peace brought him again from the dead (13:20), the better resurrection these martyrs died for is not a hope in the dark. They will follow him out.

Where Christians differ: does this make the Maccabean books Scripture? Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches include 1 and 2 Maccabees in their Old Testament, and Protestants too have long valued them as history. This commentary’s view: the author refers to events of the Maccabean period, as he refers to the tradition about Isaiah, as true history, without quoting those books as Scripture. Referring to historical events recorded in a book does not make that book inspired. The Old Testament canon received by Jesus and the apostles is the Hebrew Scriptures (Luke 24:44), which do not include the Apocrypha. The canon is closed.

Why does God deliver some believers and not others? Scripture does not give us God’s reasons in each case, and this chapter refuses to rank the delivered above the martyrs. James was killed with the sword and Peter was freed from prison in the same chapter of Acts (Acts 12:1–11). What we are told is that God is wise and good in both, that he is with his people in the fire whether he takes them out of it or through it, and that every one of them will rise. If you prayed for healing and it did not come, it was not because your faith was too small. Some of God’s strongest saints are in the second half of this list.

For worship. The world saw goatskins and caves and saws, and called them worthless; God said the world was not worthy of them. He made that verdict public on the third day: the world found his Son fit only for a cross, and God raised him and seated him in glory. The verdict of the world is temporary. The verdict of God, spoken over an empty tomb, is final.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish tradition says the prophet Isaiah was sawn in two under King Manasseh.

verseByVerse.quote: And all these, though commended through their faith, did not receive what was promised, since God had provided something better for us, that apart from us they should not be made perfect.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Commended through their faith. The chapter ends where verse 13 stood, with everybody still waiting, and “commended” (as in v. 2) frames it. The conquerors and the sawn in two, the ones who shut lions’ mouths and the ones the lions ate: all commended, all approved by God.

Did not receive what was promised. “What was promised” (tēn epangelian) is the great promise: the coming of the Messiah, the new covenant, and its fulfilment in the eternal inheritance. They received many smaller promises (v. 33), but not the ultimate one.

Something better. They did not receive it because God had something better in view, and the something better involves us. “Something better” (kreitton ti) is everything the letter has been arguing: the better covenant, the better sacrifice, the better priest, the coming of Christ, the full revelation and accomplishment of salvation. They saw the shadow and greeted it from afar; we have the substance.

Apart from us. Abraham cannot be completed without the congregation that first heard this letter read; the Old Testament faithful are not brought to their end separately and earlier, but together with people not born for centuries. “Made perfect” (teleiōthōsin) is being brought to the goal God intended: sins fully dealt with, a clean conscience before God (9:14), and at last the raised body in the city God has prepared. By a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (10:14). Abraham and Moses were waiting for that offering, and their perfection will be completed with ours at his return, one family brought to glory (12:23; Revelation 7:9).

Where were the Old Testament saints in the meantime? Some traditions teach that they waited in a holding place below until Christ descended to set them free. Scripture gives little ground for that. Jesus told the dying thief, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43), and this letter speaks of the spirits of the righteous made perfect, already in God’s presence (12:23). Believers who died before Christ were with God in conscious blessing. What they wait for, with us, is the resurrection of the body, the perfection that will come to the whole church together.

A congregation that did not know what it had. These readers were drifting back toward the old order, the era these giants lived in and longed to see fulfilled. Yet the whole gallery had died waiting for what this discouraged little congregation already possessed. There is one people of God, not two: everyone in this chapter and everyone reading it arrives by the same faith, through the same sacrifice. For people who are tired, that means they are not running alone: the stands are full (12:1).

If they had such faith with so little, what does that say about me? It should humble you and encourage you. Humble, because Abraham trusted God with a promise and a tent, and you have the whole Bible, the cross, the empty tomb and the Spirit. Encourage, because the same God who sustained their faith with less will sustain yours with more. You are not asked to be a hero. You are asked to trust the God they trusted, now that he has kept the promise they died waiting for. Read their stories, and let them shame your complaints and strengthen your hope.

By this he condemned the world and became an heir of the righteousness that comes by faith.<sup>8</sup>By faith Abraham obeyed when he was called to go out to a place that he was to receive as an inheritance. And he went out, not knowing where he was going.<sup>9</sup>By faith he went to live in the land of promise, as in a foreign land, living in tents with Isaac and Jacob, heirs with him of the same promise.<sup>10</sup>For he was looking forward to the city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God.<sup>11</sup>By faith Sarah herself received power to conceive, even when she was past the age, since she considered him faithful who had promised.<sup>12</sup>Therefore from one man, and him as good as dead, were born descendants as many as the stars of heaven and as many as the innumerable grains of sand by the seashore.<sup>13</sup>These all died in faith, not having received the things promised, but having seen them and greeted them from afar, and having acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth.<sup>14</sup>For people who speak thus make it clear that they are seeking a homeland.<sup>15</sup>If they had been thinking of that land from which they had gone out, they would have had opportunity to return.<sup>16</sup>But as it is, they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for he has prepared for them a city.<sup>17</sup>By faith Abraham, when he was tested, offered up Isaac, and he who had received the promises was in the act of offering up his only son,<sup>18</sup>of whom it was said, “Through Isaac shall your offspring be named.”<sup>19</sup>He considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead, from which, figuratively speaking, he did receive him back.<sup>20</sup>By faith Isaac invoked future blessings on Jacob and Esau.<sup>21</sup>By faith Jacob, when dying, blessed each of the sons of Joseph, bowing in worship over the head of his staff.<sup>22</sup>By faith Joseph, at the end of his life, made mention of the exodus of the Israelites and gave directions concerning his bones.<sup>23</sup>By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents, because they saw that the child was beautiful, and they were not afraid of the king’s edict.<sup>24</sup>By faith Moses, when he was grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh’s daughter,<sup>25</sup>choosing rather to be mistreated with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin.<sup>26</sup>He considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking to the reward.<sup>27</sup>By faith he left Egypt, not being afraid of the anger of the king, for he endured as seeing him who is invisible.<sup>28</sup>By faith he kept the Passover and sprinkled the blood, so that the Destroyer of the firstborn might not touch them.<sup>29</sup>By faith the people crossed the Red Sea as on dry land, but the Egyptians, when they attempted to do the same, were drowned.<sup>30</sup>By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days.<sup>31</sup>By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient, because she had given a friendly welcome to the spies.<sup>32</sup>And what more shall I say? 12.title: Fix Your Eyes on Jesus: The Discipline of the Father
12.overview:
Chapter 11 filled the stadium; chapter 12 says: run. Strip off what slows you, keep going, and look at Jesus, who ran the hardest course and sat down at the finish. Then the writer reads the readers’ hardships for them: not a sign that God has left them, but the training a Father gives his children, painful now and fruitful later.

The chapter ends with two mountains. Sinai was fire, darkness and a voice the people begged to stop. The church has come to Mount Zion, to the assembly of the firstborn and to Jesus, whose blood speaks better than Abel’s. So do not refuse the one speaking, and worship with reverence, because the God of Zion is still a consuming fire.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Run the Race, and Read the Discipline
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With the witnesses of chapter 11 around them, believers are to throw off what hinders and run with endurance, looking to Jesus, who endured the cross for the joy ahead and now reigns. Their hardships are the discipline of a Father who loves his children.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Timescales

Run looking to Jesus, who endured the cross for the joy set before him. The Father's discipline is painful for the moment, but later yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those trained by it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Suffering believers wondered whether God had abandoned them.

Now: Hardship received from God's hand is a mark of sonship, not of rejection. Do not make light of it, and do not faint under it.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us also lay aside every weight, and sin which clings so closely, and let us run with endurance the race that is set before us,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Hebrews 12 turns the faith of chapter 11 into a call to run. Surrounded by a great cloud of witnesses, believers are to throw off every weight and sin and run with endurance, looking to Jesus, who endured the cross for the joy set before him (vv. 1–3). Their hardships are the Father’s loving discipline, yielding the peaceful fruit of righteousness (vv. 4–11). They must strengthen weak knees, pursue peace and holiness, and watch that no one falls short of God’s grace or becomes like Esau (vv. 12–17). They have come not to terrifying Sinai but to Mount Zion and to Jesus, whose blood speaks a better word than Abel’s (vv. 18–24). So they must not refuse the one who speaks from heaven, but receive an unshakable kingdom with grateful awe, for our God is a consuming fire (vv. 25–29).

A cloud of witnesses. “Therefore”: all of chapter 11 is now put to work. “Cloud” is a classical image for a vast multitude. The scene is a stadium, but these are not spectators watching how we do. The word for witness is martys, the root of martyr, and chapter 11 uses its verb of people witnessed to by God (11:2, 4, 5, 39). The stands are full of people who have already run, whose lives are evidence that the course can be finished. That is better encouragement than being watched.

Every weight. “Lay aside” is strip off, as clothes. A “weight” is not a sin but bulk, excess; ancient runners ran stripped of clothing that was perfectly respectable but would slow them down. So some things are not wrong and must still go, simply because they are heavy: distractions, entanglements, good things that crowd out the best. Each runner has to decide what his own are.

Sin which clings so closely. A rare word (euperistatos), possibly meaning easily entangling, readily surrounding: the picture of a long robe wrapping round the legs of a runner and tripping him. Sin is described here not as attractive but as obstructive. In context it may be especially the sin of unbelief and turning back (3:12–13), the sin that would bring the whole race to a stop.

Run with endurance. “Run” is present tense: keep running. The race is agōn, the contest, from which we get agony, and what it requires is not speed but endurance, staying under, as in 10:36. And “set before us” is a quiet comfort. The course was marked out by somebody else. A runner is not responsible for its length or its gradients, only for staying on it.

The one runner who was never tripped. Every witness in the stands ran with a robe catching at his legs: Abraham’s lie about Sarah, Moses’ anger at the rock, David’s adultery. Only one runner has gone the whole course without sin entangling him: we have a high priest who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin (4:15). The witnesses did not receive what was promised, so that they would be made perfect together with us (11:39–40), and their perfection comes through his. The crowd proves the race can be run; the Runner who finished it unentangled is the reason it can be won. None of us runs a single lap without stumbling, but his perfect obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), so a fall does not undo our standing, and that is why the writer at once turns every eye to Jesus (12:2).

Where Christians differ: are the departed saints watching us? Some read surrounded by witnesses as teaching that departed believers watch and cheer us from heaven, and some traditions draw from this the practice of praying to the saints. This commentary’s view: the main sense of witnesses is those who testify by their faith, as chapter 11 has just shown (11:2, 4, 5, 39 use the related verb, commended). Whether the departed are aware of events on earth is not clearly taught, and Scripture gives no warrant for praying to them; there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5). The departed saints are consciously with the Lord (Philippians 1:23; Hebrews 12:23), but our eyes are to be fixed on Jesus, not on them (v. 2).

What it does not mean. We do not run to earn salvation. The race is not an entrance examination; it is the life of those who have already been entered.

How do I know what my weights are? Ask what slows you down in following Christ, even if it is not sinful in itself. A useful test: what regularly crowds out prayer, Scripture, worship or love for others? What do you reach for when you should be reaching for God? It might be your phone, a hobby, an ambition, a friendship, a busy diary, or even good church work done at the expense of your family. You do not have to strip off everything at once, and other believers may carry things that you cannot. But if something keeps tripping your heart, lay it down, and see how much lighter the running becomes.

On a Tuesday. Name the sin that most often entangles you. You do not fight it on willpower: the Spirit who raised Jesus lives in you (Romans 8:11), and a friend is one of his ordinary means, so tell a trusted Christian and ask them to ask you about it.

For worship. Abel and Abraham and Moses and Rahab and the martyrs in the caves finished this course because God carried every one of them to the end. He has marked out the course for us, too, with its hills and its long stretches, and he did not set it so that we would fail. The whole crowd of witnesses is a testimony not to their strength, but to his faithfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Looking to Jesus. The participle means looking away from everything else to one thing: a deliberate turning of the eyes. A runner keeps his eyes on the goal, not on the crowd, the other runners, or the obstacles. The writer has just filled the stadium with heroes, and now turns every eye from them: the cloud of witnesses is an encouragement, not a focus.

The founder and perfecter of our faith. “Founder” is archēgos, the pioneer word from 2:10: the man at the head of the column who opens the way. “Perfecter” (teleiōtēs) is the finisher, who brings it to its end. He is at both ends of the course. The Greek has no our; it is simply the faith. He is the best example of believing, the one who trusted God perfectly to the end, but he is more: the one who begins and completes faith itself in us (Philippians 1:6).

For the joy set before him. The same phrase as the race set before us in verse 1: he ran a marked course too, with something at the end he wanted. “For” most likely means for the sake of the joy ahead, though it can mean instead of it. So he did not go to the cross grimly, as a man resigned. There was a joy he was after: completing the Father’s will, redeeming his people, being exalted (Isaiah 53:11; John 17:5; Philippians 2:9). The letter has already named it: bringing many sons to glory (2:10). His people were part of the joy set before him.

Despising the shame. Not despising the pain: the shame. For a first-century reader that was the worse half. Crucifixion was designed as public humiliation: the victim usually stripped naked, exposed, mocked, and cursed, for a hanged man is cursed by God (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13). “Despising” means thinking little of, disregarding as beneath consideration. He weighed the disgrace against the joy and judged it not worth attention. The readers were facing shame themselves (10:33; 13:13), and Jesus shows them how to bear it.

Seated at the right hand. A perfect tense: he has sat down and remains seated. The letter’s refrain since 1:3 (8:1; 10:12) here functions as the finish line. He ran, he endured, he sat down, which is the proof to every runner still on the course that the course ends.

How do I actually look to Jesus? By deliberately turning your attention to him as he is shown in Scripture: what he did, what he endured, where he is now, and what he has promised. In practice it means reading the Gospels, so that his face becomes familiar; meditating on the cross when you are tempted or ashamed; praying to him as someone present; and, when trouble fills your horizon, asking what it looks like in the light of his throne. Looking to Jesus is not a feeling you wait for. It is a habit of the mind, and it grows stronger the more it is used.

verseByVerse.quote: Consider him who endured from sinners such hostility against himself, so that you may not grow weary or fainthearted. In your struggle against sin you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consider him. The verb is an accounting word: reckon it up, compare, work out the proportion. The writer is asking for a calculation, not a sentiment. “Hostility” is contradiction, opposition, hostile speech. He endured mockery, slander, betrayal, rejection, beatings and crucifixion from sinners, the very people he came to save. Some manuscripts, including several of the earliest, read against themselves, meaning that sinners who opposed him were really harming themselves; but against himself makes far better sense of the sentence, and most translations follow it.

Weary or fainthearted. Two words for exhaustion: to be worn out, and to have the soul give way like a runner whose strength fails. The remedy offered is not rest or a change of circumstances, but a comparison: measure yourself against him.

Your struggle against sin. “Struggle” is contending against, fighting an opponent. He is reinterpreting their persecution. They thought they were enduring hostility from neighbours; he tells them they are in a fight with sin itself: both the sin of those who persecuted them, and the temptation to sin by giving up. It is the same contest Jesus was in.

Not yet to the point of blood. Then he does the measuring for them. Shedding blood means martyrdom. These people had genuinely suffered: humiliation, imprisonment, plundered houses (10:32–34), and the writer has praised them for it. And he says: nobody has died yet. He resisted to the point of blood; you have not.

Restoring the scale. It is a hard word, and a fair one. Exhaustion makes a person’s own trouble fill the whole horizon, which is a normal part of being tired rather than a moral failure. The writer does not tell them their pain is not real. He tells them it is not the biggest thing in the room.

Is it wrong to feel that my suffering is too much? No. Feelings of being overwhelmed are part of being human, and the Psalms are full of them. Jesus himself said his soul was very sorrowful, even to death (Matthew 26:38). This verse is not a rebuke to your feelings but a help for them: when your pain fills the whole horizon, look at his, and let it give you perspective and company. He knows what hostility from sinners is. Tell him honestly how hard it is, and ask him for strength for the next step. You are not being asked to pretend; you are being invited to consider him.

On a Tuesday. When you are weary, read one of the passion narratives slowly, perhaps Mark 14–15, and notice each kind of hostility he faced. Then look at your own hardest situation in that light. It will not make your trouble disappear, but it may make it the right size, and remind you that you are not alone in it.

verseByVerse.quote: And have you forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons? “My son, do not regard lightly the discipline of the Lord, nor be weary when reproved by him. For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
And have you forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons? The question is gentle and slightly reproachful. And note what it assumes: Scripture is currently speaking to them. Not spoke, but addresses (speaks with you, reasons with you), the same present tense as 3:7 and 10:15. A passage from Proverbs is treated as a word arriving in the room this morning. And the writer introduces it as an exhortation, the encouragement word. He regards what follows as comfort, which tells you a good deal about the argument he is making. “As sons”: the words of Proverbs are God’s fatherly words to his children.

In the flow. Verses 1–3 told the readers to look at what Jesus suffered; verses 5–11 teach them how to read what they themselves are suffering. The writer turns from the size of their suffering to its meaning: it is a Father’s training, which fits the letter’s great theme, that God is bringing many sons to glory through the Son (2:10–11).

My son. The quotation is Proverbs 3:11–12, and “my son” comes first and governs everything after it: whatever follows is said inside a family. “Discipline” (paideia) is training, child-rearing, the whole process of raising a child to maturity, of which correction is one part. The first error to avoid is to “regard lightly”: to shrug it off or treat a hard providence as meaningless weather.

Nor be weary. The second error: lose heart, faint, as in verse 3, collapsing under correction. We tend to one or the other. Some harden and refuse to ask what God might be doing; others are flattened and conclude he has turned against them. The verse forbids both, and leaves a narrow path between.

The one he loves. Here is the sentence the whole passage turns on, joining the two things we most naturally separate: discipline is evidence of love, not rejection (Revelation 3:19; Deuteronomy 8:5).

Every son whom he receives. “Chastises” is stronger: it means to scourge, to whip. The writer does not soften it, and the “every” leaves no exemptions. “Receives” is accepts, welcomes as his own. If you turn to Proverbs 3:12 you will read as a father the son in whom he delights: the writer is quoting the Greek translation of the Old Testament, which reads the Hebrew slightly differently, and the sense is the same.

Discipline without wrath. How can a believer hear the word scourges and still call it love? Because the punishment his sins deserve has already fallen elsewhere. Upon the Servant was the chastisement that brought us peace, and with his wounds we are healed (Isaiah 53:5), and Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many (9:28). So a Christian’s discipline is never God settling accounts with him; Christ settled them. What remains is a Father training a son. The hard providence that would be judgment for someone outside Christ is, for one inside him, the work of a Father who has received him and will never cast him off (Westminster Confession 11.5; 1689 London Baptist Confession 11.5).

What it does not mean. It does not mean every affliction is punishment for a particular sin. The letter has just spent a chapter on people who suffered because they were faithful. Discipline here includes training through suffering, including persecution. The readers’ suffering came from faithfulness, not from sin, yet God used it to train them. What the verse claims is that God is at work in the hardship of his children, forming them, not that he is settling accounts.

How can I tell whether a hardship is God’s correction for a sin? Sometimes it is plain: you sinned, and the consequences followed, and your conscience tells you so. Then repent, and receive the correction as a Father’s love. But often it is not plain, and you should not invent a sin to explain every trouble, as Job’s friends did. Ask God honestly whether there is anything he wants to show you, and listen to Scripture and wise friends. If nothing comes to light, then treat the hardship as training rather than punishment: God is using it to make you more like Christ. The question is not mainly why, but how do I respond as his child.

Is calling suffering discipline not just a way of excusing God? It would be if the verse called evil good, but it does not. The persecutors are still wrong, and the pain is still pain (v. 11). What the verse denies is that suffering is meaningless. A world without God leaves pain with no purpose at all; this passage says that, for God’s children, nothing is wasted. And the Father who says this is not a distant official who never suffers. He did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Romans 8:32), and the Son endured the cross (v. 2). The one who trains us through hardship has walked into the worst of it himself.

For worship. The God who holds the universe speaks to us in the language of a father: my son. It is the voice that said to the eternal Son, You are my Son, today I have begotten you (1:5), and now, because that Son has made us his brothers, the same voice turns to us in the same family words.

verseByVerse.quote: It is for discipline that you have to endure. God is treating you as sons. For what son is there whom his father does not discipline? If you are left without discipline, in which all have participated, then you are illegitimate children and not sons.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For discipline. The writer applies the proverb directly: the purpose of their suffering, the hostility, the confiscations, the public shaming, is training. That does not say the persecutors were doing God’s will, or that injustice was not injustice. It says God is using it, and a Christian may read his hardest circumstances as a Father’s work without excusing those who cause them.

Treating you as sons. Their suffering had raised the question of whether God had abandoned them; the writer says it is the evidence that he has not.

For what son is there whom his father does not discipline? An appeal to ordinary experience, and in that world it needed no argument (Proverbs 13:24; 19:18). A father who took no trouble over a boy’s formation was not indulgent but negligent. A father who loved his son trained him.

In which all have participated. Every true child of God shares it, including Jesus himself, who learned obedience through what he suffered (5:8). Not because he needed correcting, but because he was a true Son walking the road of sons.

Illegitimate children. The sharpest form of the argument. A man does not train somebody else’s children; in that society an illegitimate son might be housed and fed but not raised, and he usually had no right to inherit. So the absence of discipline is the frightening thing, not its presence. That is the exact inversion of what the readers felt. They looked at their troubles and wondered whether they were still his; the writer looks at the same troubles and says: this is what having a Father looks like.

Should I worry if my life is fairly easy at the moment? No. God gives seasons of rest and blessing, and they are to be received with thanks, not suspicion. Discipline does not always mean dramatic suffering; it includes the daily correction of conscience by Scripture, the frustration of plans, the small humblings that keep us dependent. If God is at work in you through his word, convicting you of sin and drawing you to holiness, you are being trained. What would be alarming is a life in which sin never troubles you and God never seems to interfere. Use the easy season to grow, to give, and to prepare for harder days.

On a Tuesday. If you are a parent, let this passage shape how you discipline: with love, for your child’s good, with the aim of forming character, never in anger for your own relief. You have a Father who raises you that way.

For worship. God does not raise strangers. In that world it was the true son, not the illegitimate one, who inherited. God has appointed his Son heir of all things (1:2), and he has made us sons in him, so that every correction we receive is a sign that the inheritance is real and our names are on it. We are not tolerated in the house and unloved. We are sons and daughters of God, fellow heirs with Christ (Romans 8:17), and the Father is taking the trouble to raise us for what we will inherit.

parallels.desc: as a man disciplines his son, the LORD your God disciplines you

verseByVerse.quote: Besides this, we have had earthly fathers who disciplined us and we respected them. Shall we not much more be subject to the Father of spirits and live? For they disciplined us for a short time as it seemed best to them, but he disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness. For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Earthly fathers. The argument runs from lesser to greater again, and the observation is a shrewd one. Children generally end up respecting the parent who took the trouble, and thinking little of the one who did not. “Earthly fathers” is literally fathers of our flesh.

Shall we not much more be subject to the Father of spirits and live?
