The title distinguishes him from fathers of the flesh: God, the creator of our spirits, the God of the spirits of all flesh (Numbers 16:22; 27:16; Zechariah 12:1). And the promise attached is not comfort but life. Submission to God’s discipline leads to life; rebellion against it leads to death (Deuteronomy 21:18–21).

As it seemed best to them. The comparison is honest about human fathers. “For a short time” is a few years of childhood. “As it seemed best to them” is the concession: human discipline is a matter of judgment, often wrong, sometimes angry, inconsistent or for the wrong things. The writer does not pretend otherwise.

For our good. For what is profitable: no guesswork and no mixed motives. God’s discipline is never mistaken, never excessive, never selfish (Romans 8:28).

Share his holiness. The aim named is startlingly high: not merely that we should behave better, but that we should partake of his holiness. God’s holiness is his utter purity, his being set apart from all that is sinful; he alone is holy in himself, and no creature will ever become God. But his children are made like him in character, pure as he is pure: be holy, for I am holy (1 Peter 1:15–16). Suffering refines character as fire refines gold (1 Peter 1:6–7).

The holiness he bought, the holiness he trains. Where does this holiness come from in the first place? We have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all (10:10); Jesus suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people through his own blood (13:12). So Christ’s death has already set believers apart as God’s own, clean in his sight. Discipline does not add to that; it works it out. The Father trains his children until what is already true of them in Christ becomes true in their character, and they grow like the one who sanctifies them and is not ashamed to call them brothers (2:11).

Painful rather than pleasant. A humane sentence. It is not supposed to feel good. The writer concedes it flatly, and “all” leaves no heroic exceptions.

Later. “Later” is the word to watch. Two timescales are in the verse, and almost everything depends on which one a person is standing in. At the moment: pain. Later: fruit. The “peaceful fruit of righteousness” is a harvest of righteous character and of peace with God (James 3:18).

Trained by it. The fruit is not automatic; it comes to those who have been trained, the gymnasium word from 5:14, exercised as an athlete is. The same trouble can leave one person bitter and another gentle, and the difference lies in whether it was received as training or merely endured and resented. Bitterness is the sign that trouble is being endured but not received; confess it, and ask God to turn the pain into training.

How can I think of God as a Father if my own father was harsh or absent? Slowly, honestly and with help. This passage itself admits that earthly fathers fail; God is not a larger version of your father, but the true Father of whom every good human father is a faint copy. Look at how the Father is revealed in Jesus: the Father who runs to the prodigal (Luke 15:20), who knows what you need before you ask, who gave his Son for you. Let Scripture redefine the word for you, and if the wounds are deep, talk with a pastor or a trusted counsellor. If your father abused you, that was wrong, and God hates it; it was never his discipline.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The tired are to get up, smooth the road for the limping, pursue peace and holiness, and watch that no one falls short of grace or trades the inheritance away like Esau. Then come two mountains: not Sinai, with its fire and terror, but Mount Zion, where believers already stand with angels and saints before God, through Jesus and his blood. So do not refuse the one who speaks from heaven; receive the unshakable kingdom with thankful awe.
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Mountains

Believers have not come to the terrors of Sinai but to Mount Zion, to Jesus and his sprinkled blood. And our God is still a consuming fire: what has changed is our access, not his nature.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Esau sold his birthright for a single meal.

Now: Watch for anyone falling short of grace, and ask what you could not bear to lose: that shows what your life rests on.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore lift your drooping hands and strengthen your weak knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not be put out of joint but rather be healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Drooping hands and weak knees. “Therefore”: since hardship is God’s loving training. The words are Isaiah’s (Isaiah 35:3), spoken to a weary people waiting for God to act. It is a runner whose arms drop and knees buckle near the end: the writer’s picture of his readers is not wicked or rebellious, but tired. Being told to get up and keep going is itself part of the help.

Straight paths. From Proverbs 4:26 in the Greek. The image shifts from the runner to the road: smooth the way, remove what would turn an ankle, and live in a straightforward, obedient way, without crooked compromises.

That what is lame may be healed. The reason for the road-mending is corporate. A rough path is manageable for a sound man and dangerous for an injured one, and the same ground a healthy Christian crosses without noticing can turn a struggling one off the road altogether. So the church must consider its limping member when deciding how it walks (10:24): not merely what I can manage, but what the weakest person in the room can manage. And the note to end on is hope. The lame are not written off; the expectation is that they recover, and the straightening of the path is part of how.

Because your God will come. The verses around Isaiah’s words give the reason for strengthening weak knees: say to those who have an anxious heart, Be strong; fear not! Behold, your God will come and save you, and then the lame man shall leap like a deer (Isaiah 35:4–6). Matthew records that when John the Baptist asked from prison whether Jesus was the one to come, Jesus answered from this very chapter: the lame walk (Matthew 11:4–5). The command rests on the coming of God in Christ. And the one who came is a high priest who sympathises with our weaknesses (4:15), so the limping member is not pushed along by the strong alone. Christ walks the path with him.

What does making straight paths look like in a church? It means arranging our common life so that the weakest can keep walking. Practically: not flaunting a freedom that will stumble a weaker brother (Romans 14:13–21); being honest and consistent, so that young believers are not confused by the gap between what we say and do; welcoming those who struggle instead of making them feel they must pretend to be strong; preaching and teaching clearly; and helping in concrete ways, a meal, a lift to church, a listening ear. It also means removing obstacles that we ourselves put there: gossip, cliques, harshness. A straight path is one a limping person can walk.

On a Tuesday. If you are the one limping, do the one small thing this verse asks: lift your hands, in prayer, and take the next step. He gives power to the faint (Isaiah 40:29).

verseByVerse.quote: Strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peace with everyone. Two pursuits held together, because each without the other goes wrong. “Strive” is the pursuing word: chase it down (Psalm 34:14; Romans 14:19). And “with everyone” is as wide as it sounds, including the neighbours who had plundered their houses. Paul adds the necessary qualification: if possible, so far as it depends on you (Romans 12:18). Peace-making is a duty, though not always in a Christian’s power, since it takes two.

And for the holiness. Here holiness is sanctification, the process of being made holy, and it too is to be pursued. Holiness is God’s gift and work in us (v. 10; 10:10, 14), but we must actively seek it. Peace pursued alone becomes appeasement, a willingness to agree with anything for the sake of quiet. Holiness pursued alone becomes a separatism that treats other people as contaminants. The verse chases both, and the tension between them is where most pastoral wisdom lives.

Without which no one will see the Lord. A hard clause, and it needs handling carefully, because read on its own it could terrify a believer into thinking his sight of God depends on his own achieved purity. To see the Lord is to enter his presence and enjoy him for ever: blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God (Matthew 5:8; 1 John 3:2–3; Revelation 22:4). Practical holiness is not optional for believers: those who show no desire for holiness show that they do not know God.

Status and pursuit. The whole letter forbids the terrifying reading. By a single offering Christ has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (10:14): the status is settled, and Christ settled it. This verse describes the holiness that necessarily accompanies that settlement, not a qualification earned to obtain it. Nobody will see the Lord who has not been made holy by Christ; and nobody who has been made holy by Christ will fail to pursue holiness. The pursuit is the evidence, as with the conditional clauses of 3:6 and 3:14. Holiness is the fruit, not the root, of salvation, and at death believers are made perfect in it (12:23).

In the flow. Verses 14–17 widen the view from the single runner to the whole congregation, and to anyone in it who might not finish. The holiness pursued here is the holiness the Father’s discipline was producing (v. 10), and seeing the Lord points ahead to verses 22–24.

How holy do I have to be to see the Lord? As holy as Christ, and in him you already are. Your right to see God rests entirely on his righteousness counted to you and his blood that cleanses you. But the same Christ who justifies you also sanctifies you, and the proof that you belong to him is not that you have arrived, but that you are pursuing. Ask: do I want to be holy? Do I hate my sin and fight it? Am I, over the years, being changed? If so, you are on the road, however slowly. On the last day God will finish the work, and you will see him and be like him.

Must I make peace with someone who keeps hurting me? You must be willing for peace, and do what is in your power: forgive in your heart, refuse revenge, speak the truth kindly, and seek reconciliation where it is safe and possible (Matthew 5:23–24; Romans 12:17–21). But peace with everyone does not mean pretending wrong is right, or putting yourself or others in danger. Reconciliation needs repentance on both sides, and where someone is abusive or unrepentant, you may and sometimes must keep your distance while still wishing them good and praying for them. Holiness and peace go together; neither requires you to stay under abuse.

On a Tuesday. Peace and holiness are usually lost in small places: the message you did not answer because silence was easier, the habit you stopped fighting because it seemed too small to matter. The verb is chase, and nobody catches anything standing still. If a sin you have made terms with still troubles you, that trouble is the Spirit keeping you in the race.

verseByVerse.quote: See to it that no one fails to obtain the grace of God; that no “root of bitterness” springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled;
verseByVerse.commentary:
See to it. “See to it” is to oversee, watch over, the root of overseer and bishop, and it is addressed to the whole congregation, not its leaders. “Fails to obtain” is to fall short, to lag behind and miss it, as in 4:1. God’s grace is not insufficient; the danger is that someone falls back before reaching it. The letter keeps scanning the room for the single person quietly slipping, and makes that scanning everybody’s job.

A root of bitterness. The phrase is from Deuteronomy 29:18, where Moses warns against anyone whose heart turns away from the LORD to other gods, lest there be among you a root bearing poisonous and bitter fruit. The root is a person whose heart has turned. So this is not first about private resentment, though that application is fair, but about what one turned-away heart does to a community: it begins hidden underground, then sprouts and spreads poison.

Many become defiled. The three verbs trace the progress. It springs up, already established by the time it surfaces; it causes trouble; and many are defiled, because the damage is never contained to one person. A bitter grievance that seems reasonable gathers sympathisers and leaves people who have caught something they did not go looking for. Apostasy and bitterness are contagious, which is why the whole congregation is told to watch early, before roots surface.

The grace that tasted death. What is the grace of God that a person might fall short of? In this letter it has a cross in it. Jesus was made lower than the angels so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone (2:9), and because of him believers may draw near to the throne of grace to receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need (4:16). To fall short of the grace of God is to drift back from Christ himself and from the open throne he secured. That is why the whole church watches: what one person slipping stands to lose is nothing less than him.

How do I know if bitterness is taking root in me? Watch for the signs: you replay the hurt over and over; you rehearse speeches you will never give; you find yourself telling others about it to gather sympathy; you cannot hear the person’s name without a tightening inside; you begin to resent God for allowing it. Those are roots surfacing. The remedy is to bring the hurt to God honestly, to forgive as you have been forgiven (Ephesians 4:31–32), which means releasing the debt to God even when feelings lag behind, and, where possible, to speak to the person directly rather than about them. Bitterness grows in the dark; take it into the light.

How should I watch over others without becoming a busybody? By caring, not policing. Watching over one another in Scripture looks like noticing who is missing, asking how someone really is, praying for them, and speaking gently when you see someone drifting or bitter (Galatians 6:1). It does not look like gossip, suspicion or checking up on people’s private lives. If you are concerned about someone, go to them, not to others about them. And let others watch over you: the person who receives loving correction gratefully is the one best placed to give it.

verseByVerse.quote: that no one is sexually immoral or unholy like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal. For you know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sexually immoral. Esau is the letter’s final warning, but was he sexually immoral? Genesis does not say so, though his marriages to two Hittite women grieved his parents (Genesis 26:34–35). Some later Jewish writings did describe him that way, and the writer may have that tradition in mind. But the more likely reading is that only unholy describes Esau: the writer warns against two dangers, sexual immorality and the godlessness of a man like Esau.

Or unholy like Esau. Esau is a well-chosen warning, because he is not a monster. He is a man who was hungry. The word for “unholy” means profane, godless: the opposite of holy, someone who treats sacred things as common. It describes a person for whom nothing is sacred, not because he is wicked, but because he cannot see why it would be.

A single meal. The “birthright” was the rights of the firstborn: a double inheritance, family leadership, and, in this family, a share in the promise made to Abraham (Genesis 25:29–34). Esau traded it for a bowl of stew. Genesis records the exchange in a few words: he ate and drank and rose and went his way. Thus Esau despised his birthright (Genesis 25:34). No agonising, no calculation. He was hungry now, and the birthright was a thing you could not eat.

Drift with a price tag on it. That is exactly the danger these readers were in. Nobody was asking them to renounce Christ in a formal ceremony. They were being offered relief, property restored, neighbours placated, an end to the shame, in exchange for something that could not be seen or eaten. Esau’s trade is drift with a price tag on it.

One meal, or the joy set before him. The writer has set Esau beside someone else in this chapter, and the Greek makes the comparison plain. Esau sold his birthright for (anti) a single meal (v. 16); Jesus, for (anti) the joy that was set before him, endured the cross (v. 2). The same small word, opposite choices. Esau gave up the future for the present because he was hungry now; Jesus gave up the present, its comfort, honour and life, for the joy ahead. Every temptation to trade the inheritance for relief is a choice between Esau’s bowl and Christ’s cross, and the one who endured the cross always lives to intercede for those tempted to sell (7:25).

He was rejected. Later, when Isaac blessed Jacob instead, Esau wanted the blessing back but could not have it (Genesis 27:30–40). “Rejected” is disqualified, failed the test.

No chance to repent. A distressing sentence, to be read exactly. Literally he found no place for repentance (metanoias topon ouch heuren), and it is debated. One reading: Esau could not change his father Isaac’s mind, because the blessing once given was irrevocable (Genesis 27:33). The other: Esau himself could not find genuine repentance, because his tears were for the lost blessing, not for his sin. The “it” probably refers to the blessing, which he sought with tears (Genesis 27:34, 38). It does not say Esau repented and was refused forgiveness, which would contradict everything Scripture says about God. He cried for the inheritance he had thrown away, and there is no record of his ever regretting the contempt that threw it. Some decisions cannot be unmade, and grief afterwards does not restore what was sold. That is the warning, and it is a mercy that it comes while there is still time to hear it.

Is it too late for me, as it was for Esau, if I have made choices I deeply regret? If you are grieving over your sin and turning to Christ, no. The very fact that you are sorry for the sin itself, and not only for its consequences, shows that you are not where Esau was. Some consequences of past choices may remain: a marriage ended, health damaged, years lost. But God’s forgiveness is never closed to the one who comes to him through Christ, and he is skilled at bringing good out of ruined things (Joel 2:25). Do not let Esau’s story frighten you away from God. Let it send you to him now, while it is called today.

Why does Scripture put sexual sin next to Esau’s godlessness? Because both trade something holy for a momentary appetite. Sexual immorality takes a gift God made sacred, the union of a husband and wife, and treats it as common, something to be grabbed for immediate pleasure. It is the same contempt for holy things that Esau showed. And it is often how drift happens: not by argument, but by appetite. If you are struggling here, do not hide it. Confess it to God, tell a trusted believer, put practical barriers in place, and remember that Christ’s blood cleanses sexual sin as fully as any other (1 Corinthians 6:9–11).

For worship. The birthright Esau sold for a bowl of stew was the right of the firstborn, and he held it cheap. God’s own Firstborn, whom all the angels worship (1:6), held his far higher and still did not cling to it. He is the heir of all things (1:2), and he went to the cross to share his inheritance with people who had sold theirs for less than a meal. Now the church is the assembly of the firstborn, every name enrolled in heaven (12:23), and what was thrown away at a cooking pot is restored at a cross. Esau found no place for repentance; at the throne of grace, no sinner who comes in that Son’s name is ever turned away.

verseByVerse.quote: For you have not come to what may be touched, a blazing fire and darkness and gloom and a tempest and the sound of a trumpet and a voice whose words made the hearers beg that no further messages be spoken to them. For they could not endure the order that was given, “If even a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned.” Indeed, so terrifying was the sight that Moses said, “I tremble with fear.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
What may be touched. The letter’s final great contrast begins, and it is between two mountains. “Come” is a perfect tense: you have come and are there, the same verb the letter uses for drawing near to God (4:16; 7:25; 10:22). The first mountain is tangible: Mount Sinai. And the writer’s first word about the mountain is the one thing nobody was allowed to do: touch it. The boundary was set, and the penalty was death.

In the flow. The word For ties this to the warning about Esau: do not sell your birthright, because of where you now stand. Verses 18–24 turn the argument of chapters 8–10 into two pictures: Sinai, where sinners were kept at a distance, and Zion, where they are welcomed through Jesus.

Fire and darkness. Sinai when God gave the law (Exodus 19:16–19; 20:18–21; Deuteronomy 4:11–12; 5:22–26): seven terrifying features, and the combination is deliberately disorienting: fire that gives no light, darkness with a storm in it.

A voice they begged to stop. They said to Moses: you speak to us, and we will listen; but do not let God speak to us, lest we die (Exodus 20:19; Deuteronomy 5:25–27). It is a sobering request. Offered the direct voice of God, a nation asked for a mediator, more out of terror than reverence, and yet they were not wrong to ask.

If even a beast touches the mountain. From Exodus 19:12–13. The severity extended to animals, which is the point: an ox that wandered across a line it could not understand was killed. God’s holiness at Sinai kept sinners at a distance.

I tremble with fear. The final touch. Exodus does not record these words at the giving of the law; the writer is drawing on Deuteronomy 9:19, where Moses recalls his fear of God’s anger after the golden calf, at the same mountain. Moses, who spoke with God face to face, who went up the mountain when nobody else could, was shaking. If the mediator was frightened, what was it like at the bottom?

The request God answered with a Prophet. Israel’s terrified plea was answered. Moses recalled that day at Horeb, when the people said, Let me not hear again the voice of the LORD my God or see this great fire any more, lest I die; the LORD said they were right, and promised: I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers, and I will put my words in his mouth (Deuteronomy 18:16–18). Peter announced that this Prophet had come in Jesus (Acts 3:22). God gave them the mediator they asked for, and far more: not another trembling Moses, but his own Son, who speaks God’s words without fear because he is the radiance of God’s glory (1:3).

What it does not mean. The God of Sinai is not a different God from the God of the gospel. He is the same holy God (v. 29). The difference is the covenant: at Sinai sinful people met God’s holiness without a perfect mediator; in Christ they meet the same God through the blood that brings peace.

Why did God make Sinai so terrifying? To show what his holiness means for sinners who approach him without a perfect mediator. The fire, the darkness and the boundary were not cruelty; they were truth. Sin cannot stand in the presence of a holy God, and Israel needed to learn it before they could understand why a sacrifice and a priest were needed. The terror of Sinai is the background against which the welcome of Zion becomes good news. Without it we would think God easy to approach; with it we see what Christ has done in bringing us near.

On a Tuesday. Read Exodus 19 slowly and feel the fear of it: the boundary, the smoke, the command not to touch. Then begin your prayer by thanking God that you may come near, and why.

verseByVerse.quote: But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to innumerable angels in festal gathering, and to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, and to God, the judge of all, and to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you have come to Mount Zion. The tense is the astonishing thing: arrived and standing there. Not one day, but already, by faith, especially in worship. These people were sitting in an ordinary room in a hostile city, and the writer tells them where they actually are. Zion was the hill of Jerusalem where God dwelt in the temple, the sign of his presence and kingship (Psalm 2:6; 48:1–2).

The heavenly Jerusalem. The city with foundations that Abraham was looking for (11:10, 16), the Jerusalem above, which is free, and she is our mother (Galatians 4:26; Revelation 21:2). He never reached it. They have.

Angels in festal gathering. “Innumerable” is myriads, tens of thousands. “Festal gathering” means a festival assembly, a crowd gathered for celebration (Revelation 5:11–12). At Sinai the angels attended the giving of the law amid fire and fear (Deuteronomy 33:2; Acts 7:53); here they keep festival.

The assembly of the firstborn. The “assembly” is the church, and every member is a firstborn (the word is plural). Not one heir and a crowd of others; everyone has the birthright, sharing the privileges of the firstborn Son as heirs (Romans 8:29). That lands with some force a few verses after Esau, who sold his. “Enrolled” is registered, written down: their names are written in heaven (Luke 10:20; Philippians 4:3; Revelation 21:27). This is the whole church, on earth and in heaven. And it frees the heart from a quiet tyranny. Many of us live for a name written somewhere: in a newspaper, on an office door, in other people’s good opinion. The one whose name is written in heaven no longer needs it written anywhere else.

God, the judge of all. The title is not softened. He is still the judge, even in the festal gathering. But we come to him through Jesus (v. 24), and that changes everything about how the judge receives us. The festival has not dethroned the judge. It rejoices because his justice has been fully satisfied in Christ, so that the holy God can welcome sinners without ceasing to be holy (Romans 3:26).

The spirits of the righteous made perfect. The believing dead, and the whole of chapter 11 among them, existing consciously in God’s presence before the resurrection of their bodies. “Made perfect”: completed at last, as 11:40 promised, and not apart from us. Their salvation is complete in that they are free from sin and in God’s presence, though they await the resurrection. This verse is strong evidence for what is called the intermediate state: conscious life with Christ between death and the resurrection.

Jesus, the mediator. The climax, and the reason for all the rest: Jesus himself. “New” here is young, fresh. A mediator is a go-between who brings two estranged parties together and guarantees the agreement between them. The new covenant is the agreement God promised through Jeremiah: I will put my laws into their minds, and I will remember their sins no more (8:10, 12; Jeremiah 31:31–34). Jesus guarantees it with his own blood, and so it cannot fail. At Sinai the people begged for a mediator and got a frightened one; at Zion they have a mediator who is not afraid of God, because he is God’s Son, and who is not distant from them, because he is their brother.

A better word than the blood of Abel. The “sprinkled blood” is Christ’s blood, which cleanses (9:13–14, 19–22; 10:22). Abel’s blood cried from the ground for justice (Genesis 4:10; Hebrews 11:4). This blood speaks too, and it says something better: Christ’s blood pleads mercy even for those who shed it.

Two mountains side by side. Put them together, and the contrast is complete. There: fire, darkness, a boundary, and a voice people begged to stop. Here: a city, a festival, a family of firstborn sons, and blood that speaks in your favour. And the readers were considering going back to the first one.

Where Christians differ: do the dead sleep until the resurrection? Some teach that the soul sleeps, or ceases to exist, between death and resurrection. This commentary’s view: this verse speaks of the spirits of the righteous made perfect as already present in the heavenly assembly. Jesus promised the thief, today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43), and Paul longed to depart and be with Christ (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8). Believers who die go immediately and consciously into Christ’s presence, made perfect in holiness, awaiting the resurrection of their bodies.

Why does Sunday worship feel so ordinary if this is where we are? Because we see with our eyes, and this verse describes what is true by faith. The building may be plain, the singing thin, the sermon unremarkable, and still, every time God’s people gather in Christ’s name, they are joined to the worship of angels and of the saints in glory, before the Judge of all, through Jesus. The readers of this letter met in a house in a hostile city, and this was their reality. Come to worship expecting to meet God, not to be entertained, and ask the Spirit to open your eyes to where you really are.

On a Tuesday. When you think of believing loved ones who have died, remember that they are in the same assembly you join every Sunday. You worship with them, though you cannot see them. Grieve, but grieve as one who belongs to the same gathering.

For worship. Israel stood at a distance from a mountain it could not touch. We have been brought into a city, and not by climbing. Jesus went ahead of us into the holy place as a forerunner on our behalf (6:20), and he has brought his brothers in after him: the names written in heaven, the faithful dead made perfect, the angels keeping festival. The Judge of all looks at that assembly and sees in it every one of his firstborn, washed and welcomed. There is no better place in the universe to be, and in Christ we are already there.
verseByVerse.note: Abel’s blood cried out for justice; Jesus’ blood speaks of pardon.

verseByVerse.quote: See that you do not refuse him who is speaking. For if they did not escape when they refused him who warned them on earth, much less will we escape if we reject him who warns from heaven. At that time his voice shook the earth, but now he has promised, “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Him who is speaking. The fifth and final warning of the letter. “Him who is speaking” is present tense: not him who spoke, but God, who speaks now through his Son (1:1–2) and through the sprinkled blood of Christ, which speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (12:24). That present tense sums up the letter’s view of Scripture: in it God is still speaking (3:7; 12:5). “Refuse” is to beg off, to ask to be excused, the word used in verse 19 of the people at Sinai begging that no further message be spoken.

Declining without disputing. That is a subtle and searching form of the danger. Nobody at Sinai denied that God was speaking. They simply asked him to stop, because hearing him was unbearable, and the writer says the same thing is available to his readers in a more comfortable form. You can decline a word without disputing it. You can own a Bible, agree with every line of it, and quietly arrange your life so that it never actually speaks to you. And if you fear you have been doing this, the fear itself shows you are still listening; the voice that warns is the same voice that invites.

Him who warns from heaven. At Sinai God warned them on earth, through Moses, and those who rejected him perished in the wilderness (3:16–19). It is the letter’s standing argument from lesser to greater, as at 2:2–3 and 10:28–29: God now speaks from heaven, through his exalted Son, and the responsibility is greater, because the speaker is greater and the word is clearer.

In the flow. Here the letter sounds the last of its five warning passages (2:1–4; 3:7–4:13; 5:11–6:12; 10:26–39; 12:25–29), and they all say one thing: do not drift away from the Son through whom God has spoken.

Yet once more. At Sinai the whole mountain trembled greatly (Exodus 19:18; Psalm 68:8). The quotation is Haggai 2:6, spoken to men rebuilding a modest temple after the exile and grieving over how small it was. There God promised to shake the nations and fill his house with glory. The writer sees its final fulfilment in the last great shaking at Christ’s return, when the whole created order will be transformed (2 Peter 3:10–13). The first shaking rattled a mountain; the second takes in the heavens. And it is called a promise rather than a threat, which tells you on which side of it the writer expects his readers to stand.

When is this final shaking? At Christ’s return, when the present heavens and earth give way to new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (2 Peter 3:13). Some apply it to the end of the old covenant order in AD 70, when the temple was destroyed, and that event was a foretaste; but a shaking of heaven as well as earth looks to the end. Meanwhile the kingdom that cannot be shaken is already ours (v. 28).

What it does not mean. It does not mean God speaks new revelation from heaven today. He speaks through his Son, whose word is recorded in Scripture, and to refuse Scripture is to refuse him. This commentary holds that, with the Son’s word delivered through those who heard him (1:1–2; 2:3–4), revelation of that kind is complete; Christians who believe God still gives prophetic words usually agree that nothing they hear may add to Scripture or overrule it, and that is the point that matters here.

How might I be refusing God without realising it? By hearing without heeding. Common forms are: always applying sermons to other people; reading the Bible for information but never asking what it requires of me; skipping the passages that make me uncomfortable; filling every quiet moment so that there is no room to listen; agreeing with a command but postponing obedience indefinitely. None of these is open rebellion. All of them are ways of begging God to stop speaking. The remedy is simple, and hard: when God’s word touches something in your life, respond to it that day, in some concrete way.

verseByVerse.quote: This phrase, “Yet once more,” indicates the removal of things that are shaken—that is, things that have been made—in order that the things that cannot be shaken may remain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This phrase. The writer draws an argument from two small words, as he did from the single word new in 8:13. “Once more” is literally yet once for all, the word used of Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice (9:26–28). Once more implies a last time, and a last shaking implies that whatever survives it is permanent.

The removal of things that are shaken. “Removal” is change, transformation, transfer, the same word used of the change of priesthood (7:12). Then the definition of what goes: created things, the present heavens and earth, everything temporary, everything belonging to this passing age. It is a large category, and it includes the temple these readers were probably being drawn back to, along with everything else visible.

That the things that cannot be shaken may remain. The purpose clause changes the character of the whole event. The shaking is not destruction for its own sake. It is a sifting, and its object is to leave standing what was always going to stand: God himself, Christ, his people, his word, which stands for ever (Isaiah 40:8; 1 Peter 1:23–25), and the new creation.

A mercy inside a frightening image. A shaking removes only what was going to fall anyway, and the tremor is a mercy to anyone whose house is built on the right ground. These readers had already rehearsed it: their property had been shaken out of their hands (10:34), and they discovered that they still had a better and abiding possession. And the verse supplies a question worth asking now. If everything that can be shaken will be, a person can find out in advance what his life is built on, by noticing what he cannot bear to lose.

The one who remains. Why can anything survive the final shaking? Because what remains is anchored in the Son. Hebrews has already applied the Psalm to him: the heavens are the work of your hands; they will perish, but you remain; they will all wear out like a garment, but you are the same, and your years will have no end (1:10–12). The letter will end by saying it plainly: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever (13:8). Everything made will be rolled up, and the Son through whom it was made will not. Whatever belongs to him, his people, his word and his kingdom, stands on the side of what remains.

Will the things I love on earth be lost? Everything that belongs to the old order of sin and decay will go. But the new creation is this creation renewed, not abandoned, and God is not a wasteful builder. Whatever is good and done in Christ is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58), believers who have died will be raised in bodies, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into the city (Revelation 21:24). We do not know every detail, and should not pretend to. But what you love rightly, in God, you will not finally lose; you will find it again, purified, in him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and thus let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A kingdom that cannot be shaken. The response commanded is gratitude, which is not what we might expect in a passage that ends with a consuming fire. The phrase can also mean let us have grace, and both fit: grace received produces thanks, and thanks is how grace is held. “Receiving” is present tense. Nobody in this letter builds a kingdom or earns one; it is handed over. It is God’s eternal kingdom, promised in Daniel, where the saints of the Most High receive a kingdom that will never be destroyed (Daniel 7:14, 18, 27). Christ reigns now, and his kingdom grows through the gospel until it is revealed in fullness at his single, visible return. This commentary takes the amillennial view, that the thousand years of Revelation 20 picture Christ’s present reign, and expects one public coming (Matthew 24:27, 30–31) with no separate secret rapture; many faithful Christians expect a rapture or a future earthly reign, and they share the same hope of his coming.

Acceptable worship. The word for worship is the term for priestly service, and by now the reader knows that the whole congregation is doing what priests once did. The right response to grace is a whole life of worship (Romans 12:1), expressed especially in praise and good works (13:15–16).

The kingdom given to the Son of Man. Daniel saw the kingdom given first to one like a son of man, who came with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days and received a dominion that shall not pass away (Daniel 7:13–14), and then to the saints of the Most High. Jesus took that title as his own, and Hebrews shows him crowned with glory and honour, seated and waiting until his enemies are made a footstool for his feet (2:9; 10:12–13). So the kingdom we are receiving is not an idea or a mood. It is his reign, shared with those who belong to him, and nothing can shake it, because to shake it you would have to unseat him.

With reverence and awe. “Reverence” is godly fear, devout respect, as of Jesus in 5:7; “awe” is fear, dread. This is the note the letter refuses to drop. It has spent twelve chapters removing the barriers, opening the curtain, and telling frightened people to come boldly, and it will not let that boldness slide into familiarity. We come with confidence (4:16) but also with awe.

A consuming fire. The last sentence of the chapter quotes Deuteronomy 4:24, a startling place to end. The chapter contrasted Sinai’s blazing fire with the festival of Zion, and it closes by saying the God of Zion is the same God, and still a fire. The mountain has changed, and God has not. What has altered is our access, the blood, the curtain, the priest, and anyone who concludes from the open way that God has become manageable has misunderstood it. For those outside Christ he is a consuming fire of judgment (10:27). For those in Christ his fire purifies (1 Corinthians 3:13–15; Malachi 3:2–3). Grace and holiness are not opposites.

Our God. Note the pronoun the writer chooses: our God. He does not say God is a consuming fire, in the abstract, to be feared from a distance. He says the fire is ours, which is either a frightening sentence or a deeply comforting one, depending entirely on which mountain you have come to.

What does reverence look like in worship today? It is mainly a matter of the heart, not of style. It shows itself in coming prepared rather than distracted; in singing words you mean; in listening to God’s word as God’s word; in confessing sin honestly; in taking the Lord’s Supper soberly; and in a sense that the God you meet is holy and great. Reverence can be joyful and loud, as the Psalms are, or quiet; it can be in a cathedral or a front room. What it is never is casual, as if God were a friend we could take or leave, or a performance we have come to judge. Come gladly, and come awed.

How can God be both a consuming fire and my loving Father? Because in Christ the fire has already fallen. The holiness of God is unchanged, and it is a fire against sin. But for those in Christ, the judgment that sin deserves was borne by him at the cross; the fire burned there, on him. What remains for believers is the same holy God, now our Father, whose fire refines rather than destroys, burning away what is unworthy in us so that we may share his holiness (12:10). The same sun that would scorch a man without shelter warms one who lives in its light. Fear him rightly, and you will find there is nothing to fear in him.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted to grumble, say what you are receiving instead. A grateful person is hard to shake.

For worship. The kingdom we are receiving was purchased by the blood of the Son and handed to us as a gift. We did not build it, and we cannot lose it. And the King of it is a consuming fire, holy beyond our thought, who nevertheless lets us call him ours. There is no other God like him.

12.text: <sup>1</sup>Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us also lay aside every weight, and sin which clings so closely, and let us run with endurance the race that is set before us,<sup>2</sup>looking to Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is seated at the right hand of the throne of God.<sup>3</sup>Consider him who endured from sinners such hostility against himself, so that you may not grow weary or fainthearted.<sup>4</sup>In your struggle against sin you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood.<sup>5</sup>And have you forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons? “My son, do not regard lightly the discipline of the Lord, nor be weary when reproved by him.<sup>6</sup>For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and chastises every son whom he receives.”<sup>7</sup>It is for discipline that you have to endure. God is treating you as sons. For what son is there whom his father does not discipline?<sup>8</sup>If you are left without discipline, in which all have participated, then you are illegitimate children and not sons.<sup>9</sup>Besides this, we have had earthly fathers who disciplined us and we respected them. Shall we not much more be subject to the Father of spirits and live?<sup>10</sup>For they disciplined us for a short time as it seemed best to them, but he disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness.<sup>11</sup>For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.<sup>12</sup>Therefore lift your drooping hands and strengthen your weak knees,<sup>13</sup>and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not be put out of joint but rather be healed.<sup>14</sup>Strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord.<sup>15</sup>See to it that no one fails to obtain the grace of God; that no “root of bitterness” springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled;<sup>16</sup>that no one is sexually immoral or unholy like Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal.<sup>17</sup>For you know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears.<sup>18</sup>For you have not come to what may be touched, a blazing fire and darkness and gloom and a tempest<sup>19</sup>and the sound of a trumpet and a voice whose words made the hearers beg that no further messages be spoken to them.<sup>20</sup>For they could not endure the order that was given, “If even a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned.”<sup>21</sup>Indeed, so terrifying was the sight that Moses said, “I tremble with fear.”<sup>22</sup>But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to innumerable angels in festal gathering,<sup>23</sup>and to the assembly of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, and to God, the judge of all, and to the spirits of the righteous made perfect,<sup>24</sup>and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.<sup>25</sup>See that you do not refuse him who is speaking. For if they did not escape when they refused him who warned them on earth, much less will we escape if we reject him who warns from heaven.<sup>26</sup>At that time his voice shook the earth, but now he has promised, “Yet once more I will shake not only the earth but also the heavens.”<sup>27</sup>This phrase, “Yet once more,” indicates the removal of things that are shaken—that is, things that have been made—in order that the things that cannot be shaken may remain.<sup>28</sup>Therefore let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and thus let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe,<sup>29</sup>for our God is a consuming fire.

13.title: Outside the Camp: The Unchanging Christ
13.overview:
The sermon lands in ordinary life: love, hospitality, prisoners, marriage and contentment. This is not a change of subject. People who have come to Mount Zion live this way in their own streets.

At the centre stands verse 8: “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.” The founding leaders have died; Christ has not changed, so there is nothing newer to chase. Then the letter’s last appeal: Jesus suffered outside the gate, so go out to him, bearing his disgrace, for here we have no lasting city. The Christian’s sacrifices now are praise and practical kindness. The letter closes with a great benediction: the God who raised the great Shepherd works in us what pleases him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter turns to practical life: love that keeps going, welcome for strangers, solidarity with prisoners, marriage honoured and kept pure, and contentment instead of the love of money. Contentment rests on God’s own promise never to leave his people.
verseByVerse.theology:
Where the Argument Lands

The letter's theology ends in hospitality, prison visiting, marriage and money. Contentment rests on a promise: “I will never leave you nor forsake you.”
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Visiting prisoners marked a believer out publicly, and these readers had done it before.

Now: Keep loving, keep welcoming, keep remembering those in prison as though in prison with them.

verseByVerse.quote: Let brotherly love continue. Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meaning first. Hebrews 13 shows life in the unshakeable kingdom day to day: practical love (vv. 1–6); leaders, the altar outside the gate, and the sacrifices of praise and sharing (vv. 7–19); then the benediction and greetings (vv. 20–25). After twelve chapters inside the sanctuary, the letter walks out into the street: the worship of the heavenly Zion looks like a spare bed, a prison visit, a faithful marriage and a contented heart.

Let brotherly love continue. The word is philadelphia, love of brothers and sisters, the affection between members of a family. And the verb is continue, remain: the love is already there. The writer is not telling a cold congregation to start loving; he is telling a tired one not to let go. These readers had served the saints, visited prisoners and shared each other’s losses (6:10; 10:33–34). What was failing was not their love but their stamina.

Hospitality to strangers. The Greek is one word, philoxenia, love of strangers, set deliberately beside philadelphia: family affection is to widen into welcome for people you do not know. Inns were often dangerous, dirty and immoral, and the travelling teachers, missionaries and refugees of a persecuted movement depended entirely on believers’ homes (3 John 5–8). This was not a social grace but infrastructure. And it carried risk: opening your house to an unknown Christian in a city that was confiscating Christian property had consequences.

Angels unawares. The reference is Abraham at Mamre, running out to meet three travellers in the heat of the day and hurrying to feed them (Genesis 18:1–8), and Lot at Sodom (Genesis 19:1–3). In each case the guests were more than they appeared, and the host did not know it at the time. “Unawares” is the point. The writer does not promise angels; he says that some who opened their doors found later that they had done something far larger than they knew.

The brother at the table. Both loves in these verses rest on Christ. The church is a family because the Son took our flesh and blood and is not ashamed to call us brothers (2:11, 14); the affection we owe one another is his affection, continuing in us. And the welcome of strangers has a hidden guest greater than any angel. Jesus said that whoever welcomes the least of his brothers welcomes him: I was a stranger and you welcomed me (Matthew 25:35, 40). The Christian who pours tea for a tired traveller is serving the King without knowing it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean angels regularly come to our doors in disguise, and it does not require naivety: wisdom in protecting one’s household, especially children, is still needed.

How can I show hospitality if I am not a good host and my home is small? Hospitality is not entertaining; it is welcome. It does not need a large house, good cooking or a tidy kitchen. It needs an open door and a willing heart: soup at the kitchen table, a cup of tea, a sofa for a night, an invitation to Sunday lunch for the person sitting alone at church. If your home is not suitable, take someone out for coffee, or host with a friend. Start small and ordinary. The point is that strangers become guests and guests become family, and Christ is welcomed in them.

On a Tuesday. Think of one brother or sister in your church with whom love has cooled, through a disagreement, a slight or simple neglect, and send them a message today.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham, Lot and others welcomed angels without first knowing who they were.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember those who are in prison, as though in prison with them, and those who are mistreated, since you also are in the body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember those in prison. “Remember” is keep in mind and act on it. Roman prisons gave inmates little or nothing; a prisoner without visitors bringing food and clothing simply deteriorated. So remembering meant a basket of bread carried through a door that everyone in the street could see you entering, and it identified you publicly with his offence. These readers had done it before (10:34), when it was dangerous.

As though in prison with them. Literally bound together with them: not remember them charitably, from a safe distance, but as if you were in the cell. It refuses the natural instinct of a frightened community, which is to distance itself from the members who have been arrested.

Those who are mistreated. The word is ill-treated, tortured, the same word as 11:25 and 11:37, of Moses and the prophets. The persecuted of the present are put in the same company as the heroes of chapter 11.

Since you also are in the body. It may mean the body of Christ, in which what happens to one member happens to all (1 Corinthians 12:26). More probably it means a physical body: you are made of the same material, and a Christian who imagines himself exempt from what has happened to another is not merely unkind but mistaken.

The prisoner who sympathises. This is exactly what the Son of God did for us. He did not pity us from heaven. He took the same flesh and blood (2:14), and was himself arrested, bound, beaten and mocked. So the letter can say that we have a High Priest who is able to sympathise with our weaknesses, tested in every respect as we are (4:15). To feel another’s chains as your own is to have the mind of Christ. And he still feels them: when Saul struck the church, the risen Lord did not ask him why he was persecuting the church, but, why are you persecuting me (Acts 9:4)?

What it does not mean. It does not limit care to Christian prisoners, though they are the focus. Compassion for all who suffer, including those imprisoned for real crimes, reflects Christ’s heart: I was in prison and you came to me (Matthew 25:36).

How can I remember prisoners when I do not know any? Start by finding out. Several organisations publish the names and stories of Christians imprisoned for their faith around the world, with addresses for letters and guidance on how to pray; choose one person and pray for them by name each week. Many prisoners say that letters from strangers made all the difference. Nearer home, prison chaplaincies and prison fellowship ministries welcome volunteers, letter-writers and supporters, and the families of prisoners often need practical help. Remembering begins with knowing one name.

On a Tuesday. Think of anyone in your church whose suffering isolates them, a carer, a long illness, a believer cut off by family, and do one concrete thing for them this week.

verseByVerse.quote: Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled, for God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterous.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Marriage held in honor. “Honor” is precious, valued. “Among all” means by everybody, the single included. Marriage is God’s good gift from creation (Genesis 2:18–25), and the command had two contemporary edges. Some in the ancient world despised marriage as a spiritual encumbrance, and Paul warned of an ascetic strand that would forbid marriage (1 Timothy 4:3). Others, influenced by pagan culture, treated it as no obstacle to anything they wanted. Both are wrong, and the verse faces both directions at once, honouring the institution and guarding it.

The marriage bed undefiled. “Marriage bed” is a euphemism for sexual union, and “undefiled” is pure, unstained, the word used of Christ himself in 7:26: clean, honourable, and not to be spoiled.

What does undefiled require? Faithfulness. Sex belongs to one man and one woman within marriage and nowhere else: not in adultery, not in pornography, not in the lustful look that Jesus called adultery of the heart (Matthew 5:28). Within marriage Scripture is glad and generous (Proverbs 5:18–19; the Song of Songs), and it calls husband and wife to give themselves to each other freely and not to withhold themselves (1 Corinthians 7:3–5). Scripture gives no list of acts. It gives the principles: faithfulness, mutual consent, love and care, and nothing that degrades or harms.

God will judge. The reason given is the striking part. Not that adultery damages people, though it does; not that it is socially destructive, though it is. God will judge (1 Corinthians 6:9–10). The matter is between the person and God before it is between the person and anybody else, and the verse assumes a court that meets whether or not the injured party ever knows.

Pressure does not exempt. Sexual sin is not usually what a persecuted congregation is warned about, and the writer includes it without comment among prison visits and hospitality. Pressure does not exempt anybody from ordinary temptations, and it frequently increases them: people who are frightened and exhausted reach for comfort.

A living picture of Christ and his church. The deepest reason marriage is to be honoured is that God made it to show something. Paul quotes Genesis 2:24, the two shall become one flesh, and says that this mystery is profound, and refers to Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32). Christ is the Bridegroom who loved his bride and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25), and he has never once been unfaithful to her. That is why adultery is so grave: it breaks a promise, and it also tells a lie about him. And that is why a faithful marriage, through ordinary years, is a quiet sermon on the faithfulness of Jesus.

Where Christians differ: what counts as marriage, and how should the church respond to sexual sin? Some Christians today accept sexual relationships outside marriage, or marriages other than between a man and a woman. This commentary’s view: Scripture consistently teaches that sexual union is reserved for the lifelong covenant of marriage between one man and one woman (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:4–6). Asked about marriage, Jesus went back to creation, God made them male and female and joined them as one flesh, and Paul sees in that union a picture of Christ and his church (Ephesians 5:31–32); the church did not invent this pattern and cannot redraw it, however sincerely others see it differently. All sexual activity outside marriage is sin. This is held with compassion: many struggle in this area, and the gospel offers full forgiveness and cleansing to all who repent (1 Corinthians 6:11). The church must uphold the standard and extend grace together.

What it does not mean. It does not mean single people are less honourable. Singleness is also a good gift (1 Corinthians 7:7–8), and the Lord Jesus himself was single. Nor does honouring marriage mean that anyone must stay in a home where they are being abused; abuse dishonours marriage, and the victim should be protected and helped.

Can I still honour marriage if I have fallen sexually in the past? Yes, and you must not let shame tell you otherwise. If you have confessed your sin and turned to Christ, you are washed, sanctified and justified in his name (1 Corinthians 6:11), and God does not hold it against you. Honouring marriage now means guarding your present purity, speaking well of marriage, and if you marry, giving yourself wholly to your spouse. There may be consequences to deal with, trust to rebuild, or things to tell a future spouse honestly. Get wise help from a pastor if you need it. But your past is not the final word about you; Christ’s blood is.

Is the Bible’s sexual ethic not simply repressive? It can sound that way in a world that measures freedom by the absence of limits. But this verse begins by calling the marriage bed honourable and undefiled; Scripture is not embarrassed by sex, and it calls it good. The boundary is like the banks of a river, which do not stop the water but give it depth and direction. A love that makes and keeps a lifelong promise is not less free than one that keeps its options open; it is the only kind that can bear the full weight of trust. And it is the kind of love Christ has shown his bride, whom he will never leave for another.

On a Tuesday. If married, do one thing this week to honour your spouse: a word of thanks, an evening protected for each other, a filter put on a device. If you are struggling with sexual sin, tell one trusted Christian this week. Secrecy is where it grows.

verseByVerse.quote: Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, “I will never leave you nor forsake you.” So we can confidently say, “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear; what can man do to me?”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Free from love of money. The word is literally not silver-loving. Money is not evil, but the love of it is a root of all kinds of evils (1 Timothy 6:10). And there is a particular sting in saying this to these people. They had watched their property carried out of their houses (10:34), and they had accepted it joyfully at the time. Now, years later, the sting of the loss had presumably settled in, and going back to the old ways might well have won some of it back.

Content with what you have. “Content” is satisfied, having enough, as in Philippians 4:11 and 1 Timothy 6:8. The cure for wanting more is not having more, but being satisfied with what is already in the house.

I will never leave you. “He” is emphatic: God himself. The words are God’s to Joshua at the border of the land (Joshua 1:5), and behind that to Israel and Joshua through Moses (Deuteronomy 31:6, 8). The Greek piles up negatives, five of them, in a way English cannot reproduce: never, not ever, by no means will I let you go; never, no never, will I forsake you. Not provision, though God provides. Not the restoration of the property. Himself.

The Lord is my helper; I will not fear; what can man do to me? From Psalm 118:6. “Helper” is one who comes to another’s aid, the word used in 2:18 of Christ helping those who are tempted. It is a defiant question rather than a naive one. Man can do a great deal: these people knew it, and had the empty houses to prove it. The psalm does not deny the capability. It asks what any of it finally amounts to, when the one who has promised never to leave is standing beside you. If God is for us, who can be against us (Romans 8:31; Matthew 10:28)?

Forsaken so that we never would be. The promise has a price, and Christ paid it. On the cross he cried, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me (Matthew 27:46)? He bore the abandonment that sin deserves, so that God can say to everyone who trusts in him, I will never forsake you, and mean it without exception. Christ is also the pattern of contentment. Though he was rich, for our sake he became poor (2 Corinthians 8:9), and had nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8:20), yet he never lacked his Father’s presence. A Christian with little money and that same presence is living as Jesus lived.

How do I know if I love money? Watch what makes you anxious, what makes you envious and what you are reluctant to give; the test is not your bank balance but whether you could lose it and still be content, because you have God. (See 1 Timothy 6:9–10 for the fuller answer.)

What if I genuinely do not have enough? Contentment does not mean pretending that need is not real, or refusing help, or not seeking work or better provision. Paul knew hunger and need, and learned contentment in it (Philippians 4:11–13). It means trusting that God, who has promised never to leave you, will give you what you truly need (Matthew 6:31–33), and that your worth does not depend on what you have. Pray honestly, take the practical steps you can, and let the church know; it is part of the church’s calling to share with those in need (v. 16). Being content and asking for help are not opposites.

On a Tuesday. When a money worry wakes you at night, say the psalm back to it: the Lord is my helper. And give away a sum you will notice; it is one of the quickest ways to find that money’s grip on you is weaker than his.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Former leaders have died, but Christ does not change, so strange teachings about foods have nothing to add to grace. Christians have an altar, Christ’s sacrifice, and since he suffered outside the gate, they go out to him bearing his disgrace, offering praise and practical kindness. They are to follow their present leaders and pray for the writer.
verseByVerse.theology:
Outside the Camp

Jesus suffered outside the gate, as the sin offering was burned outside the camp. Go to him there, bearing his reproach, and offer the sacrifices that please God: praise, doing good and sharing.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: For these readers the camp was home: temple, synagogue, festivals and family table.

Now: Leaving what is not lasting is not homelessness; it is going to where he is.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember your leaders, those who spoke to you the word of God. Consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith. Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember your leaders. The tense suggests men who had finished: the founding generation of that church, perhaps including apostles, who first preached the gospel to them (2:3), and quite possibly some who had died for it. They are identified not by office but by what came out of their mouths: their authority was the word they preached.

The outcome of their way of life. “Outcome” is how it ended, for some perhaps in martyrdom. Doctrine is tested over a lifetime, and the end of a life is where the verdict shows. Anybody can hold a position at forty; what a man is at the close is the evidence.

Imitate their faith. As in 6:12: not their manner, not their gifts, not their personalities or methods, not their circumstances. Their faith: the one transferable thing.

The same yesterday and today and forever. Verse 8 arrives here for a reason. “The same” echoes 1:12: you are the same, and your years will have no end. Read where it stands, it answers a specific grief. The founders die, the teachers die, and a congregation that has buried the men who brought it the gospel feels the ground move. The leaders had an outcome, an end to their course; Christ has none. He is the same today, interceding for them (7:25), and he will be the same past every succession of leaders they will ever have. And a Christ who does not change is the reason strange new teachings are not worth chasing (v. 9): there is nothing later to be had.

Does this verse mean the miracles of the apostles continue today? This verse is often quoted to argue that if Jesus healed and worked miracles then, he must do the same through his people now. But the context is about who Christ is. The leaders have died, strange teachings are blowing about (v. 9), and Christ remains the same: his character, his saving work and his word do not change. That does not mean every gift he gave in every age continues. The signs that confirmed the apostles’ message belonged to that first generation (2:3–4; 2 Corinthians 12:12). Continuationists, who believe all the gifts continue, reply that an unchanging Christ will act as he acted. But the Christ who does not change no longer walks in Galilee either: his person stays the same while his ways of working through history move on. What stays the same is Jesus Christ himself, and that is enough. God still answers prayer and heals as he wills; this commentary holds, charitably, that the sign gifts of the apostolic age have ceased. Many faithful churches believe otherwise, and they worship the same unchanging Lord.

How do I imitate someone’s faith without copying their personality? Look at what they trusted and how it shaped their choices, not at their style. Ask: what did they believe about God that made them live and die as they did? How did they handle suffering, money, temptation and death? What did they do when they failed? Then ask God for the same trust, expressed in your own temperament and circumstances. A quiet person need not become loud to imitate a bold preacher’s faith; he needs to trust the same Christ as fully, in the place God has put him.

On a Tuesday. Name one person who first taught you the gospel: a parent, a pastor, a Sunday school teacher, a friend. If they are alive, write and thank them this week; if they have died, thank God for them, and ask what one thing about their faith you could imitate.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be led away by diverse and strange teachings, for it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace, not by foods, which have not benefited those devoted to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Diverse and strange teachings. “Led away” is carried aside, swept off course, like a ship drifting (2:1). “Diverse” is of many kinds, and the plural is itself an argument, since truth does not come in a range. “Strange” is foreign, alien to the gospel. Set against verse 8 the contrast is complete: Christ is the same; teachings are diverse.

Strengthened by grace. “Strengthened” is made firm, established, and grace is God’s free favour in Christ. With the words not by foods the actual issue surfaces. Whatever these teachings were, they were about eating, and the old covenant sacrificial meals may be in view, given verse 10.

Two ways of steadying a heart. One is grace: something received, from outside, on the basis of what somebody else has done. The other is food: something managed, on the basis of what you take in and abstain from. The second is attractive because rules about eating are measurable: you know whether you have kept them, and they produce a sense of progress that grace never does. The irreligious have their own version: the clean diet, the morning routine, the self-improvement plan that promises a steadier self. Grace is more humbling than all of them, and far more freeing.

Grace with a face. The grace that steadies the heart is not a substance, a mood or a force. It has appeared in a person: grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (John 1:17). Food rules ask what you have kept; grace points to what he has done, the will of God fulfilled by the offering of his body once for all (10:10). A heart resting on its own record shifts with every good or bad week. A heart resting on Christ rests on something already finished, and it cannot be moved.

Not benefited. “Devoted to them” is literally those who walk in them, who live by them. The verdict is empirical: look at the people who have given their lives to this, and ask whether it has done them any good (9:9–10; Colossians 2:16–23).

Are Christians bound by the Old Testament food laws today? No. Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19; the KJV words Mark’s comment differently), Peter was told, what God has made clean, do not call common (Acts 10:15), and Paul says that everything created by God is good (1 Timothy 4:4). Those who still keep such rules out of conscience are not to be despised (Romans 14:1–3). The danger the writer warns against is trusting rules about food to strengthen the heart. Only grace can do that.

How can I tell a strange teaching from a true one? Test it against Scripture, and above all against the Christ of Scripture (Acts 17:11; 1 John 4:1–3). Warning signs include: teaching that adds something to Christ as necessary for salvation or spiritual strength; teaching that promises secret knowledge or a higher level of Christian life through special practices; teaching that cannot be found in the plain words of the Bible; teaching that flatters the hearer or centres on the teacher; and teaching that leaves you anxious about rules rather than resting in grace. Ask what it does with the cross. True teaching always makes Christ larger and grace sweeter.

verseByVerse.quote: We have an altar from which those who serve the tent have no right to eat. For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp. So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have an altar. The sentence is startling, because Hebrews has spent twelve chapters dismantling the apparatus of altars, and now claims one. The claim is not to a piece of furniture. It is to the cross, to Christ’s sacrifice itself, and to the meal that cannot be had without it. We eat from it by faith, feeding spiritually on Christ crucified: whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life (John 6:53–58).

No right to eat. The exclusion is pointed. “Those who serve the tent” are those who cling to the old tabernacle worship. Under the old covenant the priests ate portions of many sacrifices, but never of the Day of Atonement sin offering, which was wholly burned (Leviticus 6:30; 16:27). Christ is the true sin offering, and those who stay with the old system cannot share in him. You cannot hold both. That is the sharpest thing the letter has yet said to people considering a quiet return.

So Jesus also suffered outside the gate. Golgotha was outside the walls of Jerusalem (John 19:17, 20; Matthew 27:32), and the writer has noticed that this is not an accident of Roman administration, but the pattern of the ritual, kept to the letter. Like the sin offering, he was put outside, rejected, treated as unclean. Outside the camp was the place of the unclean, the leper and the blasphemer (Leviticus 13:46; 24:14). The place of ultimate rejection, where the refuse went, is where the sanctifying happened. Jesus was not merely executed; he was put out.

To sanctify the people. “Sanctify” is make holy, as in 10:10 and 10:14. Christ’s blood washes away the guilt and defilement of sin and sets his people apart as God’s own, fit to come into his presence, as the priests were once consecrated with blood to serve in his house (Exodus 29:20–21). The one thrown outside is the one who makes those inside holy. Any reader who has felt himself on the wrong side of a boundary may take that sentence home.

Where Christians differ: is the Lord’s Table an altar? Roman Catholic and some Anglo-Catholic traditions identify this altar with the communion table, on which the sacrifice of the Mass is offered. Others take it as the Lord’s Supper understood as a meal. This commentary’s view: the New Testament never calls the Lord’s Table an altar. The altar here is Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice on the cross (7:27; 10:10–14). This letter has said again and again that Christ’s sacrifice was offered once for all and is never repeated (7:27; 9:25–28; 10:12–14), so the verse gives no support to a sacrifice in the Mass. We eat from the altar by faith in his finished work, especially as we receive the Lord’s Supper, where Christ is spiritually present and we feed on him by faith; but there is no new sacrifice offered.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should despise Jewish people. The old covenant system cannot give access to Christ’s benefits; only faith in him can. The gospel is for the Jew first, and many of the first readers of this letter were Jews who had found their Messiah.

What does it mean to eat from this altar? It means to receive by faith the benefits of Christ’s death: forgiveness, cleansing, peace with God, and life. You feed on him when you trust him, when you meditate on his cross, when you hear the gospel preached and believe it, and in a special way at the Lord’s Supper, where the bread and the cup are given as signs and seals of his body and blood, and faith receives him spiritually. It is not a matter of physical eating, but neither is it merely remembering; it is real communion with the living Christ who died for you.

For worship. On the Day of Atonement the blood went in and the body went out. In Jesus both happened, to one person. His body was led outside the gate to the place of the unclean, and by his own blood he entered once for all into the holy places, into heaven itself, to appear in the presence of God for us (9:12, 24). So he stands at once with the outcasts and before the face of the Father, and in him the outside and the inside meet. He went outside so that we could come in.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured. For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Outside the camp. This is the letter’s whole appeal in a single line. For these readers, very probably Jewish Christians, the camp was not paganism. It was the temple, the synagogue, the festivals, the family table, everything that had made them who they were. Going out meant being cut off from their own people, and losing the measure of toleration Judaism enjoyed under Roman rule. The pull backwards was not toward sin. It was toward home.

Not into nothing. Look where the invitation points: let us go to him. He is not inside the camp any more. The argument is not primarily about courage but about location: following Jesus means going where he went.

Bear the reproach. The writer does not pretend the cost is small. “Reproach” is disgrace, insult, as of Moses in 11:26: the shame Jesus despised (12:2).

No lasting city. Verse 14 removes the objection before it forms: if we go out, we lose everything. The answer is that what you have was never permanent. Jerusalem itself would be rubble in AD 70, probably within a few years of this letter. No earthly city, nation or institution is our permanent home.

The city that is to come. The city is the heavenly Jerusalem (11:10, 16; 12:22), the one Abraham looked for while he lived in tents. You are not being asked to trade a permanent home for homelessness, but to stop pretending a temporary one is permanent, and to go and find the man who is standing outside it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should withdraw from society or not care about their earthly cities. We are to seek the welfare of the city where we live (Jeremiah 29:7). But we do not put our ultimate hope there.

What does outside the camp look like for me? For the first readers it meant leaving the security and respectability of the temple system. For you it means wherever loyalty to Christ costs you belonging. It may be the family that thinks your faith is an embarrassment, the workplace where honesty marks you out, the friends who drift away when you stop joining in, the culture that calls biblical convictions hateful. You go out not by being needlessly odd or harsh, but by refusing to deny Christ to keep your place. And remember: outside the camp is where he is. You never go out alone.

verseByVerse.quote: Through him then let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name. Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A sacrifice of praise. If Christians have an altar (v. 10), what do they put on it? Two offerings, and anybody can bring both. The first is praise, offered through Christ our High Priest (1 Peter 2:5). Even praise goes up through the priest, which means the worship of a struggling Christian is acceptable for the same reason his forgiveness is. And “continually” is deliberate in a letter that insists the sacrifice for sin was made once for all. That one is finished; this one never stops.

The fruit of lips. The phrase is from Hosea 14:2 in the Greek translation; most English Bibles, following the Hebrew, speak there of paying with bulls the vows of our lips, but either way the offering is what the lips give. “Acknowledge” is confess, profess.
