Praising God and confessing Christ openly: the very thing the readers were tempted to stop doing. Praise is not only singing in church; it is saying his name aloud in a world that would prefer you kept quiet.

To do good and to share. Then the second offering, and it is the surprise. “Share” is koinōnia, fellowship, generosity, sharing possessions. Practical kindness is put on the altar beside praise, and verse 16 calls both by the same word: sacrifices.

Pleasing to God. Praise Godward and good works manward are both worship (Romans 12:1). Hebrews has spent chapters on blood, sanctuaries and mediation, and when it finally names what we offer, one of the two items is sharing what you have.

How can I praise God continually when life is hard? By remembering that praise is a sacrifice: it costs something, and it is often offered through tears. The psalmists praised God in caves and exile, and Paul and Silas sang in prison at midnight (Acts 16:25). Praise does not require you to feel happy; it requires you to say what is true about God, even when your circumstances say otherwise. Start small: thank him for one thing each hour, sing one line of a hymn you know, read a psalm aloud. Praise offered through Christ is always acceptable, and it often lifts the heart that offers it.

On a Tuesday. A meal left on a new mother’s doorstep and a hymn hummed over the washing-up are, by this passage, the same kind of thing: sacrifices God is pleased with.

For worship. Our praise does not climb to God alone. The Son who sat down at the right hand is not ashamed to call us brothers, and he says to the Father, in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise (2:12). He leads the song. Every halting hymn and every quiet act of sharing is taken up into the worship of the great High Priest and carried into the presence of the Father as though it were his own.

verseByVerse.quote: Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they are keeping watch over your souls, as those who will have to give an account. Let them do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would be of no advantage to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Obey your leaders. These are the present leaders, in contrast with the former (v. 7). “Obey” is be persuaded by, follow; “submit” is yield, defer. The command is real and should not be softened. But look at the reason the writer gives for it: not office or rank, but watchfulness and accountability.

Keeping watch over your souls. Literally staying awake, losing sleep, being vigilant: the sentry image, the shepherd on the hillside at night keeping watch over his flock (Luke 2:8). Faithful elders lose sleep over their people.

Give an account. The accounting word: these men will stand before God and be asked about the people entrusted to them (James 3:1; Ezekiel 34). That is the reason submission is owed. Not because they are senior, but because they are answerable. Which cuts in both directions, and the passage means it to. It tells a congregation to be led. And it tells anyone who leads that the job is night-watch and audit, not position, a fact that should make a man think twice before wanting it.

Not with groaning. The word means sighing, grieving: the sound a man makes when the weight is more than the encouragement.

Of no advantage to you. The reason given is entirely practical: a congregation that exhausts its leaders damages itself, because a discouraged man watches less well. There is no version of this where the church wins and the leaders lose.

Under the great Shepherd. The account these leaders must give is given to someone. The flock is not theirs. It belongs to Christ, who obtained it with his own blood (Acts 20:28), and its elders are under-shepherds who will answer to the chief Shepherd when he appears (1 Peter 5:2–4). So following faithful leaders is finally a way of trusting him. He has chosen to care for his sheep through men who watch over their souls, and he will hold those men to account.

What it does not mean. It does not support a single ruling bishop: leaders is plural. Christians differ over church government, and this verse does not settle every question.

How far must I obey? The leaders in view are those who speak the word of God (v. 7), and they are to be followed as they lead by it. Their authority is real but not unlimited. Where they command what Scripture forbids, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29); the Bereans were commended for checking even an apostle’s teaching against the Scriptures (Acts 17:11); and elders are not to be domineering over those in their charge (1 Peter 5:3). A leader who uses this verse to control, silence or exploit people has left the ground it stands on. He should be confronted, and if he will not listen, brought before the other elders (1 Timothy 5:19–20); a believer harmed by him may seek help and, if need be, leave. Where abuse is a crime, it should be reported to the authorities.

What if I disagree with my elders on something? Most disagreements are not about sin, but about judgment: a decision, a style, a priority. Then the godly course is to speak to them directly and respectfully, give your reasons, listen to theirs, and if they still decide otherwise, defer gladly unless conscience is at stake. Do not gather a faction or complain to others; that is exactly how leaders come to groan. If the disagreement concerns the gospel itself or a clear command of Scripture, it is more serious, and you should press it humbly, and if necessary seek help from outside. Trust that God holds them accountable, and pray for them.

On a Tuesday. Make your elders’ work a joy this week: tell them specifically how God has used their teaching or care, and come to them with problems rather than talking about them to others.

verseByVerse.quote: Pray for us, for we are sure that we have a clear conscience, desiring to act honorably in all things. I urge you the more earnestly to do this in order that I may be restored to you the sooner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pray for us. The verb is keep praying, and “us” is the author and his companions. The writer has spent twelve chapters and more instructing this congregation with complete authority, and now asks them for something. The traffic in a healthy church runs both ways, and a teacher who can only give is not in fellowship with anybody.

A clear conscience. Literally a good conscience. The claim is slightly defensive. It suggests somebody had said otherwise: that his motives had been questioned, perhaps by people who resented the letter’s pressure. He does not argue the point. He states it and moves on, which is usually the right handling of an accusation you cannot disprove. Not sinlessness, but integrity in everything is his goal.

A conscience Christ has cleansed. A good conscience is not a boast in this letter; it is a gift. Hebrews has said that the old sacrifices could not perfect the conscience of the worshipper (9:9), but that the blood of Christ purifies our conscience from dead works to serve the living God (9:14), so that we draw near with our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience (10:22). When this writer says his conscience is clear, he is standing where every forgiven believer stands: nothing hidden, and nothing that the blood of Jesus has not already covered.

Restored to you the sooner. “Restored” is given back. Something he does not explain, illness, imprisonment or distance, has separated him from them, and he believes their prayers will make a real difference. He asks to be given back to these particular people. He misses them.

A name nobody recorded. One of the most polished writers in the New Testament is a man whose name has not come down to us. That fits a letter which tells its readers to seek a city that is to come: the work outlasts him, and his name was never the point.

Does my prayer really make a difference to whether God acts? Yes. God has ordained to work through the prayers of his people, and he does not merely tolerate them; he answers them (James 5:16–18). The writer expected that their prayers would hasten his return. God’s sovereignty does not make prayer pointless; it makes it effective, because we are asking the one who rules everything. You may not see how your prayer fitted into his purposes, and he may answer differently from what you asked. But no prayer offered in Christ’s name is wasted, and the prayers of ordinary believers have upheld missionaries, pastors and persecuted churches across the centuries.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The letter closes with a benediction, asking the God who raised the great Shepherd to work in his people what pleases him, and then with news, greetings and grace.
verseByVerse.theology:
The God Who Works in Us

The God of peace, who brought again from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep, equips his people and works in them what pleases him. What he requires, he supplies.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The writer calls his letter a “word of exhortation”, a sermon sent to people he knows and misses.

Now: After its hardest warnings, the letter ends with grace for all.

verseByVerse.quote: Now may the God of peace who brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep, by the blood of the eternal covenant, equip you with everything good that you may do his will, working in us that which is pleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now may the God of peace. This is a benediction in which every phrase gathers up something the letter has argued. “The God of peace” is the title Paul reaches for when relationships are in view (Romans 15:33; 16:20; 1 Thessalonians 5:23): the God who has made peace with sinners through Christ’s blood, and who gives peace. It is apt here, since this congregation is under strain, tempted toward division, and its leaders are groaning.

Brought again from the dead. This is the only explicit mention of Jesus’ resurrection in the whole letter. It has been assumed on every page; a seated priest is necessarily a living one, and his priesthood rests on the power of an indestructible life (7:16).

The great shepherd of the sheep. The one pastoral image in a letter full of priests and sanctuaries, and it echoes Isaiah 63:11, where in the Greek translation God brought up from the sea the shepherd of the sheep, Moses. A new exodus, a greater shepherd, brought up not out of water but out of death. Jesus is the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep, the chief shepherd who will appear (John 10:11; 1 Peter 5:4).

By the blood of the eternal covenant. The phrase most likely tells us on what ground God raised him. The blood was not the power that raised Jesus; it was the reason he was raised. His sacrifice had been accepted, and the covenant it sealed could not have a dead mediator. The resurrection is the Father’s seal on the covenant. And “eternal” is the letter’s answer to everything the readers were tempted back toward. The old covenant was becoming obsolete and growing old, ready to vanish away (8:13); this one does not, and will never be replaced (Jeremiah 32:40).

Equip you. Then the petition. The verb means to put right, to make complete, to fit out, to mend: it is used of setting a broken bone, and of the fishermen mending their nets. God is asked to repair them into working order. “Do his will”: as Christ came to do God’s will (10:7, 9), so his people do it by his equipping.

Working in us. The sentence turns on a hinge: not merely equipping them to work, but working in them. It is the principle of Philippians 2:13, it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure, and it is the only reason the whole letter’s demand, go outside the camp, bear the reproach, is not crushing. What he requires, he supplies. Our obedience is real, but it is God’s work in us, and even at its best it is flawed; it is pleasing in his sight through Jesus Christ, whose own obedience was perfect and is counted as ours, so that our imperfect works are accepted for his sake (1 Peter 2:5).

To whom be glory. Probably Christ, though possibly the Father. The letter that has exalted Christ above angels, above Moses and above Aaron ends by giving him eternal glory.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we are passive. God equips us by the Spirit he has put within us, so that we do his will: his work is the cause of our obedience, not a replacement for it.

If God works in me what pleases him, why do I struggle so much? Because his work in you is real but not yet finished, and it works through your struggle, not around it. Sanctification is God mending a broken net, and mending takes time and sometimes hurts. The struggle itself, your hatred of sin, your desire to please him, your getting up after falling, is evidence that he is at work. Do not wait to feel equipped before you obey. Obey, trusting that he is working in you as you do, and when you fail, return to the great Shepherd who was brought back from the dead for you.

On a Tuesday. Pray this benediction by name over one person who is struggling. And when a task this week feels beyond you, ask him to work in you what is pleasing in his sight, and then step into it.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you, brothers, bear with my word of exhortation, for I have written to you briefly. You should know that our brother Timothy has been released, with whom I shall see you if he comes soon. Greet all your leaders and all the saints. Those who come from Italy send you greetings. Grace be with all of you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My word of exhortation. “Bear with” is listen patiently: the warnings have been severe. And “word of exhortation” is the phrase Acts uses for a synagogue sermon: it is what Paul was invited to give at Antioch, if you have any word of encouragement for the people (Acts 13:15). So Hebrews is a sermon sent as a letter. It closes like a letter, but it has no opening greeting, and it argues like a preacher.

Briefly. Either dry humour or an honest estimate: Hebrews takes under an hour to read aloud, and for the vastness of its subject it is brief (9:5; 11:32).

Timothy has been released. The one name in the letter, and it is a tantalising one: Timothy had evidently been in prison. This is the only mention of Timothy’s imprisonment in the New Testament, perhaps after Paul’s death in Rome. And the writer means to come with Timothy if he arrives soon: the sermon would be followed by the preacher.

All your leaders and all the saints. The elders (v. 17), and every believer, holy in Christ: all, twice. This has been a hard letter, with warnings in it that have frightened readers for two thousand years. It ends by including everybody.

Those who come from Italy. The phrase can mean Italians living abroad, sending greetings home to Rome, or people in Italy sending greetings elsewhere. The first reading suggests the letter went to Rome, which fits other evidence: the earliest known use of Hebrews was by Clement of Rome, around AD 95.

Grace be with all of you. The last word of the letter: grace. The letter has warned, exhorted and taught, but all rests on grace, and in Hebrews grace always has Christ at its centre. By the grace of God Jesus tasted death for everyone (2:9), and the throne of grace is reached through him, the great High Priest who has passed through the heavens (4:14–16). So the letter closes not with a demand but with the one who makes every demand possible.

Who wrote the letter? Some early Christians thought Paul did, and the mention of Timothy points to Paul’s circle. But the style differs from Paul’s letters, and the writer says he received the gospel from those who heard the Lord (2:3), which Paul insisted he did not (Galatians 1:12). Apollos, Barnabas, Luke and Priscilla have all been suggested, and none can be proved. The more likely conclusion is that the author was a gifted teacher in the apostolic circle whose name God has not preserved. The letter’s authority does not rest on its author but on the God who speaks in it, and the church received it as Scripture.

How should I respond to a hard word from Scripture or a preacher? Bear with it, as this writer asked. Do not dismiss it because it stings, and do not be crushed by it as if it were God’s rejection. Ask whether it is true to Scripture; if it is, receive it as the loving word of a Father who disciplines his children. Take it home, pray over it, and act on what it shows you. The warnings of Hebrews were written by a man who loved his readers and wanted them to arrive. Hard words in Scripture are always spoken inside grace, and they end, as this letter does, with grace.

For worship. The letter to the Hebrews began with God speaking by his Son, the radiance of his glory, who made purification for sins and sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high. It ends with grace. Everything between has been the unfolding of that grace: a better priest, a better covenant, a better sacrifice, a better hope, and he is ours. The writer’s name is lost, but his Saviour’s name is above every name. Grace be with all of you, and glory to the one who gives it, for ever and ever.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy had evidently been in prison. “Those who come from Italy” may be Italians abroad sending greetings home, or believers in Italy itself.

Consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith.<sup>8</sup>Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.<sup>9</sup>Do not be led away by diverse and strange teachings, for it is good for the heart to be strengthened by grace, not by foods, which have not benefited those devoted to them.<sup>10</sup>We have an altar from which those who serve the tent have no right to eat.<sup>11</sup>For the bodies of those animals whose blood is brought into the holy places by the high priest as a sacrifice for sin are burned outside the camp.<sup>12</sup>So Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people through his own blood.<sup>13</sup>Therefore let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured.<sup>14</sup>For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come.<sup>15</sup>Through him then let us continually offer up a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name.<sup>16</sup>Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God.<sup>17</sup>Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they are keeping watch over your souls, as those who will have to give an account. Let them do this with joy and not with groaning, for that would be of no advantage to you.<sup>18</sup>Pray for us, for we are sure that we have a clear conscience, desiring to act honorably in all things.<sup>19</sup>I urge you the more earnestly to do this in order that I may be restored to you the sooner.<sup>20</sup>Now may the God of peace who brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep, by the blood of the eternal covenant,<sup>21</sup>equip you with everything good that you may do his will, working in us that which is pleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever.
